explanation_en: Members and candidates who are in advisory relationships with clients should document unsuccessful attempts to update client information and circumstances. Because risk is to be evaluated in a portfolio context, there is no prohibition against the purchase of a security that is risky on a stand-alone basis, as long as the risk of the client's overall portfolio is consistent with their ability and willingness to assume investment risk. While lack of client information could make suitability a difficult question, Standard III(C) Suitability does not prohibit managing assets for clients who withhold information about their financial circumstances and needs.
question_en: According to the Standard concerning suitability, it is most likely that members and candidates in advisory relationships with clients should:
option_a: document unsuccessful attempts to update client information.
option_b: purchase only securities with low to medium risk for a client with moderate risk tolerance.
option_c: decline to manage assets for clients who withhold important information about their financial circumstances and needs.

explanation_en: Callable shares have more risk than otherwise equivalent non-callable shares because the possibility of the shares being called limits their potential price gains. Putable shares have less risk than otherwise equivalent non-putable shares because the option to put the shares back to the issuer for a predetermined price effectively places a floor under their price. Cumulative preference shares have less risk than otherwise equivalent non- cumulative preference shares because any scheduled dividends the issuer misses are still owed to the preferred shareholder.
question_en: Other things equal, preference shares have the most risk for the investor when they are:
option_c: non-callable and non-cumulative.

explanation_en: The diversification ratio measures the risk reduction benefit achieved by holding a portfolio compared to holding a single security, calculated as the ratio of the equally weighted portfolio's standard deviation to a randomly selected security's standard deviation.
question_en: In an equally weighted portfolio, the diversification ratio is best described as a measure of the:
option_a: relative level of risk between any two individual assets.
option_b: amount of risk an asset contributes to the portfolio's risk.
option_c: risk reduction benefit of investing in the portfolio versus a security from the portfolio.

explanation_en: Investors with limited resources and/or experience generally enter into alternative investments through fund investing, where the investor contributes capital to a fund and the fund identifies, selects, and makes investments on the investor's behalf.
question_en: Investors with limited resources and experience enter into alternative investments most likely through:
option_c: direct investing.

explanation_en: Under Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, fiduciaries must evaluate management's proposals during proxy fights to see if they are in the best interest of the plan participants. If management's ideas are justifiable and reasonably ensure plan participants' betterment, then fiduciaries can support them. If management is only trying to further its own objectives, especially at the cost of plan participants, then fiduciaries must vote against management in proxy fights.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely required of fiduciaries who are responsible for pension plans?
option_a: Supporting the sponsor's management during proxy ghts.
option_b: Judging investments in the context of the total portfolio.
option_c: Acting solely in the interest of plan participants.

explanation_en: Fixed income securities can be classified in a number of different ways; the most common classifications are shown above. Bilateral and syndicated are types of loans, not types of bonds, made by banks to corporations and other entities. A bilateral loan is made from a single lender to a single borrower who needs funding. A syndicated loan is made by a syndicate (ie, a group of lenders who share the credit risk of the loan). Note that although a bond issuance may, in some cases, be purchased by a single institutional investor, this bond is not called "bilateral." (Choice B) Bonds may be classified by coupon type, so fixed versus floating is a valid distinction. The "rate" refers to the coupon rate paid by the issuer, so fixed-rate bonds maintain the same rate or coupon over time. Floating-rate bonds have a rate that varies based on a reference rate such as LIBOR. (Choice C) Bonds may be classified by issuer type, so corporate versus nonsovereign is a valid distinction. There are four broad bond sectors: financial institutions, nonfinancial corporates, governments, and households. Within the government sector, nonsovereign bonds are issued by authorities (eg, municipal governments) subordinate to national governments.
question_en: An analyst is classifying bonds within the global fixed income market. Which of the following is least likely a valid distinction for the analyst to use?
option_c: Corporate versus nonsovereign

explanation_en: Lockup periods provide the hedge fund manager the required time to implement and potentially realize a strategy's expected results by restricting investor withdrawals.
question_en: A measure that restricts new investors in a hedge fund from redeeming their capital for a set amount of time in order to implement the fund's investment strategy is known as a:
option_c: lockup period.

explanation_en: The CAPM assumes frictionless markets, i.e., no taxes or transactions costs. Among the other assumptions of the CAPM are that all investors have the same one-period time horizon and that all investments are infinitely divisible.
question_en: One of the assumptions underlying the capital asset pricing model is that:
option_a: there are no transactions costs or taxes.
option_b: only whole shares or whole bonds are available.
option_c: each investor has a unique time horizon.

explanation_en: In a scenario analysis used to forecast a change in sales, the probabilities associated with each scenario must be between 0% and 100% and must sum to 100%. The correct answer choice sums to 100% (40% chance of an increase + 30% chance of no growth + 30% chance of sales decreasing). The other two choices do not sum to 100%.
question_en: Which of the following scenarios may an analyst use to forecast sales growth for a company in the next fiscal year?
option_a: 20% chance of sales increasing, 50% chance of no growth, 20% chance of sales decreasing.
option_b: 40% chance of sales increasing, 30% chance of no growth, 30% chance of sales decreasing.
option_c: 30% chance of sales increasing, 40% chance of no growth, 40% chance of sales decreasing.

explanation_en: An individual's beliefs are not ethics as it is used in the Level I CFA curriculum. Ethics are described as commonly accepted principles of good and bad behavior and the study of good and bad behavior.
question_en: Ethics least likely refers to:
option_b: a person’s beliefs about right and wrong behavior.
option_c: the study of good and bad behavior.

question_en: Assume the exchange rate between the Trotter (TRT) and the Roeckl (RKL) is 5.50 TRT/RKL and the exchange rate between the Roeckl and the Passage (PSG) is 8.00 RKL/PSG. The cross rate between the PSG and the TRT is closest to:

explanation_en:
The two-stage dividend discount model (two-stage DDM) is used to find the value of a company expected to have high growth (short term),
followed by lower constant growth (long term). The high growth stage is assumed to last for a certain number of (n) years, followed by an infinite
long-term growth stage.
In the two-stage DDM, the Gordon growth model (GGM) is used to find the value of the second stage, which has constant dividend growth. The
GGM value of the long-term growth stage is used as the terminal value input for valuation of the high growth stage. The value is discounted
back to the present using the required rate of return (r) and added to the present value of the first (high growth) stage to find the security's intrinsic
value.
(Choice B) The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) is not a dividend discount model and is used to find the expected return of a security, not its
current intrinsic value. The CAPM can be used to find the required rate of return, a variable of the two-stage DDM.
(Choice C) The free cash flow to equity (FCFE) model is based on free cash flows and not dividends, so FCFE would not be used in the two
stage dividend discount model.
question_en: The two-stage dividend discount model is most appropriate for a company expecting:
option_a: high growth for a specified number of years, then higher growth.
option_b: constant growth for a specified number of years, then high growth.
option_c: high growth for a specified number of years, then lower, long-term growth.

explanation_en: The price (or premium) of an option is its intrinsic value plus its time value. An out-of-the- money option has an intrinsic value of zero, so its entire premium consists of time value. Time value is zero at an option's expiration date. Time value is the amount by which an option's premium exceeds its intrinsic value.
question_en: The time value of an option is most accurately described as:
option_a: the amount by which the intrinsic value exceeds the option premium.
option_b: equal to the entire premium for an out-of-the-money option.
option_c: increasing as the option approaches its expiration date.

explanation_en: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Hirsh to receive her employer's permission in writing before she can accept the offer from Advisors, because it can reasonably be expected to create a conflict with the college's interests in that it may induce Hirsh not to seek better execution from other brokers.
question_en: Jan Hirsh, CFA, is employed by a college to manage its endowment fund. The endowment carries out its transactions primarily through the brokerage firm Advisors, Inc. Over the years, Hirsh has developed a solid relationship with Advisors. Advisors offers Hirsh their highest level of service for her personal account if the endowment continues to exceed a minimum number of transactions per year with Advisors. The Code and Standards most likely require Hirsh to:
option_a: disclose this benefit to the college, but it does not require her to receive the college’s permission.
option_b: receive the college’s permission before accepting this benefit.
option_c: decline this benefit because it represents a conflict of interest with the college.

explanation_en: Investing in fund of funds is likely to result in lower returns net of fees over time compared to investing directly in hedge funds. Fund of funds receive net-of-fees returns from the funds in which they invest, and charge their own investors an additional layer of management and incentive fees.
question_en: Assume most hedge funds have a 2-and-20 fee structure and most fund of funds have a 1-and-10 fee structure. Over a long investment horizon, compared to net returns from investing directly in hedge funds, net returns from investing in fund of funds are most likely to be:
option_c: the same.

explanation_en: As the economy approaches its peak, sales growth begins to slow, unsold inventories begin to accumulate, and the inventory-to-sales ratio increases
question_en: As an economic expansion approaches its peak, the economy is most likely to show:
option_c: an increase in the inventory-to-sales ratio.

explanation_en: Oligopolistic markets are characterized by a small number of competitors selling nondifferentiated products.  Kinked demand curves reflect the way competitors respond to any firm's attempts to increase market share or profitability.  The dotted black demand curve shows the hypothetical quantities demanded for a single oligopolist's product assuming naïve responses by competitors to different pricing strategies. The adverse outcomes likely confronting oligopolists are reflected in the red and blue segments of the kinked demand curve (DED).  Price cuts by one firm will likely be matched by competitors acting to defend their market shares.  The result is less elastic demand (ie, red demand curve segment, D) at price levels below the initial equilibrium (E). Competitor reaction is quite different if oligopolists attempt to increase profitability by raising prices.  The greater elasticity of demand (ie, the blue demand curve segment, D) at prices above the initial equilibrium results from competitors not matching a price increase.  Some of the price- raising firm's customers switch suppliers to avoid the price hike. The unit sales decrease after a price hike will proportionally be greater compared with the unit sales increase if prices were cut.  For example, whereas a 1% price cut might have resulted in a unit sales increase of 3%, a 1% price increase might cause a 5% decrease in unit sales. (Choice B)  A monopolist is the only seller in their market segment.  Monopolists are free to raise or lower price in search of profit maximization. (Choice C)  Firms in purely competitive markets are price-takers.  Each is so small relative to the total market that their actions cannot impact the equilibrium price; these firms therefore face flat (ie, infinitely elastic) demand curves.
question_en: Kinked demand curves are most likely associated with which type of market structure?
option_c: Pure competition

explanation_en: The Procedures section of the IPS explains the steps to take to keep the IPS current and the procedures to follow to respond to various contingencies, while the Investment Guidelines section covers leverage and derivatives, and the Strategic Asset Allocation or Rebalancing Policy sections (typically in appendices) detail rebalancing policies.
question_en: The Procedures section of an investment policy statement (IPS) most likely:
option_a: explains the steps to keep the IPS current.
option_b: provides information about the permissible use of leverage.
option_c: details the investor's policy with respect to rebalancing asset class weights.

explanation_en: The balance of payments (BOP) summarizes a country's international capital inflows and outflows. BOP accounting is based on a double-entry bookkeeping system. All transactions are allocated to either the current account, the capital account, or the financial account. Broadly speaking, the current account reflects the net value of imported and exported goods and services but can be further subdivided into: Merchandise trade: Import and export of physical commodities and manufactured goods Services: Service industry imports and exports (eg, software, movies, legal services) Income receipts: Income from foreign assets, such as dividend income or interest payments Unilateral transfers: One-way transfers, such as foreign aid or worker remittance In each account, debits increase assets or decrease liabilities whereas credits decrease assets or increase liabilities. In this instance, a US investor receiving a dividend payment from a French company (which is an income receipt in the US) results in a debit (ie, increase in assets) to the US current account. (Choice B) The financial account captures cross-border transfers of assets, not the income or interest received from owning an asset. (Choice C) The capital account captures sales and transfers of nonproduced and intangible assets, such as mineral rights or patents.
question_en: If a Brazilian converts BRL 781.25 to EUR 125, then the direct exchange rate from the Brazilian's perspective is closest to:
option_c: 6.25 BRL/EUR

explanation_en: An income statement shows the results of a firm's business activity over a specific period (eg, fiscal year, quarter). It displays how much expense the firm took to produce the revenue generated during the period. (Choice A) Balance sheet elements (ie, assets, liabilities, equity), not income statement elements, are reported as a snapshot in time. question_en: Income statement elements most likely reflect:

explanation_en: Because the coupon rate is greater than its yield to maturity, the bond price is at a premium to par value. If the yield remains unchanged, the price will decrease toward par value along its constant-yield price trajectory.
question_en: A 7.5% coupon, semiannual-pay, five-year bond has a yield to maturity of 6.80%. Over the next year, if the bond's yield to maturity remains unchanged, its price will:
option_c: remain unchanged.

explanation_en: Increased volatility of the underlying asset increases both put values and call values. A higher exercise price or an increase in cash flows on the underlying asset decrease the value of a call option.
question_en: Which of the following will increase the value of a call option?
option_a: An increase in the exercise price.
option_b: A dividend on the underlying asset.
option_c: An increase in volatility.

explanation_en: Add-on pricing refers to a pricing model in which a company sells its products at normal margins, but it offers additional (add-on) products to its customers at high margins. Bundling is a pricing model for multiple complementary products (like renting an apartment with furniture). Hidden revenue is a pricing model in which a product is usually free (like an app for a smartphone), but revenue is generated through advertising sales in the app.
question_en: Pro-X Cycle (Pro-X) is a bicycle manufacturer specializing in custom bicycles. The company sells all bikes for $1,200, but it offers high-margin packages like custom paint and premium tires and brakes ranging between $1,000 and $2,000. The pricing model that best reflects Pro-X's strategy is:
option_c: add-on pricing.

explanation_en: Cash flow statements show how a company collects cash (ie, cash inflows) and spends cash (ie, cash outflows). Cash flows are classified as operating, investing, or financing activities based on their source or use. Cash from operations (CFO) shows how the company generated cash from its core business. CFO is typically a cheaper and more sustainable source of cash than investing or financing activities; a company that reliably generates CFO is in a better position to fund growth opportunities than one that does not. Analysts can examine multiple years of CFO to determine whether the company consistently generates cash from its core business; this gives investors confidence that the company can continue to fund growth opportunities. (Choice A) An income statement exhibits a company's profitability (ie, revenue minus expenses). In this case, it is not the best statement to use since accrual accounting aligns revenues with expenses during a period, regardless of whether cash was exchanged. Although profitability is important, it does not reflect cash generation. (Choice C) A statement of changes in equity presents the increases (eg, issuances of capital) and decreases (eg, dividend payments) to the value of owners' investment in the firm. Analyzing a statement of changes in equity does not explain how the company could fund new projects.
question_en: An analyst examines the last five years of a company's financial statements. Which of the following would be best to use to analyze the company's ability to fund growth opportunities?
option_c: Statement of changes in equity

explanation_en: Option holders will exercise call options if strike price is below market price and put options if strike price is above market price, allowing profit from market declines through put options.
question_en: If a European investor believes the US equity market will decline in the next three months, the transaction most likely to allow the investor to profit from this view is the purchase of a:
option_c: currency swap.

explanation_en: An FRA can be used to lock in a fixed rate on a loan or deposit between two dates in the future. A long position in a bond and a loan that has already been made have current exposures not covered because the FRA covers a notional borrowing period starting in 30 days.
question_en: A 30-day forward rate agreement on 90-day LIBOR is most likely to be used by:
option_a: a lender to lock in an interest rate on a loan it has made to a third party.
option_b: a borrower to lock in an interest rate on a loan it will take out in 30 days' time.
option_c: an investor to offset the risk of a long position in a zero coupon bond maturing in 90 days.

question_en: A random variable Y = exp(X) is lognormally distributed, where X is normally distributed. The distribution of Y:
option_b: is often used to model stock prices.

explanation_en: Goodwill is not amortized, so it will not impact the income statement (unless subject to impairment). By allocating more of the acquisition price to goodwill and less to the acquired identifiable assets, the firm will charge less depreciation on the identifiable assets—and, as a result, increase net income. In future years, overvaluing goodwill could cause a higher chance of impairment if revalued appropriately. Overvaluing the identifiable assets will lead to higher depreciation and lower net income. Overvaluing both will cause the balance sheet to no longer balance.
question_en: If a firm wishes to manipulate its net income upward in the year it purchases another company, which of the following would most likely make this possible?
option_a: Overvaluing goodwill and overvaluing the acquired identiable assets.
option_b: Overvaluing goodwill and undervaluing the acquired identiable assets.
option_c: Undervaluing goodwill and overvaluing the acquired identiable assets.

explanation_en: An analyst is allowed to expand his knowledge through interaction with industry experts. Nothing in the case tells us that the information obtained by Teshima can be classified as material non-public information.
question_en: Paul Teshima is preparing a research report on a new drug called ABXV IV in the oncology industry. He gets in touch with a few scientists and medical professionals working in the field of oncology and obtains information about some competing oncology treatments. Most of these drugs are in the pre- clinical development phase, which is public information. Teshima concludes in his research report that ABXV IV might have some competing drugs coming into the market in the next few years if the pre- clinical and clinical trials prove to be successful. Has Teshima violated any Standard of Professional Conduct?
option_a: Yes, Teshima has violated the Standards by relying on material non-public information.
option_b: Yes, Teshima has violated the Standards by not performing due diligence to confirm the reliability of the information.
option_c: No, Teshima did not violate any Standard.

question_en: Which of the following is required to compute the standard error of a sample mean usingthe bootstrap resampling method?
option_b: The mean of the original sample

explanation_en: Credit risk is calculated with the probability of default (estimated from the bond rating) and the estimated recovery value should the bond default. Yield volatility is combined with duration to estimate the price risk of a bond.
question_en: The factors that must be considered when estimating the credit risk of a bond include:
option_a: only the bond rating and the recovery rate.
option_c: the bond rating, the recovery rate, and the yield volatility.

explanation_en: Neither the concentration ratio nor the Herfindahl–Hirschman index accounts for the possibility of new entrants into an industry; both measures only reflect current market concentration.
question_en: The possibility of new entrants into an industry is considered in the calculation of:
option_c: neither the concentration ratio nor the Herfindahl–Hirschman index.

explanation_en: Compared to the S&P 500 index, which is market cap weighted, an index that is weighted based on fundamentals will have a value tilt. Firms that have a higher earnings weight than market cap weight will be those with higher earnings yields. Weights are based on firm earnings, not earnings per share.
question_en: Compared to S&P 500 index weighting, an equities index that is weighted based on a fundamental factor, such as earnings, will most likely:
option_c: overweight rms with high EPS.

explanation_en:
The Sharpe ratio is one method used to evaluate the performance of an asset or portfolio relative to its risk. It measures an investment's return in excess of the risk-free rate, then scales that return by the amount of risk the investor assumed to achieve the return. An investment with a greater Sharpe ratio indicates that the investment produced greater excess return for its risk.
The Sharpe ratio uses total risk, as measured by standard deviation, as its risk metric. Asset risk refers to either the asset's systematic risk or its total risk, which is the sum of its systematic risk and unsystematic (ie, diversifiable) risk.
In this scenario, the portfolio's Sharpe ratio is calculated as:
(Choice A) 0.06 is the portfolio's Treynor ratio. This ratio represents the portfolio's excess return relative to its systematic risk, as measured by beta.
(Choice C) 0.70 is the ratio of the portfolio's excess return to the market's, not the portfolio's, standard deviation.

An analyst gathers the following information:

| Beta | 1.4 | 1.0 |
| Standard deviation | 15% | 12% |

If the risk-free rate is 2%, the portfolio's Sharpe ratio is closest to:

explanation_en: As part of an industry evaluation, analysts often examine the industry concentration and market shares of the largest competitors, which can indicate how competitive an industry is. High industry concentration usually indicates a smaller number of companies with greater market shares, suggesting less competition. Low industry concentration usually indicates a larger number of companies with smaller market shares and greater competition. Exceptions are cases where companies do not compete with others, such as localized services (eg, hospitals) or differentiated products (eg, food and beverage). Industry concentration can be calculated in multiple ways.  One common method is the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), which sums the squares of companies' market shares.  Larger (smaller) HHI values indicate greater (lesser) industry concentration and less (more) competition.  The largest HHI is 10,000 (= 100 ) for a pure monopoly, as is the case in this scenario since a pharmaceutical company with a patent would be the only producer of that drug.  When the patent expires and new entrants enter the market, the HHI would be expected to shrink as industry concentration declines (Choice B). (Choice C)  The HHI for an industry typically increases when the biggest companies become even larger, such as through acquisitions.
question_en: A pharmaceutical company's exclusive patent for a popular drug expires at the end of 20X1.  All else equal, at the end of 20X2, the Herfindahl- Hirschman Index for the market for that drug will most likely be:
option_c: larger.

explanation_en: Both equity and fixed income indexes can be constructed according to sector; similar to equities, fixed-income securities can be categorized according to the issuer's economic sector, the issuer's geographic region, or the economic development of the issuer's geographic region.
question_en: Both equity and fixed income indexes can be categorized according to the:
option_c: degree of inflation protection.

explanation_en: Lending money to government agencies is not typically a function of a central bank. Central bank functions include controlling the country's money supply to keep inflation within acceptable levels and promoting a sustainable rate of economic growth, as well as issuing currency and regulating banks.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a function or objective of a central bank?
option_b: Keeping ination within an acceptable range.
option_c: Lending money to government agencies.

explanation_en:
Liquidity ratios measure a firm's ability to pay its short-term liabilities. A company's defensive interval ratio (DIR) measures the time (eg, days) it
would take for the company to exhaust its quick assets (eg, cash + short-term marketable investments + receivables) when paying for its
ongoing expenses. If its DIR is low, the company may not be able to pay its bills.
Some may understand this ratio as a burn rate (ie, how long it will take the company to burn through its cash and quick assets). To find the
company most likely to meet its daily cash expenditure, first use the quick ratio to find the quick assets; use the quick assets to determine the DIR.
In this scenario, since all three companies have the same daily cash expenditures of $50,000 and the same current liabilities of $1,500,000, the

explanation_en: Net present value (NPV) analysis evaluates investments based on the present value of a project's cash flows.  NPV is the difference between the present value of the cash outflows and inflows generated by the project.  The present values are the nominal cash flows discounted by the project's required rate of return (r). Investment in a project means forgoing the return that could have been earned from investing in other projects (ie, opportunity cost of funds). Therefore, companies require a return that is at least equal to the rate of return available from comparable projects, given that return also meets the investors' requirements. (Choice A)  A company's average cost of debt capital is inappropriate for valuing an individual project since the average cost is not based on the project's risk or required return. (Choice C)  The discount rate that results in projects having an NPV of zero is the internal rate of return (IRR).  IRR is an alternative capital budgeting method to NPV analysis.
question_en: Which of the following most accurately describes the opportunity cost of funds used in net present value (NPV) analysis of investment projects?
option_a: Company's average cost of debt capital
option_b: Expected return on comparable investment projects
option_c: Discount rate that results in projects having a zero NPV

explanation_en:
Investor redemptions can significantly impact the performance of hedge funds. Unplanned redemption requests may force the fund manager to
sell illiquid or volatile assets at unfavorable prices. This may harm fund performance and result in losses for the remaining investors.
Hedge funds often impose restrictions on investors, discouraging or prohibiting redemptions during specific periods:
A lockup period is the minimum time an investor is committed to a fund after the initial investment. This restriction should give the fund
manager a reasonable time frame to select and acquire assets that optimize the fund's strategy. Withdrawals are not allowed during this
period, but nothing restricts redemptions after the lockup period ends (Choice B).
A notice period is the length of time an investor is required to wait to receive a redemption after requesting it. This restriction gives the fund
manager more time to convert assets into cash, which reduces the risk of forced selling and makes the notice period the most appropriate
choice for fund managers concerned about liquidity.
Redemption fees are paid by investors when redeeming their capital and are generally added back to the fund. The fees compensate the
remaining investors for losses the fund may eventually suffer when liquidating positions in an accelerated way. Redemption fees
discourage but do not prohibit redemptions at any time (Choice C).
question_en: A hedge fund manager wants the power to liquidate positions in a well-organized way whenever necessary and plans to impose restrictions on investors' ability to redeem capital. Which of the following restrictions would be most appropriate?
option_c: Redemption fee

explanation_en: As yields increase, bond prices fall, the price curve gets flatter, and changes in yield have a smaller effect on bond prices. As yields decrease, bond prices rise, the price curve gets steeper, and changes in yield have a larger effect on bond prices. Thus, the price increase when interest rates decline must be greater than the price decrease when interest rates rise (for the same basis point change). Remember that this applies to percentage changes as well.

explanation_en: Each bond issue has unique characteristics (eg, coupon, maturity, call features), resulting in thousands more individual securities than the equity markets.  For example, the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Aggregate Bond Index includes roughly 8,000 US-issued securities, combining various bond types and credit ratings that range from Treasury and agency debt to mortgage- and asset-backed securities and corporate bonds. The lack of daily transactions and the general illiquidity for many of these bonds create a burdensome and expensive pricing process compared with exchange-traded equities.  These factors combine to make fixed income index construction more costly and difficult for an investor to replicate than equity indexes. (Choice B)  Due to the vast variety and characteristics of bonds outstanding, it is difficult for an index to precisely replicate the composition of a bond universe with a small sample of securities. (Choice C)  Although the bond markets are much larger than equity markets and there are some issues that are very liquid and actively traded, the vast majority of bond pricing occurs through dealer quotes or a matrix pricing process, making price transparency more burdensome and less clear.

explanation_en: Sources and uses of capital Sources Uses Cash flows from operations Cash and investments Net working capital (negative) Net working capital (positive) Debt issuance Capital expenditures Equity issuance Intangible asset purchases Asset disposal Acquisitions Debt paydown Dividends Share repurchases Company research typically involves identifying and analyzing sources and uses of capital. Evaluating trends over time and comparing company data with peers can help analysts identify strengths and weaknesses or competitive advantages and disadvantages. Sources of capital are any activities that generate capital to fund operating, investing, and financing activities. Uses of capital are activities that invest in operations, including capital expenditures, or that return capital to stakeholders. A company's capital is commonly sourced from operations (ie, cash flow from operations) and from third parties (eg, issuance of equity or debt). However, sources of capital also include one-time infusions, such as asset disposals or sales. (Choices B and C) Cash and investments and positive net working capital are uses of capital. Cash and investments are used to maintain liquidity for business operations, interest payments, or other items. Positive net working capital is used to support operations.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely a source of capital for a company?

explanation_en:
The steepness of the risk-averse investor's indifference curve indicates that if risk increases (portfolio standard deviation), then a risk-averse
investor will need more return to keep the same level of investor utility. Further, the additional amount of return needed is greater than the
increase in risk.
In the example above, an investor has a risk aversion measure of 7, an expected return of 5%, and risk (standard deviation) of 10%. At a risk of
20%, the slope of a risk-averse investor's indifference curve is steeper than when the risk is 10%.
Using the utility formula, if the investor's risk doubles from 10% to 20%, then the return must more than double. In this example, the return more
than triples (15.5% ÷ 5.0% = 3.1x). This illustrates the concept of diminishing marginal utility of return. As risk increases, return must
increase by more than risk to maintain the investor's utility.
(Choice A) There is a positive risk-return relationship in this situation. Over long periods of time, data indicate that higher returns are associated
with higher risks.
(Choice C) The convexity of the efficient frontier explains how the efficient frontier is shaped, but it does not impact how indifference curves
become steeper as risk increases.
question_en: According to utility theory, which of the following best explains why an indifference curve of a risk-averse investor becomes steeper as risk increases?
option_c: The convexity of the efficient frontier

explanation_en: The ethical decision-making framework is designed to help identify important factors in the decision-making process. After identifying relevant information, the next step is to consider situational influences, additional guidance or advice, and alternative actions and consequences. After a decision is made and implemented, the decision-maker should assess the outcome. One relevant factor is to identity all stakeholders (both internal and external) involved and the responsibilities that may be owed to each. It is also important to identify all potentially relevant facts of the situation, whether verifiable or not (Choice B), and any conflicts of interest, existing or potential, that impact this decision. Finally, it is important to identify the ethical principles that bear on the decision. The framework is presented as a guide to a decision-making process, and while it is presented in a logical order (identify, consider, decide, assess), the steps may be applied in any order in practice (Choice C). Some steps may be repeated. For example, considering alternative actions may lead to identifying additional stakeholders or ethical principles.
question_en: A framework for ethical decision-making will most likely be effective when:

explanation_en:
Gold is a commodity, and like other commodities, it can be purchased. A trader can create a long position by purchasing physical gold (eg, bullion)
in the spot market, by buying a forward contract or by buying a standardized futures contract. As with most commodities, trading in the spot and
forward markets entails costs and risks that are avoided by trading gold futures.
Storage costs: Commodities are typically expensive to hold given the cost of storage and security, but futures positions can be offset by
taking an opposite position to avoid delivery and storage costs.
Transaction costs and risks: The quality of a commodity (eg, the purity of gold) can vary, creating risk, but standardized futures contracts
specify such characteristics, removing those transaction risks.
Counterparty risk: Buying the commodity or a forward contract is a bilateral trade that creates counterparty risk, but futures trade on an
exchange with a clearinghouse that guarantees performance, resolving counterparty risk.
Since futures contracts resolve these issues and minimize the costs of trading, they are more liquid than a long position in either the physical
commodity or a forward contract.
(Choice B) The arbitrage-free pricing of commodities such as gold versus gold futures insures their prices must track one another over time.
Adjusted tor the cost of carry, price changes in physical gold and gold futures must be almost the same.
(Choice C) Commodities futures exceed the price of bullion by the cost of holding bullion (ie, cost of carry), and holding costs increase with the
holding period. Consequently, returns on long futures positions will be less than returns from owning bullion. After adjusting for the cost of holding
bullion, the return on both positions is the same.
question_en: For an investor wanting to make a long-term bullish bet on gold, which of the following is the best reason to go long on a futures contract rather than buying physical gold?
option_a: Gold futures are more liquid than physical gold.
option_b: Gold futures have less price risk than physical gold.
option_c: The return on gold futures is not impacted by storage costs.

explanation_en: According to Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, members and candidates shall not knowingly participate or assist in any violation of laws, rules, regulations, or the Code and Standards. When members suspect a client or a colleague of planning or engaging in ongoing illegal activities, members should take the following actions: Consult counsel to determine if the conduct is, in fact, illegal. Disassociate from any illegal or unethical activity. When members have reasonable grounds to believe that a client's or employee's activities are illegal or unethical, the members should disassociate from these activities and urge their firm to attempt to persuade the perpetrator to cease such activity. Note: The Code and Standards do not require that members report legal violations to the appropriate governmental or regulatory organizations, but such disclosure may be prudent in certain circumstances.

option_a: consult with the company counsel to determine if in fact a law is being violated.

explanation_en: The forward price reflects the value of buying an asset in the future; the spot price reflects the value of holding the asset now.  The market sets the forward price based on three factors: the spot price, the costs of holding the asset, and the benefits of holding the asset.  Owning the forward contract means avoiding the costs and forgoing the benefits of holding the asset.  Therefore, the costs' future value is added and the benefits' future value is subtracted to determine the forward price. As new forward contracts are written each day, the forward price of contracts on the asset fluctuates due to changes in the three factors.  If the spot price of the asset increases or if the costs of holding the asset increase, the forward price of the asset increases on new contracts: If the benefits of holding the asset increase, the forward price decreases: A convenience yield, normally associated with a commodity, is the value of the nonmonetary benefits of holding an asset.  Since the convenience yield is a benefit of holding the asset, if it increases, the forward price of the asset decreases relative to its spot price for new contracts written on the asset (Choices B and C).

explanation_en: The implied forward rate (or just "forward rate") is an interest rate derived from the current zero-coupon bond term structure (ie, spot curve). Arbitrage-free pricing enforces the consistency of forward rates with spot rate differences. A forward rate can be interpreted as the incremental return required for extending the time-to-maturity by an additional period. For example, in this scenario an investor would be indifferent to investing in a three-year zero-coupon bond at 2.15% or investing in a two-year zero-coupon bond at 1.85% and then, two years from now, in a one-year zero-coupon bond at 2.75% (ie, the "2y1y" forward rate), since both result in the same return in three years. The implied forward rate is the breakeven reinvestment rate required to make the two transactions equivalent. If an investor believes that the one-year rate two years in the future will be lower than the breakeven rate of 2.75%, the investor is better off buying the three-year zero-coupon bond today. (Choice A) The implied spot rate of a two-year zero-coupon bond in one year is quoted as 1y2y, not 2y1y. (Choice B) The rate of return of the three-year zero-coupon bond is known (ie, 2.15%); it is the return of the one-year zero-coupon bond in two years that is uncertain. The implied forward rate is the required rate of return for the investor to be indifferent to the two transactions.

explanation_en: Unconditional probability is the likelihood that an event will occur, regardless of another event's occurrence.  The unconditional probability of selling the stock can be calculated from the conditional probabilities of selling the stock. The conditional probability of selling the stock, given that its price closes higher, is 0.9.  Since the probability of the stock closing higher is 0.6, the probability of both the stock closing higher and the trader selling the stock is 0.6 × 0.9, or 0.54. The conditional probability of selling the stock, given that the price does not close higher, is 0.2.  Since the probability of the stock not closing higher is 0.4 or (1 − 0.6 probability of the stock closing higher), the probability that the stock won't close higher and the trader will sell the stock equals 0.4 × 0.2, or 0.08. Since the unconditional probability of selling the stock is the likelihood of the trader selling the stock regardless of whether the stock closes higher, the answer is the sum of the probabilities of the selling the stock under both scenarios above, or 0.62 (ie, 0.54 + 0.08). (Choice A)  0.54 is the joint probability of selling the stock and the stock closing higher. (Choice B)  0.60 is the probability of the stock closing higher.

explanation_en: An issuance of corporate bonds typically has one of two principal repayment structures: In a term maturity, the entire principal amount for a bond is due on the same date. With a serial maturity, the bond issue has multiple maturity dates; the principals of certain bonds are retired on each of the maturity dates. Since a term maturity involves the issuer retiring the entire bond issue at one maturity date, it exposes bondholders to greater risk of default than a serial maturity structure. A sinking fund can mitigate this risk: the issuer is required to retire a certain minimum percentage of the bonds each year, according to a schedule designated in the bond indenture. This means that redemptions to bondholders happen over time, similarly to how cash flows occur for a bond issuance with a serial maturity structure. (Choice A) A coupon strip refers to the securities created when the interest payments from a government bond are separated ("stripped") from their principal payment and the two types of obligations trade as separate securities in the market. In this process, the date of the principal payment is not changed and occurs on the same single date, so the resulting securities are not similar to a serial maturity. (Choice B) Payment-in-kind (PIK) refers to a type of bond coupon, not a type of principal repayment structure. A PIK coupon bond pays the periodic coupon in the form of common stock shares of the company or in bonds, not cash.
question_en: With respect to principal repayment structures, a serial maturity bond is most similar to a:
option_c: bond with a sinking fund.

explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: a. Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this information regularly. b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio." CFA Members (including CFA charterholders) and Candidates are obligated to abide by and advocate for the Code of Ethics (ie, the Code) and the Standards of Professional Conduct (ie, the Standards), which provide guidance for appropriate ethical behavior. The Code includes general principles to which Members and Candidates must adhere. In contrast, the Standards address the principles' more specific applications, which must be followed. Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the Members' and Candidates' responsibilities to assess the suitability of investments for each client. A Member or Candidate does this by researching each client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance, which are compared to the characteristics of each proposed investment. Specifically, a Member or Candidate must determine suitability based on a client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before taking investment action. (Choice A) Investment suitability is based not only on the merits of a specific investment but also how that investment fits within a client's total portfolio. (Choice B) Low-fee investments are preferred if they are suitable and appropriate. However, the highest expected return may entail greater risk (ie, returns cannot be ensured) than a client is willing or able to bear and so may not be suitable for that client.

explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase In a system of fractional reserve banking, reserve requirements are one policy tool used by central banks to control the money supply and, in turn, spending and economic growth. Reserve requirements set the minimum percentage of commercial banks' deposit liabilities that must be held as reserves; banks make loans with the excess deposits. Lowering the reserve requirements for commercial banks allows those banks to lend more money. In theory, this should increase the money supply since additional money lent by banks can be deposited and lent multiple times. Thus, there is an inverse relationship between reserve requirements and the amount of money created, as reflected by the money multiplier. All else being equal, the smaller (larger) the reserve requirement is: the larger (smaller) the money multiplier, and the more (less) money is created by fractional reserve banking, and the greater (smaller) the money supply. (Choice A) Increasing the policy rate makes taking out short-term loans from the central bank more expensive for commercial banks. This typically causes commercial banks to increase their own lending rates, which lowers demand for loans and reduces the money supply. (Choice C) Selling securities to commercial banks reduces the commercial banks' reserves and typically makes them less willing and/or able to make loans, which reduces the money supply.
question_en: If a central bank wants to increase the money supply, the most appropriate action it can take is to:

explanation_en: Secondary bond market liquidity Not simply about how quickly a bond can be bought or sold The ability to buy and sell quickly at prices close to fair value The secondary bond market is dominated by institutional investors and central banks, with only limited retail participation. Securities are most often traded through a broker-dealer in over-the-counter (OTC) transactions. Outside of a handful of very liquid bonds (eg, sovereigns) that can be traded on an electronic order execution system (ie, "screen"), the liquidity of bonds is largely dependent on getting manual quotes from brokerage firms. Secondary bond market liquidity is determined by both how fast a bond can be bought or sold and how closely the price approximates fair value. For example, suppose an institutional investor is interested in selling a high-quality bond and, due to the decentralized nature of the OTC market, the investor requests bids (ie, price the buyer is willing to pay) from numerous brokerage firms (ie, manual quotes). Depending on the bond and market conditions, the price dispersion may be quite wide. In this case, suppose the best bid received is 2% below what the investor believes is a fair market price. This bond would not be considered liquid in the sense that even though the bond can be sold quickly, the price is too far below fair market value. (Choice A) Numerous bidders alone do not constitute a liquid market, particularly if the bids are materially below fair value. (Choice B) The market convention for settling most corporate bonds is trade date plus two or three days (eg, t + 3). Same-day settlement is often possible, but it frequently comes at a price further from fair market value, indicating a less liquid market.
question_en: The secondary market for a particular bond is most likely deemed liquid if the bond can be sold quickly:
option_c: at close to fair market value.

explanation_en:
A fixed-rate coupon Treasury bond can be replicated from a series of zero-coupon bonds (strips) with the same pattern of cash flows. The
price of the fixed-rate bond should equal the sum of the face values of the individual strips discounted by their corresponding spot rates (ie, the
market discount rate for zero-coupon bonds). This is known as the arbitrage-free valuation approach since the same price applies to both
instruments; otherwise, arbitrage opportunities will be present.
The YTM is the rate that discounts a bond's future cash flows to its current price. To calculate the YTM (r) of a fixed-rate bond, first calculate the
bond's present value (ie, price) using the cash flows of the zero-coupon strips, and then input the present value and other parameters (ie, maturity,
coupons, par value) on the calculator to solve for r.
(Choice A) 3.00% results from incorrectly using 8 (ie, assuming semiannual periods) for the number of periods.
(Choice C) 4.43% results from failing to include the last coupon payment of 20 in period 4's cash flow when computing the bond's present value.

explanation_en: Valuation ratios compare a stock price to a value measure, such as book value (BV), earnings, cash flow, or sales. A price-to-book (P/B) ratio indicates the price of a company's stock as a multiple of the company's BV of net assets (ie, assets minus liabilities). The price per share is the quoted market price. The P/B ratio can be calculated using per-share or total values: Market price per share divided by BV of net assets per share; Total market capitalization divided by total BV of net assets. The per-share calculation is more common since the market price is quoted on a per-share basis. In this scenario, Company C has a higher P/B ratio (1.71) than the other two companies (Choices A and B).

explanation_en: Skewness measures how nonsymmetrical a distribution is. Skewed distributions typically have more extreme values in one tail and more moderate values in the other. As a distribution becomes more skewed and either the left or right tail grows higher or longer, the values farther from the middle of the distribution are more likely to pull the arithmetic mean (simple mean or average) away from the distribution center than the median or mode. Because the arithmetic mean weights every value equally, it is more heavily influenced by outliers and extreme data points. A normal distribution, which is symmetrical, has a skewness of 0. A distribution with a skewness of 0.8 is positive, suggesting that there is a larger number of higher-valued data points. Since the tail to the right is longer in a distribution with positive skewness, the arithmetic mean is more affected than the median and mode. (Choice A) The mode (most common value) normally is least affected by skewness in a unimodal distribution. The presence of skewness in a distribution suggests a lack of symmetry (ie, one of the tails is higher or longer than the other). Altering the size of a distribution's tails typically will not change the most frequent data point. (Choice B) The median (middle value) is normally more affected than the mode by skewness in a unimodal distribution, although less affected than the arithmetic mean. In a positively skewed distribution, the greater number of larger values will pull the median to the right. Although the median is affected by the values in the right tail, the arithmetic mean is more affected by the larger values.
question_en: A distribution of returns has the same mean, standard deviation, and skewness as a normal distribution but has a kurtosis of 3.4.  Compared with a normal distribution, this distribution indicates returns are more likely:
option_a: near the mean and in the extremes.
option_b: near the mean and less likely in the extremes.
option_c: in the extremes and less likely near the mean.

explanation_en: Regulatory agencies usually require that publicly traded companies have their annual financial reports audited by an independent accounting firm. Auditors use sampling techniques with an overall goal to: provide reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free from material errors or misstatements and determine whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the applicable accounting standards (eg, US GAAP, IFRS). The auditor then gives an opinion based on what is sampled. A qualified opinion is used when financial statements are largely presented fairly but: the audit is limited in scope (eg, incomplete records) or there is an exception from the applicable accounting standards. A qualified audit opinion suggests that a company's financial statements are less reliable than statements with an unqualified, or "clean," opinion. In this situation, the auditor appends the opinion with additional details explaining the exception so users of the financial statements can decide whether the exception is important. (Choice A) An adverse opinion is given when an auditor determines that a company's financial statements differ materially from applicable accounting standards in a way that would affect investors' decision-making. (Choice C) An unqualified opinion is given when an auditor deems that the financial reports are fairly presented in all respects and in accordance with applicable accounting standards.
question_en: An independent auditor determines that a company's financial statements are fairly presented except that the company's records regarding accounts payable are materially incomplete. The auditor will most appropriately give an opinion that is:
option_c: unqualified.

explanation_en:
Correlation (ρ) measures the extent to which two variables (eg, asset returns) move together. Correlation can be used to calculate portfolio
variance, which is a measure of portfolio risk.
Variance measures the magnitude of the dispersion of portfolio returns whereas
correlation reflects both the direction and magnitude of the movement of asset returns relative to each other.
All else equal, for a two-asset portfolio, a lower correlation between the two stocks results in a lower portfolio variance. The lower correlation
implies that the stocks are less alike in the behavior of their returns. This dissimilarity can create a more diverse portfolio.
Therefore, a lower correlation means less dispersion of portfolio returns, which indicates that the portfolio has less risk. In this scenario, the
portfolio would have the least amount of risk if the correlation between the two stocks is less than zero (Choices B and C).
question_en: All else equal, if a portfolio consists of two stocks, the portfolio will have the least risk if the correlation between the two stocks is:
option_c: greater than zero.

explanation_en: Instruments for compliance with professional ethics Instrument Owner Describes Code of ethics Professional organization Shared principles Standards of conduct Professional organization Minimally acceptable behavior Laws and regulations Government Legal limits of behavior A code of ethics is a professional organization's statement of shared principles. Standards of conduct provide a guide to practicing the principles outlined in the code of ethics. Standards of conduct also clarify the minimally acceptable behaviors required to conform to the code of ethics. Although not addressed directly in standards of conduct, adherence to civil laws and regulations may be the minimally acceptable behavior in some cases. Standards of conduct may be principle-based or rule-based. Principle-based standards are universally applicable to members of the profession and are based on the principles outlined in the code of ethics. Rule-based standards, while also relating to the principles in the code of ethics, are usually more narrowly applicable and specific to certain members or scenarios that may arise. A code of ethics may or may not be accompanied by standards of conduct whereas standards of conduct exist only to enhance their associated code of ethics. CFA Institute has adopted both a code of ethics and standards of conduct (the "Code and Standards"); CFA charterholders and candidates are expected to know and comply with both. (Choice A) Standards of conduct are used to describe minimally acceptable behaviors or practices, given the shared principles of the code of ethics. The code of ethics describes the shared principles. (Choice B) Standards of conduct do not describe civil laws and regulations.
question_en: If a professional organization has standards of conduct in addition to its code of ethics, the purpose of the standards is most likely to describe:
option_c: acceptable behaviors.

explanation_en:
A bond's yield describes and quantifies its return. One yield measure used for corporate bonds is the government equivalent yield. Many
corporate bonds use a 30/360 day-count convention, whereas government bonds, particularly US Treasury notes and bonds, use an actual/actual
day-count convention. Each bond's YTM is based on its day-count convention, so the yields cannot be directly compared.
The government equivalent yield results from converting a corporate bond's YTM, which is based on a 30/360-day basis, to the YTM based on the
actual/actual basis of a government bond. This makes the yields directly comparable and shows the additional yield required to compensate
investors for the corporate bond's additional risk.
(Choice B) The true yield is similar to the yield obtained from using the street convention but is modified to account for the actual day that a
payment occurs (eg, an interest payment scheduled for a Sunday is instead made on the following Monday).
(Choice C) The street convention is a bond's YTM calculated under the assumption that all payments are made on their scheduled dates,
regardless of whether a scheduled date is a trading day.
question_en: Of the following, the government equivalent yield best describes yield to maturity (YTM):
option_a: restated from a 30/360 day-count basis to an actual/actual day-count basis.
option_b: calculated based on the actual dates that the bond pays interest and principal.
option_c: calculated by assuming that interest and principal are paid on their scheduled dates.

explanation_en: Co-investing in alternative investments Advantages Disadvantages Offers direct investing experience Requires more resources and expertise Leverages the investment firm's process than fund investing and expertise Direct investing opportunities are Reduced management fees dependent on the investment firm More active approach Potential adverse selection bias Coinvesting occurs when an investor in an alternative fund (eg, hedge fund, venture capital) accepts the opportunity to invest directly (ie, direct private investment outside the fund structure) by committing additional capital in specific investments alongside the fund manager who introduced the idea (ie, acted as an intermediary). Coinvesting requires two processes that demand more resources and expertise from the investor: fund-specific due diligence and asset-specific due diligence. Considerable asset-specific due diligence is performed by the investment firm (ie, general partner and fund manager) when it acts as an intermediary and presents the opportunity to the investor. Coinvesting is often a transitional step for investors to learn the details and fine points of direct investing. In addition, decisions to coinvest are often made under tight deadlines, putting considerable pressure on the investor to thoroughly complete the required level of due diligence. For these reasons, many investors rely heavily on the fund manager's due diligence expertise when evaluating a coinvestment opportunity. (Choice B) The investment firm, not the investor, sources the investment idea and has others invest alongside. (Choice C) Since the deadlines for decision-making and funding are usually tight, raising additional funding capital is not normally an option once the decision to coinvest has been made.
question_en: When co-investing, investors most likely:
option_a: rely heavily on the fund manager's due diligence.
option_b: source the investment idea and have others invest alongside.
option_c: raise additional capital to fund the investment once the investing decision has been made.

explanation_en: Total expenses = £780,000 initial testing costs + £95,000 training costs = £875,000. Under IFRS, any costs incurred during the research phase should be expensed (the initial £780,000). Costs incurred during development are capitalized. Heath Ltd. moved from research to development at the point where the vaccine was proven technically feasible, a market exists for the product (the contract with the government), and it has the intention and resources to complete and sell the vaccine. Training costs are always expensed, regardless of whether they are incurred during research or development. The development costs for materials, direct labor, and production overhead will be capitalized. Note that if the firm incurred any costs for administrative overhead, these would also be expensed.

explanation_en: In an informationally efficient market, prices are unbiased estimates of securities' intrinsic values. Therefore, active management cannot consistently generate positive risk-adjusted returns compared to a passive index strategy. Because transactions costs reduce its net return, an active strategy underperforms a passive index strategy on average over time.
question_en: In an informationally efficient capital market, a portfolio manager who follows an active investment strategy is most likely to:

explanation_en: An investment policy statement (IPS) is a written document that describes the client's investment objectives (eg, risk and return) and constraints. Prior to drafting it, the manager and the client examine the reasonableness of the required return and the suitability of the amount of risk. An IPS does not guarantee that the manager will meet the objectives or abide by the constraints. The process of preparing an IPS includes the manager's review of the client's overall suitability and risk tolerance. The manager ascertains the client's willingness and ability to take risk. A client's willingness to take risk is an assessment of the client's tendency to favor safety-conscious or speculative financial behaviors. The ability to bear risk reflects the client's financial flexibility to tolerate the periods of below-average returns. (Choice A) The return objective is determined by both the client and the manager. It should be reasonable relative to the client's risk tolerance. It can be measured either gross of (before) or net of (after) fees, so measurement gross of fees cannot be counted on as an advantage. (Choice C) One investment objective is to have an absolute or relative level of return when defining success. The IPS does not guarantee or provide evidence that the manager will meet the stated return objective; it simply acts as a plan for meeting the return objective.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely an advantage of using an investment policy statement?
option_a: Return objectives are expressed gross of fees.
option_b: The manager can assess the client's willingness to take risk.
option_c: The client receives assurance that the required rate of return will be met.

explanation_en: Alternative investments refer to investments in nontraditional assets such as commodities, real estate, private equity, and hedge funds. The term also refers to vehicles, such as limited partnerships, created to invest in traditional asset classes (eg, stocks, bonds). Alternative investments are attractive since they give investors access to a broader range of assets classes and have the potential to provide diversification benefits when added to a traditional asset portfolio. Typically, alternative assets have lower correlations with traditional assets. (Choice A) The markets for these assets are typically less liquid (ie, assets cannot be sold as quickly for cash) than markets for traditional assets. As a result, adding alternative assets to a traditional asset portfolio most likely decreases the portfolio's liquidity. (Choice B) Alternative investments are subject to less regulation than traditional investments, which results in fewer reporting requirements and therefore less transparency. Alternative investments also have higher fee structures (eg, hedge funds have both management and incentive fees).
question_en: Which of the following choices most likely describes a benefit of adding alternative investments to a portfolio of traditional investments?
option_c: Lower correlations with other assets

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Use reasonable judgement in identifying which factors are important to their investment analyses, recommendations, or actions, and include those factors in communications with clients and prospective clients." Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients requires Members and Candidates to inform both clients and prospective clients about the limitations and risks of an asset or investment process.  The communications must use plain language that is easy for clients to understand but also conveys enough information for them to recognize the relevant risks and limitations. In this instance, Lee violated the Standard by oversimplifying the exchange traded fund (ETF) as an "enhanced index fund," which inappropriately downplays the underlying risks associated with the investment.  Specifically, the ETF is not an index fund and employs an active approach, leverage, and short positions, which should all be clearly acknowledged and detailed when communicating the risks of the investment with clients and prospects (Choice A). (Choice C)  The fact that Lee uses the ETF as primary equity exposure for retail clients does not specifically violate the Standard.  Lee conducted considerable research before recommending this investment and is acting in what she believes to be in the best interest of her clients.  The issue is in how she communicated the favorable aspects of the investment but failed to mention the considerable risks that a well-informed investor would want to know.
question_en: Grace Lee, CFA, is an investment advisor at Apex Investments.  After considerable research, Lee recommends the XYZ 130/30 long/short exchange traded fund (ETF) to her retail clients as their primary equity exposure, if it is suitable for their portfolios.  The XYZ fund invests in a selection of benchmark equity securities while employing leverage (130% long) and short positions (30% short) to arrive at an equivalent 100% long position. Lee is very comfortable recommending the ETF, as it has historically outperformed the benchmark index while exhibiting a similar level of volatility. When discussing the ETF with clients and prospects, Lee touts the relative outperformance and low tracking error versus the benchmark, referring to it as an "enhanced index fund."  Lee has most likely:
option_a: remained in full compliance with the Standards.
option_b: violated the Standards by not adequately disclosing the risks of the ETF.
option_c: violated the Standards by using the ETF as equity exposure for retail clients.

explanation_en: Securitization refers to the process of bundling (ie, pooling) cash-generating loans, such as mortgages or credit card receivables.  The original lenders sell the assets to an entity that issues bonds secured by the assets, which are broadly referred to as asset-backed securities.  The cash flows from these assets are used to pay the bonds' interest and principal. Although securitization offers many benefits, it can also present increased risks.  A lender that plans to sell a 30-year home mortgage immediately after originating it, rather than keeping the loan until it matures, has less incentive to conduct proper due diligence concerning the borrower's credit quality or the collateral securing the loan.  This can lead to later defaults, as in the financial crisis of 2006-2008. (Choices A and C)  Traditionally, lenders kept loans on their balance sheets until they matured; therefore, they were not liquid.  However, bonds that are secured by bundled assets can be traded in the secondary market; therefore, they are liquid.  This liquidity is a benefit of securitization.  In addition, securitization provides lenders with another source of capital aside from borrowing or selling equity.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a benefit of securitization?
option_b: Lenders can relax credit standards in their lending decisions.
option_c: Asset-backed securities are more liquid than the collateral used to create them.

explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV(A) Loyalty is one of the broader Duties to Employers addressed in Standard IV.  It places specific requirements on members or candidates who intend to engage in independent practice for compensation when that practice may conflict with the employer's interest or deprive the employer of business opportunities.  Members or candidates who plan to engage in such independent practice must notify their employer prior to offering the services. In this instance, there is no violation of the Standard since Bright's teaching does not compete with QED's business model.  Furthermore, based on the information provided, teaching the classes will not deprive his employer of any of his skills or time, and the teaching may benefit his employer by improving his skill set. (Choice B)  If Bright's independent practice competed with QED's business, he would have to wait for permission prior to teaching a class to comply with the Standard. (Choice C)  In this case, Bright is not required to provide notice.  When the Standard does apply, members and candidates are required to provide a description of the services to be offered, compensation to be received, and expected duration of services.
question_en: Hudson Bright, CFA, just received his certificate in quantitative finance.  As part of his studies, he developed training modules for financial modeling.  Soon after receiving his certificate, Bright joins QED Consulting, a quantitative analysis consulting firm, and posts news about his certificate and new job on social media.  The local CFA Society president sees his post and asks him to teach financial modeling classes.  After determining that the time commitment will not hinder his performance at QED, Bright agrees to teach a monthly, one-hour class for 6 months at €500 per class.  He advises QED of his plans in an email that states, "I am writing to inform you that I have agreed to partner with the local CFA Society to teach financial modeling classes.  Please contact me with any questions."  He does not receive a response and begins teaching the classes.  Has Bright most likely violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty to Employer?
option_b: Yes, since he started teaching prior to receiving approval from QED.
option_c: Yes, since his notice to QED left out required information on compensation and duration.

explanation_en: Days sales outstanding (DSO), sometimes referred to as days in receivables, calculates the number of days, on average, for a company to collect cash from its customers after sales are made on credit. It measures how quickly a company converts its receivables into cash. Faster collection of receivables results in a lower DSO, and this enhances a company's liquidity. By contrast, a higher DSO indicates that customers are too slow to pay invoices or that the company has poor credit extension policies (eg, not granting trade discount incentives for early payment), both of which can act as a drag on liquidity. It is helpful to gauge a company's DSO performance by comparing it across time, to that of the industry average, or to peers. Company 3 showed the most improvement from the previous year. It reduced its DSO by 2.4 days, meaning that it collected its receivables, on average, 2.4 days faster than it did for the previous year. (Choice A) Company 1 took 5.0 days longer, on average, to collect its receivables compared to its performance the prior year. (Choice B) Although Company 2 improved its DSO from the previous year (−0.3 days), the improvement was less than that of Company 3.
