explanation_en: Slope of the futures curve Contango Backwardation Futures price > spot price May result if No convenience yield or Convenience yield < storage costs Futures price < spot price May result if Convenience yield > storage costs An investor who owns a physical commodity (eg, wheat, copper) incurs storage costs until the commodity is used or sold.  In contrast, an investor who owns a futures contract on the same commodity incurs no storage costs until the contract matures and delivery is accepted. All else equal, to prevent arbitrage, a commodity's futures prices are set higher than the spot price by the cost of holding the commodity.  An upward-sloping futures curve (ie, futures prices > spot prices) is the typical forward pricing structure for physical commodities.  This structure is called contango. Convenience yield, which offsets the storage costs, is the benefit the investor receives from directly owning the commodity (eg, immediate availability).  Contango results if the convenience yield is less than the storage costs, which is usually the case.  When the futures contract is in contango, there is little to no convenience yield (ie, benefit) to owning the commodity directly. (Choice A)  Backwardation has a negatively sloped (ie, downward-sloping) forward price curve since the futures price is less than the spot price. (Choice B)  Roll yield is the return (positive or negative) that occurs when the contract nears its expiration and the futures price converges with the spot price.  The roll yield for a forward price curve in contango is negative since the futures price is moving toward the lower spot price.
question_en: When a commodity's futures prices are in contango, its forward price curve most likely has:
option_c: little to no convenience yield.

explanation_en: Asset-based valuation models An asset-based valuation model estimates a company's value as the common shareholders' claim on the company's net assets. These models calculate the company's value as: the market value of its assets, less the market value of its liabilities and the value of its preferred shares. These market values include any off–balance sheet items that have value. The value of preferred shares must be removed from net assets in asset-based models since preferred shareholders' claims have priority over those of common shareholders (Choice B). Capital expenditures are a cash flow item measuring the value of new fixed assets a company has purchased during a period. Capital expenditures increase the company's assets but are not needed for asset-based valuation models since their value will already be reflected in the company's assets. Similarly, any debt required to fund the purchase of capital expenditures would be reflected in the company's liabilities. (Choice A) The value of liabilities is needed in asset-based valuation models since liabilities are subtracted from assets to calculate the net value of the assets.

If the events A and B are independent, then P(A) = P(A|B) (ie, probability of A is the same as probability of A given B) since the probability of A occurring is the same whether or not B occurs. If this is the case, the multiplication rule simplifies to P(AB) = P(A)P(B). In this scenario, P(A) is not equal to P(A|B): 0.31 ≠ 0.28. Therefore, events A and B are not independent. Substitute into the multiplication rule: (Choice A) 0.0868 is equal to P(A|B)P(A). (Choice C) 0.2790 is the result of incorrectly treating events A and B as if they were independent [ie, P(AB) = P(A)P(B)]. Since the events are not independent, P(AB) = P(A|B)P(B) must be used instead.

explanation_en: Derivatives can be traded on an exchange, which acts as a central counterparty for buyers and sellers of different types of futures contracts and options. This eliminates counterparty risk (ie, the risk that the other party to a contract will default). This is significantly different from derivatives traded "over-the-counter" (OTC), which are bilateral agreements (ie, directly between two parties). OTC contracts have little regulatory oversight since most participants in the OTC market are large institutions that can evaluate the risks of both the contract and the counterparty. Exchanges attract a wide range of participants, including less sophisticated investors. Regulations are designed in part to provide assurance that institutional investors do not have an unfair advantage (Choice A). To better facilitate its role as the only counterparty, as well as to provide liquidity, an exchange imposes a high degree of standardization on the contracts traded on the exchange. Terms such as dates, quantities, and delivery specifications are identical for all traders in a given contract. In contrast, parties to OTC contracts can negotiate all the terms of the contract (Choice B).
question_en: Compared with over-the-counter derivatives, derivatives traded on an exchange are least likely to be characterized by:
option_c: counterparty risk.

explanation_en: US GAAP require companies using LIFO to report inventory at the lower of cost or market value. US GAAP define market value as replacement cost, subject to upper and lower limits. The company's original cost is $105 per unit, which is higher than the $90 replacement cost, so this company must write down its inventory to market value. "Market value" is a range defined by the upper limit of net realizable value ($100) (Choice C) and the lower limit of net realizable value minus a normal profit margin ($100 - $7 = $93). The actual replacement cost ($90) is less than the lower limit ($93), so the company can write down its inventory to only $93 per unit. (Choice A) This is the company's actual replacement cost, but since it is less than the GAAP-specified lower limit of net realizable value minus a profit margin, the company cannot reduce the inventory value below the lower limit of $93 per unit.

explanation_en: Equity securities' characteristics Common Preferred Voting rights Some corporate actions (eg, M&A) and board seats Usually none Dividends Payable only after preferred Payable in full before common Assets Residual claim after all other obligations retired Priority claim over common for asset distributions There are two types of equity securities: common stocks and preferred stocks (ie, preference shares). Corporations must have common shares outstanding, which represent the ownership interests in the company. As owners, common stockholders: share in the company's operating performance, participate in its governance through voting rights, and have a residual claim on the company's assets in the case of liquidation. Companies may raise additional equity capital by issuing preferred stock. Unlike common stock, preferred shares normally carry no voting rights and do not participate in company operating performance. However, preferred shares rank ahead of (ie, have preference over) common shares, as preferred shareholders receive: preferred dividends, once declared, before any common stock dividends can be paid (Choice B), and shares' par value before common shareholders receive any distributions, upon liquidation (Choice C).
question_en: The priorities that preferred shareholders have compared to common shareholders are least likely related to:

explanation_en: In addition to measuring operating risks, analysts typically evaluate a company's risks related to its capital structure (ie, financial risk). Larger amounts of debt in a company's capital structure will increase the company's obligated principal and interest payments, and therefore its financial risk. The degree of financial leverage (DFL), which is the rate of change in a company's net income compared with the change in its operating income, measures this risk. A company's DFL is directly affected by interest expense. Interest expense is a nonoperating cost and therefore affects net income, but not operating income. Larger interest payments result in a larger DFL, thus making net income more sensitive to changes in operating income since the company has a riskier capital structure that relies more on debt financing. A DFL close to 1 indicates there is little interest expense as the company largely uses equity financing. (Choice A) Contribution margin is the difference between a product's unit price and unit variable costs. For a nonbank company, contribution margin would be unaffected by increases in the amount of debt in a company's capital structure. (Choice C) Degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures the rate that operating profit increases (decreases) in relation to sales increases (decreases). For nonbank companies, DOL is affected by the company's operating cost structure (ie, fixed versus variable costs) but would not be impacted by changes in interest rates.

explanation_en:
An impairment is an unanticipated decline in an asset's value. An asset is impaired when its carrying amount is greater than its recoverable
amount. Under US GAAP, the recoverable amount is the sum of the asset's undiscounted future cash flows (ie, total future economic benefit).
An asset is impaired if its expected future benefit is below its current book value.
After its initial impairment, the asset's value may increase. However, under US GAAP, if the asset is considered held for use (ie, PPE), a
reversal of the impairment is not allowed (Choices B and C). If the asset is considered held for sale, the company may record an increase in
the asset's carrying value limited to the amount of the initial impairment.
Under IFRS, there is no distinction between held for use and held for sale; all assets may increase in value after an initial impairment charge.
However, the increase is limited to the original impairment, even if the recoverable amount is greater than the asset's carrying value before the
initial impairment.

explanation_en: Using the new information we can use Bayes' formula to update the probability. P(economy does not expand | tech does not outperform) = P(economy does not expand and tech does not outperform) / P(tech does not outperform). P(economy does not expand and tech does not outperform) = P(tech does not outperform | economy does not expand) × P(economy does not expand) = 0.90 × 0.40 = 0.36. P(economy does expand and tech does not outperform) = P(tech does not outperform | economy does expand) × P(economy does expand) = 0.30 × 0.60 = 0.18. P(economy does not expand) = 1.00 – P(economy does expand) = 1.00 – 0.60 = 0.40. P(tech does not outperform | economy does not expand) = 1.00 – P(tech does outperform | economy does not expand) = 1.00 – 0.10 = 0.90. P(tech does not outperform) = P(tech does not outperform and economy does not expand) + P(tech does not outperform and economy does expand) = 0.36 + 0.18 = 0.54. P(economy does not expand | tech does not outperform) = P(economy does not expand and tech does not outperform) / P(tech does not outperform) = 0.36 / 0.54 = 0.67.

explanation_en: Derivative contract comparison Forward commitments Contingent claims Contract Exchange of obligations Conveyance of rights Counterparties Both obligated to perform Buyer has the right, but no obligation, to exercise; seller's obligation is contingent on exercise Cost at initiation Usually no cost to either party Buyer pays premium to seller Examples Futures, forwards, most swaps Options, credit default swaps, total return swaps Contingent claims are derivatives that give holders the right to trade the underlying asset at a specified price at a future date.  Contract holders do not have to exercise that right, but if they do the original contract seller is obligated to take the other side of the trade that results from the exercise.  For a contingent claim, sellers must fulfill their obligations contingent on the contract holders exercising their rights. Contingent refers to the counterparties exchanging a right for an obligation.  This is unlike forward commitments, in which both buyers and sellers exchange obligations that each must fulfill. (Choice A)  Contingent claim sellers receive a premium for granting contract buyers specified rights. (Choice C)  Counterparty credit risk is the uncertainty that a counterparty will fulfill its obligation under a derivative contract.  The presence or absence of counterparty credit risk is not a factor in determining whether a derivative is considered a contingent claim.

option_b: Incorrect because Chan has also violated Standard II(C), Misrepresentation. Standard II(C) states that CFA Institute members and candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentation relating to professional or investment activities. Chan's post was based on prediction and contrary to the facts. Chan knew or should have known that his statements were false and misleading. The online or interactive aspects of social media do not remove the need to be open and honest about the information being distributed. Chan disseminates the news of launching a new medicine for heart disease on social media. This is false and misleading information. Therefore, Chan has also violated Standard II(C).
option_c: Correct because Standard II(C), Misrepresentation, states that CFA Institute members and candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentation relating to professional or investment activities. Chan's post was based on prediction and contrary to the facts. Chan knew or should have known that his statements were false and misleading. The online or interactive aspects of social media do not remove the need to be open and honest about the information being distributed. Chan disseminates the news of launching a new medicine for heart disease on social media. This is false and misleading information. Therefore, Chan has violated Standard II(C). In addition, Standard II(B), Market Manipulation, requires that members and candidates uphold market integrity by prohibiting market manipulation. Market manipulation includes practices that distort security prices or trading volume with the intent to deceive people or entities that rely on information in the market. Information-based manipulation includes, but is not limited to, spreading false rumors to induce trading by others. Chan spreads the false and misleading information to push up WPC's stock price. explanation_en: Given a forecasted change in a noncallable bond's yield, the bond's price can be estimated using duration and convexity.  The estimated price based on duration alone is always less than the bond's actual market price since duration assumes that bond price sensitivity is constant.  (In the image above, the constant slope of the blue tangent lines represents duration).  So, estimating bond value based on duration alone and ignoring convexity underestimates bond value. The blue and green functions in both graphs illustrate the relationship between such estimated and actual prices, respectively.  The two functions touch at only the single point Y , which implies no change in yield.  At any other yield, the estimated price is less than the actual price. In fact, price sensitivity changes as yields change, as indicated by the curvature (ie, convexity) of the actual price/yield (green) function in the image. The convexity of noncallable bonds is always positive, which means that: As yields rise, prices become less sensitive to yield changes (ie, prices decline more slowly), so duration alone overestimates the size of price declines and the duration-estimated price < actual price. As yields fall, prices become more sensitive to yield changes (ie, prices increase more rapidly), so duration alone underestimates the size of price increases and the duration-estimated price < actual price.
question_en: If the yield to maturity of a noncallable bond changes, then compared with the actual market price of the bond, duration-based estimates of bond value most likely:
option_a: underestimate the market price if yield increases or decreases.
option_b: overestimate the market price if yield increases and underestimate it if yield decreases.
option_c: underestimate the market price if yield increases and overestimate it if yield decreases.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts defines a conflict as a matter that reasonably could be expected to "impair [members' or candidates'] independence or objectivity or interfere with their respective duties…."  Beck's spouse serves as a director of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst.  This must be disclosed since it potentially interferes with Beck's objectivity.  It is irrelevant that Beck wrote reports on the company for his previous employer since he cannot assume the new employer is aware of the relevant facts. The Standard includes all conflicts, not just financial conflicts.  Beck's soccer trusteeship is a potential conflict since Beck will have to devote significant time to the association in the coming months.  This could interfere with his duties to his employer as well as to his clients.  The Standard does not require an actual conflict to exist to trigger disclosure, only that one could "reasonably be expected" to occur (Choice A). (Choice C)  Both Beck's spouse serving as a trustee of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst and his soccer trusteeship pose actual or potential conflicts of interest, which Standard VI(A) requires him to disclose to his new employer.

The weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is a company's weighted average after-tax cost of capital from all sources. The most common sources of capital include equity, preferred stock, and debt. The WACC also represents the weighted average required return of all capital providers.

WACC = (wd)(rd)(1 - t) + (we)(re) + (wp)(rp)

For this question, use the steps below to calculate WACC using CAPM:

1. Determine current market values of capital (GBP millions): Debt: 30.00; Common: 1,000,000 x 47.60 = 47.60; Preferred: 800,000 x 28.0 = 22.40; Total: 100.00
2. Determine weight of each capital source: wd = 30%, we = 47.6%, wp = 22.4%
3. Recall given pre-tax cost of debt: rd = 6%
4. Use CAPM to determine cost of common equity: re = Rf + B(ERP) = 0.03 + 1.2(0.05) = 0.09
5. Determine the cost of preferred equity: rp = 1.80 / 28.00 = 0.0643
6. Input WACC variables:

WACC = (0.3)(0.06)(1 - 0.20) + (0.476)(0.09) + (0.224)(0.0643) = 7.16%

explanation_en: Greenfield vs. brownfield infrastructure characteristics Greenfield Brownfield Infrastructure that has yet to be built Expansion or improvement of existing infrastructure No operating or financial history May already be generating regular cash flow or dividends Usually higher risk, higher return potential Usually lower risk, lower return potential The terms brownfield and greenfield refer to the development stage of infrastructure investments. Greenfield investments build new infrastructure (eg, a new toll road). Brownfield investments expand or improve existing infrastructure (eg, adding a new hospital wing). Unlike brownfield assets, greenfield assets have no financial or operating history. An investor in a greenfield project may have the promise that a government will purchase or lease the asset once it is built, or the investor may be planning to own and operate the completed asset. Given the long time required to construct a greenfield asset, the risks for a greenfield investor are that the completed project may get a lower price or face lower demand than expected. It may also be difficult to obtain needed financing for a greenfield investment, and construction or operating costs could be higher than expected. (Choice B) Greenfield investments have higher potential returns since the latest technology can be used to maximize the efficiency of the asset's operations and maintenance. (Choice C) It takes a long time to construct greenfield investments and make them operational. During that time, they typically do not generate cash flows, whereas brownfield projects may generate predictable cash flows even before they are completed.
question_en: Compared to a brownfield infrastructure investment, a greenfield investment most likely has:
option_c: more current cash flows.

The returns on a price-weighted index can be matched by purchasing a portfolio with an equal number of shares of each stock in the index.

explanation_en: Companies can be classified based on their sensitivities to the business cycle. Cyclical companies exhibit profits that strongly vary with the state of the economy (ie, expansion or contraction). Whereas noncyclical companies exhibit stable profits independent of the state of the economy. Cyclical products (eg, high-end cars) tend to be expensive or discretionary, with demand directly tied to consumer disposable income. Since disposable income is strongly correlated with the economy, product demand is high during economic expansion, which leads to higher sales and profits. Product demand is low during economic contraction, which leads to lower sales and profits (Choice C). Furthermore, the generally capital-intensive nature of cyclical companies (eg, manufacturing) translates to high fixed costs, which further amplifies profit fluctuation. (Choice A) Noncyclical products (eg, consumer staples such as food) exhibit relatively stable demand that is not strongly correlated with the economy. These products are either inexpensive or necessities. Therefore, noncyclical companies have sales and profits that do not fluctuate significantly with periods of expansion or contraction.
question_en: Compared with noncyclical companies, cyclical companies most likely:
option_c: have strong revenue during economic contractions.

explanation_en: Covered bond redemption regimes If fund sponsor defaults: Hard bullet Default triggered; payments accelerate Soft bullet Default delayed; final maturity date extended Conditional pass- through Pass-through mode triggered only if bonds are not retired at original maturity date A type of asset-backed security (ABS), a covered bond is secured by collateral consisting of a pool of loans (eg, auto loans, home mortgages). Interest and principal payments on ABS depend exclusively on the timely payment of the interest and principal on the underlying loans. Unlike other ABS, covered bonds offer an additional layer of protection since bondholders have dual recourse, which allows a claim on both the issuer and the cover pool (ie, underlying pool of loans).  Other kinds of ABS are typically issued by a special purpose entity so that the issuer remains bankruptcy remote. If payments on covered bonds are not received as scheduled, stipulations in the issuing documents (ie, loan covenants) called redemption regimes determine how the bonds are impacted.  The three types of covered bond redemption regimes are as follows: Hard bullet:  Bond default is triggered and all payments are due immediately.  This is the typical treatment for bonds of all types in the event of issuer default (Choice B). Soft bullet:  Bond default is delayed and payments continue on the original schedule.  The issuer's failure to pay does not trigger default since the maturity date is extended (eg, to 12 months).  A failure to pay principal and interest on the new, extended maturity date will trigger default. Conditional pass-through:  Bond default is not triggered and payments continue on the original schedule.  If payments are not fully satisfied at maturity (ie, conditional), the bond is converted to pass-through mode, in which payments are funneled directly from the underlying pool to bondholders until the original expected cash flow payments are met (Choice C).
question_en: If covered bondholders do not receive payments as scheduled and the bond has a soft-bullet redemption regime, the bond default is most likely:
option_a: delayed, and final maturity is extended.
option_b: triggered, and bond payments are accelerated.
option_c: delayed, and the bond converts to a pass-through structure.

explanation_en: Market share instability is primarily determined by the degree of competition and the expense customers must incur to switch suppliers. Market share instability is increased by: Low barriers to entry that allow new competitors to enter an industry and take market share from incumbents Rapid rates of product innovation that make competition more intense and increase the likelihood of customers changing to suppliers whose products offer new features or higher quality Low switching costs that allow customers to shift their purchases to new suppliers without incurring significant extra expense (Choice A) High barriers to entry reduce the threat posed by firms entering an industry and upending the existing competitive balance, which results in greater market share stability. (Choice C) High switching costs (eg, the cost of creating new supply chains, new software when a company upgrades its computer system) mean substantial additional expense for customers. The greater such costs are, the less likely customers will change to new suppliers, which leads to more market share stability.
question_en: In equity analysis, market share instability is most likely linked with:
option_c: high customer switching costs.

explanation_en: A repurchase agreement (ie, repo) is structured as two paired transactions. The first trade is a sale of securities for a specified amount of cash. At that time, the counterparties agree to a second trade in which the initial seller repurchases the securities for a slightly higher price. There is no price risk with a repo since the prices for both trades are agreed to at initiation; in effect, the price difference is interest earned on the purchase (ie, loaned) amount. The original buyer is protected from default by the securities (ie, collateral) received in the initial trade. As a result, a repo is the equivalent of a collateralized loan. (Choice A) The put provision in a putable bond does give bondholders the right to force the issuer to repurchase the bond prior to maturity, but there is no collateral (ie, no assets are pledged against the risk of default). (Choice B) An interbank loan is unsecured. In a repo, the assets purchased function as collateral.
question_en: Which of the following fixed-income instruments is most similar to a collateralized loan?

explanation_en: Chung violated both Standard I(C) by making a misrepresentation about stock price increases without clarifying it is his opinion, and Standard V(B) by failing to explicitly discuss the assumptions and limitations of his analysis with clients.
question_en: A financial analyst, Chung, who works for an investment firm states the following to clients: "ATC is scheduled to announce a substantial stock repurchase program and its stock price will increase significantly." Does Chung's statement violate the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct?
option_a: Incorrect because Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, prohibits members and candidates from guaranteeing clients any specific return on volatile investments. Most investments contain some element of risk that makes their return inherently unpredictable. For such investments, guaranteeing either a particular rate of return or a guaranteed preservation of investment capital is misleading to investors. Chung states ATC is scheduled to announce a substantial stock repurchase program and its stock price will increase significantly, and does not clarify that it is based on his opinion. Therefore, Chung has also violated Standard V(B).
option_b: Incorrect because Standard I(C), Misrepresentation, prohibits members and candidates from guaranteeing clients any specific return on volatile investments. Most investments contain some element of risk that makes their return inherently unpredictable. For such investments, guaranteeing either a particular rate of return or a guaranteed preservation of investment capital is misleading to investors. Chung states ATC is scheduled to announce a substantial stock repurchase program and its stock price will increase significantly, and does not clarify that it is based on his opinion. Therefore, Chung has also violated Standard I(C).
option_c: Correct because according to Standard I(C), Misrepresentation, prohibits members and candidates from guaranteeing clients any specific return on volatile investments. Most investments contain some element of risk that makes their return inherently unpredictable. For such investments, guaranteeing either a particular rate of return or a guaranteed preservation of investment capital is misleading to investors. In addition, Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, members and candidates should explicitly discuss with clients and prospective clients the assumptions used in the investment models and processes to generate the analysis. Caution should be used in promoting the perceived accuracy of any model or process to clients because the ultimate output is merely an estimate of future results and not a certainty. Chung states ATC is scheduled to announce a substantial stock repurchase program and its stock price will increase significantly, and does not clarify that it is based on his opinion. Therefore, Chung has violated to both Standard I(C) and Standard V(B).

explanation_en:
A bond with an embedded option trades at a price that reflects both the value of the option and the risk of an otherwise similar bond (ie, same
credit quality, coupon rate, maturity) with no embedded option.
An embedded call is a disadvantage to a bondholder since the call can be exercised by the issuer when market conditions are favorable. Thus,
issuers must offer callable bonds with higher yields (implied by the benchmark rate + Z-spread) than the yields required by investors for
comparable bonds with no embedded option (implied by the benchmark rate + OAS). The difference between those bonds is the presence of the
option, and the difference in their spreads is the value of the option (Z-spread − OAS = option value).
To calculate the OAS of a bond, subtract the call option value (in basis points/year) from the Z-spread (eg, 760 − 208 = 552 basis points).
question_en: An analyst has compiled the following data about a bond that has an embedded call option and matures in 8 years: If an option pricing model determines that the value of the embedded call is 208 basis points/year, the option-adjusted spread for the bond (in basis points/year) is closest to:

explanation_en: While an investment advisor might have success in mitigating cognitive errors through educating clients, emotional biases are more difficult to overcome and may need to be accommodated. Processing errors and belief perseverance both describe cognitive errors. There is no support for the idea that cognitive errors typically lead to errors of commission while emotional biases typically lead to errors of omission.
question_en: A distinction between cognitive errors and emotional biases is that cognitive errors:
option_a: are more likely to be mitigated through education than emotional biases.
option_b: are essentially processing errors, while emotional biases tend to involve belief perseverance.
option_c: typically lead to errors of commission, while emotional biases typically lead to errors of omission.

explanation_en: Identifying the risk tolerance of the organization and aligning risks with risk tolerance is a key element of the risk management process. An organization will not use the risk management process to generate returns equal to just the risk-free rate, nor will it necessarily seek to minimize risks.
question_en: As part of its risk management process, an organization should most appropriately seek to:
option_a: generate a return equivalent to the risk-free rate.
option_b: minimize the risks inherent in its investment portfolio.
option_c: align the organization’s risk level with its risk tolerance.

explanation_en: One of the assumptions of the CAPM is that investors plan for the same single holding period.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely an assumption of the capital asset pricing model (CAPM)?
option_a: Investors are different only with respect to theirunique holding periods.
option_b: An investor can invest as much as he or she desires in any asset.
option_c: Security prices are not affected by investor trades.

explanation_en: A European put option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at the exercise price on the date of the option's expiration.  If the market price is less than the exercise price, then the put buyer has the right to sell the underlying asset at a higher price than the existing market price.  The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the put buyer's payoff. If the market price is not lower than the exercise price, then the put buyer will not exercise the option, and there is no payoff.  Therefore, the put buyer's payoff is the greater of (exercise price – market price) and zero. In this scenario, the put's exercise price at expiration is GBP 76, and the value of the underlying is GBP 83.  The payoff is the greater of (76 – 83) = GBP −7 and zero, so the payoff is GBP 0. (Choice A)  GBP −3 is the put buyer's profit, which equals the payoff minus the amount paid to purchase the option: (0 – 3) = GBP −3. (Choice C)  GBP 7 is the result of subtracting the exercise price from the value of the underlying asset.
question_en: On the day of expiration, a European put option's underlying asset has a price of GBP 83.  The option's exercise price is GBP 76, and the put buyer paid GBP 3 to purchase the option.  The payoff to the put buyer is closest to:
option_c: GBP 7

explanation_en: Leveraged accounts in the foreign exchange market refer to investment accounts that use derivatives.
question_en: In the context of the foreign exchange market, investment accounts are said to be leveraged if they:
option_c: use derivatives.

explanation_en: A box and whisker plot shows how data is distributed across quartiles.  The box always displays and encloses the interquartile range (IQR) of an ordered distribution.  Thus, the upper boundary of the box marks the third quartile (Q ), and the lower boundary marks the first quartile (Q ). The whiskers extend from the upper and lower bounds and mark the range of acceptable observations above Q  and below Q .  Values beyond the ends of the whiskers (ie, the "fences") represent outliers.  In this scenario, the upper fence is determined by adding 1.5 times the IQR to Q , and the lower fence by subtracting the same value from the Q . 3 1 3 1 3 1 Therefore, the outliers are values above 17% and below −7%. (Choice A)  The values of 14% and −4% result from incorrectly using the mean (5%) instead of the upper and lower bounds of the box (Q  and Q ) to define the fences. (Choice B)  The maximum and minimum values of 15% and −3% result from incorrectly using the median (6%) instead of the upper and lower bounds of the box to define the fences.
question_en: An analyst prepares the following box and whisker chart that displays a summary of the daily returns on an indexed fund: The analyst uses 1.5 times the interquartile range for the whiskers and considers all values beyond the upper and lower fences as outliers. Outliers are best described as observed values:
option_c: above 17% and below −7%

Parametric tests concern the hypothesized value of a parameter (eg, mean, variance) and are based on distributional assumptions (eg, normally
distributed). For example, a researcher can test for the mean or variance of a population when the population is assumed to follow a normal
distribution.
Unlike parametric tests, nonparametric tests are used when a hypothesis does not concern the value of a parameter or when few assumptions
about the underlying population can be made. Instead, these tests may concern the correlation between two populations (tested by Spearman's
rank correlation coefficient which gauges correlation strength), the ranking of population members, or whether a sample is random.
question_en: A nonparametric test can be most appropriately applied to which of the following?
option_a: A chi-square test concerning a single variance
option_b: A paired comparison test concerning two means
option_c: A Spearman's rank correlation coefficient test

explanation_en: Financial strength is an important factor in an organization's risk tolerance because it reflects the organization's ability to withstand losses. Even if its risk tolerance is low, an organization may choose to bear some risks that are consistent with achieving the organization's objectives. Risk tolerance includes risks that arise from within the organization as well as risks from outside.
question_en: Which of the following statements about an organization's risk tolerance is most accurate?
option_a: An organization with low risk tolerance should take steps to reduce each of the risks it identifies.
option_b: Risk tolerance is the degree to which an organization is able to bear the various risks that may arise from outside the organization.
option_c: The financial strength of an organization is one of the factors it should consider when determining its risk tolerance.

explanation_en: In the years following the expenditures, capitalizing will result in depreciation being deducted against net income, thereby resulting in a lower net income than expensing. Furthermore, capitalizing will increase total assets and cause ROA (net income / assets) to be lower.
question_en: When comparing the financial statement effects of expensing versus capitalizing an expenditure, capitalizing will most likely result in which of the following effects in the years after the expenditure is incurred?
option_a: Lower net income and higher return on assets.
option_b: Higher net income and lower return on assets.
option_c: Lower net income and lower return on assets.

explanation_en: According to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, if the costs of voting certain proxies exceed the benefits, the member or candidate can establish a policy to not vote all proxies. The member or candidate is required to inform clients of the proxy voting policy. Jackson has met these requirements and has not violated any Standards.
question_en: Bill Jackson, CFA, has established his own investment management firm. Jackson uses cost-benefit analysis to determine whether to vote proxies, and he informs his clients and prospects of this policy. Is Jackson in compliance with the Code and Standards?
option_b: No, because he must also disclose the details of his cost-benefit analysis.
option_c: No, because he has violated his duty of loyalty to clients by failing to vote some proxies.

explanation_en: The Treynor ratio is a metric that evaluates a portfolio's performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It measures excess return per unit of systematic (market) risk. Excess return is the difference between the portfolio's return and the return of a risk-free asset (eg, US Treasury bill, or T-bill). Systematic risk is measured by beta and refers to the relative sensitivity of a portfolio's return to that of the overall market. It is important to adjust return for risk since investors require additional return for taking on more risk. (Choice B) This answer results from dividing the average portfolio return, instead of the excess return, by beta. (Choice C) The excess return was divided by the standard deviation instead of beta.
question_en:
An analyst collects the following data to calculate the Treynor ratio for a fund:

| | |
|---|---|
| Market return | 10.0% |
| US Treasury bill return | 4.0% |
| Standard deviation of portfolio returns | 22.9% |
| Fund return | 16.0% |
| Beta | 1.15 |

The Treynor ratio for the four-year period is closest to:

explanation_en: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, such that if the yield has dropped from 4.2% to 3.8%, it must be a case that the price of the bond has increased. A decrease in price would align with an increase in yield to maturity. If the price had remained flat, the yield would be unchanged.
question_en: An investor looks at her monthly brokerage statement and notices that the yield to maturity on her 5-year corporate bond with a 4% annual coupon rate has gone from 4.2% last month to 3.8% this month. The statement will reflect a bond price that, over the last month, has:
option_c: increased.

explanation_en: Conservatism, hindsight, and framing biases are examples of cognitive errors. Loss aversion, self-control, regret-aversion, and overconfidence are all emotional biases.
question_en: Which of the following are considered biases due to cognitive errors?
option_a: Loss aversion, self-control, and regret-aversion biases.
option_b: Representativeness, mental accounting, and overcondence biases.
option_c: Conservatism, hindsight, and framing biases.

buyer) pays to the short party (ie, seller) for the underlying asset at settlement. The forward contract's value (at any time) represents its worth.
The forward contract becomes more valuable to the buyer as the underlying asset's price rises above the fixed forward price.
Throughout the life of the contract:
at inception, the value is 0;
prior to settlement, the value equals the spot price minus the present value of the forward price; and
at settlement, the value equals the spot price minus the forward price.
In this scenario, the value of the forward contract (in ¥ millions) prior to settlement is calculated as follows:
At inception, the long party agrees to purchase the materials from the short party in 3 months for ¥30 million. After 1 month, the market price of
the material rises to ¥31.5 million, which increases the forward contract's value. To determine its value after the first month (at t = 1), subtract the
discounted forward price from the current spot price of ¥31.5. The forward price is discounted for 2 months (2/12 of a year) since the forward
contract is 3 months long, and 1 month has elapsed (ie, 2 months remaining). It should be noted that the months-to-year conversion is needed
since the risk-free rate is stated in annual terms.
(Choice A) −1.35 results from switching S and F in the equation.

One month after the contract's inception (t =1), the same materials cost ¥31.5 million in the open market. explanation_en: Property and casualty insurers may need to distribute funds at any time if a disaster occurs. Endowment funds have a very long horizon, as they are often expected to operate in perpetuity with only annual distributions representing a relatively small percentage of the fund value. Defined benefit plans have an investment horizon based on the years to retirement of currently covered workers and the years they (and their beneficiaries) are expected to live after retirement.
question_en: On average, which of the following types of investors has the shortest investment horizon?
option_c: Property and casualty insurer.

explanation_en: According to Standard IV(A) on Loyalty, only Statement 1 is correct because members must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive them of their skills and abilities; Statement 2 is incorrect because the standard does not require subordinating personal and family obligations to work; Statement 3 is incorrect because the standard does not prohibit independent practice while employed (though notification to the employer is required).
question_en:
According to the Standard relating to loyalty, which of the following statements are correct?

Statement 1: "Members must not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities."
Statement 2: "Members are required to subordinate important personal and family obligations to their work."
Statement 3: "Members are prohibited from entering into an independent practice for compensation while still employed."
option_c: Statement 1, Statement 2, and Statement 3

explanation_en: A history of unusual expense items indicates a pattern of management potentially manipulating investor perception of sustainable profitability through repeated misclassification, whereas diversified companies may legitimately have different operating margins, and accounting policy changes for compliance are not suspicious.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely to signal manipulation of financial reporting for a large, diversified company?
option_a: A history of large expense items classified as unusual
option_b: Operating margins out of line with other diversified companies
option_c: Changes in accounting policies to reflect new accounting standards

explanation_en: Milton did not violate any CFA Institute code or standard because he developed a new model and re-created supporting records by directly gathering information from Indigo Corp.
question_en: Gilbert Love worked as financial analyst at Milton Securities. During his employment at Milton, Love covered Indigo Corp and developed detailed financial models, assumptions and supporting reports. When Milton switched his job, his new employer assigned him to analyze Indigo Corp. Milton developed a new model with improved assumptions and specifications and re-created the supporting records by gathering data from the covered company. Has Milton violated any CFA Institute Code and Standards?
option_a: No, he is in compliance with the Code and Standards.
option_b: Yes, he has violated Standard V-C ‘Record Retention’ by re-creating thesupporting records.
option_c: Yes, he violated ‘Misrepresentation’ and ‘Record Retention’ bydeveloping the model and re- creating the supporting records for Indigo Corp.

explanation_en: Regulation of digital assets compared with traditional financial assets Digital assets Traditional financial assets Clarity Ambiguous and still being developed Clear and well-defined rules Inconsistent across regulatory bodies: Asset class categorization US classifies as commodities Consistent asset classification Others classify as nonfinancial assets Legality of market behaviors Legality may vary across accepted guidelines Legality standardized across jurisdictions Traditional financial assets, such as stocks and bonds, are clearly defined and regulated under well-established legal frameworks across jurisdictions. A robust regulatory framework protects capital market integrity and safeguards investors from illegal activities such as price manipulation and fraud. In contrast, the regulatory framework for digital assets poses significant challenges for investors. As digital assets are a relatively new asset class, regulation is still underdeveloped and inconsistent across regulatory bodies. This lack of an established framework leads to poor legal guidelines. Thus, certain activities that are illegal on traditional asset exchanges, such as price manipulation and fraud, may be legal on digital exchanges. (Choice A) The use of digital assets is illegal in some countries, where legal and regulatory standards vary widely. (Choice C) US regulatory bodies treat cryptocurrencies as commodities, whereas some other regulatory bodies treat cryptocurrencies as nonfinancial assets.
question_en: Which of the following statements regarding the regulation of digital assets is correct?
option_a: Use of digital assets is legal in every country.
option_b: Price manipulation and fraud may be unregulated on digital exchanges.
option_c: Digital assets are globally considered commodities for regulatory purposes.

explanation_en: Standard V(B), Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. Members must distinguish between fact and opinion in the presentation of a research report or investment recommendation. option_a: not violated CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct because she had reasonable reason to believe that the statements in her report were true.
option_b: violated CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct because she did not check the accuracy of the statements that management made.
option_c: violated CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct because she misrepresented the optimism by turning it to certainty.

question_en: Which of the following statements about legal and ethical standards is most accurate?
option_a: Ethical and legal standards often intersect, but not always.
option_b: Ethical standards are a subset of legal standards.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Disclose to clients and prospective clients significant limitations and risks associated with the investment process." Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients requires Members and Candidates to discuss the limitations and risks of recommendations of an investment strategy or process. This is especially imperative when the investments are in new or unusual financial instruments with which the client may be unfamiliar. To comply with the Standard, Members and Candidates must communicate with clients in plain language. The communication must also convey enough information that clients can recognize the risks and limitations of the recommendation. When explaining key attributes of an investment recommendation, Members and Candidates must use reasonable judgment in providing the appropriate level of transparency without unnecessary or confusing details of the strategy. In this scenario, Steinhardt communicated the positive pro forma performance data, but she failed to discuss the significant risks of the strategy. A strategy consisting of only long-term options is aggressive and the risk of loss is very high, particularly in a different market environment (eg, bear market). (Choice A) The basic format, structure, and security selection process of the investment was sufficiently described, meeting the Standard. (Choice C) Advisors must not impose their own biases (ie, conservatism) on the client. In this instance, after discussion with Steinhardt, the client specifically requested an IPS with a greater risk/reward profile. Since the high-net-worth client can be assumed to have adequate risk tolerance, there is no indication that the original IPS was more appropriate.
question_en: Ivan Petrovich, CFA, manages the Emerging Markets Private Equity Fund.  Twelve of the fund's 87 holdings may go a week or more without a quoted price.  Petrovich believes that this is normal for some private equity holdings, so when reporting performance he uses the last available market price for the holdings that do not price daily.  According to Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Petrovich should:
option_a: provide only GIPS-compliant performance reports to potential clients.
option_b: inform current and potential clients about the fund's pricing methodology.

The angel investing stage is when investment funds are used for business plans and assessing market potential. The early stage refers to investments made to fund initial commercial production and sales.
question_en: The formative stage of venture capital investing when capital is furnished for market research and product development is best characterized as the:
option_c: early stage.

explanation_en:
The value of a forward contract is the spot price of the underlying minus the present value of
the forward contract. Calculating the present value requires adjusting the time period to account
for the remaining term ofthe contract.
question_en: During its life, the value of a forward contract is most likely equal to the price of the underlying minus the price of the:
option_a: forward, discounted over the remaining term of the contract.
option_c: forward, discounted over the original term of the contract.

explanation_en: Markets are informationally efficient if security prices adjust rapidly and rationally to the release of new information. Informational efficiency is fostered when information is widely available at low cost and there are numerous market participants adjusting their expectations of risk and return as new information is released. CFA Institute curriculum defines new information as the "surprise" or "unexpected" component of newly released information. For example, an earnings report in line with expected earnings is not considered new information. In an informationally efficient market, prices adjust only when information releases contain a surprise (ie, new information), such as when reported earnings fall short of expectations. (Choice A) Security prices cannot accurately anticipate new information, since new information is defined as being unexpected, that is, information that could not have been expected or anticipated. (Choice B) Since most markets restrict trading on the basis of nonpublic (ie, private) information, informational efficiency is indicated by prices' reaction to newly public information; it does not depend on security prices reflecting private information.
question_en: A market that is informationally efficient is most likely one where security prices:
option_b: reflect all public and private information.
option_c: react quickly and rationally to new information.

explanation_en:
Performance evaluation analyzes a portfolio's return and degree of risk. In portfolio management, risk is quantified as either systematic risk, as measured by beta, or total risk, as measured by standard deviation. Total risk includes both systematic and unsystematic risk.

The Treynor ratio, which is the ratio of excess return to beta, allows the isolation of systematic risk using beta. This distinguishes it from the Sharpe ratio, which is the ratio of excess return to total risk as measured by standard deviation.

In this question, the portfolio with the highest systematic risk is identified as follows:

| Calculations | Steps |
|---|---|
| βp = (Rp − Rf) / Treynor ratio | Rearrange Treynor ratio formula to solve for beta |
| β1 = (0.18 − 0.015) / 0.11 = 1.50 | Solve for beta for Portfolio 1 |
| β2 = (0.10 − 0.015) / 0.13 = 0.65 | Solve for beta for Portfolio 2 |
| β3 = (0.075 − 0.015) / 0.06 = 1.00 | Solve for beta for Portfolio 3 |

Portfolio 1 has the highest systematic risk, with a beta of 1.50.

Things to remember:
The Treynor ratio measures excess return relative to systematic risk, as measured by beta. This distinguishes it from the Sharpe ratio, which also uses excess return but relative to total risk as measured by standard deviation.
question_en:
An analyst provides the following performance information for three portfolios over the past year:

| | Mean Annual Return | Sharpe Ratio | Treynor Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Portfolio 1 | 18.0% | 0.83 | 0.11 |
| Portfolio 2 | 10.0% | 0.34 | 0.13 |
| Portfolio 3 | 7.5% | 0.50 | 0.06 |

Based only on this information, if the risk-free rate is 1.5%, which portfolio has the highest systematic risk?
option_c: Portfolio 3

option_a: put buyer’s maximum loss is the put option’s premium.
option_b: maximum loss to the put writer is the exercise price less the premium.

question_en: Which of the following statements about moneyness is most accurate? When the stock price is:
option_a: below the strike price, a call option is in-the-money.
option_b: above the strike price, a put option is in-the-money.

explanation_en: Both Gordon and Haney violated Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs by compromising the integrity of the exam. The Standard prohibits candidates from discussing specific exam questions or which topics were tested or not tested.
question_en: Lindsay Gordon is a Level II CFA candidate. Gordon's best friend, Steve Haney, is also a Level II candidate and has registered for the same exam window as Gordon. Because Haney's exam appointment is the day before Gordon's appointment, Gordon suggests that Haney try to remember some of the exam questions and let her know what they asked. After Haney takes his exam, he reminds Gordon that the Code and Standards prohibit candidates from disclosing specific exam questions, and only gives her a general idea of what topics were tested or not tested. Which of the following statements regarding Gordon and Haney is most accurate?
option_a: Gordon is in violation of the Code and Standards, but Haney is not in violation.
option_b: Both Gordon and Haney are in violation of the Code and Standards.

explanation_en: Common behavioral finance biases Loss aversion Disliking losses more than one appreciates gains of equal magnitude Mental accounting Separating wealth into different mental buckets with different risk and return expectations Overconfidence Being overconfident in one's ability to estimate prices and select stocks Herding Following and mimicking the decisions of the masses Making oversimplified assessments on new information based on conclusions drawn from past experiences (eg, Representativeness stereotypes) Conservatism Reluctance to accept new information and clinging to past views Focusing on issues in isolation instead of considering the broader context in conjunction with other interrelated Narrow framing factors Behavioral finance is the area of study that examines how behavioral biases influence investment decisions. Often, biases lead to irrational decision-making. Conservatism bias occurs when individuals are reluctant to accept new information and instead adhere strictly to past information. In this scenario, the analyst refuses to revise the previous EPS forecast of $0.21 despite receiving updated information on supply chain disruptions that will decrease earnings. explanation_en: In a price-weighted index, the weight of each constituent security is its price as a proportion of the sum of all the securities' prices in the index. In addition, if a company splits its stock, the weighting of every security in the index must be revalued, although stock splits do not affect a company's total market value. (Choice A)  Price-weighted indexes have no inherent value tilt.  Value tilt is an issue for fundamentally weighted indexes since their weights are based on fundamental factors (eg, sales, earnings).  Compared to growth stocks, value stocks have higher ratios of such factors relative to their market values.

explanation_en:
Mean absolute deviation (MAD) measures dispersion (ie, variability) of observations around the mean. Dispersion refers to the difference
between an observation and the mean. Higher dispersion means that the observations are more spread out around the mean, which indicates a
greater probability of observations that are significantly higher or lower than the mean. In finance, dispersion indicates risk.
Since the sum of all dispersions around the mean equals 0, MAD instead uses the absolute value of each dispersion. The sum of all the absolute
values is divided by the number of observations, which produces the average dispersion. The calculations are shown below:
(Choice A) Data in a sample will be both above and below the mean, so some dispersions around the mean are negative and others are
positive. The sum of all dispersions equals 0, so the average also equals 0. By using the absolute value of the dispersions, MAD always
generates a number ≥ 0.
(Choice C) 6.0 results from dividing the sum of the absolute values by (n − 1), or 4, instead of 5. The number of observations minus 1 is used
only when calculating the standard deviation of a sample. MAD uses the actual number of observations.

explanation_en:
This question uses the total probability rule to estimate the probability of a compensation increase. The compensation increase is impacted by
whether the company's EPS increases. One scenario is that EPS does not increase, which has a probability of 0.6. Since the probability of EPS
increasing is mutually exclusive and conditional, the probability of an EPS increase is (1 − 0.6) = 0.4.
After the independent probabilities of an EPS increase are determined, the next step is to identify and calculate the conditional probabilities of
compensation increasing, given that EPS increases and also given that it does not. The sum of those conditional probabilities is the total
probability that compensation increases.
The likelihood that compensation increases given that EPS increases is 0.8, so the joint probability that both EPS and compensation increase is
0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32 (Choice B). This is not the total probability of a compensation increase since it does not address the scenario of compensation
increasing given that EPS does not increase.
Conditional probabilities can also be mutually exclusive and exhaustive. The probability of no compensation increase given no EPS increase
is 0.9, so the conditional probability that compensation increases given that EPS does not increase is 1 − 0.9 = 0.1. The joint probability of no EPS
increase and a compensation increase is 0.6 × 0.1 = 0.06 (Choice C). The result is the total probability of a compensation increase of 0.32 + 0.06
= 0.38.

explanation_en: A fixed-for-floating swap is a contract in which the counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. To achieve an initial contract value of zero, the fixed swap payments are set so that their present value equals the present value of the floating payments. The process involves replicating the swap cash flows. The fixed swap payments can be viewed as a blended average of the floating payments, locked in by the replicating strategy of a forward contract. When a market is in contango, forward contracts with different expirations must have different agreed-on prices to be at market (ie, have initial values of zero). Therefore, for a market in contango a series of forward contracts with the same agreed-on price (ie, fixed swap payments) have different values. Some of the fixed swap payments have negative values (ie, fixed payment > forward price) and others have positive values (ie, fixed payment < forward price). The fixed swap payments are set so that their net value is zero when the swap is initiated. (Choice A) The series of fixed swap payments is equivalent to a series of forward contracts that have the same agreed-on price, not different agreed-on prices. (Choice C) When a market is in contango, forward contracts in a series with the same agreed-on price cannot all have an initial value of zero.

explanation_en: Categorization of behavioral biases Cognitive errors Emotional biases Decisions made on innate feelings or emotion Flawed reasoning or thought process Difficult to correct as often based on intuition Description Can often be corrected with better and subconscious influences information, advice, or education Awareness that these biases exist is the best defense Bias Confirmation, hindsight, representative Loss aversion, regret aversion, overconfidence examples Behavioral biases that impact financial decisions are categorized as either cognitive errors, resulting from flawed logic, or emotional biases, resulting from subconscious influences or emotion. Although cognitive errors can often be remedied by additional information or better education, emotional biases are more difficult to overcome. Emotional biases are based on intuition and subconscious influences, which often go undetected by the biased individual. Thus, having self- awareness and recognition that a bias exists is the first step in adapting to and mitigating the potential for negative outcomes based on bias. There are six identified emotional biases: Loss aversion Overconfidence Self-control Status quo Endowment Regret aversion Cognitive errors are classified as either belief perseverance bias or processing errors. Belief perseverance bias relates to firmly adhering to previously held beliefs and ignoring facts rather than facing potentially mentally uncomfortable situations (ie, cognitive dissonance) (Choice B). Processing errors relate to illogical or irrational financial decision-making; they can be corrected with better education, information, or advice (Choice C).

explanation_en:
The F-statistic is used to test the statistical significance of a linear regression by testing whether results are random. In the F-test for a simple
linear regression, if the F-statistic is greater than the critical F-value, there is evidence that the single independent variable (X) helps to explain
changes in the dependent variable (Y) (ie, results are not random).
The F-statistic is the ratio of the mean square regression (MSR) to the mean square error (MSE) and can be interpreted as the ratio of the
explained variance to the unexplained variance. The greater (smaller) the F-statistic, the more (less) of the variation is explained by the
regression. In the current scenario:

| Steps | Calculations |
|---|---|
| 1. Calculate MSR | MSR = Sum of squares regression / Number of independent variables = 20.601 / 1 = 20.601 |
| 2. Calculate MSE | MSE = Sum of squares error (residual) / (Total observations − Total variables) = 8.326 / (12 − 2) = 0.8326 |
| 3. Calculate the F-statistic | F = MSR / MSE = 20.601 / 0.8326 = 24.74 |

Note that the denominators used to calculate MSR and MSE are the degrees of freedom (df) in each case:
df(model), denominator of MSR, is the number of independent variables, which is 1 in a simple linear regression.
df(residual), denominator of MSE, is the difference between the sample size (n) and the number of parameters (2 in a simple linear
regression), so 10 = 12 − 2.
df(total) is the sum of df(model) and df(residual), or 11.
(Choice B) 27.22 is obtained by incorrectly using total df in the denominator of MSE [20.601 / (8.326 / 11)].
(Choice C) 29.69 is obtained by incorrectly using the total observations in the denominator of MSE [20.601 / (8.326 / 12)].

explanation_en: The security market line (SML) is a graph of the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). The CAPM is used to estimate a security's expected return based on its beta, the market's expected return, and the risk-free rate. If a stock's non-CAPM expected return is greater than its CAPM expected return, then the market assumes that the stock is mispriced and undervalued relative to the CAPM's valuation. Undervalued securities plot above the SML, and overvalued securities plot below it. Securities that are valued fairly are located on the SML. Rational investors buy the undervalued asset, causing its price to increase and its expected return to decrease. This process continues until the security is priced fairly and plots on the SML (Choices B) Selling the stock is a result of misinterpreting its valuation as overvalued. According to CAPM, rational investors buy undervalued securities and sell overvalued ones. (Choices C) By taking no action the investor cannot capture the price appreciation. Market orders determine how an order is completed. Execution instructions define how an order is filled, and validity instructions state the
time frame and conditions under which an order is filled. In this scenario, a combination of execution and validity instructions is used:
The instruction "stop $72" is a stop-loss order, used to contain potential losses. Once the stock falls to the stop price or below it, the
execution instructions are triggered.
The instruction "limit $70" links the stop-loss order with a limit order, executing the trade at a price of $70 or better. Since this is a sell order,
the price must be $70 or higher for the order to fill.
In this scenario, the immediate outcome is that no action is taken. The stop is triggered when the price falls below $72. However, the stock opens
$1 below the $70 limit, preventing the order from being filled. As a result, no trade is executed, and the current unrealized loss stands at $900
[(69 − 78) × 100]. The order remains valid (ie, good till canceled), so if the stock price rises to $70 (ie, lowest acceptable limit price), the trade will
be executed.
(Choice A) A $600 loss incorrectly assumes the trade is executed at the stop price of $72.
(Choice B) An $800 loss incorrectly assumes the trade is executed at the limit price of $70.

Then, prepayments stabilize at a constant 6% rate until the bond is retired. A mortgage-backed security with a value of 100 PSA assumes prepayments fit the standard model. A value of 50 PSA assumes prepayments occur at half the rate of the standard model, and a 200 PSA assumes twice the rate of prepayments (Choice B). If prepayments were assumed to be double the benchmark (200 PSA), the underlying mortgage collateral must have had much higher mortgage rates than the current market environment, as many homeowners were incentivized to refinance their mortgages at lower rates. explanation_en:
The purchasing power of one currency versus another is measured by the real exchange rate between the two. The real exchange rate is a function of both the quoted (ie, nominal) exchange rate between the currencies and the price level in each currency; changes in real exchange rates result from changes in one or more of those factors.

Considered from the perspective of the price currency versus the base currency, a change in the real exchange rate reflects the cumulative impact of changes to the: spot exchange rate, the net inflation rate in the base currency (ie, NZD), and the net inflation rate in the price currency (ie, SGD).

The more precise measure of changes in real exchange rates is calculated as 0.85% = 1%:
[(1 + %DeltaS(SGD/NZD)) x (1 + %DeltaP(NZD))/(1 + %DeltaP(SGD)) - 1] = [(1.06) x (0.98/1.03) - 1] = 0.0085 = 0.01

However, the change in the SGD/NZD real exchange rate change may also be estimated using a second formula. This formula estimates the net change in the real exchange rate as the expected change in the spot rate, adjusted for the difference between the expected change in the price currency's inflation and the expected change in the base currency's inflation; the three expected changes are expressed as percentage changes.
%DeltaR(SGD/NZD) = %DeltaS(SGD/NZD) + %DeltaP(NZD) - %DeltaP(SGD) = +6% + (-2%) - (+3%) = 1%

(Choice B) 5% results from incorrectly treating NZD deflation as reinforcing, not offsetting, the impact of the increase in the SGD/NZD spot exchange rate.
(Choice C) 11% results from incorrectly treating both NZD deflation and SGD inflation as factors that reinforce the impact of the increase in the SGD/NZD spot exchange rate.

explanation_en: Covenants are legally enforceable promises made by a bond issuer to its bondholders. These promises are set forth in the bond indenture, which is the legal contract that establishes all rights and obligations of the issuer and bondholders. There are two main types of covenants: affirmative covenants and negative covenants. Affirmative covenants are actions the issuer is required to perform; negative covenants address prohibited actions by the issuer. One type of affirmative covenant is the issuer's promise to pay interest and principal on the dates required by the bond. (Choice A) Collateral consists of assets that the issuer pledges as security for the bonds. Generally, the bond indenture gives the bondholders the right to sell the collateral to satisfy their claims under the bond if the issuer defaults. Collateral can consist of the asset purchased with the bond proceeds or other assets (including securities and other bonds). (Choice C) Credit enhancements consist of security in addition to any collateral backing the bond. They can be provided by the issuer (ie, internal enhancements) or other entities (ie, external enhancements). Examples include additional collateral and third-party guarantees.

explanation_en: Asset-backed securities are bonds created from securitizing cash-generating assets, such as residential mortgages or credit card receivables. As the schematic above shows, the assets are bundled and sold to a special purpose entity (SPE) that uses them as collateral for bonds.  The cash flows from the loans pay the bonds' interest and principal.  Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are a type of ABS. One type of risk that RMBS present to bondholders is default risk.  This refers to the possibility that borrowers of the loans serving as collateral default, either in full or in part.  Since the cash flows from the collateral are the primary source of payments for the bonds, defaults can significantly impact the bondholders' expected returns. Some securitization structures attempt to mitigate the risk of defaults through credit tranching.  Instead of issuing only one class of bonds from the securitization, a credit-tranched structure uses multiple classes.  Subordinate classes are the first to absorb losses caused by defaults in the collateral, which shields senior classes from some default risk. (Choices B and C)  Extension risk and contraction risk are two types of prepayment risks.  Securitizations may offer different classes of bonds that allow investors to determine how much prepayment risk they want to be exposed to; this is known as time tranching.
question_en: In securitizations that create residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS), credit tranching most likely refers to multiple classes of bonds that offer unequal:
option_c: contraction risk.

explanation_en: Arbitrage based on put-call parity ensures that puts and calls are fairly valued relative to each other.  The equivalent portfolios approach to put-call parity (above) illustrates the pricing relationship.  Both portfolios have the same value at expiration, so they must have the same value at any time prior to expiration. Synthetic positions are derived by isolating one position on one side of the equation.  The combination of positions is the synthetic equivalent of the isolated position. Plus and minus signs designate long (+) or short (−), so a long bond position is indicated by X / (1 + r) .  This is a zero-coupon, risk-free bond with a face amount equal to the strike price (X) and a price equal to the present value of X.  The long bond's synthetic equivalent is Long asset, S Short a call, −c Long a put, +p The long bond's value is its face amount (X).  The synthetic long bond position also has a value of X, regardless of the asset price (S ).  Either one of the options is in the money or both options are at the money.  If one option is in the money, the long asset is sold for the exercise price (X), and if both options are at the money (S  = X), the asset has a value equal to the maturing bond.

option_a: Long asset, short call, long put
option_b: Long asset, long call, short put
option_c: Short asset, long call, short put

explanation_en: Characteristics of preference shares (preferred stock) • Rank above common shares in respect to ◦Dividend payments ◦Asset distribution during liquidation • Do not generally offer voting rights • Can be callable, putable, or convertible • Dividends are ◦Not contractual obligations ◦Generally fixed at issuance Preference shares are a type of equity security that provides financing for the issuing company.  Preference shareholders receive a regular dividend payment from the company that is fixed at issuance.  Like dividends on common shares, preferred dividends are not contractual obligations, and missing payments will not send a company into default. Preference shares rank above common shares when dividends and claims on a company's net assets are paid during liquidation.  In that situation, preference shareholders must receive their dividends before common shareholders can receive theirs. This requirement is taken a step further in regard to cumulative preference shares: A company must pay any current and previously unpaid dividends to cumulative preference shareholders before common dividends can be paid. (Choice A)  Unlike common shares, preference shares usually do not provide voting rights to the shareholders.  When exceptions occur, preference shareholders are typically allowed to vote on only those matters relevant to their shares. (Choice B)  Dividends on preference shares are fixed and generally larger than those on common shares.  This helps to make preference shares more attractive to potential investors, despite lacking the upside potential of common shares.
question_en: Which of the following best describes a fundamental difference between preference shares and common shares?
option_a: Preference shares carry more voting rights than common shares.
option_b: Common shares typically have larger dividends than preference shares.
option_c: Preference shareholders receive dividends before common shareholders.

The required return on equity, k, must be greater than g. The constant growth DDM is unlikely to be appropriate for valuing growth companies. A multistage dividend discount model that accounts for a supernormal growth period is likely to be more appropriate.

explanation_en: Liabilities are debts that a company owes to others.  Noncurrent liabilities are debts due in more than 12 months.  If a debt is due to be paid in 12 months or less, it is classified as a current liability. Unearned revenue is a liability recorded when a company receives cash in advance of the delivery of goods or services; only when the company delivers the goods can it consider the revenue earned.  In this scenario, since the company received cash in 20X3 and will not deliver the goods until 20X5, the time elapsed between cash received and delivery is greater than 12 months. (Choice B)  The current portion of long-term debt represents the amount of repayment due (in less than 12 months) in the current period, so it is a current, not a noncurrent, liability. (Choice C)  If a company buys inventory in the second half of the year and repays it in the first half of the following year, the debt is considered current, not noncurrent, since it is paid within 12 months.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) addresses compensation arrangements from third parties that can challenge loyalty to an employer by competing with and/or creating a conflict with the employer's interests.  A Member or Candidate should receive written consent from all parties involved for any such compensation. In this scenario, Miah's investment advisory for friends and family can be reasonably seen as competing with Tenor's business, since Miah would be doing the same type of work that he currently does for Tenor.  Therefore, Miah needs to obtain written permission from Tenor and from his friends and family before he starts advising (Choice C).  The ridesharing role does not compete directly with Tenor's business, so Miah does not need to obtain written permission for this arrangement (Choice B). Standard IV(B) recommends that Members and Candidates make a written report to their employer detailing the compensation from any third- party sources before engaging in such activities.  However, obtaining written permission is only required before entering into arrangements that could be seen as competing or creating conflicts of interest.
