The returns on assets C and D are strongly correlated with a correlation coefficient of 0.80. The variance of returns on C is 0.0009, and the variance of returns on D is 0.0036. What is the covariance of returns on C and D?

explanation_en: The straight-line method will result in the least depreciation expense in the first year. This will allow the firm to report the highest net profit margin. In the early years of depreciating a fixed asset, straight-line depreciation will be lower than the double-declining balance method. Furthermore, the straight-line method has lower depreciation expense than the units-of-production method in this scenario because the machine will be producing an above-average number of units in its first year of service. This high production will result in higher depreciation expense under the units-of-production method.
question_en: A firm buys a new machine that has a 5-year life. This new machine will be used heavily in the first two years of its service, and then its output is expected to decline significantly each year thereafter. If management wants to maximize the firm's reported net profit margin for the first year of the machine's life, the depreciation method they are most likely to use is:
option_c: double-declining balance.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation focuses on knowingly misrepresenting or misusing information, and as a result, undermining investor trust in the integrity of the profession and financial markets.  The standard applies whether information is prepared for clients, colleagues, or the public —and whether it is a verbal or published statement. Misrepresentation can consist of omission: not presenting complete information or data in order to mislead plagiarism: quoting information without acknowledgement or citation exaggeration: inflating professional credentials or performance results In this scenario, Zheng violates the standard in two ways.  First, by not citing the source of the research and by reproducing it as though it were her own, she engages in plagiarism.  Although she does not know the author's full name, she should not mislead her readers as to the information's source.  Second, she exaggerates the validity of the research by stating that it is endorsed by an "expert" when she does not know that to be the case. (Choice B)  Using research available on social media is not a violation of the Standard; social media is a legitimate outlet for information.  As with all sources, material from social media should be properly cited. (Choice C)  Although Zheng does not know the real name of the source of the research since the author chose not to share it, she should not reproduce the research without attribution.  Since she omits any citation, it is plagiarism.
question_en: Bo Shun Zheng, CFA, is a journalist who writes articles on market sentiment for a major news organization.  She uses various sources, including social media, analyst interviews, and more conventionally published research.  In one article, she reproduces research published on social media by an analyst known only as "Big Alpha."  Since she does not know Big Alpha's real name, she includes the research without citation, noting only that it has been endorsed by "a leading investment expert."  Regarding Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, does Zheng most likely violate the Standard?
option_a: Yes, by not citing the source of the research.
option_b: Yes, by using research available only on social media.
option_c: No, because she protects Big Alpha's choice to hide his true identity.

explanation_en: While all three questions are legitimate questions, for understanding a company's business model for the first time, asking about the products and services the company offers is an appropriate first (or early) question to ask. How the company obtains customers is important as well, although the retention ratio is very specific. Debt covenants associated with bond issuances must be met, but that is not one of the first questions to ask in understanding a company's business model.
question_en: Laurie Palmer, CFA, is analyzing the business model for ABC Corp. Given that this is a new company for Palmer, what is one of the first questions she will need to answer?
option_a: “What is the company’s customer retention ratio?”
option_b: “Has the company been able to meet its debt covenants related to its outstanding bond issuances?”
option_c: “What products and services does the company offer?”

explanation_en: Correct because investors compare these scenarios with other analysts' forecasts for a company, as well as forecasts implied by current valuations, to make investment decisions.
question_en: Which of the following statements about scenario analysis is most accurate?
option_a: Scenario analysis provides a point estimate forecast
option_b: Forecast scenarios can be compared to forecasts implied by current valuations
option_c: Generic risk factors in scenario analysis are assumed to affect all companies in the same way

explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Expansionary monetary policies are used to increase economic growth during periods of decline (eg, when output is below potential GDP).  For example, a central bank can implement an expansionary policy of increasing excess reserves in the commercial banking system by: making open market purchases, reducing reserve requirements, which turns some required reserves into excess reserves, or reducing the policy interest rate, which reduces the costs banks incur when borrowing reserves. Excess reserves encourage increased lending since banks can earn higher returns by making loans than by holding reserves.  This expands the money supply and lowers interest rates, leading to growth in borrowing, investment, and consumption, and thus an expanded GDP. (Choice B)  A central bank conducts open market sales to reduce its holdings of government bonds when implementing a contractionary monetary policy.  Commercial banks use reserves to purchase the bonds, which contracts the money supply. (Choice C)  A central bank holds its policy interest rate constant as the neutral rate of interest falls below the policy rate in order to tighten credit conditions.  This inaction by a central bank is contractionary, not expansionary.
question_en: Which of the following central bank actions is most likely considered expansionary monetary policy?
option_b: Selling government bonds through open market operations
option_c: Holding the policy rate constant as the neutral rate falls below it

explanation_en: Expensing or capitalizing an asset purchase impacts the company's financial results differently each year, but the cumulative impact to net income and total cash flow under both methods is the same over time.  In this scenario, when the company expenses the asset, the full cost of €120,000 is reported on the income statement this year.  Subtracting €120,000 from revenue of €300,000 results in pretax income of €180,000, which yields €135,000 of net income after deducting €45,000 of taxes. Had the company capitalized the asset, at initial recognition €120,000 would be reported on the balance sheet as a long-term asset.  At year-end, €40,000 of depreciation (ie, €120,000 purchase price less 0 salvage value over 3 years) is reported as depreciation expense on the income statement and reduces pretax income to €260,000, which yields €195,000 in net income after subtracting €65,000 in taxes.  Therefore, expensing the asset would result in net income that is 135,000 − 195,000 = €60,000 lower in the first year. (Choice A)  €120,000 lower net PPE results from not subtracting depreciation of €40,000.  Net PPE at year-end is €80,000. (Choice C)  Cash from operations (CFO) is actually €100,000 lower when the asset is expensed.  This is because expensing the entire purchase cost reduces net income in the first year, which also reduces CFO.
question_en: At the beginning of this year, a company purchased electronic goods that cost €120,000 and chose to expense the purchase instead of capitalizing it.  The electronics have a useful life of 3 years with zero salvage value, and the company uses straight-line depreciation.  The company reports €300,000 in revenue each year and is taxed at 25%.  There are no other expenses aside from the purchase cost and corporate tax.  Based only on this information and compared to capitalizing the asset, expensing the asset most likely results in:
option_a: net PPE that is €120,000 lower in the current year.
option_b: net income that is €60,000 lower in the current year.
option_c: cash from operations that is €100,000 higher in the current year.

explanation_en: Both the debt to capital ratio decreased from 12.7% to 11.9% and the interest coverage ratio increased from 2.9 to 3.5, both indicating improved solvency in Year 2.
question_en: The best conclusion the analyst can make about Year 2 is that compared with Year 1, the company's solvency has:
option_a: deteriorated because both ratios have weakened.
option_c: improved because both ratios have strengthened.

explanation_en:
The quoted market price, or the flat price (ie, clean price) of a bond, does not include accrued interest. Therefore, all else being equal, on the
coupon payment date the quoted price of a bond remains the same. Quoting only the flat price separates the accrued interest component,
which always increases the price, from other factors (eg, changes in interest rates or credit quality) that are more relevant to investors.
The bond's full price (ie, dirty price), or the total amount an investor pays for a bond, is equal to the flat price plus the accrued interest. Interest
accrues each day; therefore, the full price increases each day until the coupon payment is made, at which point accrued interest falls to zero (as
shown in the image above). On the coupon payment date, the flat price and the full price are the same.
(Choices A and C) The standard market quoting convention is to quote the flat price, which does not include accrued interest. Therefore, a
coupon payment does not affect the bond's quoted price.
question_en: All else being equal, as soon as the coupon on a bond is paid, the quoted price of that bond from a bond dealer will most likely:
option_c: increase.

explanation_en: Portfolio 1 does not lie on the efficient frontier because it has a lower return than Portfolio 2 but has equal risk. Portfolio 4 does not lie on the efficient frontier because it has higher risk than Portfolio 3 but has the same return.
question_en:
Which of the following possible portfolios cannot lie on the efficient frontier?

| Portfolio | Expected Return | Standard Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8% | 6% |
| 2 | 10% | 6% |
| 3 | 14% | 12% |
| 4 | 14% | 16% |
option_c: Portfolios 2 and 3.

explanation_en: Issuing additional equity will increase the number of common shares outstanding, which will decrease earnings per share. A company does not have to retire debt to fund an equity issuance. The cost of capital for equity is higher than the cost of capital for debt because debt is less risky and because interest payments are tax deductible.
question_en: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the impact on a public company and its stakeholders from issuing additional equity rather than debt?
option_a: The company must retire debt to fund the equity issuance.
option_b: The additional shares will have an initial negative impact on earnings per share.
option_c: The cost of capital for the new equity issuance will be lower than the cost of capital for debt.

explanation_en: Spot interest rates can be used to price coupon bonds by taking each individual cash flow and discounting it at the appropriate spot rate for that year's payment. Note that the yield to maturity is the bond's internal rate of return that equates all cash flows to the bond's price. Current spot rates have nothing to do with the bond's yield to maturity.
question_en: Current spot rates are as follows: 1-Year: 6.5% 2-Year: 7.0% 3-Year: 9.2% Which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: For a 3-year annual pay coupon bond, all cash flows can be discounted at 9.2% to find the bond's arbitrage-free value.
option_b: The yield to maturity for 3-year annual pay coupon bond can be found by taking the geometric average of the 3 spot rates.
option_c: For a 3-year annual pay coupon bond, the first coupon can be discounted at 6.5%, the second coupon can be discounted at 7.0%, and the third coupon plus maturity value can be discounted at 9.2% to find the bond's arbitrage-free value.

explanation_en: Production-flexibility options offer operational flexibility to alter production when demand varies from forecast, allowing companies to reduce supply on lower demand.
question_en: In capital investing, a production-flexibility option allows a company to:
option_c: increase prices on excess demand.

explanation_en: Overview of Big Data Traditional: includes financial reports, census reports Data sources Alternative: includes social media, sensor networks Volume: large number of data points Data set characteristics Velocity: high speed of data collection Variety: many different formats and sources Structured: tabular data with distinct fields (eg, address database) Data structure Unstructured: unorganized data not in tabular format (eg, audios) Semistructured: mixture of structured and unstructured formats Big Data is a term referring to enormous amounts of data generated by businesses, governments, and individuals that can be captured through sources that are either traditional (eg, census reports) or alternative (eg, social media posts) (Choice A). These data sets are typically characterized by high volume (data points), velocity (speed), and variety (formats). The data can be structured, unstructured, or semistructured (Choice B). Structured data is stored in a tabular format where a unique record is stored in each row and various fields are stored in each column. Unstructured data such as data from an audio file is not stored in a tabular form. Semistructured data is a combination of the two.
question_en: Big Data most likely:
option_a: excludes data generated from traditional sources.
option_b: excludes unstructured data and includes only structured data.
option_c: is typically composed of data sets generated at high velocities.

Diluted EPS = 200,000 / (50,000 + 20,000) = $2.86 per share. The warrants are out of the money at a stock price of $20.
question_en: An analyst has gathered the following information about Zany Corp. Net income of $200,000 for the year ended December 31, 2004. During 2004, 50,000 common shares were outstanding. Zany has 10,000 shares of 7%, $50 par convertible preferred stock outstanding, each convertible into two shares of common. 5,000 warrants are outstanding with an exercise price of $24. Each warrant is convertible into one common share. The average market price per common share during 2004 was $20. Calculate Zany's basic and diluted earnings per share (EPS) for 2004. Basic EPS Diluted EPS

explanation_en: Internal rates of return are appropriate for measuring returns of investments that are characterized by cash inflows and outflows that may vary in their timing and magnitude, such as real estate and private capital investments. Neither multiple of invested capital nor time-weighted rate of return account for the timing of cash flows.
question_en: Which measure of return is most appropriate for investments with cash flows that may vary in their timing and amounts?
option_c: Internal rate of return over the investment’s life.

explanation_en:
The time-weighted rate of return (TWR) and the money-weighted rate of return (MWR) are both portfolio return measures. The TWR measures
the compound growth rate of a portfolio and excludes impact from contributions and withdrawals. The MWR is the internal rate of return on a
portfolio and accounts for the impact of contributions and withdrawals.
The MWR equates the present value of the cash outflows to the present value of the investor's cash inflows. The outflows (contributions) are

explanation_en: Farmland and timberland investments Farmland Timberland Common to both Harvest quantities Sources of returns Commodity prices Lumber prices Land price changes Possibly ESG Inflation hedge ESG-friendly Investment Regular income Low correlation with traditional Long new growth cycle attributes Harvest inflexibility; at least annual assets Harvest flexibility harvest cycle Can hedge with futures Direct purchase, but for largest Investment vehicles Publicly traded REITs investors only Private investment funds ESG = environmental, social, and governance REIT = Real estate investment trust Farmland and timberland have three principal components of return: harvest quantities, changes in commodity prices, and changes in land prices. Both types of land are desirable investments due to: a low occurrence of negative historical annual returns; income streams derived from the sale of crops or timber; low correlations with other financial assets; and providing an inflation hedge due to exposure to commodity and land prices. The most significant difference between farmland and timberland is the harvest cycle. Farm crops, whether row crops (eg, corn, wheat) or permanent crops (eg, almonds, grapes) must be harvested when ripe, with little flexibility in production. By contrast, timber does not have to be harvested regularly, so if market conditions are unfavorable, the harvest can be delayed indefinitely. Timberland can serve simultaneously as a production facility (when timber is harvested) as well as a source of raw material (ie, uncut trees). (Choice A) Both timberland (ie, lumber) and many farmland crops (eg, corn, wheat) can be hedged through futures on the commodities produced. (Choice B) Both farmland and timberland are viewed as inflation hedges.

When using a cash flow statement prepared under US GAAP, the interest coverage ratio is CFO plus back interest and taxes paid (similar to EBIT)
divided by interest paid. Adding back interest and taxes paid is necessary since net income (ie, net of interest and tax expense) is the starting
point for operating cash flow.
Under IFRS, if interest paid is classified as a financing activity, that portion of interest paid should not be added back to the numerator to determine
interest coverage.

(Choice C) 5.9 times coverage is the result if all cash flow metrics (ie, CFO, cash flow from investing [CFI], cash flow from financing [CFF]) are

The value of a price-weighted index is the sum of the market prices of the constituent stocks divided by the index divisor. The initial divisor is
usually either the number of stocks in the index or a divisor that results in a round number (eg, 1,000) as the initial index value. Use of a round
number makes the index return since inception easier to quantify. In the example above, an initial divisor of 0.87 would cause the three-stock
sample index to have an initial value of 100.
Price-weighted index divisors are adjusted to prevent the index value from being impacted by stock price changes that do not reflect changes
in the fundamental values of the component companies. This makes an index's value over time more easily comparable. Divisors are adjusted
for:
Stock splits
Stock dividends
Index reconstitutions (ie, changes to constituent stocks).
The divisor adjustment for stock splits is illustrated above. A similar process is followed when adjusting for stock dividends and index
reconstitutions.
(Choice B) Price appreciation of a constituent stock increases the value of a price-weighted stock index but does not impact the index divisor.
(Choice C) All else equal, stock prices fall by the amount of cash dividends paid; therefore, cash dividends impact the value of a price-weighted
index but do not affect the divisor.
question_en: The divisor used to calculate the value of a price-weighted stock index is most appropriately adjusted if a constituent company's stock:

explanation_en: The distinction between effective convexity and approximate convexity is that effective convexity accounts for the effects of embedded options on the bond's cash flows at different yields. For bonds that do not have embedded options, there is no difference between effective convexity and approximate convexity. Both measures are used to improve the estimate of the change in a bond's price for a given change in yield.
question_en: In what way is approximate convexity different from effective convexity?
option_a: Effective convexity takes embedded options into account, while approximate convexity does not.
option_b: Effective convexity results in a more accurate estimate of an option-free bond’s change in price than approximate convexity.
option_c: Approximate convexity can be used with an unequal increase and decrease in yield, while effective convexity can only be used with an equal increase or decrease in yield.

explanation_en: Bonds with contingency provisions combine the cash flows of a debt contract with an option referred to as an embedded option.  Three common examples are: callable bonds, which issuers can retire prior to maturity, putable bonds, which holders can force issuers to repurchase prior to maturity, and convertible bonds, which holders can exchange for issuers' common stock. Owning an option provides an advantage, so the effective price of such bonds reflects whichever counterparty is implicitly "paying" for the embedded option.  Since issuers must pay for the right to retire bonds early, the issuer compensates investors by selling the bonds at a lower effective price and at a higher yield than equivalent noncallable (eg, putable, convertible) bonds. (Choices A and C)  In putable and convertible bonds, investors own the option.  Investors must pay the issuer a higher effective price for those rights, which is reflected in a lower yield compared with bonds not containing such options.
question_en: All else being equal, for an issuer selling 10-year bonds, which of the following most likely requires the highest yield at issuance?  A bond that is:
option_c: convertible.

explanation_en: Forwards and futures are similar in that both are firm commitments: One party agrees to deliver (ie, sell) to another party (ie, the buyer) a specific quantity of an underlying asset or commodity, at a predetermined price and within a specified time frame. A forward contract is a negotiated (ie, non-standardized) over-the-counter derivative with settlement (ie, exchange of cash and assets upon delivery) at contract expiration.  Forwards carry significant counterparty risk as they are private agreements between two parties (ie, bilateral) and as such are illiquid, making it difficult for one of the parties to exit the agreement prior to expiration. Futures trade on an exchange with standardized contracts (eg, price, delivery dates/locations) brokered by a clearinghouse that guarantees both parties' performance with daily mark-to-market and settlement.  Exchange-traded options are also standardized contracts that give owners the right but not the obligation to buy (call) or sell (put). In this instance, a forward contract is most appropriate as the contract is bilateral and it is negotiated, which means the terms (eg, delivery location) are nonstandard.  The miner does bear counterparty risk, and although the standardized features and clearinghouse oversight of futures and options could mitigate that risk, the quantity, price, or delivery location may not be optimal (Choices A and B).
question_en: A silver producer negotiates an agreement to deliver a specific amount of silver ore to a local ore processor for a specified price in six months. This arrangement is most appropriately done with which type of contract?
option_c: Forward

option_b: the average time until the receipt of the bond’s cash ows.

A yield spread is the difference between a bond's YTM and a benchmark yield. The bond's yield can be expressed as the sum of
the benchmark rate, which represents factors that affect all bonds, and
the spread, which represents factors that are more specific to a bond or issuer.
Different yield spreads result from the use of different benchmarks. Bond yields are often used as a benchmark, but benchmarks can also be
derived from an interest rate swap curve. The I-spread is defined as the spread that a bond earns versus a swap rate of the same tenor.
(Choice B) The spot curve is used to derive the Z-spread, which is a spread applied across the benchmark curve that allows the bond's
discounted cash flows to equal the bond's price.
(Choice C) The excess yield a bond earns over a government bond is the G-spread.
question_en: The I-spread is most appropriately defined as the difference between a bond's yield and:
option_c: a government bond's yield.

In this scenario, the analyst is using the EV to estimate an appropriate value per share of the company's preferred stock.  Using the components of EV listed above, solve for the market value (£ thousands) of preferred equity as follows: Since there are 1,160,000 preference shares outstanding, the appropriate market value per share is: 30,920,000 / 1,160,000 ≈ £26.66 (Choice A)  £16.79 results from incorrectly subtracting cash equivalents and short-term investments, along with market capitalization and the market value of debt, from EV to arrive at the market value of preferred stock.  Cash equivalents and short-term investments are added to EV to arrive at the market value of preferred stock since those items are subtracted when calculating EV. (Choice C)  £29.58 results from adding accounts receivable, along with other items, to arrive at the market value of preferred stock.  This is incorrect since accounts receivable is not part of the calculation of EV.

explanation_en: Performance measures comparison Performance measure Diversification Description Risk measure Risk Sharpe ratio No Excess return per unit of total risk Standard deviation Total M-squared No Excess market-risk- adjusted return Standard deviation Total Treynor ratio Yes Return per unit of systematic risk Beta Systematic Jensen's alpha Yes Excess of actual vs. expected return Beta Systematic In theory, fully diversified portfolios have no nonsystematic (company-specific) risk.  For those portfolios, an appropriate performance measure is one that uses beta to measure market risk.  Portfolios that are not fully diversified contain both nonsystematic (company-specific) and systematic (market) risk.  For these portfolios, a suitable performance measure is one that uses total risk (standard deviation). Here, the portfolio is fully diversified, so an appropriate performance measure should be based on beta, not standard deviation (Choices A and B).  Using the Treynor ratio or Jensen's alpha is appropriate.  The Treynor ratio is a performance measure that determines a portfolio's excess return per unit of systematic risk.  For example, if the return of a portfolio is 20%, the risk-free rate is 5%, and its beta 1.2, then the portfolio's Treynor ratio is 0.125, or (0.20 − 0.05)/1.2.  This means that the portfolio earned 0.125 units of excess return per unit of systematic risk.
question_en: Which of the following performance measures is most appropriate for evaluating the risk-adjusted returns of a fully diversified portfolio?
option_c: Treynor ratio

explanation_en:
Types of call provisions
American style Continuously callable: the issuer has the right to call at any time beginning on the call date until maturity
European style Only one call date, and the issuer can call bonds only on that date
Bermuda style Can be called on one of multiple call dates, but only on those dates
A call provision allows the bond issuer to redeem a bond prior to its final maturity. This allowance exposes bondholders to reinvestment risk, as
the call provision is unlikely to be exercised unless yields are lower than when the bond was issued. To compensate for the call risk, investors
require higher yields for callable bonds than for noncallable bonds.
Most callable bonds have an initial call protection period during which the bonds cannot be called. Once the call protection period has passed, the
bond is callable within the constraints of the embedded call provision. Specific call dates usually coincide with coupon payment dates.
In this scenario, the bond is callable on multiple specific dates and is, therefore, a Bermuda-style call rather than an American- or European-
style call (Choices B and C). Bermuda-style calls often require a premium to par on the earliest call dates, which serves as a "sweetener" for the
bondholder since it discourages the issuer from exercising the call provision early in the life of the bond.

explanation_en: Falling interest rates will decrease the value of a call option. Decreasing the risk-free rate will increase the risk neutral probability (π) of a price decrease and decrease the present value of the expected option payoff. Since the value of a call option is positively related to the price of the underlying asset, an increased probability of a downward price move will reduce the expected payoff from the call. As a result, both of those effects will reduce the call option value as the return on risk-free investments decreases.

Probability estimates are often revised based on new information. In this scenario, the conditional probability that the CEO is not fired depends on
whether the company's earnings per share (EPS) have decreased. Two relevant conditional probabilities are as follows:
The CEO is not fired given that EPS did not decrease [P(CEO not fired | no EPS decrease)]
The CEO is not fired given that EPS decreased [P(CEO not fired | EPS decrease)]
The diagram above shows that the probabilities that the CEO is not fired are:
0.0525 if EPS decreased and
0.4875 if EPS did not decrease.
The total probability that the CEO is not fired, regardless of what happens to EPS, is 0.0525 + 0.4875 = 0.54. Bayes' formula can be used to
reverse the conditional probability and answer the question, "What is the probability that EPS decreased given that the CEO was not fired"? However, it is often easier to invert the tree diagram using previously calculated probabilities than to memorize and apply Bayes' formula:
Before the analyst learned the outcome for the CEO, the estimated probability of an EPS decrease was 0.35. Given the updated information (ie,
CEO was not fired) and using Bayes' formula, the revised probability that EPS decreased is reduced to approximately 0.10 (ie, 0.0972).
(Choice A) 0.05 (ie, 0.0525) represents the joint probability that the CEO is not fired and that there is a decrease in EPS.
(Choice C) 0.15 is the conditional probability that the CEO is not fired given that EPS decreased.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts aims to protect employers and clients by promoting transparency, allowing them to evaluate whether a Member or Candidate is acting independently and objectively when offering investment advice or recommendations.  When a conflict can be reasonably viewed as interfering with a Member's or Candidate's ability to conduct unbiased investment evaluations, the employer and clients must be informed on all pertinent details of the conflict. Garcia does not have a disclosable relationship with the company currently. explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities. Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires Members and Candidates to refuse any compensation that could reasonably be expected to compromise their independence and objectivity. Sell-side analysts can be compensated by companies for writing research reports about the company. However, analysts must be careful not let the compensation affect their judgement. The report must reflect an independent opinion following diligent and thorough research. Compensation from the company should not be linked to the conclusion of the report. Forms of compensation that violate that Standard are those that can reasonably be expected to bias the analyst's opinion directly (eg, payments based on the rating) or indirectly (eg, stock options, warrants). Best practice calls for a flat fee paid by the company. Analysts are required to disclose the compensation in their report, including the nature of the compensation, but disclosure does not offset a violation of accepting influential compensation (Choice C). (Choice B) Although the report reflected Huang's independent opinion, this opinion can be reasonably viewed as biased by clients due to the nature of the compensation (ie, stock options) for writing the report, thus violating he Standard.

The absorption approach to analyzing the balance of trade implies that national saving must increase relative to domestic investment for a currency devaluation to narrow a trade deficit, which in turn depends on whether the economy is producing at maximum capacity (full employment or potential GDP) when the devaluation occurs.

explanation_en: American depository receipt (ADR) overview Rule 144A Level I Level II Level III Yes, but only QIB private Raise new US capital No No Yes, public offering placement Yes, more robust filing SEC registration None Yes, basic Yes, basic required Over-the- NYSE, NASDAQ, Trading venues Unlisted NYSE, NASDAQ, AMEX counter AMEX Listing fees Low Low High High Size/earnings None None Yes Yes requirements QIB = Qualified institutional buyers Foreign companies can access US investors and broaden their equity investor base by creating American depository receipts (ADR). In a sponsored ADR, a foreign company deposits shares of its stock with certain banks that create dollar-denominated certificates (ie, ADRs), which will usually be listed on an exchange. An ADR trades just like a stock and generally tracks the underlying value of the company's shares that trade on a foreign exchange. There are four primary types of ADR listings, each with progressively more stringent listing and corporate governance requirements: Rule 144A ADR: unregistered and privately sold only to qualified investors, with resale restrictions Level I: SEC-registered and trades over-the-counter (OTC) with basic access to US investors Level II: SEC-registered and exchange-traded with better investor access but higher cost and more requirements Level III: most stringent SEC registration requirements; can be used by foreign-listed firms to raise new equity capital and for acquisitions (Choices B and C) Level I ADRs give foreign-listed firms the most basic access to US markets and investors. SEC filing requirements are less stringent, and these ADRs may not be sold to raise new equity capital in the US.

explanation_en: A key component of a comprehensive industry analysis, the experience curve displays the direct cost per unit of a good produced or service delivered relative to the quantity produced. The curve declines with an increase in asset utilization as fixed overhead costs are spread over an increasing number of units produced. The cost of production can also decline due to efficiency gains in labor, production, or design. The experience curve is a particularly important concept for industries with high fixed costs or industries that can take advantage of economies of scale. Examples include heavy machinery, auto, and aircraft manufacturing and could also include consumer electronics manufacturers. (Choice A) Service industries tend to be asset-light businesses that do not have high fixed overhead infrastructure costs to overcome; therefore, the cost of production does not change much with each unit or service produced. (Choice C) The experience curve is unlikely to be useful for an embryonic-stage (ie, early life cycle) industry that is just beginning to develop. Many companies in the industry are likely to be start-ups, which have significant investment needs and high failure rates.
question_en: When preparing a thorough industry life cycle stage analysis, the experience curve is most appropriate for which type of industries?
option_c: Embryonic-stage industries.

explanation_en: Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps are over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives in which counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. At each swap payment date: the floating payer owes cash to the fixed payer if the reference interest rate is greater than the swap's fixed rate, or the fixed payer owes cash to the floating payer if the reference interest rate is less than the swap's fixed rate. Swap cash flows are similar to forward rate agreements' (FRAs') cash flows (at expiration) since: the FRA seller (ie, short) pays the buyer (ie, long) if the reference interest rate is greater than the agreed rate, and the FRA buyer (ie, long) pays the seller (ie, short) if the reference rate is less than the agreed rate. Given this similarity, the swap's cash flows can be replicated by a portfolio of FRAs with expirations matching each swap payment date, all having agreed interest rates equal to the swap's fixed rate. (Choice A) Unlike FRAs, futures are exchange-traded derivatives that generate daily cash flows since they are marked to market every trading session. Although a portfolio of interest rate futures could create similar market exposure to that of an interest rate swap, a portfolio of futures could not replicate a swap's cash flows. (Choice B) Holders of interest rate calls never incur negative cash flows at expiration. Holders receive either the in-the-money call value in cash or nothing. In contrast, swaps may have positive or negative cash flows on the payment dates.
question_en: Which of the following best replicates the cash flows of an interest rate swap? A series of:
option_c: forward rate agreements.

explanation_en:
The price impact of a change in a bond's yield-to-maturity can be estimated using duration and convexity. Estimates based on duration
capture most of the price change but fail to reflect the change in price sensitivity as yield changes. Adjusting for a bond's convexity greatly
improves the accuracy of price change estimates.
The impact of convexity is always positive for noncallable bonds. As yields fall, prices become more sensitive to yield changes (ie, bonds
appreciate more rapidly). As yields rise, prices become less sensitive to yield changes (ie, prices decline more slowly). The convexity impact is
added to duration-based estimates of price change when prices are rising. When prices are falling, the decline is reduced by the convexity impact.
(Choice A) 3.51% results from subtracting the convexity impact from the percentage price increase based on duration.
(Choice C) 3.76% results from failing to square the yield change and then mistakenly adjusting the decimal point two columns to the right in the
calculation of the convexity impact.

Tax laws allow companies to report balance sheet and income statement items differently for tax and financial reporting purposes. These
differences cause pretax income and taxable income to diverge. The differences are classified as either temporary or permanent.
Deferred taxes arise only from temporary differences in pretax income and taxable income. For example, a company may choose to
depreciate assets more rapidly for tax purposes than for financial reporting. When this happens, compared to the financial reports, in tax
reporting:
depreciation is higher,
taxable income is lower,
tax obligation is lower, and
taxes payable is lower.
The difference is temporary since an asset will be depreciated by the same amount over its useful life, regardless of the depreciation methods.
When the discrepancy is permanent (ie, never to be reversed), no deferred tax item is created (Choices B and C). For example, companies
include interest on municipal (state and local) bonds as revenue for financial reporting, but municipal bond interest is never taxable to the
recipient. Similarly, fines imposed by a government agency are deducted as an operating expense for financial reporting, but fines cannot be
deducted when calculating taxable income.
question_en: Deferred taxes most likely result from:
option_c: both temporary and permanent tax differences.

explanation_en: For a firm with fixed costs to be profitable, its contribution margin (= P − VC) must remain positive and greater than its fixed costs, so that operating profit (= Q(P − VC) − FC) is positive: If FC > 0, then P − VC > 0 and P − VC > FC, and as a result, Q(P − VC) − FC > 0. P = Price per unit VC = Variable cost per unit FC = Fixed cost Q = Quantity sold Operating leverage refers to the proportion of fixed costs in a company's cost structure. Holding other factors constant, a company that increases fixed costs as a percentage of total costs will increase the rate at which operating profit changes. When the proportion of fixed costs increases and: contribution margin is positive, operating income will increase (decrease) faster as quantity increases (decreases). contribution margin is negative, operating income will decrease (increase) faster as quantity increases (decreases). The degree of operating leverage (DOL) measures the rate that operating profit increases (decreases) relative to increases (decreases) in sales. Since a greater proportion of fixed costs will increase the rate that operating profit changes for a given change in quantity, it will also increase the DOL, all else equal. Therefore, a firm that reduces a variable cost such as temporary labor while increasing a fixed cost such as equipment, all else equal, will report an increase to its DOL (Choices A and B).
question_en: A company purchases a piece of equipment that reduces its need for temporary labor, thus increasing its fixed costs as a percentage of total costs. All else equal, the company's degree of operating leverage will most likely:
option_c: increase.

explanation_en:
Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) represents the remaining cash available to shareholders after making investments in working capital, fixed capital (ie, property plant and equipment), and servicing debt. Companies may use FCFE to pay dividends to shareholders or buy back shares.

In this scenario, take the following steps:

- Begin with net income (600 million), an accrued figure that includes noncash components
- Add back depreciation (90 million) since it is a noncash expense
- Subtract the investments in net working capital (20 million) (eg, accounts receivable, accounts payable, inventory) and fixed capital (300 million) that are required to sustain operations
- Add the change in net debt (an increase of 30 million) to reflect additional cash from net borrowing

FCFE = NI + NCC − ΔWC − ΔFC + ΔDebt
= 600 + 90 − (220 − 200) − 300 + (780 − 750)
= 400

This results in FCFE of MXN 400 million, which may be used to pay dividends to shareholders or to buy back shares.

(Choice A) MXN 370 million results from failing to include changes to debt.

(Choice C) MXN 440 million is the free cash flow to the firm (FCFF). The calculation for FCFF involves adding back after-tax interest expense and excluding changes to debt.

Things to remember:
Free cash flow to equity is the cash flow available to equity providers (ie, shareholders) after accounting for investments in fixed capital, working capital, and changes in debt.

explanation_en:
Investors require higher returns for assuming more risk. The Sharpe ratio is one metric that evaluates returns on a risk-adjusted basis, measuring excess return per unit of total risk. Excess return is the difference between the portfolio's return and the return of a risk-free asset (eg, US Treasury bill, or T-bill). Total risk is measured by the standard deviation of returns and captures both systematic (market) risk and nonsystematic (nonmarket) risk. The Sharpe ratios for the three portfolios are calculated below:

| | Portfolio 1 | Portfolio 2 | Portfolio 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sharpe ratio | (10% − 3%) / 18% = 0.39 | (9% − 3%) / 12% = 0.50 | (11% − 3%) / 22% = 0.36 |

Portfolio 2 has the highest Sharpe ratio, and therefore has the greatest excess return per unit of total risk compared to its peers.

Things to remember:
The Sharpe ratio measures excess return per unit of total risk. Standard deviation, not beta, is used to calculate the Sharpe ratio. The portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio produces the best risk-adjusted result.

explanation_en: Categories of capital projects Rationale Decision considerations Replacement Worn, broken, or inefficient assets Most accurate cash flow projections, greatest certainty of decisions Expansion Add capacity for existing products Greater uncertainties over cost and revenues compared with replacement projects New products and services Research and development, and investment in products not yet offered by the company Greater uncertainties than expansion projects, most complex investment decisions Regulatory, safety, and environmental Driven by external party (eg, government, insurance company) Necessary to stay in business, not directly profit- driven like other categories Pet projects or high-risk investments Capital allocation error Overly optimistic projections, or failure to apply proper project analyses Profit-motivated capital budgeting decisions are classified as replacement projects, expansion projects, or introduction of new products and services.  Since replacement projects are projects that replace assets already in use, net cash flows can be estimated much more accurately compared to other capital budgeting decisions: Acquisition and operating costs:  Such assets have been purchased or constructed previously, and there is an operating history on which to base cost estimates. Revenues:  Previous period revenues and familiarity with the product market's competitive environment allow for better revenue estimates. More accurate cash flow estimates allow managers a higher degree of confidence regarding decisions on replacement projects compared to decisions on other types of projects. (Choice A)  Although expansion projects also imply an extension of previous investments, they entail more uncertainties than replacement projects.  There may be advantages and disadvantages related to the larger scale of operations and reactions of competitors that are difficult to quantify.  These factors cause expansion project decisions to be more complex. (Choice C)  Decisions to invest in new products or services are the most complex capital budgeting decisions since they have the greatest uncertainties regarding initial cost, operating expenses, and revenues.
question_en: When making capital budgeting decisions, which of the following types of investment projects most likely allow management to have the highest level of confidence?
option_c: New products and services

explanation_en:
A yield curve allows comparisons between yields of bonds over different maturities (ie, term structure of interest rates). Most yield curves are
based on government bonds, which have no risk of defaulting on principal or coupon payments. However, government bonds have different
coupon rates for different maturities, so each maturity reflects some degree of reinvestment risk. This risk can prevent accurate analysis of the
term structure.
The spot curve is the government bond yield curve constructed from a series of government zero-coupon bonds of different maturities. Zero-
coupon bonds do not pay periodic interest, so they have no reinvestment risk since there is nothing to reinvest until maturity. Although the spot
curve reflects the absence of both credit and reinvestment risks, it addresses neither liquidity risk nor inflation risk.
(Choice B) The demand for government bonds is not the same for all maturities. Bonds for which there is low demand can exhibit lack of liquidity,
posing liquidity risk. This would manifest as a higher spread between the bid and ask prices that dealers quote for the bonds.
(Choice C) Most government bonds do not adjust their coupon rates or principal to keep pace with inflation, so government bond yields do not
account for inflation risk.
question_en: The risk-free yields for a spot curve constructed from government debt instruments most likely refer to the absence of:
option_c: inflation risk.

explanation_en: An amortizing loan is characterized by a payment schedule that gradually increases principal repayments over time. In a traditional fixed-rate mortgage loan, the total payment is fixed, but over time the underlying principal component increases while the interest component decreases. Fully amortizing loans completely pay both principal and interest by the time the last scheduled payment is made. Thus, the mortgage loan has been fully satisfied, and the borrower is under no additional obligation. (Choice A) Interest-only loans do not include any principal payments. At the end of the mortgage period, the entire original principal balance is due as a balloon payment. (Choice C) Partially amortizing loans do not completely retire the principal, resulting in a balloon payment, which is the remaining principal needed to retire the loan. Balloon payments often require the borrower to refinance the remaining principal into a new mortgage loan.
question_en: Which of the following types of residential mortgage loan is least likely to result in a balloon payment at maturity?
option_c: Partially amortizing

explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must:… b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio.…" Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the adviser's responsibility to assess the suitability of investments for each client.  The adviser does this by researching a client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance, which together form the building blocks of the client's investment policy statement (IPS).  The IPS can be used to determine the suitability of proposed investments. Clients and advisors may disagree regarding investment suitability.  Best practices regarding unsolicited requests for unsuitable investments include: Refrain from making the trade until discussing it with the client. Educate the client regarding divergence from the IPS. Consider the trade's potential impact within the context of the client's entire portfolio. Be sure the client acknowledges being advised that the trade is unsuitable. Update the IPS if the trade is executed and its portfolio impact is material. In extreme cases, determine whether to continue the advisory relationship. In this scenario, Tim Green complies with the Standard since he: discusses the trade with the client, educates the client regarding the trade's conflict with the IPS, considers the trade's immaterial portfolio impact (Choice B), and has the client sign the unsolicited trade request form before the trade is executed. question_en: Tim Green, CFA, is an investment advisor for Steady Hand Advisors (SHA).  While attending a charity function, Green runs into one of his clients, Dr. Walter Kowalski.  Kowalski tells Green about a small-cap biotechnology company developing a new process that could be a medical breakthrough.  Green says he is familiar with the company but considers its stock to be very speculative since the company has never been profitable or even produced a viable product. Nevertheless, Kowalski instructs Green to buy 10,000 shares of the stock when the market opens the next day.  Green advises against the trade: although an investment of this size will have an immaterial impact on Kowalski's portfolio, it does not meet his investment objectives and violates the constraints of his investment policy statement (IPS).  Still, Kowalski insists that Green execute the trade. The next morning, Green documents his rationale for why the trade is unsuitable on SHA's unsolicited trade request form.  Green emails the form to Kowalski to sign and return so the trade can be executed at the market open.  Do Green's actions comply with Standard III(C) Suitability?
option_b: No, the investment is unsuitable regardless of portfolio impact.
option_c: No, since Green is required update the investment policy statement.

The Gordon growth model uses the difference between a company's required rate of return (r) and its long-term growth rate (g) as the
denominator of the equation. Since the denominator is the difference between rand g, an identical increase to both variables will result in no
change to the denominator.
The numerator in the calculation of justified forward P/E is next year's dividend divided by next year's earnings (D / E ). An increase to g will

explanation_en: Industries evolve over time and experience different levels of growth and profitability in each stage of their life cycle. Each stage exhibits different characteristics that affect the competitive dynamics of an industry, such as the level of product demand and intensity of competition. The growth phase, which is the second stage, is characterized by rapidly growing demand, rising profitability, and limited competition. During the growth stage, customers become familiar with an industry's product. As such, the industry attracts new customers, which drives higher product demand. The growing market draws many new entrants (companies) while the barriers to entry are still low. Despite the influx of entrants, competition among companies is low (or limited) since the vast market allows companies to grow without having to take market share from competitors. (Choices A and C) In the growth stage, companies within the industry achieve economies of scale and better distribution channels, which allow them to reduce prices to further increase product demand. The combination of increased sales volume and economies of scale results in higher industry profitability.
question_en: An industry experiencing the growth phase in the industry life cycle is most likely characterized by:
option_c: falling economics of scale.

Hypothesis tests are classified as either parametric or nonparametric. A parametric test focuses on the value of a population parameter (eg,
mean, variance) based on the value of a sample drawn from that population. A parametric test should be used only if certain assumptions can be
made concerning the population's distribution (eg, distribution is known, data use a ratio measurement scale).
By contrast, a nonparametric test is appropriate when:
It is difficult to make assumptions about the population's distribution;
Data are ranked using a weaker measurement scale such as interval or ordinal scaling; or
The test does not involve a parameter.
(Choices B and C) When the sample size is large (ie, ≥ 30), a z- or t-test can help to validate a hypothesis that a sample mean equals the
population mean. Both tests are parametric and can be used regardless of what is known about the population's distribution (normal vs. non-
normal) or variance.
question_en: When testing a hypothesis that concerns a sample mean, it is most appropriate to use a nonparametric (rather than parametric) test if the sample size is large and:

explanation_en:
The harmonic mean is a weighted average. It is a measure of central tendency typically used for averaging ratios (stated as "amount per unit")
where an observation's value is inversely proportional to its weight in the average. It can be used for cost averaging (ie, finding average price per
share) when fixed amounts are invested periodically.
In this instance, since the investor is investing annually the same total amount, €1,000,000, a lower stock price implies that a larger number of
shares can be purchased. Thus, the lower (higher) share prices should be assigned larger (smaller) weights in the average since a greater
(smaller) number of shares in the investment portfolio was purchased at that price. The harmonic mean assigns a larger weight to smaller
observations and therefore is appropriate.
(Choice B) The geometric mean is most appropriate for calculating the average growth rate over multiple consecutive return periods by taking
compounding into account. It is not a weighted average.
(Choice C) The arithmetic mean is a simple average of the purchase prices, assigning equal weight to all observations.

explanation_en: Geopolitical risks Type Description Known event date, unknown event outcome Event risk (eg, political election, new legislation) Unanticipated event (eg, sudden uprisings, impact Exogenous risk from natural disasters) Known risks that evolve over time (eg, displacement Thematic risk of fuel vehicles, rise of political factions) Geopolitical risks can have major impacts on investment returns globally and can be identified as different risk types: event risk, exogenous risk, and thematic risk. Analysts often model such risks as a part of their investment decision-making process. Thematic risks arise from events that evolve over a long period of time, such as climate change, rising political trends, and technological innovation. For example, the reduction in energy costs due to the displacement of gasoline cars is a thematic risk. This phenomenon may be driven by the gradual passage of climate-friendly regulations and may negatively affect major oil-producing economies. Event risk describes the uncertain outcome of an event that will occur on a known date. For example, the date of a US presidential election is known, but the winner is unknown until the event occurs (Choice A). Exogenous risk describes sudden or unanticipated geopolitical risk. One example is the aftermath of a sudden natural disaster, such as the Mount St. Helens eruption in 1980, which caused significant environmental harm in parts of the US and Canada (Choice C).
question_en: Reduction in energy costs due to displacement of gasoline cars is most likely a type of:
option_c: exogenous risk.

JPY appreciation against EUR means JPY 1 is worth a greater amount of EUR in Year 1 than it was in Year 0. Since the exchange rate quote is given as the number of JPY per EUR 1, the question requires the relationship between the currencies to be viewed from the opposite perspective, with EUR as the price currency and JPY as the base currency. Appreciation of JPY means the same thing as depreciation of EUR. The EUR depreciation means EUR 1 buys fewer JPY. Consequently, JPY/EUR will be quoted at a lower number since it will take a smaller amount of JPY to buy EUR 1.

Contractionary monetary policy should cause both securities prices and expectations for economic growth to decrease, each of which is likely to cause consumers to decrease spending.
question_en: Contractionary monetary policy is least likely to decrease consumption spending by decreasing:
option_c: the foreign exchange value of the currency.

explanation_en: The interbank funds market refers to short-term unsecured loans between banks. It does not refer to trading of negotiable certificates of deposit. Borrowing from the central bank is said to occur in the central bank funds market.
question_en: The interbank funds market is most accurately described as:
option_a: banks’ borrowing of reserves from the central bank.
option_b: trading of negotiable certicates of deposit.
option_c: unsecured short-term loans from one bank to another.

explanation_en:
Real estate return indexes are categorized as appraisal, repeat sales, or real estate investment trust (REIT) indexes. Repeat sales indexes are
constructed using the average price change of the same property as a result of a sale or refinancing. This transaction-based approach
provides a timely and accurate valuation for a broad range of properties (eg, residential single-family homes).
A repeat sales index does have limitations, including sample selection bias. The selection process is nonrandom since it uses properties with
prior sales. Thus, the index may have a bias toward properties that turn over at a higher rate but are not necessarily representative of the broader
geographic scope of the index. Selection bias could also occur if sales in a specific area are infrequent, making the results less reliable.
(Choice A) REIT indexes are based on the underlying prices of publicly traded REITs. Although useful for the valuation of the real estate asset
class, valuation of publicly traded REITs may not align with the specific circumstances (eg, geography, quality, property type) for valuing a
particular investment property.
(Choice B) Appraisal indexes rely on appraised property values, which are typically based on comparable properties or cash flow estimates.
Limitations of the appraisal index include the subjectivity of the appraisal process and the reliance on appraisals to calculate returns, all of which
may result in understated return volatility.
question_en: An analyst is using a real estate valuation index to estimate the value of an investment property and wishes to avoid sample selection bias. The analyst's least appropriate choice is to use a(n):
option_c: repeat sales index.

option_b: that a maximum level of professional responsibility and conduct dictates that members be aware of and comply with laws, rules, and regulations governing their conduct.

option_a: Firms were including only top performing funds to represent their performance history.

explanation_en: According to Standard V (A), Diligence and Reasonable Basis, a member or candidate may rely on others in their firm to determine whether secondary or third-party research is sound and use the information in good faith unless they have reason to question its validity or the processes and procedures used.
question_en: Emma Berkstein, CFA, uses third-party data to prepare a report on a company. Berkstein does not check the validity of this data herself, but instead relies on her senior colleagues to conduct due diligence. Another analyst at the same firm, Jimmy Brooks, CFA, prepares an industry report with a group of colleagues. After thorough research, the group agrees to issue a report with a positive outlook for the industry. Brooks disagrees with this conclusion, but leaves his name in the report. Has the Standard relating to diligence and reasonable basis most likely been violated?
option_c: Yes, by Brooks only

explanation_en: Passive investment strategies attempt to match the returns on a benchmark index by holding all index securities or using statistical techniques to replicate index returns. Active investment strategies attempt to outperform a benchmark index by overweighting and underweighting index securities or by holding securities that are not in the index. Active strategies typically create more fees and expenses for the investor than passive strategies. Security prices in semi-strong-form efficient markets reflect all publicly available information. When this information is accurate, on average, securities trade at prices that match or are close to their intrinsic value. Based on net returns, when securities trade at intrinsic value, active strategies should underperform the market due to their fees and expenses. Passive strategies outperform active strategies by avoiding those costs in semi-strong-form efficient markets (Choices B and C).
question_en: In security markets that are semi-strong-form efficient, passive investment strategies will most likely:
option_c: perform the same as active strategies.

explanation_en: Geographic classification of bonds Domestic bonds Foreign bonds Eurobonds Issuer Same as country Different from country of issuance domicile of issuance Currency Domestic (local) currency Foreign currency Jurisdiction Domestic legal, regulatory, and tax rules Numerous exemptions Foreign bonds are debt securities issued in the domestic market by foreign-domiciled issuers. Foreign issuers issue such securities to reduce currency risk for earnings of domestic subsidiaries and/or to gain access to capital at attractive interest rates. In this scenario, the debt of the Japanese corporation issued in France and denominated in EUR, which is the local currency where the bond is issued, is considered a foreign bond in the French bond market. (Choice C) Domestic bonds are debt securities issued within the country in which the issuer is domiciled and denominated in that country's currency. explanation_en: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) engages in the broadest range of activities compared to the other international organizations. The IMF's responsibilities fall into four main categories: addressing international monetary problems; facilitating growth of trade and poverty reduction; supporting exchange rate stability; and lending foreign exchange to address balance of payments problems. IMF loans are temporary and are not considered foreign aid or a source of long-term funding. Loans are made only with adequate safeguards (ie, senior creditor status) and only after countries have filed a plan with the IMF to resolve their difficulties. (Choice A) The World Bank Group (World Bank) is primarily involved (through affiliate organizations) in long-term lending to facilitate economic development in developing countries. The World Bank also provides advice and analysis to foster economic and social improvements. It does not directly assist in resolving problems due to trade imbalances. (Choice B) The World Trade Organization (WTO) fosters global trade through a variety of means. It administers bilateral and multilateral trade agreements as well as related dispute resolution. The WTO seeks to reduce tariffs and non-tariff barriers to trade. It does not help resolve problems involving trade imbalances.

option_c: International Monetary Fund (IMF).

explanation_en:
The price value of a basis point (PVBP), a measure of yield duration, is an estimate of how much a bond's price changes given a change of 1 basis point in its yield-to-maturity. A basis point is 1/100th of a percentage point, or 0.0001. The PVBP of a bond is also called the bond's PV01 or DV01, meaning "price value" or "dollar value" of a 1-basis-point change.
In this scenario, Bond Z's YTM (6.2%), annual coupon (5%), and time-to-maturity (11 years) are given. A 1-basis-point increase in Bond Z's YTM results in a new YTM of 6.21%, and a 1-basis-point decrease results in a new YTM of 6.19%. PV− and PV+ are calculated for Bond Z as follows:
PV− = 5/(1+0.0619)^1 + 5/(1+0.0619)^2 + ... + (5+100)/(1+0.0619)^11 = 90.7052
PV+ = 5/(1+0.0621)^1 + 5/(1+0.0621)^2 + ... + (5+100)/(1+0.0621)^11 = 90.5585
PVBP = (90.7052 − 90.5585)/2 = 0.0733
For Bond Y, PV− and PV+ are given. Substitute to calculate Bond Y's PVBP:
PVBP = (87.25 − 87.15)/2 = $0.05

| | Bond X | Bond Y | Bond Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| PVBP (USD) | 0.04 | 0.05 | 0.07 |

Therefore, Bond Z has the greatest yield duration based on its price value of a basis point compared to Bond X and Bond Y (Choices A and B).
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about three bonds:

|  | Bond X | Bond Y | Bond Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yield-to-maturity (%) |  |  | 6.2 |
| Coupon paid annually (%) |  |  | 5 |
| Time-to-maturity (in years) |  |  | 11 |
| Price when yield decreases by 1 basis point |  | 87.25 |  |
| Price when yield increases by 1 basis point |  | 87.15 |  |
| Price value of a basis point | 0.04 |  |  |

As measured by price value of a basis point, which bond is most sensitive to changes in its YTM?
option_c: Bond Z

A probability can be sorted into one of three broad categories. In this question, the analyst uses historical information for stock splits to derive
the probability of a future stock split on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSE). Since the probability was derived from the historical data method, it is
classified as an empirical probability.

question_en: An analyst studies 10 years of historical data on stock splits for companies listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSE) to determine the probability that a firm listed on the TSE will have a stock split this year. The probability derived from this method is best described as:
option_c: subjective.

explanation_en: The long party in a forward contract forgoes the benefits and avoids the costs of holding the underlying asset by purchasing that asset in the future, rather than the present.  To calculate the forward price: subtract the future value of the asset's benefits and add the future value of the costs of holding the asset to the future value of the spot price. Therefore, if the forward price of the asset is less than the spot price, the future value of the benefits of holding the asset must be greater than the future value of the costs. For example, suppose the spot price on a one-year contract is 100, the risk-free rate is 3%, the present value of asset costs is 2, and the forward price is 99.  In that case, the future value of the benefits of holding the asset must be greater than the future value of the costs (6.06 > 2):
question_en: On the day a forward contract is initiated, the spot price of the underlying asset is greater than the forward price.  This implies that the future value of the asset's benefits is most likely:
option_a: less than the future value of the costs of holding the asset.
option_b: the same as the future value of the costs of holding the asset.
option_c: greater than the future value of the costs of holding the asset.

However, Logan is violating the Standard on communication with clients and prospective clients by excluding relevant factors of the investment process. The use of his model is an important aspect of the investment process and should be disclosed to clients. Brisco is not violating the Standards by not considering Logan's research.
question_en: Victor Logan is a portfolio manager for McCoy Advisors, and Jack Brisco is the Director of Research for McCoy. Brisco has developed a proprietary model that has been thoroughly researched and is known throughout the industry as the McCoy model. The model is purely quantitative and screens stocks into buy, hold, and sell categories. The basic philosophy of the model is thoroughly explained to clients. Brisco frequently alters the model based on rigorous research—an aspect that is well explained to clients, although the specific alterations are not continually disclosed. Portfolio managers then make specific sector and security holding decisions, purchasing only securities that are indicated as "buys" by the model. Logan has conducted very thorough research on his own, using the same process that Brisco uses to validate his findings. Logan feels the model is missing some key elements that would further reduce the list of acceptable securities to purchase, however, Brisco has refused to look at Logan's research. Frustrated by this, Logan applies his own version of the model, with the justification that he is still only purchasing securities on the buy list. Because of the conflict with Brisco, he does not disclose the use of the model to anyone at McCoy or to clients. Which of the following statements regarding Logan and Brisco is CORRECT? Logan is:
option_a: not violating the Standards by applying his version of the model, but is violating the Standards by not disclosing it to clients. Brisco is not violating the Standards.
option_b: violating the Standards by applying his version of the model and by not disclosing it to clients. Brisco is not violating the Standards.
option_c: violating the Standards by applying his version of the model and by not disclosing it to clients. Brisco is violating the Standards by failing to consider Logan's research.

explanation_en: Deflation is often associated with liquidity trap conditions. A liquidity trap is a situation in which demand for money becomes highly elastic. Expanding the money supply has little effect on economic activity under these conditions because individuals and firms choose to hold the additional money in cash. "Bond market vigilantes" is an expression referring to the fact that expansionary monetary policy may cause long-term interest rates to increase, instead of decreasing as intended, if bond market participants expect the expansionary policy to increase future inflation rates.
question_en: The most likely reason for deflation to persist despite expansionary monetary policy is:
option_c: inelastic demand for money.

explanation_en: Normally, public companies have a share structure that grants each shareholder proportional voting power based on the number of shares held. For example, a shareholder who owns 50% of the company controls 50% of the votes. One exception to the general rule is a dual-class structure, where different share classes allow different numbers of votes per share (eg, Class A at one vote per share vs. Class B at two votes per share). A dual-class structure may create disproportional voting power relative to share ownership. Insiders (eg, founders) commonly hold Class B shares, which grant them dominant voting control on important issues (eg, board elections or strategic decisions) even if their share ownership falls below 50%. (Choice A) Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of share ownership only if all shares grant the same number of votes. Different share classes allow for different votes per share in a dual-class structure. (Choice C) Class B shares are granted mainly to insiders and family members and not to outside shareholders; therefore, greater voting power is typically held by insiders and family members.
question_en: Which of the following is most accurate with regard to a dual-class share structure?
option_a: Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of ownership.
option_b: It may grant founders superior voting control even if their ownership level falls below 50%.
option_c: It typically grants outside shareholders greater voting power than insiders and family

explanation_en: A company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is its marginal cost to raise additional capital.  If each source of capital has a different component cost of capital, WACC is the weighted average of these costs of capital.  The costs are weighted by the proportions of capital the company currently uses to support all its business activities. In this question, to calculate the WACC the weights of debt and equity must be derived from the company's debt-to-equity ratio (D/E).  The company's D/E ratio of 25% means it has $0.25 of debt for every $1.00 of equity, or 25% as much debt as equity.  The weights can be derived as follows: Note:  Since the proportions of debt and equity must equal 100%, the weight of equity is 80% = 100% − 20%. To calculate WACC, the company's component costs of capital are multiplied by their weights.  To account for the after-tax cost of debt, be sure to apply the company's tax rate: WACC = [(0.20) (0.05 × (1 − 0.20))] + [(0.80) (0.09)] WACC = 8.00% (Choice A)  7.75% results from incorrectly interpreting the company's D/E ratio of 25% to mean that 25%, instead of 20%, of the company's cost structure is debt. (Choice C)  8.20% results from using the company's pretax, instead of after-tax, cost of debt.

| Total capital $2 | billion |
|---|---|

| Pretax cost of debt | 5.0% |
| Tax rate | 20% |

If the company has only common equity and debt in its capital structure, the company's weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is closest to:

explanation_en: One difference between a forward contract and a futures contract relates to the daily mark-to-market process for futures contracts.  Each day's change in the futures price generates a gain for one side and an identical loss for the other.  The exchange deducts the losses from the loser's accounts and transfers them to the winner's accounts.  The winner reinvests the daily cash flows, which generates interest income. The graph above shows the advantage of holding a futures contract rather than a forward contract.  Both contracts expire in one year and have a forward price of $25.  It is assumed that the underlying asset increased by $0.10 per day.  The gain on the underlying asset was $36.50 for both contracts but reinvesting the cash flows from the daily mark-to-market of the futures contract generated nearly $1 in interest. When interest rates and asset prices are positively correlated, rising prices create gains for the long futures holders, which in turn can be invested at higher interest rates.  This is disadvantageous to sellers of futures contracts.  To induce participants to take short futures positions, the futures price must be set higher than for a forward contract, which does not settle gains and losses each day. (Choice A)  Futures prices are lower than forward prices when interest rates are negatively correlated to futures prices. (Choice B)  When interest rates are constant, futures prices and forward prices are the same in most cases.
question_en: Compared with a forward contract on the same underlying asset, when interest rates are positively correlated to futures prices, the futures price is most likely:
option_b: the same as the forward price.
option_c: higher than the forward price .

explanation_en: Able's basic earnings per share ((Net Income − Preferred Stock Dividends) / weighted average shares outstanding) for 2004 was [($720,000 − ($500 × 6,000 × 0.03) − ($1,000 × 1,000 × 0.08)] / 1,000,000 = $0.55. If the convertible preferred were converted to common stock on January 1, 6,000 × 40 = 240,000 additional shares would have been issued. Also, dividends on the convertible preferred would not have been paid. So diluted EPS was ($720,000 − 80,000) / (1,000,000 + 240,000) = $0.52.
question_en:
Selected information from Able Company's financial activities is as follows:

- Net Income was $720,000.
- 1,000,000 shares of common stock were outstanding on January 1.
- 1,000 shares of 8%, $1,000 par value preferred shares were outstanding on January 1.
