Companies can utilize one, or several, strategies to grow their business and generate economic profit. Companies with successful strategies
tend to outperform those without. Three common strategies, based on Michael Porter's research, are:
Cost leadership
Differentiation
Focus
The differentiation strategy involves a company making its products or services stand out from those of its competitors in the broad market.
There are many ways for companies to accomplish this. One is investing more heavily into the product or service itself. A company that uses
higher-quality materials for its product will stand out from its peers in the market. The goal is for consumers to associate the company with
superior products and unique features.
(Choice A) Closer proximity to customers provides focus on a niche of customers, but this strategy would not necessarily differentiate the product
or service at a broad level and is therefore more accurately associated with the focus strategy.
(Choice C) Gaining access to cheaper raw materials would allow a company to reduce its costs, but this strategy would not necessarily
differentiate the product or service and is therefore more accurately associated with the cost-leadership strategy.
question_en: Which of the following would most effectively support execution of a differentiation strategy?
option_c: Gaining cheaper access to raw materials

explanation_en: The central clearinghouse does not originate trades, it acts as the opposite party to all trades. In other words, it is the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. This action guarantees that all obligations under the terms of the contract will be fulfilled.

explanation_en: Corporate bonds are most often issued in an underwritten offering; this is also known as a firm commitment offering. In an underwritten offering, the underwriter (eg, investment bank) guides the issuer through the issuance process (eg, size, structure, pricing) by conveying investors' preferences. The underwriter then buys the entire issue to resell to investors, thus guaranteeing that the issuance is successful for the issuer but taking a financial risk if not all the bonds are sold. (Choice A) Auctions utilize a bidding process for price discovery and are more typical in the issuance of sovereign government debt. Sovereign bonds are well known to investors; combined with the standardized nature and regular issuance of these bonds, they enable the lowest cost issuance method, namely an auction. (Choice B) In a best effort offering, the investment bank is acting only as a broker and will sell the issue only on a "best efforts" basis for a commission. Best effort offerings are not as common and usually reserved for high-risk issues.
question_en: Typically, corporate bonds are most likely issued through a(n):
option_c: underwritten offering.

explanation_en: The types of issued securities and the provisions (ie, indentures) of debt contracts determine the priority of claims for different classes of creditors and owners.  Strict adherence to the priority of claims results in sequential payment in full according to the seniority of each class of claimants. The class of claimants with the most senior status at the point when the last of the assets are distributed receives only partial payment.  Those with more junior claims receive nothing.  Therefore, preferred shareholders receiving distributions only after all liability holders' claims (including those of subordinated lenders) are paid in full is consistent with strict adherence to the priority of claims. (Choice A)  All creditors accepting partial settlement of their claims is not strict adherence to the priority of claims.  However, senior creditors often accept immediate, partial settlement of their claims to avoid protracted litigation and obtain higher recovery rates. (Choice C)  Secured creditors have a claim only to the money they are owed.  Collateral sale proceeds in excess of their claims are used to make distributions to other claimants.  Shortfalls are given a status equal to the claims senior unsecured creditors.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely considered strict adherence with the priority of claims in a bankruptcy proceeding?
option_a: All creditor classes receiving only partial settlement of their claims
option_b: Preferred stockholders receiving distributions only after all creditors are paid in full
option_c: Secured lenders receiving 100% of collateral sale proceeds to fully retire their claims

Exercising a warrant causes the number of common shares outstanding to increase. This increase usually causes the company's earnings-per-

When calculating EPS, warrants are treated as having been exercised at the earlier of the beginning of the accounting period, if the warrants
were then outstanding, or the date of issuance. Both IFRS and GAAP require companies to use the treasury stock method for calculating the
effect of warrants on EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below.
A key assumption underlying the treasury stock method is that the average market price of the stock is more than the exercise price, so the
proceeds will purchase fewer shares than were issued from the warrants' exercise. The resulting weighted average is then used to calculate
diluted EPS. An example of XYZ's use of the treasury stock method is shown below.
(Choice A) $1.36 is obtained when the denominator is increased by the total number of shares issued from the warrants' exercise (1,000,000)
instead of the net shares added (250,000).

explanation_en: The capital allocation line (CAL) represents portfolios with the highest return for a given level of risk.  Those portfolios contain a combination of the optimal risky portfolio and the risk-free asset.  The optimal risky portfolio lies on both the efficient frontier and the CAL. The optimal risky portfolio is located at the point of tangency where a straight line originating from the risk-free rate touches the efficient frontier. The risk-free rate is what an investor earns by taking no risk.  If any other portfolio along the efficient frontier, such as the global minimum variance portfolio, is used to create an alternative CAL, then the resulting portfolios would be suboptimal to the dominant CAL using the optimal risky portfolio. If the optimal risky portfolio has a risk of 20% but the investor prefers half that risk (10%), then the investor allocates 50% of the investment to the optimal risky portfolio and 50% to the risk-free asset.  If another investor prefers 50% more risk than the optimal risky portfolio (30%), then this investor would borrow 50% at the risk-free rate and invest 150% in the optimal risky portfolio. Describe and interpret the minimum variance and efficient frontiers of risky assets and the global minimum variance portfolio LOS
question_en: Portfolios along the capital allocation line are most likely to:

explanation_en: The coupon rate of a floating rate note (FRN) is reset regularly and often, typically every three months, based on market rates.  Therefore, increased volatility in interest rates between coupon dates will not have much impact on the price of an FRN.  If the issuer's credit quality has not changed, the price of the bond is equal to par value at each reset. Callable and putable bonds have embedded call and put options.  Whether those options are exercised depends on interest rates.  A rise in interest rate volatility increases the range of possible interest rates.  With more possible outcomes, there is a higher probability that a bond's option will be exercised, which makes the option worth more. Interest rate volatility affects the prices of both callable and putable bonds.  The price of a putable bond is the price of an otherwise identical option-free bond plus the value of the put option.  As the put option increases in value, the price of the bond rises.  The opposite applies for callable bonds: An increase in the value of the call option reduces the price of the bond (Choices A and B).

explanation_en:
Hedge funds charge a management fee and an incentive fee. The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the total value of the fund's assets under management (AUM). It is assessed each year regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is levied against the fund's annual gains, subject to certain conditions. It is calculated either gross or net of the management fee. The net calculation subtracts the management fee from AUM to arrive at an adjusted AUM that is used to calculate the fund's profits.
The high-water mark represents the value of AUM, net of fees, at any time during the fund's existence. To earn an incentive fee, the fund must exceed the high-water mark, the base from which the fee is calculated.
The hurdle rate is the minimum profit that the fund must earn (usually annually) before it receives an incentive fee. The hurdle rate can either be "soft," meaning that the incentive fee is calculated based on the entire profit, or "hard," meaning that the incentive fee is based on only the excess profit above the hurdle rate.
In this scenario, the fund generated net returns in 20X5 of 18.9% ( = (29.725 – 25) / 25 ), above the soft hurdle rate of 6%, and eclipsed the high-water mark of $27 million. Therefore, the fund earned an incentive fee of 10% of profits, net of the management fee on average assets of $27,500,000:
0.10 × (29,725,000 − 27,000,000) = $272,500.

explanation_en: Cash flow treatment of investment income taxes paid US GAAP IFRS Investment income CFO CFO or CFI Income taxes CFO CFO, but can treat taxes paid on CFI income as CFI Cash flow statements divide cash inflows and outflows into three categories: cash from operations (CFO), cash from investing (CFI), and cash from financing (CFF).  CFO encompasses cash inflows and outflows related to a company's daily activities.  In contrast, CFI refers to inflows and outflows from noncore activities, such as passive investments in other companies.  There are no income tax implications for CFF. In most cases, IFRS classify all taxes paid as CFO regardless of the underlying source of income.  However, when a portion of the taxes can be specifically identified as paid on investment income, IFRS permit (but do not require) the company to classify that portion of the taxes as CFI. This company attributes €3 million of its total taxes paid to the rental income, which is not part of its core operations.  The rents received constitute CFI, and the company may classify the taxes associated with those rents as CFI.  The balance of the tax payment is classified as CFO. (Choices A and C)  Financing activities that give rise to CFF entries include borrowing or repaying debt, issuing stock, and paying dividends. None of the taxes paid relate to any type of financing activity, so none can be classified as CFF.

explanation_en: In a securitization, a company may sell an asset (eg, accounts receivable) to a special purpose entity (SPE), which then issues asset-backed securities, using the bundled receivables as collateral. If customers continue to pay the receivables, the SPE can make interest and principal payments so that all bond classes are unaffected by the company's bankruptcy.  For that reason, the SPE is commonly referred to as "bankruptcy remote" since, all else being equal, the company's bankruptcy does not affect to the SPE's ABS investors (Choices A and C).

explanation_en:
Options embedded in callable bonds complicate comparisons with other bonds. Adjusting the market price of callable bonds for the value of
embedded options makes it easier to assess the impact of other risk factors (eg, credit quality, liquidity) on relative value. For this analysis, the
option-adjusted spread (OAS) is estimated by subtracting the value of the option (in basis points per year) from a bond's Z-spread.
The Z-spread is the constant spread to a benchmark (ie, government or swap) curve that results in a series of periodic discount rates that equate
the present value of a bond's cash flows to its market price. Discount rates based on a Z-spread capture all risks affecting price, including any
embedded options. An option pricing model estimates how much narrower the Z-spread would be for an equivalent noncallable bond. The
callable bond's OAS is used to calculate an option-adjusted price and yield, allowing better comparisons with other securities.
(Choices A and C) The G- and I-spreads are based on the difference between a bond's YTM and a benchmark rate of the same maturity (eg, 5-
year corporate bond versus a 5-year government bond or swap). Since these spreads are computed separately for each maturity, they widen as
maturities increase, reflecting the greater relative risk of corporate securities for longer time horizons.
question_en: A callable corporate bond's option-adjusted spread (OAS) is most likely calculated using the value (in basis points per year) of the embedded option and the:
option_c: G-spread.

explanation_en: There are two formats for a common-size cash flow statement, expressing each type of outflow as a percentage of total cash outflows or as a percentage of total revenue for the period. Operating cash flow for the period mixes inflows and outflows and is not used to calculate percentage flows for payment made.
question_en: A common-size cash flow statement is least likely to provide payments to employees as a percentage of:
option_b: operating cash ow for the period.
option_c: total cash outows for the period.

explanation_en: A box and whisker plot illustrates the dispersion of data across quartiles.  The box's: upper boundary marks the third quartile (Q ) and 75% of the data fall at or below that point; lower boundary marks the first quartile (Q ) and 25% of the data fall at or below that point; and upper and lower boundaries include 50% of the data, the interquartile range. The whiskers extend from the upper and lower boundaries and mark the range of acceptable observations above Q  and below Q .  Single values beyond the ends of the whiskers (ie, the "fences") represent outliers, typically marked with asterisks or dots.  The largest data point (ie, maximum) is the fourth quartile (Q ) since 100% of the data falls at or below that point. Outliers are actual data points in the data set, so Q  would include outliers.  In this question, Q  is 15, which is the upper bound of the box; Q  is 20, which is an outlier and the largest value. Calculate, interpret, and evaluate measures of central tendency and location to address an investment problem
question_en: An analyst collects P/E ratios from companies within an industry and plots them on a box and whisker chart: The third and fourth quartiles are closest to:
option_c: 17 and 20

question_en: A semiannual-pay bond is callable in five years at $1,080. The bond has an 8% coupon and 15 years to maturity. If an investor pays $895 for the bond today, the yield to call is closest to:

question_en:
An analyst estimates the following information from a simple linear regression:

- Sum of squares error: 280
- Sum of squares regression: 25
- Number of paired observations: 30

The standard error of the estimate is closest to:

explanation_en: If the NPV is positive, this implies that the IRR must be greater than the discount rate.
question_en: A project with a conventional cash flow pattern has a net present value of $15,000. If the discount rate used was 6%, the project's internal rate of return is:
option_c: greater than 6%.

explanation_en: The correct answer uses the effective duration formula with PV₋ and PV₊ values (101.12 and 103.74 respectively) in the denominator: EffDur = (103.74 - 101.12) / (2 × 102.31 × 0.002) = 6.40, whereas option A incorrectly uses 103.74 in the denominator and option C incorrectly uses 101.12.
question_en: A bond is currently selling for 102.31. A valuation model estimates the price will fall to 101.12 if interest rates increase by 20 bps and rise to 103.74 if interest rates decrease by 20 bps. Using these estimates, the effective duration of the bond is closest to:

explanation_en: Return on invested equity is ($45 – $40) / $10 = 50%. The leverage ratio is purchase price / equity = $40 / $10 = 4. Margin call price is $40 × [(1 – 0.25) / (1 – 0.20)] = $37.50.
question_en: An investor purchases stock on 25% initial margin, posting $10 of the original stock price of $40 as equity. The position has a required maintenance margin of 20%. The investor later sells the stock for $45. Ignoring transaction costs and margin loan interest, which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_c: Return on investment is 50%.

explanation_en: According to the CAPM, an asset's expected return is a function of its sensitivity to systematic risk as measured by beta, the market risk premium, and the risk-free rate. The market's beta is always equal to 1.0. If a security's beta is greater than 1.0, that security has more exposure to systematic risk and a higher expected return than the market. In this case, Stock A's beta (1.3) is greater than the market beta (1.0), so Stock A has an expected return greater than the market's expected return (Choices B and C). Alternatively, a security's expected return can be calculated using the CAPM and then compared to the market's return. Stock A's expected return of 15% is greater than the market's expected return of 12%.
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information on three stocks:

| Stock | Expected Standard Deviation | Beta |
|---|---|---|
| A | 20% | 1.3 |
| B | 13% | 0.8 |
| C | 31% | -0.3 |

The market's expected return is 12%. Based on the CAPM, if the risk-free rate is 2%, then the stock with an expected return greater than the market's expected return is most likely:
option_c: Stock C.

explanation_en: Price discrimination is setting different prices to different identifiable groups of customers. Peak and off-peak pricing is an example. Penetration pricing is setting a low price temporarily to grow market share and achieve greater scale. Cost-based pricing is setting prices based on production costs plus a profit margin.
question_en: Pricing strategies that involve price discrimination most likely include:
option_c: penetration pricing.

explanation_en: Standard I(D) addresses conduct reflecting poorly on professional integrity, and accepting oversubscribed IPO shares for personal gain violates this standard and also violates Standard I(B) regarding independence and objectivity, as it allows managers to profit from opportunities unavailable to clients.
question_en: Which of the following statements best describes the application of Standard I(D), Misconduct, to a member who declares personal bankruptcy due to a large loss from investing in a startup company and accepts an allocation of shares in an oversubscribed IPO for her personal account?
option_a: Incorrect because according to Standard I(D), Misconduct, the Code and Standards are primarily aimed at conduct and actions related to a member's or candidate's professional life. Also, personal bankruptcy may not reflect on the integrity or trustworthiness of the person declaring bankruptcy, but if the circumstances of the bankruptcy involve fraudulent or deceitful business conduct, the bankruptcy may be a violation of this standard. Therefore, a member does not violate Standard I(D), Misconduct, by declaring personal bankruptcy because of a large loss from investing in a startup company.
option_b: Correct because Standard I(D), Misconduct, addresses all conduct that reflects poorly on the professional integrity, good reputation, or competence of members and candidates. Any act that involves lying, cheating, stealing, or other dishonest conduct is a violation of this standard if the offense reflects adversely on a member's or candidate's professional activities. Accepting allocation of shares from an issuer in an oversubscribed IPO for her personal account reflects poorly on the member's professional integrity. Therefore, the member violates Standard I(D). The member's conduct also violates Standard I(B), Independence and Objectivity. One type of benefit is the allocation of shares in oversubscribed IPOs to investment managers for their personal accounts. This practice affords managers the opportunity to make quick profits that may not be available to their clients. Such a practice is prohibited under Standard I(B).
option_c: Incorrect because Standard I(D), Misconduct, addresses all conduct that reflects poorly on the professional integrity, good reputation, or competence of members and candidates. Any act that involves lying, cheating, stealing, or other dishonest conduct is a violation of this standard if the offense reflects adversely on a member's or candidate's professional activities. Accepting allocation of shares from an issuer in an oversubscribed IPO for her personal accounts reflects poorly on the member's professional integrity but declaring personal bankruptcy does not relate to the member's professional life. Therefore, the former is a violation of Standard I(D), Misconduct, while the latter is not.

explanation_en: With a finance lease, the lessor will recognize a lease receivable asset and amortize it over the lease term. With an operating lease, the lessor retains the leased asset on its balance sheet and records depreciation expense over its useful life.
question_en: A lessor will recognize a lease receivable asset if the lease is classified as:
option_c: either an operating or a nance lease.

explanation_en: Security 2 should receive the highest weight because the information ratio (alpha divided by nonsystematic risk) best measures the abnormal return per unit of risk added to a well-diversified portfolio, making it the most valuable metric for determining relative weights when maximizing risk-adjusted returns.
option_c: Security 3.

explanation_en: The capital market line graphically relates total risk, σ (on x-axis) and expected return (on y-axis), and effectively prices total risk because pricing or valuing an asset is equivalent to estimating its expected rate of return.
question_en: The capital market line is best described as pricing:
option_c: only nonsystematic risk.

explanation_en: Factors that increase market efficiency Fair and orderly markets Low cost of information gathering Company financial disclosure Investment by foreigners permitted Arbitrage and short selling Low transaction costs Availability of daily market data Existence and prevalence of exchanges Large number of analysts and investors An efficient market is one in which new information is reflected quickly in asset prices. Market participants acquire market information from company reports and use that data to make investment decisions. Factors that increase the speed at which participants have access to information for valuation and trading facilitate faster price adjustments. This tends to increase market efficiency. Less frequent financial reporting impedes valuation and investing and increases the cost of gathering information. More financial disclosure contributes to a fairer and more orderly market, as well as broader availability of information to analysts and investors, both of which tend to increase market efficiency. As a result of these factors, less frequent financial disclosure by companies decreases market efficiency (Choices B and C).
question_en: After an election, new political leadership in a country allows more flexibility on the frequency of financial reporting. Consequently, many companies report financial results less often. Market efficiency will most likely:
option_c: increase.

explanation_en: Fintech refers to technological innovation in designing and delivering financial information and products. One practical application of fintech concerns how investment companies can utilize machine learning to analyze and manage risk. Machine learning is the creation of algorithms that analyze enormous amounts of qualitative and quantitative input data to predict future outcomes or to identify patterns that would not otherwise be obvious. Risk analysis uses data from multiple sources, many of which are classified as alternative sources (eg, photographs, text messages). Machine learning is easily adapted to determine whether this data contains errors, bias, or outliers that would distort the predictive ability of a risk model that will use the data. In other words, if the data contains errors that were missed during human quality control processes, machine learning can help validate the data before it is used by the algorithm that manages risk. (Choice B) Risk management uses both quantitative and qualitative data. (Choice C) Operational risk is the risk of loss caused by failed systems or processes within the firm. Fintech can use algorithms that analyze a variety of input data to predict events that result in losses from operational risk.
question_en: Use of fintech most appropriately enhances a company's risk analysis capabilities when:
option_a: machine learning analyzes input data for errors.
option_b: the data to be analyzed excludes quantitative data.
option_c: the risk analysis focuses mainly on market and trading risk rather than operational risk.

explanation_en: According to Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, members and candidates must disclose to their clients, prospects, and employer all situations that could reasonably be expected to compromise their independence and objectivity. Stock ownership of a company in which clients are invested would need to be disclosed to clients and the employer since a member may be tempted to purchase more stock for client accounts in order to increase the value of personal holdings. Participation on the board of directors of a company in which clients are invested would also need to be disclosed to both clients and the employer. Board positions may inhibit the member's ability to objectively determine when to sell the stock of the company and may expose the member to material nonpublic information.
question_en: Giselle Holt, CFA, is a portfolio manager in the trust department of State Bank. Holt recently inherited a substantial amount of stock of Brown & Company and accepted a position on the board of directors for TVC Plastics, Inc. Many of the trust clients at the bank hold positions in Brown & Company and in TVC Plastics. According to CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Holt must disclose:
option_a: both the stock ownership and board position to her clients.
option_b: the board membership to her clients and the stock ownership to State Bank.
option_c: both the stock ownership and board position to her clients and State Bank.

explanation_en: The one year forward rate is 0.6243 × (1 + 0.03016) = 0.6431.
question_en: The spot exchange rate is 0.6243 USD/GBP and the 1-year forward rate is quoted as 3.016%. The 1-year forward exchange rate for USD/GBP is closest to:

explanation_en: Allen's notes from his research are employer records and even though he prepared them, it is a violation to take them from his employer without permission. Soliciting former clients' business is not, in itself, a violation as long has Allen has not misappropriated client information from his former employer. Preparations to start a new business are not necessarily a violation of the Standard, although soliciting current clients or recruiting other firm personnel for the new venture, before formally leaving his employer, would be violations of the Standards.
question_en: Jacob Allen, CFA, decides he could make more money if he started his own company. Which of the following steps would most likely violate Standard IV(A) Loyalty?
option_a: Renting space for his new company and interviewing several candidates for the position of manager at the new company.
option_b: Soliciting, without written permission from his current employer, the business of former clients after he leaves his current employer.
option_c: Using his notes from prior research of a firm in a creating a new research report on the firm, after leaving his current employer.

explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." To comply with Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Members and Candidates must use credible return data when preparing performance information for current or potential clients.  Clients must receive performance information that is free from distorted data that may be misleading. To comply with the Standard, Members and Candidates need to fully disclose exceptions and avoid any disclosures that may misrepresent performance. Shepherd accurately portrays her work with the Green Fund and does not mislead her clients, who are made aware that she worked for the Green Fund from 20X6 to 20X8. (Choice B)  Shepherd does not violate the Standard by reporting the Green Fund's performance gross of fees since she discloses its fee schedule. (Choice C)  An advisor must report an account's returns even if the advisor is no longer associated with that account.  Otherwise, the advisor might conceal accounts that performed poorly, leading to the advisor's termination.
question_en: In 20X6, Shepherd Financial, Inc. (SFI), headed by founder Lillian Shepherd, CFA, is engaged by the Green Fund to manage part of the fund's assets.  SFI, with Shepherd as the advisor for the account, is one of 10 subadvisors hired by the Green Fund to select securities.  Two years later, in 20X8, the Green Fund terminates SFI.  In 20X9, Shepherd delivers performance reports to prospective clients that include the Green Fund's historical gross performance.  The reports also include the Green Fund's fee schedule and disclosures that SFI was one member of a 10- subadvisor team for the Green Fund from 20X6 to 20X8. According to Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, does Shepherd most likely violate the Standard?
option_b: Yes, since she reports the Green Fund's gross performance.
option_c: Yes, since she claims performance for a fund SFI no longer advises.

explanation_en: Operationally efficient markets are characterized by liquid markets with low commissions and order price impacts, which directly reflects the costs of arranging trades.
question_en: The financial systems that are operationally efficient are most likely characterized by:
option_a: security prices that reflect fundamental values.
option_b: the use of resources where they are most valuable.
option_c: liquid markets with low commissions and order price impacts.

explanation_en: Edwin's statement is consistent with both behavioral finance and informationally efficient markets. While behavioral biases that cause individuals to act irrationally can cause assets to be mispriced, markets can still be considered efficient if asset mispricing cannot consistently be exploited to earn positive risk-adjusted returns on average over time.
question_en: Tom Edwin, CFA, states, "Individuals exhibit biases, such as loss aversion and herding, that result in observed pricing anomalies in financial markets. However, a strategy based on exploiting these anomalies will not earn positive abnormal returns over time." With regard to the efficient markets and behavioral finance views of market pricing, Edwin's statement is most likely consistent with:
option_a: behavioral nance, but not informationally ecient markets.
option_b: neither behavioral nance nor informationally ecient markets.
option_c: both behavioral nance and informationally ecient markets.

explanation_en: In open-end funds, new shares are issued at the net asset value of the fund at the time of investment. An open-end fund is a collective investment scheme that can issue and redeem shares at any time. An investor will generally purchase shares in the fund directly from the fund itself rather than from the existing shareholders. It contrasts with a closed-end fund, which typically issues all the shares it will issue at the outset, with such shares usually being tradable between investors thereafter.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a characteristic of open-ended mutual funds?
option_a: Open-end funds accept new investment money and issue additional shares to existing or new investors. Therefore, the number of outstanding shares changes after every new investment.
option_b: In open-end funds, new shares are created and sold at a premium or a discount to net assets values depending on the demand for the shares.
option_c: An open-end structure makes it easy to grow in size but creates pressure on the portfolio manager to manage the cash inflows and outflows.

explanation_en:
A holding period return (HPR) is a single-period measurement of return. The period can represent a day, a year, or any other timeframe. The
difference between the security's ending price and its beginning price is its capital gain or loss during the holding period. Also affecting the HPR
are company distributions to bondholders (interest) or shareholders (dividends). These distributions are the income part of a security's return and
increase HPR.
(Choice A) This answer incorrectly applies the HPR using the ending price, rather than the beginning price, to find the HPR.
(Choice B) This incorrect choice does not include the stock's dividend and therefore results in an understatement of HPR.
question_en: A manager buys 500 shares of a stock at $15.00 per share at the beginning of the year. At the end of the year, the stock's price appreciates to $18.50. If this stock pays its annual dividend of $0.50 at the end of the year, then the manager's holding period return is closest to:

explanation_en: Other things being equal, the amount of reinvestment risk embedded in a bond will decrease with lower coupons as there are fewer coupons to reinvest and with shorter maturities because the reinvestment period is shorter. A lower Macaulay duration may reflect more or less reinvestment risk, depending on what causes Macaulay duration to be lower. A lower Macaulay duration could result from a shorter maturity (which reduces reinvestment risk) or a higher coupon (which increases reinvestment risk).
question_en: All else being equal, which of the following bond characteristics most likely results in less reinvestment risk?
option_c: A lower Macaulay duration.

explanation_en: High operating leverage, other things held constant, means that a relatively small change in sales will result in a large change in operating income. Therefore, during a period of increasing sales, a highly leveraged firm will have higher earnings growth than a lesser leveraged firm.
question_en: During a period of increasing sales, compared to firms with lower operating leverage, earnings growth for firms with high operating leverage will be:
option_c: lower.

explanation_en: Ethics refers to the study of moral principles. Ethics is broader than written codes of standards or a particular belief about proper conduct.
question_en: Ethics are most accurately defined as:
option_c: the study of moral principles.

explanation_en:
An interest rate can be used to express the percentage growth in money between two different points in time. For example, $100 invested today
at an annual interest rate of 5% will grow to $105 in a year. Depending on the circumstances, an interest rate can be interpreted in many ways: as
a required rate of return, as a discount rate, or as an opportunity cost.
The student forgoes the future investment return (ie, the interest rate) by choosing to spend the money today. The foregone return is the
opportunity cost of current consumption.
(Choice A) A sunk cost is an actual cost that has already been incurred. In this question, the $100 spent on the purchase, not the foregone
interest, is the sunk cost.
(Choice C) The required rate of return is the minimum return percentage that an investor requires for accepting an investment. Since the student
did not accept the investment, the interest rate offered on the account is not the student's required rate of return.
question_en: A student chooses to spend $100 today on a concert ticket instead of investing that money in a savings account that earns interest. The interest that could have been earned can be best interpreted as this student's:
option_c: required rate of return.

explanation_en: Ineffective internal controls over accounting may provide opportunities for low-quality financial reporting.
question_en: Jordan Loney issues a "sell" recommendation on Sullivan Company because she believes its financial reporting quality is low. Loney writes, "Rapid turnover of key employees in its information systems and accounting units have made Sullivan's internal monitoring controls ineffective." Which condition that may lead to low-quality financial reporting has Loney detected at Sullivan?
option_c: Rationalization.

explanation_en: A simple capital structure contains no potentially dilutive securities such as stock options, warrants, or convertible preferred stock.
question_en: Which of the following securities would least likely be found in a simple capital structure?
option_c: 7%, $100 par value non convertible preferred.

explanation_en: Classifications of big data Traditional Prices of stock trades Company reports Sources Alternative Social media Satellite images Structured: Tabular depiction (eg, spreadsheets) Data types Unstructured: Requires additional applications such as image recognition software and use data Fintech refers to technological innovation in designing and delivering financial information and products. One area of fintech concerns ways to efficiently use data generated by businesses, governments, and individuals. This data can arise from both traditional and alternative information sources; collectively, this data is commonly referred to as Big Data. Big Data can be categorized as structured or unstructured. Structured data refers to data that can be easily stored in a database. Historical stock prices, company earnings. and economic statistics are examples of structured data. Unstructured data largely encompasses alternative data sources such as social media postings and transaction information from point-of-sale registers in retail stores (Choices B and C). Unstructured data requires special applications to process the information before investment professionals can use it.
question_en: When considering different sources of Big Data, structured data most likely includes:
option_a: computer spreadsheets of historic company information.
option_b: postings by users of consumer products on social media.
option_c: point-of-sale information transmitted by cash registers in stores.

explanation_en: DuPont decomposition: ROE = Net Profit Margin x Asset Turnover x Financial Leverage. This separates profitability, efficiency, and leverage into analysable drivers. Option B incorrectly replaces Asset Turnover with Equity Turnover. Option C uses Gross Profit Margin and Return on Assets, which are not standard DuPont components.
question_en: Which of the following is the most appropriate equation for calculating the return on equity ratio?
option_a: Return on Equity = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage.
option_b: Return on Equity = Net Profit Margin × Equity Turnover × Financial Leverage.
option_c: Return on Equity = Gross Profit Margin × Return on Assets × Financial Leverage.

explanation_en: A point estimate is a single value that is used to estimate a parameter of the population. For instance, the mean of each sample drawn from a population is a point estimate of the population mean. Since each sample mean is a unique number based on the sample from which it was calculated, a point estimate has no sampling distribution (Choice A). Due to sampling error, a point estimate is usually different from the parameter. A confidence interval is a range of values greater or less than a point estimate that, for a given level of probability (ie, confidence), includes the actual population parameter. In the diagram above, the sample mean (4%) is a point estimate of the actual population mean (5%), which is greater than the sample mean. The 90% confidence interval around the sample mean (shown on the left) is too narrow to include the population mean, but the wider 95% confidence interval does include the population mean. A greater confidence level results in a wider confidence interval. (Choice B) Confidence intervals, not point estimates, are calculated using the standard error.
question_en: Which of the following characteristics of point estimates and confidence intervals is most likely correct?
option_a: A point estimate has a sampling distribution.
option_b: The standard error is required to calculate a point estimate.
option_c: A confidence interval widens as the confidence level increases.

explanation_en: The change in bond price can be calculated using the following formula: price change = -annual modified duration (Delta YTM) + 1/2 annual convexity (Delta YTM) squared. For a 25 basis point decrease in yields, the calculation is equal to (-3.27 x -0.0025) + (0.5 x 15.74 x -0.0025^2) = .008224, or 0.8224%.
question_en: A bond is currently priced at 92.35. If the calculated modified duration is 3.27 and the convexity is 15.74, the expected price change due to a 25 basis point decrease in yields is closest to:

explanation_en: Derivatives have lower transaction costs relative to trading directly the underlying. The other two options talk about the other benefits that come with derivatives.
question_en: "Derivatives have many uses and benefits relative to trading the underlying." Which of the following would most likely refute the above statement?
option_b: The use of a large amount of leverage
option_c: Increase in the amount of speculative trading

explanation_en: Soprano is violating the Standard on portfolio investment recommendations and actions by excluding relevant factors of the investment process. The fundamental research aspect is highly relevant to the process and should be disclosed to clients. It is acceptable for Melfi to use two investment processes that may be in conflict with each other and to use a process that was not developed by her.
question_en: Janice Melfi is a portfolio manager for Soprano Advisors. Soprano has developed a proprietary model that has been thoroughly researched and is known throughout the industry as the Soprano model. The model is purely quantitative and screens stocks into buy, hold, and sell categories. The basic philosophy of the model is thoroughly explained to clients. The director of research frequently alters the model based on rigorous research—an aspect that is well explained to clients, although the specific alterations are not continually disclosed. Portfolio managers use the model to assist them in making portfolio decisions, but, based on their own fundamental research, are allowed to purchase securities not recommended by the model. This fact is not disclosed to the clients, because the head of marketing does not think it is relevant. Which of the following statements regarding the portfolio manager's investment decisions is CORRECT?
option_a: Soprano is violating the Standards by not disclosing the fundamental research aspect of the investment process.
option_b: Melfi is violating the Standards by using two investment processes that are in conflict with each other.
option_c: There is no violation of the Standards.

explanation_en: The growth rate cycle shows peaks and troughs earlier than the classical cycle or the growth cycle.
question_en: Peaks and troughs in the business cycle are most likely to appear earliest as measured by the:
option_c: growth rate cycle.

explanation_en: Cumulative voting allows shareholders to direct their total voting rights to specific candidates, as opposed to statutory voting having to allocate their voting rights evenly among all candidates.
question_en: The voting method that allows shareholders to cast all their votes for a single candidate is best described as:
option_c: cumulative voting.

explanation_en: According to Standard VI(B), an analyst must give clients the first opportunity to buy or sell a security before the analyst acts on his own behalf. A 24-hour waiting period seems reasonable under the circumstances presented. The analyst seems to have a reasonable basis, and there is no reason to believe that he is violating Standard III(B) since he contacted all of the clients who have a position in the security.
question_en: An analyst has a large personal holding of a security, and he has just determined that market conditions warrant selling this security. The analyst contacts clients who have a position in the security and advises them to sell some or all of the security. After waiting 24 hours, he sells the security from his personal accounts. This is:
option_a: a violation of Standard III(B), Fair Dealing.
option_b: a violation of Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions.
option_c: congruent with Standard VI(B), Priority of Transactions.

explanation_en: The target semideviation correctly measures dispersion of returns below a target using n - 1 as the denominator, calculating sqrt(0.0037/3) = 0.0351 ≈ 3.5%, unlike the standard deviation which includes all deviations from the mean.
question_en: Not provided in visible text - question text not shown on this solution page
option_a: Incorrect because it wrongly uses n, not n – 1, as denominator in calculating the target semideviation. Hence, target semideviation = sqrt(0.00374) = 0.0304 ≈ 3.0%.
option_b: Correct because the target downside deviation, also referred to as the target semideviation, is a measure of dispersion of the observations (here, returns) below the target. The target semideviation, s_target, is: s_target = sqrt[Σ_for all X_i<B (X_i - B)² / (n - 1)].
option_c: Incorrect because it is the standard deviation, not the target semideviation. The mean is (5% + (–2%) + 3% + 8%)/4 = 3.5%. The standard deviation is sqrt[((5% – 3.5%)² + (–2% – 3.5%)² + (3% – 3.5%)² + (8% – 3.5%)²)/3] = sqrt(0.0053/3) = 0.0420 ≈ 4.2%.

explanation_en: If a stock's continuously compounded return is normally distributed, then the future stock price is necessarily lognormally distributed.
question_en: If a stock's continuously compounded return is normally distributed, the future stock prices most likely:
option_c: lognormally distributed.

explanation_en: A company running high-end hotels with high average room rates is executing a differentiation strategy, where customers see value in paying more for a product or service. A culture of strong customer experience lends itself to this strategy. Economies of scale, low variable costs, and strong cost controls are needed with a cost leadership strategy.
question_en: Company X runs a series of high-end hotels in the Northeastern United States. The average room rate per night is higher than any other hotel in the region. Which of the following best allows the company to build upon its differentiation strategy?
option_a: Economies of scale and low variable costs.
option_b: Strong cost controls, which allow the company to maintain prot margins.
option_c: A culture of strong customer experience.

Year | Net Return (%)

2009 | 32.2

The 2012 return needed to achieve a trailing five-year geometric mean annualized return of 5% when calculated at the end of 2012 is closest to:

explanation_en:
Common-size cash flow statements display each statement item either as a percentage of revenue or as a percentage of the company's total cash inflows or outflows. This allows analysts to compare the receipts and expenditures for companies of different sizes or for one company over time.

In this scenario, the common-size cash flow statement indicates that the company's free cash flow to equity (FCFE) as a percentage of revenue increased between 20X4 and 20X5: from 3.5% (= 9% + 5% − 5.5% − 5% + 6% − 6%) in 20X4 to 4.4% (= 11.1% + 6.7% −7.2% − 6.7% + 2.2% − 1.7%) in 20X5. This equates to FCFE of MXN 35 million in 20X4 (= 1,000 × 0.035) and MXN 40 million in 20X5 (= 900 × 0.044).

Note: After-tax cash paid for interest is used in the calculation of free cash flow to the firm (FCFF), not FCFE.

Things to remember:
Common-size cash flow statements can present each item on the cash flow statement as a percentage of revenue. They allow analysts to compare the receipts and expenditures that contribute to cash generation for companies of different sizes or for one company over time.

explanation_en: Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients requires members to distinguish between fact and opinion. "Blanding's earnings will grow at 12.5% annually in each of the next two years" violates the Standard by stating an uncertain future outcome as a fact. Preceding the statement with a qualifier such as "We expect..." identifies the forecast as an opinion.

explanation_en: As financial reporting standards evolve, analysts must monitor ongoing developments since new and changing standards can impact financial analyses. Since they are not accountants, analysts should monitor standards from a user's, not a preparer's, perspective. They can accomplish this by staying aware of new products and transactions, reviewing the actions of standard setters, and identifying new critical accounting policies from company disclosures. It is important to stay current on new financial businesses, such as fintech companies, by reviewing business journals. Reading exposure drafts from the International Accounting Standards Board, Financial Accounting Standards Board, and CFA Institute websites increases awareness of upcoming changes in financial reporting. However, analysts should expect a lag between a new accounting transaction and its eventual reporting standard. Reviewing a company's annual report provides information about new accounting policies (Choices A and C).
question_en: An analyst is responsible for monitoring developments in financial reporting standards. Which of the following is least likely to help the analyst?
option_b: Monitoring changes in standards from a preparer's perspective.
option_c: Checking companies' disclosures regarding their new accounting policies.

explanation_en: Capital market theory suggests that all investors should invest in the same portfolio of risky assets, and this portfolio is located at the point of tangency of the CML and the efficient frontier of risky assets. Any point below the CML is suboptimal, and points above the CML are not feasible.
question_en: According to capital market theory, which of the following represents the risky portfolio that should be held by all investors who desire to hold risky assets?

option_b: Any point on the efficient frontier and to the right of the point of tangency between the CML and the efficient frontier.
option_c: Any point on the efficient frontier and to the left of the point of tangency between the CML and the efficient frontier.

explanation_en: A residual is the difference between the observed value of the dependent variable and the value predicted by the regression.  In a simple linear regression (SLR), residuals are the vertical distance between the actual observations and the regression line, which is the straight line that minimizes the sum of the squares of all residuals (ie, the sum of squares error). Ideally, the residual plot is randomly scattered; the presence of a pattern often indicates the violation of one or more assumptions underlying the simple linear regression model. In this scenario, there is a pattern: the variance increases as the value of the independent variable increases.  This indicates a violation of homoskedasticity, which assumes that observations have a similar dispersion and residuals have constant variance.  That violation is called heteroskedasticity. (Choice A)  Linearity assumes that the variables have a linear relationship.  Nonlinearity, the violation of this assumption, is indicated by a concentration of positive residuals in a range (or ranges) of the plot and of negative residuals in other range(s).  No concentration exists in this scenario's residual plot. (Choice B)  Independence assumes that observations are uncorrelated.  Autocorrelation, the violation of this assumption, is often indicated by plotting the residuals against time (ie, observation order), and identifying that neighboring residuals have similar signs and magnitudes.  There is no evidence of autocorrelation in this residual plot.
question_en: After running a simple linear regression, a trader analyzes the resulting residual plot: Based on only the residual plot, this regression model most likely violated which of the following linear regression assumptions?
option_c: Homoskedasticity

explanation_en: Traders must meet an initial margin requirement in cash when initiating a futures position. To ensure there are adequate funds to cover losses, the margin account value must be maintained above a minimum amount known as the maintenance margin. If the account value falls below the maintenance margin, there is a demand for additional funds, which is referred to as a margin call. The amount of the margin call is the cash necessary to raise the account value to the initial margin requirement. The €10 price decline results in an equal loss on the long futures position (ie, -150 + 140 = −10), which reduces the account value to €5 (15 −10). The margin call is for the difference between the account value and the initial margin, €10 = 15 − 5. Failure to meet the call in full can result in a liquidation of positions. (Choice A) €1 is the shortfall of the account value relative to the maintenance margin. A margin call that brings the account equity back up to the maintenance margin is a requirement in the securities market, not the futures market. (Choice B) A deposit of €9 would raise the account value to €14, equal to 10% of the current cash value of the futures contract. However, futures margins are expressed as a specific money amount per contract, not as a percentage of a contract's cash value.

explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase A policy rate (or official interest rate or official policy rate) is the rate at which a central bank lends to commercial banks. Policy rates are adjusted to influence interest rates throughout the economy and affect economic activity. Since the policy rate is the cost of obtaining reserves from the central bank, commercial banks often tie base lending rates to the central bank policy rate. Therefore, commercial banks usually increase their base lending rate when a central bank increases its policy rate. Base lending rates are reference rates for setting loan interest rates for different types of clients (eg, large corporations: Base lending rate + 0.50%; privately held small businesses: Base lending rate + 3.00%). Since changing reserve requirements and buying or selling securities affects reserves, such policy actions by central banks are less likely to impact base lending rates when there are already significant excess reserves and therefore ample capacity to make loans and expand the money supply (Choices B and C).

explanation_en: Approximate modified duration (ModDur) and effective duration (EffDur) both measure the sensitivity of bond prices to changes in yields: ModDur measures sensitivity as the slope of a bond's price-yield curve, derived by calculating the bond's price at lower and higher YTMs. EffDur measures sensitivity based on parallel downward and upward shifts of the benchmark yield curve. If the government par bond (ie, benchmark) curve is flat, the spot rate curve derived from it is also flat, and the spot rates and YTMs are equal with the same value across all maturities. Therefore, if the basis point change in YTM and the shift in the benchmark yield curve are equal, the same PV and PV will be used to calculate both ModDur and EffDur since all cash flows are discounted by the same interest rate. This results in + − ModDur and EffDur being closest to each other (ie, they are equal). Regardless of the yield curve's shape, PV and PV for ModDur are calculated by using a single interest rate to discount bond cash flows. + − However, if the benchmark curve is not flat, the PV and PV used to determine EffDur are calculated by discounting each cash flow by a different + − spot rate. If the benchmark curve's slope diverges only slightly from flat, the two duration measures will be almost equal. As the curve's slope steepens, the divergence of spot rates used to calculate PV and PV will increase, leading to larger differences between ModDur and EffDur + − (Choice B). (Choice C) Neither duration measure is based on actual movements of the yield curve. Effective duration is based on assumed downward and upward parallel shifts of the yield curve.
question_en: All else equal, an option-free bond's effective duration and approximate modified duration are closest when the benchmark par bond curve:
option_c: makes a parallel shift.

explanation_en: Real exchange rates are used to measure the relative purchasing power between two currencies. Relative purchasing power is measured by adjusting the nominal exchange rate by the ratio of the aggregate price levels for similar goods in each currency. Based on the formula shown above, the real exchange rate: varies directly with the nominal exchange rate and the foreign price level, and varies inversely with the domestic price level (which itself is typically measured using a consumer price index. In this case, CAD is the domestic currency and AUD is the foreign currency. If the purchasing power of both currencies were the same, the real exchange rate would equal 1.0 and the nominal exchange rate would need to be adjusted to offset the relative price level difference (ie, the nominal exchange rate would be the inverse of the ratio of price levels). As the real exchange rate rises (falls), the relative purchasing power of the domestic currency declines (increases), such that imported foreign goods become more expensive (cheaper). If the real exchange rate falls below zero (as in this case), the domestic currency's relative purchasing power has increased (ie, imported foreign-priced goods become more affordable). (Choice B) 0.9575 results from using the relative inflation rate, instead of price levels, to adjust the nominal exchange rate. (Choice C) 1.1380 results from mistakenly inverting the ratio of foreign to domestic price levels.

explanation_en: Swaps: pricing vs. valuation Definition Method Time horizon Setting terms so contract has an Set fixed rate so present values of payments from Full length of contract from Pricing initial value of zero counterparties are equal initiation Determining contract's value after Determine difference between present values of Remaining life of contract from Valuation initiation fixed and floating payments valuation date Swaps are a type of derivative contract in which counterparties agree to exchange a series of fixed payments for a series of floating payments. Swap pricing refers to setting contract terms so the swap has an initial value of zero and neither counterparty makes a payment at initiation. A swap has a value of zero when the present values of the cash flows of both payment streams (fixed and floating) are equal. The swap's floating payment stream can be replicated as a portfolio of forward contracts that hedge the amounts due for the series of floating payments. The periodic fixed payment is priced or set so it equates the present value of the fixed and floating payment streams at initiation. (Choice A) The amount of cash owed on swap payment dates is the difference between the constant value of the fixed payment and that period's value of the floating payment, based on the market value of the underlying asset. (Choice B) Swap valuation determines the cash payment required to terminate a swap prior to expiration. A swap's value is the difference between the present values of the fixed and floating payment streams remaining until contract expiration.
question_en: Swap pricing most likely refers to:
option_a: determining the amount of cash owed on a swap payment date.
option_b: establishing the amount payable for early termination of a swap.
option_c: setting the contract terms so the swap has an initial value of zero.

explanation_en: Geopolitical tools Tool type Examples Alliances (eg, NATO) National security Armed conflict Espionage Multilateral trade agreements (eg, NAFTA) Economic Nationalization Free exchange of currencies Permitting foreign investments Financial Reducing access to local currency markets Limiting foreign investments Actors often use geopolitical tools to improve or strain relationships with other countries to achieve certain objectives. Generally, there are three types of tools: national security, economic, and financial. The positive (ie, cooperative) use of these tools can improve capital, labor, and economic flows across borders. In contrast, the negative (ie, noncooperative) use of such tools has the opposite effect and may heighten geopolitical risk and worsen investment returns. Governments can apply economic tools to impact the level of cooperation with others globally. One cooperative tool is a multilateral trade agreement. For example, the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) was created to facilitate the cross-border exchange of goods and services among Canada, the US, and Mexico. In contrast, nationalization, which involves the state seizure of a private industry, is a noncooperative economic tool. For example, Britain's government nationalized its steel industry in 1967 to preserve domestic jobs (later re-privatized in 1988). (Choice A) Financial tools mainly pertain to the cross-border movement of currencies and the level of foreign investments. (Choice C) National security tools typically involve alliances, armed conflict, or espionage.

explanation_en:
Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices. Companies often update their inventory values on the
balance sheet to account for such events. US GAAP require companies to report inventory at the lower of historical cost or market value (MV).
When a company reports under US GAAP and uses LIFO as its inventory costing method, MV is the current replacement cost subject to an
upper and lower limit.
The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which is the selling price net of the costs to complete and sell the inventory. In this
scenario, NRV = Selling price − Selling cost − Completion cost, so NRV = 140 − 10 − 30 = 100.
The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin. In this scenario, the lower limit is NRV − Normal profit margin = 100 − 7 = 93.
MV is always the middle number of the replacement cost (RC), upper limit, and lower limit when ranked in order:
If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit.
If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC.
If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit.
In this case, the MV is the RC of $96 per unit since it is within the upper and lower limits and is lower than the historical cost of the inventory.
(Choice B) $100 is the upper limit for MV, which is capped at the upper limit only when RC exceeds the upper limit.
(Choice C) $105 is the company's historical cost. The inventory's NRV is lower than its historical cost, so the NRV should be reported.

explanation_en: A deferred tax liability (DTL) is created when income tax expense (for financial reporting) temporarily exceeds taxes payable (for tax reporting) in a reporting period.  This means that the company pays less taxes in the current period than it reports on its income statement.  Therefore, this temporary "underpayment" generates a DTL that is expected to reverse in a future period. For example, a company may generate a DTL by reporting unrealized gains from holding certain securities on the income statement, but delaying recognition of gains for tax purposes until the securities are sold in a future period. When the securities are sold in the future, the company will report the realized gain as taxable income and reverse the liability. Sometimes a DTL is no longer expected to reverse in the future.  For example, the company may decide to not sell the security and instead own it indefinitely.  When this happens, the company should write off the DTL and increase shareholders' equity by the same amount. (Choice A)  There is no change in total assets.  Total assets equal liabilities plus equity.  In this scenario, the decrease in the DTL is fully offset by the increase in shareholders' equity. (Choice B)  Taxable income is determined by taxable revenues and allowed expenses.  It is not determined by changes to DTL.
question_en: When a deferred tax liability is no longer expected to reverse, which of the following is the most appropriate financial adjustment?  The company should:
option_c: increase shareholders' equity.

explanation_en: Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting Deferred tax asset Income tax expense < Taxes payable Deferred tax liability Income tax expense > Taxes payable Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability A deferred tax asset is created when income tax expense is less than taxes payable.  This means that the company pays more taxes for the current year (as shown on its tax return) than it reports as income tax expense (on its income statement).  This temporary overpayment generates a future tax benefit (ie, deferred tax asset) since this difference is expected to reverse. For example, if the company receives $50,000 in cash before delivering services and the company's tax rate is 20%, then the result is as follows: Since the cash received from the customer (ie, unearned revenue) is recognized as revenue for tax purposes but not for accounting purposes, taxable income is greater than pretax income (ie, accounting profit) and taxes payable is greater than tax expense, which generates a deferred tax asset. (Choice A)  Tax base refers to the value of an asset or liability for tax purposes. (Choice C)  A deferred tax liability is created when deferred tax expense is more than taxes payable.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from trading on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information.  However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form an investment conclusion. This research approach is referred to as the mosaic theory, and it recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information. Conclusions formed through the mosaic process, even when based on information that would be considered material and nonpublic if it were coming directly from a reliable source (eg, the company), do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Lena Schmidt has used public information (eg, financial statements) and nonmaterial nonpublic information (ie, the CEO's flight) to form an investment conclusion using the mosaic approach.  Although Schmidt's conclusion, if true, would be the equivalent of material nonpublic information if disclosed directly to her by the company, her actions do not violate the Standard. (Choice B)  A CEO's travel plan is typically deemed a nonmaterial event (ie, by itself, it would not affect the company's stock price).  Therefore, Schmidt did not need to wait for the company to issue a press release to make the information public. (Choice C)  Analysts are not required to publicly disseminate their research reports.  As long as Schmidt's report was sent to clients in a fair manner, she has not violated the Standard.

explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTA) and deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise from temporary differences between pretax income and taxable income. Compensation in stock is a deductible expense, and for financial reporting, the company deducts the market value of the shares in the period that it accrues the expense.  The company will deduct the value of the shares for tax purposes in the future period when it delivers the shares. The lack of tax deductibility in the current period means that the company pays more taxes than it reports as tax expenses.  This is a temporary difference since the company will pay less tax in the period of delivery than it pays in the current period.  To account for the difference, the company creates a DTA.  This advises investors and analysts that the discrepancy between what the company pays in tax currently and what it reports as tax expense will reverse in a future period. When the discrepancy is permanent (ie, will never reverse), no deferred tax item is created.  The chart below shows items that lead to permanent differences: Major areas resulting in permanent differences between pretax and taxable income Item Impact Reason Interest on state and local government bonds Pretax income > taxable income Interest is tax-free Fines and penalties Fines are tax-deductible Certain entertainment expenses Taxable income > pretax income Not all are fully tax-deductible Certain benefits for senior management Some benefits, such as company-paid premiums on life insurance, are not tax-deductible Companies include interest on municipal (state and local) bonds as revenue for financial reporting, but municipal bond interest is never taxable to the recipient (Choice A).  Similarly, fines imposed by a government agency are deducted as an operating expense for financial reporting, but fines cannot be deducted when calculating taxable income (Choice C).

explanation_en: The capital market line (CML) is the practical form of the capital allocation line (CAL).  The CAL represents theoretical portfolios combining the optimal risky portfolio and a risk-free asset.  The CML replaces the optimal risky portfolio with the real market portfolio (eg, global market index) and uses short-term domestic government bonds (US Treasury bills) in place of the risk-free asset.  All portfolios above the CML are unattainable (gray shaded area). At each level of risk along the CML, there is no combination of assets that can produce a return greater than the return on the CML.  All portfolios below the CML (green shaded area) are attainable but are suboptimal since portfolios along the CML have the highest return at each level of risk (Choices A and B). The CML represents portfolios that hold a combination of the global market index and the US Treasury bills.  The market portfolio is the portfolio on the efficient frontier at the point where a straight line that originates from the risk-free rate is tangent to the efficient frontier.  All portfolios on the CML dominate all other achievable portfolios.
question_en: In relation to other portfolios, unattainable portfolios are located:
option_c: above the capital market line.

explanation_en:
Examining a portfolio's return is only one aspect of evaluating its performance. Another is determining how much risk it took to earn that return. This is accomplished by calculating a risk-adjusted return. In portfolio management, the return is adjusted for risk using either systematic risk (beta) or total risk (standard deviation).

Jensen's alpha is a performance measure that uses beta to determine the portfolio's risk-adjusted excess return. It is the difference between a portfolio's actual return and its risk-adjusted return as predicted by the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). Portfolio X, which has the highest Jensen's alpha, is the best performing portfolio based on its risk-adjusted excess return.

(Choice B) Portfolio Y is the best performing investment evaluated using the Sharpe ratio. The Sharpe ratio determines a portfolio's risk premium (return less risk-free rate) per unit of total risk (standard deviation).

(Choice C) Portfolio Z is the best-performing investment evaluated using the Treynor ratio. The Treynor ratio determines a portfolio's risk premium (return less risk-free rate) per unit of systematic risk (beta).

Things to remember:
Jensen's alpha is the difference between actual return and expected return as predicted by the capital asset pricing model. The portfolio with the highest Jensen's alpha outperforms its peers by having the greatest risk-adjusted excess return.

"Members and Candidates must:
1. Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions.
2. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action."
To reach an investment recommendation, each analyst may take different steps in conducting investment research. However, identifiable criteria should be measured when evaluating the research's quality. Under Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, it is recommended that analysts and supervisors establish policies and procedures that require analysts to substantiate that their research is reasonable.
One recommended procedure is that supervisors should review and approve analysts' claims of a reasonable basis; this should be completed prior to disseminating investment advice. If this is not done it raises uncertainty as to the thoroughness of diligence. Here, Chevela streamlined operations and does not evaluate each analyst's research. Reinstating a review process would lead to a greater level of diligence.

(Choice C) Conducting research with a reasonable basis does not eliminate downside risk since analysts make decisions based on information available at a point in time. The process of coming to the conclusion, not the correctness or consistency of the results, determines whether the research has a reasonable basis.

He also examines the company's financial statements, third-party research, and quantitative forecasts, which he believes cover all important issues. Over the last year, most of his sell recommendations have proven to be wrong. To ensure compliance with Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, the most appropriate recommended action is that:
option_a: Fernandez should exclude internet rumors as part of his research.
option_b: Chevela should reinstate a review process to ensure diligence when making investment recommendations.

Since common-size balance sheet items are proportional to a company's asset value, an analyst could determine whether the company is shifting its asset base to become more liquid. In this scenario, the company's current assets have increased from 44% of the company's asset base to 47%, indicating that it may be shifting to a greater proportion of more liquid assets. (Choice A) Based on the company's common-size balance sheet, its solvency risk measures are declining, suggesting decreasing solvency risk. (Choice C) The company has goodwill on its balance sheet in 20X9 and none in 20X8, suggesting that it made an acquisition during 20X9.

explanation_en:
In equity valuation, free cash flow to equity (FCFE) models estimate a company's intrinsic value as the present value of future cash flows
available for distribution to common shareholders. The starting point for calculating FCFE is cash flow from operations (CFO), which is the net
cash generated from a company's business activities. However, CFO is then adjusted for:
Cash from operations that is not available for distribution to shareholders; and
Cash from another source, not operations, that is available for distribution to shareholders
Cash from operations is unavailable for distribution when it is needed to maintain and invest in fixed assets. Cash may become available from
borrowing, a financing, not operating, activity. Therefore, the determination of FCFE starts with CFO, subtracts cash invested in fixed assets, and
adds cash from net borrowing (ie, financing activities) to derive the cash available for distribution to shareholders.
(Choice A) FCFE is defined as the cash available for distribution to shareholders. The immediate impact of borrowing is additional cash available
for distribution, so net borrowing is added to CFO.
(Choice C) Future share repurchases represent cash distributions to shareholders. Since this is cash that shareholders will receive, it is not
deducted from what is available to them.
question_en: When projecting free cash flow to equity (FCFE) to estimate a stock's intrinsic value, which of the following is subtracted from the company's projected cash flow from operations (CFO)?
option_c: Common stock repurchases

A bond's YTM is an annualized interest rate that can be stated as the product of the periodic rate (ie, the rate per compounding period) and the
periodicity (ie, the assumed number of compounding periods each year). A stated YTM can be easily converted from one periodicity to another
based on the equation above.
The left side of the equation represents the effective annual yield (ie, return) based on 4 compounding periods, whereas the right side of the
equation represents the same effective annual yield based on 12 compounding periods. To make the YTM periodicity conversion, calculate the
effective annual yield on the left side, then adjust that value for 12 compounding periods by raising it to the 12th root to derive the monthly periodic

explanation_en: The price of a putable bond equals the price of an otherwise identical, yet non- putable, bond plus the price of the bond put option. The price of the bond put option increases when interest rate volatility increases. Therefore, the price of the putable bond will rise. The price of a callable bond equals the price of an otherwise identical, yet non-callable, bond minus the price of the bond call option. The price of the bond call option increases when interest rate volatility increases. Therefore, the price of the callable bond will fall. The price of a floating rate bond will not change significantly, especially if the coupon reset dates are not far apart.
question_en: For three otherwise identical bonds, which feature would result in the largest increase in value during a period of rising interest rate volatility?
