explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation.  Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires members and candidates to understand local laws.  When members or candidates do business in more than one country, they are required to know and understand both the Standards of Professional Conduct and the laws and regulations of each country.  In all professional activities, they must follow the strictest of the applicable rules. Telluci does business in both Country Y (where Bull Advisors is based) and Country X (where the new client resides).  Before doing business with the client, Telluci must be familiar with the set of securities laws and regulations in Country X—in addition to those of Country Y and the Code and Standards—so that he knows which rules to apply if a conflict arises.  Without this knowledge, Telluci could not make an informed judgment. (Choices B and C)  Although the rules of Country X are less strict than those of Country Y or the Code and Standards, Telluci violated Standard I(A) by not familiarizing himself with and understanding all the applicable laws and regulations.
question_en: Bull Advisors, based in Country Y, expanded its operations to Country X, where securities laws and regulations are less strict than either CFA Institute's Code and Standards or Country Y's laws and regulations.  One of Bull's advisors, Joseph Telluci, CFA, travels to Country X to meet with a client.  In a rush to meet with the client before she leaves for vacation, Telluci does not familiarize himself with Country X's securities laws and regulations.  After the meeting, he begins the investment management process on behalf of the client based on the laws, regulations, and rules of Country Y and the Code and Standards.  Has Telluci most likely violated Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law?
option_b: No, since he follows the laws of Country Y.
option_c: No, since he adheres to CFA Institute's Standards of Professional Conduct.

explanation_en: If a firm sells more than it collects, accounts receivable will increase. If a firm pays suppliers more than it purchases, accounts payable will decrease.
question_en: What is the impact on accounts receivable if sales exceed cash collections and what is the impact on accounts payable if cash paid to suppliers exceeds purchases?
option_b: Both accounts payable and accounts receivable will increase.
option_c: Only accounts receivable will increase.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Under Standard VI(C), Members and Candidates must notify clients of the benefits they obtain for receiving a referral.  When an adviser's referral arrangements are disclosed, prospective clients may evaluate the adviser's objectivity. All referral arrangements between an employee and employer or an employee and a third party must be disclosed.  Clem Benson does not violate the Standard since both Sterling Hospital and the past contributors being referred to Benson are aware of the referral structure. (Choice B)  Benson may receive cash from the referral arrangement since the clients are informed of the referral structure. (Choice C)  Benson is permitted to construct any legally allowable referral arrangement, including one that generates a tax benefit.  Since the referral structure is disclosed, he does not violate the Standard.
question_en: Clem Benson, CFA, is the chief investment officer at Sterling Hospital.  Sterling's board asks Benson for fundraising ideas.  Benson suggests that if Sterling refers past contributors to him, he will conduct a personalized investment review for a fee of $1,000.  In return, Benson will donate 50% of that fee to Sterling.  After receiving board approval, Sterling promotes the fundraising campaign to its past contributors, informs them of Benson's arrangement, and refers 50 clients to Benson.  The fundraiser raises $25,000 for Sterling.  According to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, has Benson most likely violated the Standard?
option_b: Yes, since Benson receives income from the referrals.
option_c: Yes, since Benson receives the tax deduction for the donation instead of the contributors.

explanation_en: Companies with complex capital structures (ie, potentially dilutive securities) may report a diluted EPS that is different from its basic EPS. Dilutive securities, such as convertible debt, are convertible into shares of common stock.  Companies issue additional common shares upon conversion, thus increasing the number of shares outstanding and reducing EPS.  Under the if-converted method, diluted EPS is calculated assuming that conversion occurred at the beginning of the year. If the company had converted its convertible bonds at the beginning of the period to common shares, it would not have paid after-tax interest expense of HKD 6 million for the year.  Therefore, it is added back to net income in the diluted EPS numerator.  Furthermore, the company would have issued 10 million additional common shares, which increases the denominator and dilutes the EPS to HKD 1.95. (Choice B)  2.00 is the basic EPS. (Choice C)  2.11 results from subtracting the new common shares in the denominator, instead of adding.
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a company for the most recent fiscal year:

- annual net income: HKD 500 million
- weighted average common shares outstanding: 250 million
- convertible debt outstanding: HKD 100 million at 9% interest, convertible into 10 million common shares
- tax rate: 33.33%

If there are no other dilutive securities, then diluted EPS (in HKD) is closest to:

explanation_en: Bootstrap mimics the random sampling process by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from the original sample and treating it as if it were the population, without requiring analytical formulas or guaranteeing all items appear.
question_en: The bootstrap resampling method:
option_a: guarantees that all items will appear in the resamples.
option_b: relies on an analytical formula to estimate the distribution of the estimators.
option_c: mimics the random sampling process by treating the randomly drawn sample as if it were the population.

explanation_en: According to Standard VII(A), Shah violated the standard by mentioning there were no calculation questions on derivatives, which is information that cannot be disclosed by candidates sitting for an exam, while Standard VII(B) regarding misrepresentation of CFA membership was not violated.
question_en: What conduct should Shah follow regarding reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA program?
option_a: reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA program only.
option_b: both conduct as participants in CFA Institute programs and reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA program.
option_c: both conduct as participants in CFA Institute programs and reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA program.

explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV Duties to Employers addresses the Member or Candidate's responsibilities as an employee.  Standard IV(A) Loyalty notes that Members and Candidates must try to protect the interests of their employer and avoid actions that may harm those interests. Before leaving an employer, a Member or Candidate must follow its policies and procedures for notifying clients and must not make any attempt to solicit clients for another firm.  After leaving an employer, the Member or Candidate can solicit former clients as long as the contact information used is not the property of the former employer. In this case, Ostrovsky did not mention either his departure from BII or his future plans to his BII clients before leaving BII, and he did not use BII's proprietary data to contact them, so he has not violated the Standard (Choices B and C).
question_en: Andrei Ostrovsky, CFA has been employed as an advisor at Bolshoi Investments Inc. (BII) for several years.  His employment agreement does not include a "noncompete" clause or termination policies.  Ostrovsky decides to leave BII and start a new advisory firm.  Prior to giving notice to his employer, Ostrovsky spends a few weekends setting up his new office.  There he "connects" with as many of his clients as he can on social media, which is easy as he knows their names.  Before leaving BII, he does not mention his departure from BII or his plans for his new firm to any client, on or off social media.  One day after leaving BII, he posts a notice on a social media site that he has left BII and that he would be happy to continue to advise his former clients at his new firm.  With regards to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, has Ostrovsky most likely violated the Standard?
option_b: Yes, by soliciting business from BII's clients
option_c: Yes, by "connecting" with BII's clients while still employed by BII

explanation_en: The Gordon growth model is particularly appropriate for valuing dividend-paying companies that are relatively insensitive to the business cycle and in a mature growth phase, such as electric utilities.
question_en: The Gordon growth model is most appropriate for valuing the equity of a dividend-paying:
option_c: automobile manufacturer.

explanation_en: Sovereign credit analysis Sovereign debt factors Nonsovereign debt factors Basic institutional systems and risks Cash on balance sheet Economic growth prospects Operating cash flow International position and reputation Ability to pay Bank credit Access to external liquidity Asset sales Fiscal and monetary policies Raise debt/equity capital Debt burden Forced bankruptcy Sovereign immunity allows a Asset seizures Willingness to pay government to avoid legal remedies Personal liability/reputation to force debt repayment Business dissolution At a high level, sovereign credit analysis begins with an assessment of a country's ability to pay and willingness to pay. A unique feature of sovereign credits is sovereign immunity, which is the inability of investors to force debt repayment through legal means. Factors to consider when assessing a country's willingness to pay include the following: Respect for the rule of law Level of government corruption Governmental checks and balances Universal property rights Prior commitment to pay debts (Choices B and C) High-yield corporate and nonsovereign revenue bonds are issued by entities that can be forced through legal means to honor their debts. This does not mean that investors will always be repaid in full, only that legal remedies (eg, bankruptcy laws) are available.
question_en: If an investor is most concerned about being able to legally enforce payment of principal and interest in the event of default, which of the following bonds represents the least appropriate investment choice?
option_c: Nonsovereign revenue

explanation_en: The interquartile range (IQR) is the difference between the third quartile and the first quartile, or IQR = Q₃ - Q₁ = 93 - 11 = 82.
question_en: An analyst calculates the following statistics for a sample with 100 observations: The interquartile range of the sample is equal to:

explanation_en: Normally, options with greater time to expiration are worth more than otherwise identical options that are nearer to expiration. However, in some circumstances, this relationship may not hold for European puts. For example, if the price of the underlying asset goes to zero, the European put with less time to expiration may be worth more because the put holder will receive the exercise price earlier.
question_en: Compared to an otherwise identical European put option, one that has a longer time to expiration:
option_a: must be worth more than the put that is nearer to expiration.
option_b: must be worth at least as much as the put that is nearer to expiration.
option_c: may be worth less than the put that is nearer to expiration.

explanation_en: CAPM has several assumptions around investors and the investment market. It assumes markets are frictionless (no transactions costs), prices are not affected by trades, investments are infinitely divisible, and that investors are risk averse, seek to maximize utility, act rationally, plan using the same time period, and have the same expectations of a security's returns.
question_en: Which of the following is an assumption of the Capital Asset Pricing Model?
option_c: Investors have heterogeneous expectations.

explanation_en: In the case of trusts or endowments, the member must be aware that his fiduciary responsibility is not necessarily to the client (who hired him) but to the beneficiaries of the investment account. By routinely executing trades directed by Ross without making a determination that the securities transactions are consistent with the investment goals and constraints of Ross's mother, the account beneficiary, Ross has violated Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Ross has likely also violated other Standards (e.g., Standard III(C) Suitability and Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis). Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity deals primarily with conflicts resulting from gifts, compensation, or benefits that may compromise the member's independence and objectivity.
question_en: Ronald Rice, CFA, is the investment manager for a trust established for Selma Ross's mother. Ross selected Rice after interviewing several potential managers. From time to time, Ross calls Rice and asks him to purchase or sell shares in specific firms. Rice routinely complies with these requests without determining suitability for the trust. By doing so, Rice has most likely:
option_a: violated the Standard concerning loyalty, prudence, and care.
option_b: violated the Standard concerning independence and objectivity.
option_c: not violated the Code and Standards because he has followed the client’s request.

explanation_en: The time-weighted returns are what they are and will not be affected by cash inflows or outflows. The money-weighted return is susceptible to distortions resulting from cash inflows and outflows. The money-weighted return will be biased upward if the funds are invested just prior to a period of favorable performance and will be biased downward if funds are invested just prior to a period of relatively unfavorable performance. The opposite will be true for cash outflows.
question_en: Which of the following is most accurate with respect to the relationship of the money- weighted return to the time-weighted return? If funds are contributed to a portfolio just prior to a period of favorable performance, the:
option_a: money-weighted rate of return will tend to be depressed.
option_b: money-weighted rate of return will tend to be elevated.
option_c: time-weighted rate of return will tend to be elevated.

explanation_en: According to the GIPS standards, verification is performed with respect to an entire firm, not on specific composites, making Statement 3 correct and Statement 2 incorrect; Statement 1 is incorrect because verification is voluntary, not mandatory.
question_en:
Which of the following statements is accurate according to the GIPS standards?

Statement 1: A firm must perform verification to claim compliance with the GIPS standards.
Statement 2: Verification ensures accuracy of specific composite presentations.
Statement 3: Verification is performed with respect to an entire firm.
option_c: Statement 3

explanation_en: According to GIPS standards, only a firm managing assets can claim compliance once it has satisfied all applicable requirements, and a pension fund managing investments for its beneficiaries can claim compliance with GIPS standards.
question_en: Which of the following entities can claim compliance with the GIPS standards?
option_a: A pension fund that manages investments for its beneficiaries
option_b: An investment consulting firm that focuses on enabling clients to self-manage their investments
option_c: A vendor that offers software products designed to help firms achieve compliance with the GIPS standards

explanation_en: Fiscal policy can be used as a tool for redistribution of income and wealth, through a variety of taxation and spending policies.
question_en: Policies that can be used as tools for redistribution of wealth and income include:
option_a: both scal policy and monetary policy.
option_c: monetary policy only.

explanation_en: In the GICS each company is assigned to a sub-industry according to its principal business activity, with a hierarchical structure from sub-industry to industry to group to sector.
question_en: The Global Industry Classification Standard's broadest level of classification is a(n):
option_c: industry group

explanation_en: Portfolio Z has a beta of 1.3 and its required return can be calculated as 7.0% + 1.3 × (13.0% − 7.0%) = 14.8%. Because it plots on the SML, its expected (forecast) return and required return are equal. The SML plots beta (systematic risk) versus expected equilibrium (required) return. The analyst believes that Portfolio Y is overvalued – any portfolio located below the SML has a forecast return less than its required return and is overpriced in the market. Since Portfolio X plots above the SML, it is undervalued and the statement should read, "Portfolio X's required return is less than its forecast return."
question_en: Consider the following graph of the Security Market Line (SML). The letters X, Y, and Z represent risky asset portfolios and an analyst's forecast for their returns over the next period. The SML crosses the y-axis at 0.07. The expected market return is 13.0%. Using the graph above and the information provided, the analyst most likely believes that:
option_a: Portfolio X's required return is greater than its forecast return.
option_c: the expected return for Portfolio Z is 14.8%.

explanation_en: Financial reports that are of low quality make it difficult or impossible for users of the statements to assess the quality of the firm's earnings, cash flows, and balance sheet values.
question_en: If a firm's financial reports are of low quality, can users of the reports assess the quality of the firm's earnings?
option_a: No, because low-quality financial reports are not useful for assessing the quality of earnings.
option_b: Yes, because users can assess earnings quality independently of financial reporting quality.
option_c: Yes, because if financial reports are of low quality, earnings are also of low quality.

explanation_en: The lower bound on a European put option is always zero or positive, but can never be negative. The lower bound is greater than zero or the difference between the present value of the exercise price and the underlying asset price (pt ≥ Max[0, X(1 + Rf)−(T–t) – St].
question_en: Which of the following statements about the lower bound on a European put option is correct?
option_a: The lower bound can only be negative for deep out-of-the-money puts.
option_b: The lower bound is always zero.
option_c: The lower bound cannot exceed the difference between the present value of the exercise price and the underlying asset price.

explanation_en: According to Standard I (C), Misrepresentation, by showing only balanced account results and failing to disclose underperforming accounts, Luminon violated the standard requiring full disclosure of investment performance data.
question_en: Jordan Kope, CFA, is an analyst with a hedge fund and works closely with Deepa Bose who earned her CFA designation 15 years ago. Kope becomes aware that Bose uses her CFA designation even though she no longer pays her membership dues. During several meetings that Bose and Kope have with the firm's clients, Bose emphasizes that all her team members, including herself, are CFA charterholders. To be consistent with the Standards, Kope should:
option_a: only dissociate himself from activities involving Bose.
option_b: only report Bose's conduct to the fund's compliance department.
option_c: dissociate himself from activities involving Bose and report Bose's conduct to the fund's compliance department.

explanation_en: Call protection in the context of a CMBS refers to protection against prepayment risk. Structuring a CMBS with a residual (equity or first-loss) tranche provides investors in the senior tranches with CMBS-level call protection. Prepayment lockout periods and yield maintenance charges are examples of loan-level call protection because they apply to the individual loans.
question_en: In a commercial mortgage-backed security (CMBS), which of the following is an example of CMBS-level call protection?
option_c: Yield maintenance charges.

explanation_en: Hedge fund investor redemption restrictions Minimum time an investor is committed to the Lockup period fund before withdrawals are allowed Usually less than 2 years Requires investor to notify the fund of Redemption notice period planned redemption Usually 30−90 days Hedge funds commonly use leverage to implement investment strategies by borrowing from a prime broker. If the equity value of the account drops below a minimum level, a margin call is issued. The fund is then forced to reduce its leverage, usually by liquidating existing positions. Margin calls can magnify losses for a hedge fund since the forced liquidation creates a negative feedback loop: the selling forced by the margin call drives the price down even more, leading to investor redemptions, which force more selling, etc. Redemption notices and lockup periods help protect a hedge fund from investor redemptions that would further worsen its position. In this scenario, most if not all investors in the recently launched hedge fund will be subject to a lockup period, restricting withdrawals immediately following their initial investments. (Choice A) A drawdown is a reduction in a hedge fund's net asset value below the high-water mark, not a helpful development during a margin call. (Choice C) Committed capital refers to an amount the limited partners in a private equity (PE) fund (ie, not a hedge fund), agree to provide the fund upon request to finance a new investment. The PE fund will draw down this capital commitment, usually over 3 to 5 years.
question_en: A recently launched hedge fund that is subject to a prime broker's margin call will most likely benefit from a:
option_c: committed capital drawdown.

explanation_en: An economic contraction (recession) is typically characterized by decreasing inflationary pressures, increasing unemployment, and low or negative real GDP growth.
question_en: During an economic contraction:
option_b: real GDP growth is greater than its sustainable long-term rate.
option_c: the unemployment rate typically decreases.

explanation_en: Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs prohibits members and candidates from providing confidential information about the exam even after the conclusion of the exam.
question_en: Stephanie Irons, a Level II CFA candidate, regularly posts in internet chat rooms dedicated to candidates studying for the Level II exam. Throughout the season, she and other candidates discuss curriculum content in great detail. Three days after her exam window ends, she returns to the site and vents her frustrations over complicated exam questions by posting questions she remembers on the site, and asking others for their responses and reasoning. Other candidates follow suit and post the questions they remember. Irons and her fellow candidates are most likely:
option_a: in violation of the Code and Standards for discussing curriculum content in a public forum prior to the exam.
option_b: not in violation because the information about the actual exam contents was posted after the close of the exam window.
option_c: in violation of the Code and Standards for providing confidential information about the exam.

explanation_en: A stop 20, market sell order will sell the position at $20/share or under, at all prices, at the market; if the price falls to or below $20, the market order becomes valid and executes immediately at the best available price.
question_en: An investor owns a stock trading at $22 per share and would like to place an order to sell the position should the stock ever trade at or below $20 per share. The order most likely is:
option_c: stop 20, limit 20 sell.

explanation_en: The path that a bond's price follows over its maturity assuming the yield is held constant is known as the constant yield price trajectory. In this case it is being held constant at 8%. Given the bond is sold at a premium (coupon > YTM), its price will decrease as it moves toward par value. Price at issuance: N = 10; FV = 1,000; PMT = 100; I = 8; CPT → PV = 1,134 Price after one year: N = 9; FV = 1,000; PMT = 100; I = 8; CPT → PV = 1,125
question_en: Consider a 10%, 10-year bond sold to yield 8%. If after one year the bond has followed its constant yield price trajectory, its price will most likely have:
option_c: remained constant.

explanation_en: The optimal portfolio for each investor is the highest indifference curve that is tangent to the efficient frontier. The optimal portfolio is the portfolio that gives the investor the greatest possible utility.
question_en: The particular portfolio on the efficient frontier that best suits an individual investor is determined by:
option_b: the current market risk-free rate as compared to the current market return rate.
option_c: the individual's asset allocation plan.

explanation_en: Capital adequacy is a monetary measure of a firm's risk as a percentage of its equity capital. The comparison of a bank's liquid assets to certain named liabilities is known as the liquid asset requirement. The ratio of a bank's liabilities to its central bank reserves refers to the bank's reserve requirements.
question_en: Which of the following is the most accurate definition of capital adequacy in the context of financial analysis of banks?
option_a: The ratio of a bank’s liabilities to its central bank reserves.
option_b: A comparison of a bank’s liquid assets to certain named liabilities.
option_c: A monetary measure of a rm’s risk as a percentage of its equity capital.

explanation_en:
Nominal return is the expected return on an asset. Three factors influence nominal return: the risk-free rate, the inflation rate, and the risk
premium. Most investors estimate these factors, resulting in varying nominal return figures. The risk-free rate is the return received by investors
who take no risk. The risk premium is the additional return an investor receives for investing in a risky asset. The inflation rate is the percent
change in the cost of a basket of goods over time.
The nominal return (expected annual return) of equities is given at 8%. Since the return on short-term government bonds is the optimal proxy for
the risk-free rate, it can be used here to find the current inflation rate. Using the other given information, rearrange the nominal return formula to
solve for the missing variable.
(Choice A) This option incorrectly calculates inflation using the expected return on certificates of deposit as a proxy for the risk-free rate.
Certificates of deposit are bank-issued investments; they do not have the full faith and credit of the United States. This is not the best proxy for the
risk-free rate.
(Choice C) This choice calculates the inflation rate using the expected return on commercial paper. Commercial paper is a company-issued,
short-term fixed income investment. This investment is subject to more risks than affect government securities. The expected return of
commercial paper is not the best proxy for the risk-free rate and overstates the inflation rate.
question_en:
A manager is concerned about the current inflation rate and gathers the following information:

| Investment Type | Expected annual return (%) |
|---|---|
| Certificates of deposit | 1.8 |
| Treasury bills | 2.3 |
| Commercial paper | 2.8 |
| Equities | 8.0 |

If the equity risk premium is 3.5%, what is the current inflation rate?

explanation_en: The slope of the efficient frontier decreases steadily as risk and return increase. The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios with the greatest expected return for a given level of risk as measured by standard deviation of returns. That is, for a given level of risk, an expected return greater than that of the portfolio on the efficient frontier is not attainable, and a portfolio with a lower expected return is inefficient.
question_en: Which of the following statements about the efficient frontier is least accurate?
option_a: A portfolio that plots above efficient frontier is not attainable, while a portfolio that plots below the efficient frontier is inefficient.
option_b: The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios with the greatest expected return for a given level of risk.
option_c: The slope of the efficient frontier increases steadily as risk increases.

A callable bond can be analyzed as a package comprising two elements: the schedule of coupon and principal payments over the bond's
scheduled life and a call option giving the issuer the right to purchase (ie, call) the bond prior to its maturity. The option creates uncertainty about
the bond's future cash flows.
Even assuming no default, the cash flows on a callable bond are uncertain due to the possibility of early retirement. Of the choices, only effective
duration addresses the uncertainty regarding the length of time over which the bond will pay cash flows. It is necessary to value the embedded
option to address how future interest rate fluctuations may impact the bond's cash flows.
(Choices B and C) Modified and Macaulay durations can be calculated only for a stream of cash flows for a fixed time period. These duration
measures are not accurate measures for callable bonds, given the cash flow uncertainty introduced by the embedded call option.
question_en: A bond matures in 20 years and is callable at the issuer's option any time after the first call date in 3 years. Which of the following types of duration is most appropriate for quantifying the bond's interest rate risk?
option_c: Macaulay

explanation_en: Shares issued post-split need not be adjusted for the split as they are already "new" shares. Options with an exercise price greater than the average share price do not affect diluted EPS.
question_en: Which of the following statements about the calculation of earnings per share (EPS) is least accurate?
option_a: Shares issued after a stock split must be adjusted for the split.
option_b: Reacquired shares are excluded from the computation from the date of reacquisition.
option_c: Options outstanding may have no effect on diluted EPS.

explanation_en: Eurobond market Market Part of international bond market outside national markets' jurisdiction Currency denomination Major currency (usually not issuer's domestic currency) Valuation Issuance currency's benchmark rate + Yield spread reflecting issuer's credit risk and issue's liquidity risk The market value of a bond is the PV of the coupon and principal amounts discounted by the appropriate market interest rate for the bond's currency denomination.  An interest rate in the same currency must be used since it represents the opportunity cost of debt capital in that currency.  The specific rate used to value the bond is based on the currency's benchmark (eg, government bond, interest rate swap) rate, adjusted for any risk factors (eg, credit, liquidity) that are appropriate for the bond. A bond's market yield is the market discount rate used for valuing the bond's cash flows.  Therefore, the market yield on US dollar-denominated emerging market sovereign debt, as in this case, is primarily determined by US dollar interest rates regardless of where the bonds are issued. (Choice A)  Euro interest rates are used to value euro-denominated securities but have no direct effect on the value of bonds denominated in other currencies.  The Eurobond market is a segment of the global fixed-income securities markets that consists of debt issued outside the jurisdiction of any single country. (Choice C)  An emerging market's domestic interest rates are the primary determinant of the country's sovereign debt yield if the bond is denominated in that country's currency, regardless of where the debt is issued.  However, in this scenario, the bonds are US dollar-denominated.
question_en: The biggest determinant of market yields on US dollar-denominated emerging market sovereign debt issued in the Eurobond markets is:
option_c: the emerging market's domestic interest rates.

explanation_en: A portfolio manager can decrease or increase exposure to the risk and return of a market index. The issuer of a fixed-rate obligation can change risk exposure by converting to a floating- rate obligation. Converting from a fixed-rate to a floating-rate obligation does not necessarily mean increasing risk, especially if market interest rates are falling, for example.
question_en: Which of the following statements regarding the use of derivatives is most accurate?
option_a: A portfolio manager can decrease exposure to the risk and return of a market index.
option_b: The issuer of a fixed-rate obligation can increase risk exposure by converting to a floating-rate obligation.
option_c: A manufacturer can hedge the exchange risk of anticipated receipts or payments.

explanation_en: Because of the impact of income taxes, a profitable company that accounts for inventory using LIFO will have higher total cash flow than a profitable company that uses FIFO. The company that uses LIFO will have higher cost of goods sold, resulting in lower net income and thus lower taxes. The other statements are accurate: A company that issues common stock is not required to pay dividends (which would reduce cash flow from financing). Thus, it may have the same CFF as a firm that issues debt since interest paid on debt is a component of CFO. When a company issues bonds at a premium, the proceeds raised at issuance (CFF inflow) are greater than the par value repaid at maturity (CFF outflow). For bonds issued at par, the CFF inflow at issuance is equal to the CFF outflow at maturity.
question_en: Assuming US GAAP is applies, which of the following statements about accounting procedures and their impact on the statement of cash flows is least valid? All else equal:
option_a: A company that finances through common stock issues may have the same cash flow from financing (CFF) as a firm that issues debt.
option_b: A nonprofitable company that uses LIFO to account for inventory will have higher total cash flow than a nonprofitable company that uses FIFO during a period of rising prices.
option_c: Cash flow from financing (CFF) is higher over the life of a bond if a firm issues the bond at a premium, compared to issuing the bond at par.

explanation_en: In common markets, member countries remove all the restrictions regarding import-export goods and services, adopt a standard set of trade restrictions on non-members, and remove barriers to labor and capital goods movement among members. However, members do not adopt common economic policies. A is incorrect. A monetary union is basically two or more governments coming together and agreeing to share a common currency. B is incorrect. In an economic union, members adopt common economic policies on regulating products, capital and labor, and freedom of movement of goods and services.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely a trade agreement in which barriers on the movement of labor and capital goods among members are removed, but members do not adopt common economic policies?
option_c: Common markets.

explanation_en: Forwards and futures are similar in that they are both firm commitments to purchase or sell an asset at a specified time in the future. However, futures have a daily settlement of gains or losses. In contrast, the gain or loss to a forward contract occurs at contract expiration. If futures prices and interest rates are negatively correlated, futures prices rise when rates are falling. This means that holders of long futures positions reinvest daily gains at lower interest rates. Conversely, as futures prices decline, the losses on long futures positions are financed at higher rates. As a result, long futures positions are at a disadvantage compared with long forward positions. Consequently, under these conditions, futures prices will be less than the prices of equivalent forwards, reflecting the relative disadvantage of futures to forwards. Moreover, volatility increases whatever differential exists between forward prices and futures prices, so in this case an increase in interest rate volatility means an increase in the price of forward contracts relative to the price of futures contracts (Choices A and C).
question_en: If interest rates are negatively correlated with futures prices, an increase in interest rate volatility most likely increases the prices of:
option_c: futures and forwards equally.

The I-spread is the difference between the yield-to-maturity (YTM) of a given bond and the interbank lending benchmark rate with the same
time-to-maturity. A benchmark rate is a broad market measure that reflects macroeconomic risk factors. The I-spread over different times-to-
maturity indicates the term structure of spreads since the spreads differ across times-to-maturity.
To determine the I-spread of a bond, the YTM of the bond should be calculated first. In this scenario:
The periodicity (m) of the bond is 2 since the coupons are semiannual.
The number of periods is therefore 10 = (m × n = 2 × 5).
The periodic coupon payment is 3 = [(0.06 ÷ 2) × 100] since the bond's annual coupon is 6%, paid semiannually.
The present value is the price of the bond, 78.3.
The periodic discount rate is determined, using a financial calculator, according to the following formula:
The periodicity of the bond is 2, so multiplying the periodic discount rate (r) by 2 will determine the annual YTM: YTM = r × m = 5.94 × 2 = 11.88%.
The I-spread is the difference between the YTM of the bond and the interbank lending benchmark rate with the same time-to-maturity, 4.83%.
Therefore, the I-spread is 11.88 − 4.83 = 7.05%

The weight of an asset in a market-capitalization-weighted (ie, market-cap-weighted) index is the market cap of the individual asset divided by the sum of the market caps of all the assets in the index. The market cap of an asset is the product of the price of the asset and the number of shares outstanding. Dividends and end of period prices are not used in the calculation of an asset's weight in a market-cap-weighted index at the beginning of the period.

Substituting the above values into the formula:

Market-cap weight of Asset X = 100(€100) / [100(€100) + 200(€48) + 300(€80)] = 10,000/43,600 = 23%

The value of Asset X in the index is the product of its weight in the index and the index value:

23% × €1,000 = €230

(Choice B) €333 is the value of Asset X in an equal-weighted index.
(Choice C) €439 is the value of Asset X in a price-weighted index: €100 ÷ (€100 + €48 + €80) × €1,000 = €439.

Things to remember:
In a market-capitalization-weighted index, weight is apportioned to each asset based on market capitalization. Market cap is the product of shares outstanding and share price. The value of an asset in the index is the product of its weight in the index and the index value.

explanation_en: Secured debt is backed by a claim (ie, lien) on specific assets pledged as collateral. Secured creditors have the most senior claim on the cash flows and assets of a company. As a type of secured debt, a second lien obligation is ranked ahead of all unsecured creditors and equity holders. Secured creditors' claims are paid first in any liquidation or obtain the highest recovery rates in a bankruptcy reorganization. In the case of a second lien obligation, first lienholders have a prior claim on the assets pledged as collateral. However, the collateral value is typically significantly greater than the original value of the claims of all lienholders. Should the collateral prove inadequate to cover the entire debt, secured creditors are ranked equally with senior unsecured creditors for the balance of their claims. (Choice B) Senior unsecured creditors are ranked ahead of all other unsecured creditors and all equity holders. However, senior unsecured creditors rank behind the secured creditors, including second and third lienholders, with respect to any asset pledged as collateral. (Choice C) Senior subordinated creditors are junior to the other listed creditor classes. Although senior to other subordinated creditors and equity holders, senior subordinated lenders have the lowest recovery rate among the categories of creditors shown here.

explanation_en: Inventory write-downs and reversals When to write down When to reverse a write-down Maximum reversal US GAAP (FIFO, weighted average) Net realizable value < cost Reversals prohibited N/A US GAAP (LIFO, retail inventory) Market value < cost Reversals prohibited N/A IFRS Net realizable value < cost Net realizable value > carrying value Amount of write-down Inventory costs may decline due to spoilage, obsolescence, or reduced selling prices.  Companies reporting under IFRS and US GAAP using any inventory valuation method other than the LIFO and retail inventory methods must value their inventory at the lower of cost and net realizable value.  Net realizable value is the estimated selling price in the normal course of business less the costs to complete the sales of inventory. If the net realizable value of a company's inventory becomes lower than its cost, the company must write down the inventory to its net realizable value.  At the same time, the company must increase COGS by the same amount.  This becomes the inventory's new carrying value. Under US GAAP, reversals of write-downs are prohibited.  Therefore, in this scenario, the company should do nothing even though the net realizable value of its inventory rose above its carrying cost following the write-down.  It should not reduce COGS. Under IFRS, write-downs can be reversed in subsequent periods if net realizable value rises above the new carrying value.  However, a reversal cannot exceed the value of the write-down (Choices B and C).

A fund of funds (FoF) is a hedge fund that invests in other hedge funds. Hedge funds often levy both a management fee and an incentive fee.
The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund's end-of-period assets under management (AUM) and is assessed
regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits either gross (ie, before deduction) or net (ie, after deduction) of management
fees.
If fees are calculated independently, calculations are on a gross basis.
An incentive fee is often contingent on profits being greater than a hurdle rate and/or the AUM being above a high-water mark (HWM), which is
the base asset value used to calculate the incentive fee. The HWM represents the fund's previous peak AUM value that has already earned an
incentive fee.
The FoF's fees and return are calculated (with year-end values and fees in € millions) as follows:
Steps Calculations
Calculate the FoF's year-end asset value 49 + 55 + 58 = 162
Calculate management fee 162 × 0.01 = 1.62
Calculate HWM-adjusted incentive fee base 162 − 152 = 10.0
Calculate incentive fee 10.0 × 0.10 = 1.00
Total fee paid to FoF 1.62 + 1.00 = 2.62
In this scenario, the total fee paid to the FoF is €2.62 million.
(Choice A) A total fee of €2.46 million results from calculating the incentive fee on a net basis.
(Choice B) A total of €2.50 million results from inappropriately using beginning AUM to calculate the management fee.

explanation_en:
Quote-driven markets are also called dealer, price-driven, and over-the-counter (OTC) markets. In quote-driven markets, dealers provide
liquidity (ie, make markets) by standing ready to trade at their quoted prices. Most trades are between customers and dealers. Buyers must pay
the price the dealer is willing to sell for (ie, ask or offer price), and sellers must accept the price the dealer is willing to buy at (ie, bid price). Almost
all currency and bond trading as well as OTC stock trading occurs in quote-driven markets.
(Choice B) In order-driven markets, customer buy and sell orders are matched based on price priority and time precedence. All automated
trading systems and nearly all exchanges use order-driven systems.
(Choice C) Brokered markets are those in which brokers search for willing counterparties on behalf of customers. Assets traded in brokered
markets typically share several or all the following characteristics: expensive, unique, trade infrequently, and/or difficult to hold in inventory (eg,
large blocks of stock, fine art masterpieces, real estate).
question_en: Which of the following best describes a quote-driven market?
option_a: Dealers and customers trade at dealer bid or ask prices
option_b: Customer buy and sell orders are matched based on price and time precedence
option_c: Brokers search for willing counterparties on behalf of customers seeking to buy or sell

explanation_en: Dealers in the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives market act as the counterparty for participants who want to buy or sell derivatives. Dealers provide liquidity by quoting what they will pay for a derivative (ie, bid price) and a price to sell the same derivative (ie, ask price). The ask price is higher than the bid price and the spread is the difference between the ask and bid prices. Dealers may try to maintain a "flat" position (ie, long positions netted against short positions). If successful, their return consists of the spread between the bid and ask prices. However, market conditions can force dealers into a net long or short position, which exposes them to risk. Their assumption of risk distinguishes them from brokers, who facilitate transactions between two parties. Brokers do not hold positions, so they do not assume any risk. Brokers earn a commission for their services, but a dealer's spread is not a commission (Choice B). Dealers can also earn returns from intentionally taking on risk by establishing a long or short derivative position. This would occur if they believe that the price of the underlying will move favorably, which makes the derivative more valuable (Choice C).
question_en: The source of return for a derivatives dealer in the over-the-counter market is least likely to be:
option_b: dealer transactions at the bid-ask spread.
option_c: gains on the derivative caused by gains in the underlying.

application of the Z-spread concept, which requires the entire benchmark curve's spot rates, not just a single period's YTM.

explanation_en: Rejection of a null hypothesis when it is actually true is a Type I error. Here, H o : μ ≤ 18 inches and H : μ > 18 inches. Type II error is failing to reject a null hypothesis when it is a actually false. Because a Type I error can only occur if the null hypothesis is true, and a Type II error can only occur if the null hypothesis is false, it is logically impossible for a test to result in both types of error at the same time.

explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Central banks have different primary policy objectives, but one common goal is price stability. Central banks attempt to achieve this stability by influencing money supply levels with one or more monetary policy tools. When a central bank expects inflation to rise above the target, it would most appropriately seek to curb inflation by implementing a contractionary monetary policy. To accomplish this, the central bank can target an increase in commercial banks' lending rates by increasing its policy rate above the neutral rate. Commercial banks tend to base their lending rates on the policy rate plus a spread. Therefore, a higher policy rate would cause those banks to either raise their lending rates or accept lower margins, thus discouraging lending and borrowing. Less supply and demand for business and consumer loans would slow capital expenditures and consumption. In theory, these effects should lower inflationary pressures. (Choice B) Buying government bonds from commercial banks is an expansionary monetary policy that gives those banks more excess reserves to lend. This policy would be inappropriate if the goal is to reduce inflationary pressures. (Choice C) Lowering the reserve requirement for commercial banks encourages those banks to lend more money. This expansionary monetary policy would be inappropriate if the goal is to reduce inflationary pressures.
question_en: If the inflation rate is expected to rise above a central bank's inflation target, that central bank's most appropriate action would be to:
option_a: increase the policy rate above the neutral rate.
option_b: buy government bonds from commercial banks.
option_c: lower the reserve requirement for commercial banks.

explanation_en:
Characteristics of security market indexes
Represent and track the value of a given security market, market
segment, or asset class
Typically constructed as a portfolio of marketable securities
Valued on a regular basis using actual or estimated prices of
constituent securities
A security market index (eg, S&P 500, Hang Seng) is a representation of specified security market, a market segment, or an asset class.
Indexes can be designed to represent a broad universe of securities (eg, the equity market) or a narrow subsection of a specific security market
(eg, U.S. mid-cap growth stocks).
An index is usually constructed and managed as a portfolio of individual marketable securities (ie, constituent securities). The value of an
index is the combination of the value of the constituent securities, weighted by the creator of the index. The securities may represent nearly all of
the index's universe or just a sample.
(Choice A) Security market indexes are valued on a regular basis. Most high-profile indexes are updated in real time as the prices of the
underlying securities update.
(Choice B) Security market indexes can be valued using constituent securities' estimated prices when actual prices are not available. Estimated
prices are more likely to be used for assets that are not priced regularly or are illiquid (eg, bonds).

explanation_en: Replication combines an asset and a derivative to form a portfolio that is economically identical to a completely different asset.  Buying a share of stock and selling a stock futures contract produces the same economic result as buying a risk-free bond.  Logically, this makes sense: The stock/futures contract portfolio guarantees the price the investor receives (ie, eliminates price risk), so the portfolio's expected return is the risk-free interest rate.  Rearranging terms, buying a share of stock is equivalent to buying a risk-free bond and buying a stock futures contract. Replication is necessary to enforce the principle that a derivative's price must relate to the price of its underlying asset so that no arbitrage opportunities are created.  In this question, the stock/futures portfolio and its synthetic equivalent (eg, the risk-free bond) both generate the same risk-free return, so they must be priced the same.  If not, an investor can earn an arbitrage profit. (Choice A)  Buying a risk-free bond and simultaneously selling a stock futures contract replicates a short position in the underlying stock. (Choice C)  Shorting the stock and the futures contract replicates a short position in the risk-free bond.
question_en: When creating a synthetic position, owning a share of stock of a publicly traded company is best replicated by:
option_a: buying a risk-free bond and selling a futures contract on the stock.
option_b: buying a risk-free bond and buying a futures contract on the stock.
option_c: selling a risk-free bond and selling a futures contract on the stock.

An indenture or trust deed is a legal contract that specifies a bond issuer's obligations and restrictions. The indenture may include covenants that require the issuer to take or refrain from taking certain actions and may specify the source of funds for repayment, such as a project to be funded or the taxing power of a government.

explanation_en: A firm will typically increase the proportion of debt in its capital structure as it matures through its life cycle. In early (ie, start-up) stages, businesses have very limited access to debt due to high operating risk and unstable cash flows. In general, as a business gradually matures, more funds can be borrowed since increased revenues and stable cash flows are opening the firm to more potential lenders. However, there are exceptions to this tendency for capital-intensive, capital-light, and cyclical businesses. Capital-intensive firms (eg, companies operating in real estate, utilities, or transportation) require relatively high levels of debt financing to purchase fixed assets during any stage of the life cycle. For example, a real estate developer would most likely have a lot of debt, even in its early stages. Capital-light firms (eg, consulting firms, software companies) have fewer capital expenditures. Such companies often require little debt financing throughout the life cycle (Choice C). Cyclical firms (eg, car manufacturers, mining companies) have more volatile revenues and cash flows that fluctuate with economic cycles. This volatility reduces their debt capacity, especially during an economic downturn (Choice B).
question_en: Which of the following companies will most likely employ the greatest amount of debt relative to its equity?
option_a: A real estate developer during its initial growth phase
option_b: A cyclical car manufacturer during an economic downturn
option_c: A consulting firm that uses highly paid consultants and few physical assets

Although the image above illustrates volatility's effect on calls only, all contingent claims have asymmetric value profiles; therefore, both call and put values are directly related to volatility (Choices B and C).

explanation_en: The market model uses market returns to predict the expected return of a single security. The relationship between the market return and a security's expected return is estimated through linear regression of historical return data, which results in a straight line when the relationship is graphed. This line represents an estimate for the security's return for a given market return. The slope of the regression line is the individual security's beta, which measures the sensitivity of a security's return relative to the market's return. For a given market return, a higher beta translates to a higher expected return for the security. Alpha is where the market model's regression line intersects the y-axis. While it represents an estimate of the security's return if the market return is zero, alpha has less predictive value than beta. In the market model, beta represents a security's predicted return relative to the market's return. (Choice B) The market model uses the market's returns to predict a security's return. It is not used to determine asset allocation. (Choice C) The market model applies beta to determine the expected return of a security. Beta represents the systematic risk, not the nonsystematic risk, of an asset.
question_en: The market model is most likely used for determining the:

explanation_en: Co-investing in alternative investments Advantages Disadvantages Offers direct investing experience Requires more resources and expertise Leverages the investment firm's process than fund investing and expertise Direct investing opportunities are Reduced management fees dependent on the investment firm More active approach Potential adverse selection bias The three most common methods of engaging in alternative investments, ordered by the increasing level of involvement or expertise required, are: Fund investing: The fund (eg, hedge fund) makes all the investment decisions. Fund investing is an indirect method of investing. Co-investing: An investor in an alternative fund (eg, private equity fund) can invest directly (ie, privately and outside the fund structure) by committing additional capital to specific investments along with the fund manager who introduced the idea (ie, as an intermediary). Direct investing: An investor makes a direct investment in an asset (eg, takes a position in a private company directly, without using an intermediary). Certain fund managers enjoy reputational benefits that make them desirable partners in private deals. The involvement of such managers, like well-known hedge funds, creates an aura of legitimacy that boosts the chances of a successful offering for the issuer. Therefore, issuers seek out these managers, giving them better access to the best deals than other direct investors. Adverse selection bias is possible, however, since the managers may choose to keep those deals for themselves (Choice C). (Choice A) Alternative investment managers offer private deals to their fund investors, not the other way around.

option_b: have better access to private deals than direct investors.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' best interests before their employer's or their own interests." Investment managers pay a commission to a broker to execute client trades. Soft dollar brokerage is the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment services. Since it is the client who ultimately "pays" (ie, out of client assets) the commission, when a portion of the commission (ie, soft dollars) purchases additional investment services, the services "belong" to the client. The investment manager has a duty of loyalty to use such assets for the benefit of the client. Soft dollars can be used only to purchase research services that assist the manager in the investment decision-making process (ie, to make better decisions for the client). Therefore, soft dollars cannot be used to cover the investment manager's operating expenses, such as computers, office supplies, or travel expenses. Investment managers may be tempted to generate excess soft dollar commissions to purchase additional research or to gain clout with brokerage firms by generating more commission revenue. The investment manager cannot meet the Standard by paying a higher commission rate for the exclusive purpose of generating soft dollar commissions and must disclose soft dollar practices to clients. (Choices A and C) Performance attribution software and economic research will assist the portfolio management team in making more informed investing decisions for the client and is therefore permissible under the Standard.

explanation_en:
In finance, pecking order theory states that managers prefer sources of capital that require the least amount of information disclosure. On a
preference hierarchy, sourcing capital from:
internally generated funds (ie, retained earnings) requires no public disclosure and is most preferred.
publicly issued equity requires the most disclosure and is least preferred.
According to pecking order theory, a company will typically finance internally if it has sufficient funds. When internal financing is insufficient, the
company will turn to debt (Choice B). From an investor's perspective, a company issuing debt is a positive signal that management is confident
that the company can service future debt obligations.
At the bottom of the pecking order, a company will finance through issuing new equity, which is a negative signal to investors since the cost of
equity is the highest (Choice A). Furthermore, companies tend to issue shares when the stock is overvalued but will not do so if the stock is
undervalued, signaling that management is pessimistic about the company's valuation.
question_en: Which of the following is correct according to the pecking order theory? Managers prefer:
option_a: issuing new equity more than issuing debt.
option_b: issuing debt more than using internal financing.
option_c: using internal financing more than issuing new equity.

Index design entails assigning weights to constituent securities. Price weighting, equal weighting, and float-adjusted market-capitalization
weighing are the three most common methods. As index constituents and prices change over time, an index may need to be rebalanced to
maintain its weighting. Each weighting method has different rebalancing requirements to maintain consistency with the index's weighting.
Price-weighted indexes require no active rebalancing. The weight of each constituent security is based on its price, so weights automatically
adjust as prices change. Ease of maintaining the index over time (ie, managing the index) is a major advantage of price weighting.
(Choice B) Equal weighting assumes an equal value is invested in each constituent security at index inception. Any price changes result in the
weights no longer being equal. Equal weighting generally requires the most frequent rebalancing.
(Choice C) Float-adjusted market-capitalization weighting is based on the market value (ie, number of shares × market price per share) of the
shares available to public investors. Those are the shares not held by controlling shareholders or other corporations. Periodic adjustments are
made to the number of shares to account for transactions by controlling shareholders.
question_en: An analyst designing a security market index who wants to minimize the need to actively rebalance the index would most appropriately choose:
option_c: float-adjusted market-capitalization weighting.

explanation_en: The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) allows investors to estimate a security's expected return given that security's beta, the market's return, and the risk-free rate.  Beta calculates the security's expected return based on only its systematic risk. The security market line (SML) is the graphical representation of the CAPM, displaying the linear relationship between a security's expected return (y-axis) and its beta (x-axis).  The SML allows investors to identify the relative value of a security.  Securities located on the SML are deemed to be fairly valued.  In contrast: Securities that plot above the SML are undervalued (ie, greater return than expected for the amount of risk), so the value should rise and the expected return should decrease. Securities that plot below the SML are overvalued (ie, less return than expected for the amount of risk), so the value should fall and the expected return should increase. (Choice B)  The capital market line relates to only portfolios on the efficient frontier.  The SML relates to any security or asset. (Choice C)  The SML intersects the y-axis at the risk-free rate.  The market risk premium is the slope of the SML.
question_en: The security market line is best described as:
option_a: the graphical representation of the CAPM.
option_b: relating to only portfolios on the efficient frontier.
option_c: intersecting the y-axis at the market risk premium.

explanation_en: The Sharpe ratio is a performance measure that determines a portfolio's excess return (the amount of return above the risk-free rate) per unit of total risk.  For example, if the portfolio's return is 24%, the risk-free rate is 4%, and the total risk (standard deviation) of the portfolio is 20%, then its Sharpe ratio is 1.00, or (0.24 – 0.04)/0.20.  This means that the portfolio earned 1.00 unit of excess return per each unit of total risk. A useful application of the Sharpe ratio is to rank portfolios.  The portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio has earned more return per unit of risk. Rational investors prefer portfolios with the highest Sharpe ratios. (Choice A)  The Sharpe ratio measures a portfolio's risk-adjusted return.  It scales a portfolio's excess return by its total risk (standard deviation). (Choice C)  The Sharpe ratio is based on total risk.  Total risk is the sum of systematic risk and nonsystematic risk.  This performance measure would be inappropriate for a portfolio that has only systematic risk.
question_en: Which of the following statements best describes the Sharpe ratio?
option_a: It measures return without considering a portfolio's risk.
option_b: It indicates the performance of an investment on a risk-adjusted basis.
option_c: It is most appropriate for those portfolios that have only systematic risk.

explanation_en: Benefits of strong corporate governance Increased operational efficiency and improved internal controls Increased creditworthiness (eg, lower default probability, lower cost of debt) Earlier identification of potential conflicts Improved operating and financial results Better alignment of manager decisions and company value maximization Reduced legal costs and reputational damage An effective corporate governance system prevents one stakeholder group from benefitting at the expense of others by establishing strong stakeholder management guidelines and operational controls. These features lead to better relationships with investors and creditors, fewer conflicts of interest, more efficient operations, and improved financial results. A robust corporate governance system protects creditor rights by lowering default risk and improving financial transparency. The better the controls and reporting, the more confidence creditors have in the business, reducing borrowing costs and increasing access to funds. (Choice B) Strong corporate governance better aligns manager decisions to maximize shareholder wealth; it does not necessarily make management more or less risk averse. Proper controls and well-designed compensation plans may encourage potentially risk-averse managers to take on risky projects that maximize shareholder wealth. Likewise, effective governance and controls can prevent undue risk-taking that emphasizes short-term gains without enhancing long-term shareholder value. (Choice C) Effective corporate governance systems typically improve a company's decision-making process, thereby improving, not impeding, the company's ability to quickly respond to market factors.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation prohibits actions and statements by investment professionals that could undermine confidence in investment performance reporting.  Members and Candidates must provide accurate and reliable pricing information to enable informed investment decision-making by clients. Accurate values for distressed real estate are difficult to determine, and a wide range of appraised values is not uncommon.  Using the average from several appraisers is a reasonable method for estimating a property's fair value.  The method should be disclosed to clients and potential clients. (Choice B)  Using the lower estimates for asset values can lead to exaggerating the expected returns when undervalued assets are sold.  Archer Clegg potentially violates the Standard if he uses only the lowest appraisals since doing so could result in the estimates for future returns being upwardly biased. (Choice C)  The Standard recommends but does not require that Members and Candidates compare their performance results to comparable benchmarks.  CFA Institute recognizes that some assets, such as those Clegg manages, do not lend themselves to benchmark comparison.
question_en: Archer Clegg, CFA, manages a fund of illiquid distressed real estate that primarily consists of properties located in economically depressed areas.  Clegg does not report fund performance relative to a benchmark since there are no benchmarks based on distressed real estate.  Clegg uses two reputable appraisal firms to value each property annually.  Last year, a new appraisal firm was hired due to cost and timing concerns involving a previous appraiser.  Since then, Clegg has noticed that the new firm appears to consistently undervalue properties compared with the other firm doing appraisals.  Fund performance reports are prepared using the average of the two appraisals, a method that is disclosed to clients and potential clients.  Has Clegg most likely violated Standard I(C) Misrepresentation?
option_b: Yes, since he is not using only the lowest appraisal.
option_c: Yes, since he fails to compare performance to a benchmark.

Life cycle phase Financial characteristics Debt characteristics
Revenue growth: Low Availability: Little to no
Start-up Cash flow: Negative Cost: High

Availability: Moderate
Revenue growth: High

The proportion of debt in a firm's capital structure typically increases as the firm moves through its life cycle stages.
In the start-up phase, management would prefer taking on debt to avoid equity dilution but the firm lacks access to debt due to high risk. A
firm in this phase typically does not have enough assets to secure against debt or enough cash flows to service debt.
In the growth phase, debt is more available but management generally chooses to use debt conservatively. A firm in this phase has
typically started generating a positive cash flow, but the preference is to maintain operational flexibility and minimize financial risk.
In the mature phase, the firm is generating continuous cash flow and deleveraging over time, but management tries to maintain a debt level
close to that of the firm's optimal capital structure. A mature firm will often use share buybacks, financed by debt, to increase the proportion
of debt in its capital structure.
A firm's capital structure may also be dictated by the industry in which it operates. In this scenario, the company is leveraged and has access to
low-cost debt, but management is trying to minimize the risk of financial distress. These considerations suggest that the company is in the growth
phase.
(Choice A) In the mature phase, a company has a positive cash flow and less need of debt.
(Choice C) Start-up companies are riskier for capital providers; therefore lenders would not be offering low lending rates to a start-up.
question_en: Management wishes to limit a company's use of debt since its operating cash flows are unpredictable, despite the company's current lenders offering low rates. The company is most likely in its:
option_c: start-up phase.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise other personnel to take reasonable steps to prevent and detect violations of laws and regulations.  The Guidance to the Standard indicates that compliance with the Standard, at a minimum, requires supervisors to: establish written compliance procedures; and perform regular reviews to ensure that employees are following the procedures. A supervisor who does not satisfy these requirements violates the Standard even if no laws were broken.  In this question, Grimaldi violated the Standard by not implementing a regular review to ensure that employees were complying with the requirement to provide confirmations for trades occurring in outside accounts. However, the concept of "reasonableness" does not make supervisors responsible for detecting all violations; employees may be able to evade compliance in ways that cannot be detected through reasonable efforts.  It is not reasonable to conclude that Grimaldi knew or should have known in advance that an employee would try to evade the requirement by establishing a hidden account (Choices B and C).  However, now that he knows it is possible, Grimaldi should update the fund's rules to prevent future occurrences.
question_en: Stuart Grimaldi, CFA, is the compliance officer for a large hedge fund with several hundred employees.  Grimaldi has implemented a comprehensive set of rules for employees to comply with applicable laws and regulation.  He appropriately updates the rules and communicates all changes to the employees.  He also holds regular meetings to advise employees of different compliance issues. The fund permits employees to maintain investment accounts with outside firms but requires the employees to send Grimaldi duplicate confirmations for all trades.  The rule applies for accounts that the employee establishes in his or her own name as well as those for immediate family members such as a spouse, domestic partner, children, or parents.  About half of the employees have outside accounts.  Grimaldi does not regularly check the confirmations but believes that the employees are complying with the rule. Recently, an employee tried to circumvent the rule by having his neighbor open an account at another firm, with the employee directing the trades made in the account.  Grimaldi was not aware of this activity until the neighbor who "owned" the account was charged with insider trading.  The neighbor then implicated the employee who was directing the trades.  Of the following, the most appropriate statement is that Grimaldi violated Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors with respect to:
option_b: not taking appropriate actions to prevent the employee from circumventing the rule.
option_c: both not checking the confirmations and preventing the circumvention of the rule.

Market participants analyze a security to determine its current intrinsic value. Homogeneity in investor expectations, one assumption of the
capital asset pricing model (CAPM), suggests that all market participants use identical economic expectations to determine an asset's value.
Since all investors are presumed to have the same expectations, there can be only one optimal risky portfolio. Although inconsistent with
observed investor behavior, this assumption is necessary to create a portfolio that has the same consensus expectation.
(Choice A) Homogeneity in investor expectations presumes that investors use the same, not different, estimates to value assets. If they used
different economic estimates, then assets would have more than one expected return.
(Choice B) The CAPM assumes homogeneity in investor expectations. Theoretically, all market participants come to the same conclusions since
they all have the same economic expectations.
question_en: Which of the following is an assumption of the capital asset pricing model (CAPM)?
option_a: Investors use different estimates to value assets.
option_b: Analysts independently appraise a company's price.
option_c: Market participants use the same economic expectations.

explanation_en: Common misleading performance reporting practices Representative Selecting top-performing portfolios to represent overall results accounts Survivorship Excluding terminated portfolios from average performance bias Varying Presenting only selected periods of strong performance time periods The global standard for investment performance reporting known as GIPS (Global Investment Performance Standards) provides a uniform approach for calculating and presenting historical investment performance. Without the GIPS standards, a firm's reporting of its investment performance may be unreliable due to: selectively presenting top-performing portfolios to represent the firm's results for a given strategy, excluding portfolios that performed poorly and were terminated, or presenting returns for a period of strong performance while excluding periods of weaker performance. GIPS require that firms include terminated client accounts, funds, and portfolios as part of the historical performance of a composite. This practice results in a more accurate representation of a firm's complete performance. Excluding terminated portfolios that underperformed results in overstating performance and leads to misleading reporting. (Choice B) GIPS standards prevent firms from selectively presenting performance periods by mandating a minimum number of consecutive years to present. If the strategy has existed for more than the minimum number of required reporting years, firms are allowed to present fewer periods of historical performance than exist. (Choice C) Firms can present results of a single portfolio if it is the only one for a given strategy.
question_en: GIPS standards prevent firms from using misleading performance measurement practices such as presenting:
option_a: average returns that exclude terminated portfolios.
option_b: fewer periods of returns than exist for an investment strategy.
option_c: returns of investment strategies that consist of a single portfolio.

explanation_en:
In a business combination, the difference between the purchase price and fair market value of net assets (ie, assets − liabilities) is goodwill. At
the time of the merger, long-lived tangible assets and identifiable intangibles are not reported as goodwill; instead, they are revalued to their fair
market value. Intangible assets are identifiable and are included in the fair market value of net assets if:
Under US GAAP, they:
Originate as a legal claim (eg, patents, trademarks)
Are separable (ie, can be sold separately) from the acquired company
Under IFRS, they:
Originate as a legal claim (eg, patents, trademarks)
Are separable (ie, can be sold separately) from the acquired company
Are controlled by the acquiring company
Can create measurable economic benefits
Have reliably measured costs
If intangible assets do not meet these criteria, they are not included in the fair market value of net assets and are accounted for as goodwill.
(Choice A) Under US GAAP, if an intangible asset originates as a legal claim or is separable (eg, a patent), it is considered an identifiable
intangible asset and is not included in goodwill.
(Choice B) Tangible assets are revalued to their fair market value in a business combination. By definition, a tangible asset's (eg, PPE's) fair
market value is identifiable and is not part of goodwill.
question_en: A company acquires the assets of another company in a business combination and records goodwill. Under US GAAP, which of the following is most likely included in goodwill?
option_b: The fair market value of PPE
option_c: Nonidentifiable intangible assets
