explanation_en: A common share structure for public companies is the single-class structure, wherein each share grants the holder one vote so that every shareholder has proportional voting power based on the number of shares held (eg, a shareholder owning 5% of the company controls 5% of the votes). Other companies have dual-class structures, with multiple share classes that allow different numbers of votes per share (eg, Class A has one vote per share, while Class B has five votes per share). Proponents of dual-class structures argue that they provide more stability since founders and insiders can better retain control when faced with activism or a takeover attempt. In addition, shareholders and their chosen managers are insulated when voting power is controlled, so the company can focus on long-term strategic investments instead of short-term financial results. Once created, dual-class structures are difficult to dismantle. (Choice A) Dual-class structures separate voting power from economic ownership since owners of the class with more votes (usually founders or insiders) have voting power disproportionate to their share ownership. (Choice C) Critics of dual-class structures argue that they can create conflicts of interest between company executives and noncontrolling shareholders, who lack the voting power to enforce their preferences when the executives—chosen by insiders—have different goals.
question_en: An argument supporting a dual-class structure of common equity is most likely that compared to single-class structures, dual-class structures better:
option_a: align voting power with economic ownership.
option_b: promote stability and long-term strategic investments.
option_c: remove conflicts of interest between noncontrolling shareholders and management.

explanation_en:
The coefficients of a linear regression (ie, slope and intercept) can be estimated based on common statistical measures, as given in this
scenario. When the expected benchmark return (the independent variable, X) equals zero, the predicted return of the mutual fund (the predicted
dependent variable, Ŷ) equals the value of the intercept.
Based on the information given, find the intercept using the return means as the independent and dependent variable values and the slope of the
regression line. The slope is the ratio of the covariance of Y and X to the variance of X. This is derived from the least squares criterion that drives
the goal of the linear regression: to minimize the sum of the squared residuals so that the regression line is the best fit for the data.

| Steps | Calculations |
|---|---|
| Calculate the slope (b1) | b1 = Covariance of Y and X / Variance of X = 4.78 / 5.07 = 0.94 |
| Calculate the intercept (b0) | b0 = Ȳ − b1X̄ = 1.48 − (0.94 × 1.20) = 0.35 |
| Apply coefficients to linear equation | Ŷ = b0 + b1X + e = 0.35 + 0.94X + e |

It is important to note that 0.35% is the predicted mutual fund return, not the observed (ie, actual) return, and that the data set is just a sample of
the population, so the calculated coefficients will always be estimates of the population parameters.
(Choice B) 0.94% is the slope, or the change in the predicted return of the mutual fund for every unit change in the expected return of the
benchmark.
(Choice C) 1.48% is the mean (ie, average) return of the mutual fund. It is the expected return when there is no information about the
benchmark.

explanation_en: Execution instructions define how an order is filled.  A limit order instructs the brokerage firm to execute the trade only at the limit price or better.  Validity instructions state the time frame and conditions under which an order may be filled.  A day order is valid for the same day it is issued and expires at the end of that day if not filled. The investor has set a limit price of NZD 15.40, instructing the broker to sell up to 1,000 shares at this price or higher.  The 700 shares offered at or above the limit price are immediately filled with an average price of NZD 15.45.  Since no new bids are submitted before the market closes, the unfilled portion of the order is canceled. explanation_en: Defined benefit plans vs. defined contribution plans Investment Funding Defined contribution Employee Employee Defined benefit Employer Employer Employers may offer either a defined benefit (DB) or a defined contribution (DC) retirement plan as part of an employee's total compensation and benefits. Investment and funding responsibilities are distributed differently to either the employer or the employee, depending on the type of plan. In DB plans, employers are responsible for contributing assets, investing the plan assets, and assuming the risk of shortfalls if plan assets are insufficient to pay the promised benefits (Choice A). In DC plans, employees are responsible for funding, investing the contributions, and bearing the investment risks. Although an employer may contribute to an employee's DC plan, the employer is not responsible for the performance of its contributions or any assets in the plan (Choice B).
question_en: Which of the following best describes the distribution of responsibilities in an employee's retirement plan?
option_a: Employees are responsible for funding defined benefit plans.
option_b: Employers accept investment risks in defined contribution plans.
option_c: Employers ensure that assets meet liabilities in defined benefit plans.

explanation_en:
Floating-rate notes (FRN [ie, floaters]) are debt instruments that make interest (coupon) payments based on a reference rate, which can fluctuate
from one period to the next. The reference rate is typically a short-term, low-risk money market rate, such as LIBOR.
Since FRN investors may face additional credit risk, a quoted yield spread (ie, quoted margin) is added to the reference rate to compensate for
this risk. The discount margin (ie, required margin) reflects investor return expectations and is used for discounting future interest payments to the
present value of the FRN.
An FRN will trade at a premium if the quoted margin that the issuer pays is greater than the required margin that the market demands. This is
similar to a fixed-rate bond, which sells at a premium when the coupon rate is greater than its YTM.
(Choice A) The FRN will trade at a discount, not premium, when the quoted margin is less than the discount margin.
(Choice B) The size of the quoted margin relative to the reference rate has no bearing on whether an FRN trades at a premium or discount.
question_en: A floating-rate note will most likely be priced at a premium when the quoted margin is:
option_c: greater than the discount margin.

explanation_en:
Money convexity and money duration can be used to estimate a bond's price change (in currency) due to a change in its YTM. The relationship

explanation_en: The convenience yield is a non-cash benefit that comes from holding a physical commodity. explanation_en: A unique feature of ETFs is that they will create shares when institutional investors deposit securities that are included in the ETF basket and will redeem ETF shares for institutional investors. question_en: The creation and redemption of shares by authorized participants, which keeps the price of fund shares close to their net asset value, is a feature unique to which of the following types of pooled investments?

explanation_en:
Analysts use integrated financial ratio analysis to gauge a company's performance in terms of its activity or efficiency, liquidity, solvency, and
profitability.
Activity ratios measure how efficiently a company utilizes its assets.
Liquidity ratios measure how well a company can cover its short-term obligations with cash or with assets that are easily converted to cash.
Solvency ratios measure a company's ability to satisfy its long-term obligations.
Profitability ratios measure a company's return on sales and return on investments. Return on sales measures the margin earned from
sales. Return on investment measures the profit from invested capital (eg, equity).
From the information provided in the question, solvency is measured by Debt-to-EBITDA ratio, efficiency is measured by total asset turnover,
and profitability is measured by net profit margin. After calculating the three ratios, the analyst can most appropriately conclude that Company
A has better efficiency (0.83 vs. 0.50) since it is better at utilizing its assets to generate sales.
(Choice A) Company B has better solvency as measured by a lower Debt-to-EBITDA ratio.
(Choice C) Company B has better profitability as measured by net profit margin.

An analyst gathers the following data to compare two companies' performance.

| ($ millions) | Company A | Company B |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 1,000 | 800 |
| EBITDA | 200 | 250 |

| Long-term debt | 700 | 800 |

explanation_en: The law of diminishing returns states that as more of a resource is added to a production process, holding other resource use constant, increases in output will eventually decrease. Therefore, as more salespeople are added they will generate more sales at a decreasing rate. Total sales will increase and the average sales per salesperson will decrease.
question_en: According to the law of diminishing returns, doubling the number of salespeople for a firm will most likely result in:
option_a: decreasing the total sales of the firm as a result of competition amongst salespeople.
option_b: doubling the total sales of the firm.
option_c: increasing the total sales of the firm and reducing the average sales per salesperson.

explanation_en: Collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) are a type of asset securitization similar to asset-backed securities (ABS). Sponsors of both CDOs and ABS create special purpose entities that issue multiple tranches (ie, different classes) of bonds to raise funds. The funds pay for assets that become the collateral (ie, asset portfolio) for the CDO. The cash flow from the collateral is used to make distributions to investors. CDO collateral can include different types of assets with varying degrees of credit risk and rates of return (eg, commercial mortgage loans, corporate debt, credit default swaps). ABS usually are collateralized by a specific type of loan (eg, auto, credit cards). Leveraged CDOs are structured like a waterfall, with several tranches of different seniority, including an equity tranche. The CDO manager uses funds raised for investment to construct an asset portfolio designed to earn a return that is sufficient to: 1. pay bondholders the bond's interest and principal, in order of seniority, 2. then pay investors in the equity tranche, and 3. only then pay the CDO manager. This structure typically includes restrictions known as prespecified risk tests (eg, maintain agreed-upon levels of coverage ratios, collateral quality) to ensure adequate cash flows for the senior tranche. If the CDO fails any of the prespecified risk tests, a provision is triggered that requires principal payments to be redirected from junior classes to the senior class until the CDO is back in compliance with the tests. Failure to earn a return higher than the cost of issuing bonds is determined by the return on the investments made by the CDO manager. Such a failure lowers the CDO manager's compensation; it can also affect the return to the equity tranche of the CDO. However, these circumstances can occur without triggering the prespecified risk tests or affecting the senior tranche (Choices B and C).
question_en: If a collateralized debt obligation provision is triggered, requiring the return of principal to the senior tranche, the most likely cause for the trigger is the failure:
option_b: to return principal to the equity tranche investors.
option_c: to earn a return higher than the costs of issuing the bonds.

explanation_en: The comparables (comps) method is the most common way to compare and report on price multiples.  The analyst compares a price multiple of a company stock to that of a benchmark (ie, similar company stock, industry average).  If the price multiple of the stock is lower, higher, or the same as the benchmark, then the stock is considered undervalued, overvalued, or fairly valued, respectively. There are disadvantages to the comps method.  Results can be inconsistent with other types of models (eg, present value, asset-based).  Also, factors that decrease comparability, such as economic fluctuations and choice of accounting methods, may distort comparisons.  For example, companies have flexibility on the timing and amount of expenses they recognize, which can potentially impact income statement items and therefore price multiples. Using comps to make valuation decisions also has advantages.  The data needed to construct price multiples and make comparisons are publicly available, and the method is easily used and widely understood.  Compared with other valuation methods, use of comps is relatively simple and allows for relative comparisons between companies.  It is particularly suited to comparing companies in the same industry (Choices A and B).
question_en: In valuing equities, a disadvantage of using the method of comparables with price multiples is most likely that it:
option_b: does not work well for industry analysis.
option_c: is impacted by choice of accounting methods.

question_en: A form of economic integration that allows free movement of goods, services, and factors of production among member countries and has a common trade policy against non-members best describes a:

A deferred tax asset (DTA) is created when a company's accounting income is less than its taxable income. In that case, according to the tax
code, the tax expense that the company must pay is greater than its income tax expense based on financial reporting. Often, these differences
arise when the tax code and accounting standards differ on how and when companies should recognize revenues and expenses. A DTA is
temporary since its benefit is expected to offset future taxes.
For example, accounting income is less than taxable income when a company elects accelerated depreciation for financial reporting and straight-
line depreciation for tax reporting. Using straight-line depreciation for tax reporting results in lower depreciation expense and higher taxable
income than when it is used for financial reporting. Higher taxable income increases tax expense and taxes payable. Overpayment of tax today
results in a DTA since the company will pay less tax in the future.
(Choice A) Carryforwards of prior years' losses, not gains, may be used against future gains and are recorded as DTAs. Under most tax laws,
gains are immediately taxable and are usually disallowed as carryforwards.
(Choice C) Foreign or domestic currency received for revenue earned during the same period creates neither a DTA nor a deferred tax liability
since accounting standards and the tax code recognize the currency as income.
question_en: Which of the following most likely creates a deferred tax asset?
option_a: Carryforward of prior years' gains, offset by current losses
option_b: Greater expenses for financial reporting than for tax reporting
option_c: Foreign currency received for income earned during the same period

explanation_en:
The global minimum variance portfolio is the lowest risk portfolio on the efficient frontier. It is composed of only risky assets, so it excludes
risk-free assets. The efficient frontier represents all minimum variance portfolios within the investment opportunity set. Each portfolio along the
efficient frontier has the highest expected return for a given level of risk. The global minimum variance portfolio (Portfolio A) is the lowest point on
the efficient frontier (the blue curved line).
Although portfolios along the red curved line are also minimum variance portfolios, they are not part of the efficient frontier. Portfolios B and C
have the same risk, but Portfolio B is suboptimal since it has a lower expected return than Portfolio C. This holds true for all portfolios on the red
curved line.
(Choice B) The global minimum variance portfolio is the lowest risk portfolio on the efficient frontier that is composed of only risky assets and is
achievable. There are theoretical portfolios with certain combinations of risk and return that are not possible, but the global minimum variance
portfolio is not one of them.
(Choice C) The lowest-risk portfolio on the capital allocation line is the risk-free asset, not the global minimum variance portfolio. The capital
allocation line combines a risky portfolio with a risk-free asset. Portfolios on the capital allocation line do not include the global minimum variance
portfolio.
question_en: Under modern portfolio theory, which of the following best describes the global minimum variance portfolio?
option_a: A portfolio on the efficient frontier
option_b: An unachievable portfolio with the lowest risk
option_c: The lowest risk portfolio on the capital allocation line

explanation_en: Standard II(A), Material Nonpublic Information, applies in this situation. Standard II(A) suggests the use of "fire walls" to protect the firm and to conform to the Standards. A fire wall is an information barrier designed to prevent the communication of material nonpublic information between departments of a firm. Although the fire wall system should provide a means to review transactions, it is not feasible to monitor all communications into/out of departments. Placing sensitive securities/firms on "watch, "restricted," or "rumor" lists helps management target monitoring of transactions.

explanation_en:
A fixed-coupon bond's return (ie, yield) is measured in terms of percentage. The yield depends on both the amount of each coupon payment and
the bond's periodicity, which refers to the number of coupon (ie, compounding) periods per year. A bond that pays coupon interest
semiannually has a periodicity of 2, a bond that pays monthly has a periodicity of 12, etc.
A bond's price is the PV of its future cash flows. Each bond's cash flows are discounted at a periodic yield, thus prohibiting the comparison of
bonds with different periodicities. Multiplying the periodic yield by the number of compounding periods in a year produces the annual percentage
rate (APR), allowing for the comparison of APRs for bonds with different periodicities.
In this question, Bond A's periodicity is 2, and its semiannual yield is approximately 2.64%. Multiplying the semiannual yield by the number of
coupon periods (2) results in an APR of approximately 5.27%. Bond B's periodicity is 4, its periodic yield is approximately 1.41%, and its APR is
approximately 5.65% (1.41% × 4), which is greater than Bond A's APR (Choices B and C).
question_en: Information on two bonds is shown below: If the bonds are priced on a date when they both pay coupon interest, Bond A's annual percentage rate (APR) is most likely:
option_c: greater than Bond B's.

explanation_en:
A bond's yield-to-maturity (YTM) describes and quantifies the rate of return that investors demand given its maturity and perceived credit
quality. YTM is given as a percentage, and is the sum of two components:
The benchmark rate, which is also known as the risk-free rate of return; and
The spread, which consists of the additional amount of return over the benchmark rate.
The benchmark rate applies to government bonds, which are assumed to have no risk of default and are therefore referred to as risk-free bonds.
The benchmark rate incorporates macroeconomic factors such as a government's fiscal and monetary policies, expected inflation, and exchange
rates for the issuer's currency (Choices B and C).
The spread captures the impact of factors that are specific to the nongovernment issuer as well as the bond itself. These include the issuer's
credit risk, both in absolute terms and relative to that of other issuers; liquidity of the bond; and whether the bondholder is subject to income tax on
the coupon interest. All these factors are expressed as an additional percentage that compensates investors for the additional risks. A risky
bond's YTM is the sum of the benchmark rate and the spread.
question_en: Which of the following is most likely included in the spread component of a corporate bond's yield-to-maturity?
option_c: Business conditions in the issuer's country

explanation_en:
Fundamental weighting uses some fundamental measure of a company, such as earnings, to weight the assets in the index. Other usable measures include dividends, revenues, or book value.

Since fundamental weighting uses these types of measures instead of market cap or share price, it tends to favor assets normally associated with value investing. To find the weight of an asset, divide the fundamental measure of the asset by the sum of the measures of every asset in the index. In this example, the fundamental value is earnings yield, which is found by dividing earnings by share price.

Earnings yield = Earnings per share / Share price

Use the price at the beginning of the period and the earnings per share to find the fundamental weight of Asset Z. Then multiply the weight of the asset by the initial value of the index to find the value of Asset Z in the index:

| Asset | Earnings yield | Fundamental weight | Value in index |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | €3.00/€100.00 = 0.03 | 0.03/(0.03+0.10+0.05) = 16.7% | €1,000 × 16.7% = €167 |
| Y | €4.80/€48.00 = 0.10 | 0.10/(0.03+0.10+0.05) = 55.6% | €1,000 × 55.6% = €556 |
| Z | €4.00/€80.00 = 0.05 | 0.05/(0.03+0.10+0.05) = 27.7% | €1,000 × 27.7% = €277 |

(Choice B) €333 is the value of Asset Z in the index using equal weighting: €1,000 ÷ 3 = €333.
(Choice C) €351 is the value in the index of Asset Z based on its price weight. The price weight of an asset is found by dividing the price of the asset by the sum of all the asset prices in the index.

Things to remember:
To find the fundamental weight of an asset, divide the fundamental measure of the asset by the sum of the fundamental measures of all the assets in the index. Earnings yield is calculated as earnings per share divided by share price.

explanation_en:
Initiating futures positions requires traders to meet an initial margin requirement in cash, which ensures that a trader has enough funds on hand to
cover any losses. This is essential since futures settle daily, and therefore losses must be paid for immediately after every trading session.
Futures margins are described as performance bonds or good faith deposits.
To ensure that there are adequate funds to cover losses, the margin account balance must be maintained above a minimum amount known as the
maintenance margin, which is usually lower than the initial margin requirement. If the account balance falls below the maintenance margin, there
is a demand (ie, margin call) for additional funds. The amount of the call is equal to the amount of cash necessary to raise the account balance
to the initial margin requirement, not the maintenance margin. Failure to meet the call in full can result in liquidation of under-margined
positions.
(Choice A) The money to buy the underlying asset is required only at expiration and only if the long decides to buy the underlying asset at that
time. Most futures positions are liquidated prior to expiration.
(Choice C) The money required to return the account balance (ie, equity) to the maintenance margin would be correct if this were a securities
account margin call, instead of a futures margin call.
question_en: When losses on a long futures position result in a margin call, the amount due is most likely the money required to:
option_b: return the account balance to the initial margin.
option_c: return the account balance to the maintenance margin.

explanation_en: When a question requires a candidate to calculate the probability that an event occurs based on whether a different event occurs or does not occur, this signals the candidate to use the total probability rule: P(bankrupt) = P(bankrupt AND pass) + P(bankrupt AND not pass) = [P(pass) x P(bankrupt | pass)] + [P(not pass) x P(bankrupt | not pass)]. The question asks for the probability of a bank going bankrupt, an event the occurrence of which is related to whether it passes a test. The probability of not passing the test is 0.62, so the probability of passing the test is 1 - 0.62 = 0.38. The joint probability that a bank goes bankrupt and it passes the test is 0.05; the conditional probability that a bank goes bankrupt given that it does not pass the test is 0.7903. The total probability rule can be illustrated as a tree diagram: the first node shows the two unconditional probabilities of whether a bank passes the test or does not pass; the next nodes show the conditional probabilities of bankruptcy and no bankruptcy, based on whether the bank passes the test or not. The two conditional probabilities containing no bankruptcy are irrelevant since the question asks for the probability that a bank goes bankrupt. The joint probability of bankruptcy and passing the test is given in the question as 0.05. The joint probability that a bank goes bankrupt and does not pass the test is calculated as: P(bankrupt AND not pass) = P(not pass) x P(bankrupt | not pass) = 0.62 x 0.7903 = 0.4899. The total probability that a bank goes bankrupt is the sum of the two joint probabilities involving the bank going bankrupt: 0.05 + 0.4899 = 0.5399, or approximately 0.54.

explanation_en: For issuers with multiple debt issues outstanding, indentures establish seniority rankings that determine the priority of claims for the different classes of investors.  During a bankruptcy, strict adherence to the priority of claims results in sequential payment in full, according to the seniority of each class of claimants. If subordinated debtholders receive partial payment before secured and senior debtholders are paid in full, then the priority of claims was not strictly adhered to.  A likely reason is that the various classes of claimants negotiated a settlement to avoid litigation, which would reduce assets available for recovery. In this scenario, the subordinated debtholders received 15% of their claim while the senior secured debtholders received 75% of theirs, suggesting the various claimants agreed to such a settlement.  If the priority of claims were strictly followed, the senior secured debtholders would have received 100% of their claim before lower classes received any distributions. (Choice B)  In cases where the value of the secured property is less than the amount of the claim, shortfalls are given a status equal to the claims of senior unsecured creditors.  This claim still takes priority over subordinated debtholders based on the priority of claims. (Choice C)  Shareholders, including preferred shareholders, have claims junior to those of all debtholders.  They will receive distributions only after all liability holders' claims are paid in full, assuming adherence to the priority of claims.

option_b: value of the secured property was less than the amount of the claim.
option_c: preferred shareholders received distributions first based on the priority of claims.

ABS Typical collateral
Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) Residential mortgage loans
Collateralized mortgage obligations (CMO) Mortgage-related products (eg, RMBS)
Commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) Commercial mortgage loans
Collateralized debt obligations (CDO) Loans, other ABS, structured securities
Non-mortgage asset-backed securities (ABS) Credit card loans, auto loans
Securitized debt instruments, broadly known as asset-backed securities (ABS), are created using collateral which is sold to a special purpose
entity (SPE). The SPE then sells bonds backed by the collateral. As shown in the table above, there are different types of ABS, which have
different forms of collateral.
Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are bonds that are securitized by pools of residential mortgage loans. Agency RMBS are issued
and typically guaranteed by a sovereign government or one of its agencies. A nonagency RMBS is issued by a private entity and has no
government guarantee.
The collateral for agency and nonagency RMBS consists of residential mortgage loans (Choice B). Credit card receivables, which are unsecured
loans, are the collateral for credit card ABS (Choice A).
A collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) is similar to a residential mortgage-backed security except that the collateral is one or more ABS
instead of actual loans. A typical CMO is structured with multiple tranches of bonds. Payments on the loans that secure the ABS are then
distributed to the CMO investors. A sequential-pay CMO is designed so that each tranche is retired in order of seniority; only the most senior
tranche then existing receives principal payments until that tranche has been retired.

Type Turning point relative to economy Examples

Various statistics drawn from the real economy and the financial markets have historically exhibited stable patterns of change relative to turns in
the business cycle. These economic indicators are characterized as leading, coincident, or lagging indicators.
Leading indicators signal economic change several months to a year in advance of a change in real GDP growth rates. Coincident indicators
move largely in tandem with the economy. Lagging indicators trail changes in the economy by several months or quarters.
The spread between short-term (eg, three-month government security) and long-term (eg, ten-year government bond) interest rates as well as
initial claims for unemployment insurance are leading indicators. A narrowing of the spread of long-term over short-term rates and increases
in new applications for unemployment compensation usually foreshadow a weakening economy. Changes in the opposite direction forecast
economic strengthening.
In this case, both indicators are exhibiting negative signals. Before the specified changes occurred, the indicators had been consistent with a
weakening economy, and both have become even more negative. Initial unemployment claims have increased more rapidly. The spread between
short-term and long-term rates must have previously narrowed since it has recently inverted. Both indicators signify an economy going from bad
to worse.
Based on the information about the indicators, the most appropriate forecast is for further slowing of growth, if not an outright contraction of
economic activity (ie, a recession).

explanation_en: Corporate governance overview Corporate The framework of managing priorities between a company's management and board, relative to its shareholders governance and other stakeholders Shareholder theory Prioritizes maximizing returns to equity shareholders Considers shareholders' needs, but takes a more balanced approach toward managing the diverging interests Stakeholder theory that arise between all interested parties Corporate governance is the framework of managing priorities between a company's management and board, relative to its shareholders (ie, owners) and other stakeholders. There is not one universally accepted approach to corporate governance, but the two most widely practiced approaches are: Shareholder theory, in which the priority is maximizing shareholder returns above all else (Choice A). Stakeholder theory, which takes a more balanced approach in managing the conflicting interests of shareholders and all other stakeholders without unduly favoring one group over another (Choice B). The practice of corporate governance is often influenced by long-standing cultural, legal, and political factors specific to a country or geographic region. Corporate governance approaches are best seen as placed along a continuum, with shareholder theory at one end and stakeholder theory at the other. While there is not a single unifying set of global rules and regulations for what constitutes the proper model of corporate governance, the trend has been toward a convergence of ideas for a consensus framework regarding what is considered best practice.
question_en: Stakeholder theory asserts that the primary responsibility of corporate governance is to:

explanation_en: For a bond with an embedded call option, the OAS is less than its zero-volatility spread by the option cost. Therefore, the zero-volatility spread is greater than the OAS for callable bonds. If the embedded call option has any value to the issuer, a callable bond with an OAS of 75 basis points will have a Z-spread that is greater than 75 basis points. Because the OAS represents the bond's spread to the spot yield curve excluding the effect of the embedded option, it does not include any compensation for the volatility risk related to the option. The implied cost of an embedded option is the difference between the bond's zero-volatility spread (not the nominal spread) and its OAS.
question_en: If a callable bond has an option-adjusted spread (OAS) of 75 basis points, this most likely suggests:
option_a: the bond has a zero-volatility spread greater than 75 basis points.
option_b: the 75 basis points represent the investor’s compensation for credit risk, liquidity risk, and volatility risk.
option_c: the implied cost of the call option is the bond’s nominal spread minus 75 basis points.

A price multiple is a ratio that compares a company's stock price to another fundamental value. One such multiple is the price-to-earnings ratio

based on future earnings. If the forward earnings estimate is based on a model used to estimate company fundamentals or cash flows, the ratio is

To understand the relationship between justified forward P/E and company fundamentals, begin with the Gordon growth model (GGM):

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by members or candidates that distort securities prices.  Manipulation can occur through information-based activities, such as spreading false rumors, or transaction-based activities, such as exaggerated trading between two accounts. However, a key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is that the Member or Candidate must intend to deceive other market participants.  The Guidance emphasizes that intent is critical; there is no violation of the Standard without it.  Intent in each case must be inferred from relevant facts and circumstances. Here, no market manipulation occurred, as Trainor had no intent to deceive.  His recommendation was based on research from different sources, and while some of it could be characterized as rumor (eg, he heard that earnings would be "very strong"), he also offered details of the research, as well as disclosing his ownership in Ambit.  Since he engaged in no manipulative conduct, it is irrelevant that he benefitted from his recommendation (Choice C). (Choice B)  Trainor's recommendation was based on a combination of variables.  He formed an opinion based on a reasonable interpretation of those variables.  Nothing suggests any intent by Trainor to deceive his subscribers, which would have been the case had he based it on falsity or unsupportable conjecture.
question_en: Kyle Trainor, CFA, publishes a popular investing newsletter.  In the most recent edition he recommends that subscribers buy Ambit Holdings (AHC).  Trainor has owned AHC for many years and would like to sell it, but he believes that AHC is undervalued at its current price of $25 per share.  His recommendation is based on interviews with AHC's executives as well as his own independent research, and he believes that AHC's price will double when it releases its year-end earnings next month.  He includes a few details of his research, using phrases such as "I have heard that earnings will be very strong" and "Many people think that this stock will SOAR."  He also discloses his ownership of AHC stock.  Based on his recommendation, many subscribers buy AHC stock, which causes the price to rise.  Before AHC releases its year-end earnings, Trainor sells his entire AHC position at a price of $45 per share.  After AHC releases its earnings report, its price continues to rise, peaking at $64 per share before declining.  Did Trainor most likely violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation?
option_b: Yes, since his recommendation was premised on opinion, not fact.
option_c: Yes, since he benefitted from the price increase caused by his recommendation.

explanation_en: The capital allocation line (CAL) is a straight line originating from the risk-free rate and tangent to the efficient frontier. It represents portfolios that dominate all other viable portfolios with respect to risk and return. The optimal risky portfolio is the point of tangency between the efficient frontier and the CAL. An investor's risk aversion determines investor utility. Utility helps an investor choose the optimal portfolio. Plotting portfolios with the same utility but with different levels of expected return and risk creates an indifference curve. An investor prefers all portfolios on the same indifference curve equally but prefers an indifference curve with higher utility over one with lower utility. The investor's optimal portfolio is the point of tangency between the indifference curve with the highest utility and the CAL. This dominant portfolio satisfies the investor's risk aversion and is viable. Although the indifference curve with lower utility does intersect the CAL, the investor would prefer the optimal investor portfolio since it has higher utility. (Choice A) All risk-averse investors want to have the highest return for a given level of risk, or the lowest risk for a given level of return. The highest return portfolio does not satisfy all the investor's needs. (Choice B) Borrowing and lending rates are most often required to match the investor's risk to a portfolio on the CAL. The actual rate of borrowing or lending is irrelevant in determining an optimal investor portfolio.
question_en: An investor's optimal portfolio is most likely to be determined by the:
option_c: indifference curve with the highest utility.

explanation_en:
In the short run, firms in a monopolistic competition structure can earn an economic profit. Economic profit brings new entrants; the new entrants
attract customers from existing firms. In the long run, this reduces demand for all firms that produce similar products, so the price falls until per-
unit price equals per-unit cost. "Cost" in this context includes opportunity costs, and since the owners' return from the business is one type of
opportunity cost, all firms' economic profit equals zero in the long run.
In monopolistic competition, a firm maximizes profit when producing a quantity at which marginal revenue (MR) = marginal cost (MC). Producing a
higher quantity means that the incremental cost for each unit exceeds the incremental revenue generated by that unit; the firm generates a loss on
each additional unit sold. Producing a lower quantity (ie, minimizing marginal cost) means that the firm not only fails to maximize its economic
profit in the short run, but actually incurs an economic loss (Choice C).
Note: Although this question specifically addresses monopolistic competition, the condition that firms optimally produce when MR = MC applies to
all market structures. It is likely that the exam will have questions on this topic.
(Choice B) In monopolistic competition, profit maximization in the long run occurs when MR = MC, not when average cost is lowest.
question_en: For a firm operating in a monopolistic competition market structure, which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: In the long run, the firm's economic profit equals zero.
option_b: In the long run, the optimal quantity produced is that at which average cost is lowest.
option_c: In the short run, the firm should produce the quantity at which marginal cost is lowest.

explanation_en: A lognormal distribution is a positively skewed probability distribution with a lower bound of zero that models probability distributions of asset prices. Asset prices cannot be less than zero, so the distribution is positively skewed with a lower bound of zero and no upper bound. The long tail on the right reflects the reduced probability of higher prices for the asset. Random variables follow a lognormal distribution if their natural logarithms follow a normal distribution. For example, an asset's continuously compounded return for any period is the natural logarithm of the ratio of its ending price to its beginning price: An asset's continuously compounded returns may follow a normal distribution. In that case, the asset's prices follow a lognormal distribution. (Choice A) An F-distribution is used for hypothesis tests concerning the equality (or inequality) of the variances of two separate populations. (Choice B) A binomial distribution is a probability distribution based on an event having one of two possible outcomes. A binomial distribution can model the change of asset prices over time but does not model the distribution of the prices themselves.
question_en: Prices for a volatile asset most likely follow a(n):

explanation_en: The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is equal to stock price divided by earnings per share.  Trailing P/E uses past earnings, whereas forward P/E is based on future earnings.  Justified forward P/E uses earnings based on a predictive model such as the Gordon growth model (GGM).  Analysts use the justified forward P/E to compare companies and draw conclusions about stock prices. The relationship between justified forward P/E and the GGM implies that an increase in the dividend payout ratio results in a higher forward P/E. However, a relationship also exists between the dividend payout ratio and the long-term dividend growth rate: This indicates that the dividend payout ratio is also inversely related to the long-term growth rate, which is directly related to the forward justified P/E ratio.  This reflects the fact that earnings paid out as dividends cannot be reinvested into the company to fuel future growth. As a result, care must be taken when trying to understand the effect of a change in the dividend payout ratio on the P/E ratio.  The dividend payout ratio is both directly and inversely related to the P/E ratio.  Either influence may predominate in a given situation.  Therefore, if the dividend payout ratio increases, then justified forward P/E may increase or decrease—depending on the scenario. The relationship between justified forward P/E ratio and the Gordon growth model implies that if the growth rate increases, the P/E ratio increases (ie, they are directly related).  An increase in the required rate of return implies a lower justified forward P/E (ie, they are inversely related) (Choices B and C).
question_en: As a result of the relationship between the Gordon growth model and the justified forward price-to-earnings ratio, all else being equal, an increase in the justified forward P/E most likely indicates a(n):
option_a: change in the dividend payout ratio.
option_b: increase in the required rate of return.
option_c: decrease in the long-term growth rate.
