explanation_en:
Execution instructions vs. validity instructions
Market order types Examples
Market: order is immediately filled at the best available price
Execution instructions Limit: order is filled at a threshold price or better
All-or-none (AON): entire order is filled or canceled
Day: expires at the end of the trading day
Stop: contingent on a specified price to trigger action
Validity instructions
Good-till-canceled (GTC): order is good until canceled
Market-on-close (MOC): order filled at the day's closing price
Orders to buy or sell securities can include both execution and validity instructions. Execution instructions address how to fill an order with
respect to:
The price at which to buy or sell.
The size (ie, quantity) of the order.
Validity instructions refer to when an order can be filled, as well as how long an unfilled order should remain open before it expires. A stop order
is a type of validity instruction. A stop order does not become executable until the security has traded at a prespecified trigger price (ie, stop
price). A buy-stop order cannot be filled until the security has traded at a price equal to or higher than the stop price.
"All-or-nothing" refers to the quantity of the security to be bought or sold; therefore, it is a type of execution instruction. The investor in this
question would have indicated the number of shares that would be purchased in the buy-stop order. However, by adding the all-or-nothing
instruction, the intermediary cannot fill any of the order unless the entire order can be filled.
(Choices A and B) A buy-stop, all-or-nothing order contains both execution and validity instructions.
question_en: An investor places a buy-stop, all-or-nothing order for a security. The type of instruction(s) relating to this order is (are) best described as:
option_c: both validity and execution instructions.

explanation_en:
Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability
Income tax expense < taxes payable
Deferred tax asset
Created by overpaying tax in current period
Income tax expense > taxes payable
Deferred tax liability
Created by underpaying tax in current period
Deferred tax items (ie, deferred tax assets and liabilities) arise from the difference between income tax expense (for accounting purposes) and
taxes payable (for tax reporting) for a period. Differences can occur as tax expense is calculated according to accounting standards whereas
taxes payable are calculated according to the tax code.
Deferred tax assets (DTA) arise when taxable profit is greater than accounting profit and taxes payable are greater than tax expense.
Deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise when taxable profit is less than accounting profit and taxes payable are less than tax expense.
In this scenario, the value of deferred tax items is directly correlated with the tax rate. All else equal, when the tax rate decreases (as is the
case in this scenario), DTA and DTL decrease. Since the company's DTA exceeds its DTL, it has a net DTA balance, which is reported as a net
long-term asset under US GAAP. Therefore, a decrease in the tax rate ultimately reduces total assets, which increases the debt-to-asset
(debt/asset) ratio.
(Choice A) Operating profit is pre-tax, so a decrease in tax expense will not affect operating profit.
(Choice C) Since the company has a net DTA, decreasing the tax rate also reduces the DTA. From the accounting equation assets = liabilities +
equity, equity would have to decrease, not increase, to maintain the balance.
question_en: A company reporting under US GAAP has deferred tax assets that exceed deferred tax liabilities. All else equal, a reduction in the tax rate will most likely increase the company's:
option_c: shareholders' equity.

explanation_en: Derivative markets increase economic efficiency and welfare by facilitating a more optimal allocation of risks. Derivatives can be used to reduce or eliminate a party's market exposure through hedging or other risk management strategies. Those seeking increased returns on capital can take on more risk by increasing exposure to the desired assets or sectors with the appropriate derivative positions. The image above illustrates how derivatives trades transfer risk. The owner of a long asset position bears the full price risk of the asset. The asset owner can eliminate price risk by selling a futures contract. The buyer of the long futures position now bears the price risk originally borne by the asset owner. Thus, from a global perspective, price risk has not been eliminated (Choice B). Critics claim that derivative trading leads to increased financial speculation, resulting in market instability. However, financial panics occurred frequently before the advent of derivatives trading, and panics that have occurred since often originated outside of derivative markets. Further, derivative markets function more efficiently since speculators provide liquidity and assume risks that hedgers wish to eliminate (Choice C). It seems clear that use of derivatives neither increases nor decreases economy-wide risk but merely reallocates it.
question_en: Which of the following statements best describes how derivatives markets influence risk? Derivatives markets:
option_a: facilitate more optimal allocation of risk.
option_b: reduce economy-wide risk by enabling hedging strategies.
option_c: increase economy-wide risk by facilitating financial speculation.

explanation_en: Consensus protocols: proof of work and proof of stake Proof of work Proof of stake Validation Miners validate transactions by solving algorithm puzzles "Stakers" guarantee transactions Pledged stake of holdings in Validation requirements Massive amounts of computing power blockchain Protection from Computing power requirements protect against third-party "Stakers" protect access manipulation manipulation Blockchains are digital ledgers where transaction information is recorded in a series of linked "blocks" using a consensus protocol to verify and link the blocks and thus establish an unchangeable "truth." Two primary types of consensus protocols are the proof of work (PoW) and proof of stake (PoS) mechanisms. PoW protocols require crypto miners to solve complex cryptographic puzzles, a process that consumes large amounts of computing power to earn cryptocurrency as a reward. The large expenditure of time, computing power, and energy is intended to make the cost of fraud greater than its potential rewards. PoS protocols have individual validators pledge or lock up some of their holdings as a "stake" to earn the opportunity to validate and guarantee the accuracy of newly added information (Choice C). The "stakers" are assumed to control and protect the blockchain. (Choice A) Tokenization is the process of validating ownership rights to a portion of a blockchain or a distributed ledger. It is one of the applications of distributed ledger technology (DLT) to the financial services and investment management industry.
question_en: Which of the following consensus protocols most likely requires solving puzzles using large amounts of computing power?
option_c: Proof of stake

explanation_en: If the investment horizon is shorter than the Macaulay duration, the price impact of a decrease in YTM dominates the loss of reinvestment income and the realized yield will be higher than the YTM at purchase.
question_en: An investor purchases a fixed coupon bond with a Macaulay duration of 5.3. The bond's yield to maturity decreases before the first coupon payment. If the YTM then remains constant and the investor sells the bond after three years, the realized yield will be:
option_a: equal to the YTM at the date of purchase.
option_b: higher than the YTM at the date of purchase.
option_c: lower than the YTM at the date of purchase.

explanation_en: Examining a portfolio's return is only one part of evaluating a portfolio's performance.  Another part is determining how much risk it took to earn that return.  This is accomplished by calculating a risk-adjusted return.  In portfolio management, the return is adjusted for risk by using either systematic risk (beta) or total risk (standard deviation). M-squared uses standard deviation to measure the total risk-adjusted return of a portfolio.  It is the difference between a portfolio's hypothetical market-risk-adjusted excess return and the excess return of the market.  This hypothetical risk-adjusted return is found by calculating the portfolio's return using the market's risk.  If M-squared is positive, then the portfolio's risk-adjusted performance is better than that of the market. (Choice B)  The Sharpe ratio is a performance measure that determines a market premium (a security's level of return above the risk-free rate) per unit of total risk (standard deviation).  The Sharpe ratio is not the difference between two returns, but rather scales return per unit of risk. (Choice C)  Jensen's alpha measures the systematic-risk-adjusted excess return of a portfolio using beta, not standard deviation.  It is used to calculate the difference between the actual return and the return predicted by the capital asset pricing model.  A positive Jensen's alpha shows that the portfolio has outperformed the market on this risk-adjusted basis.
question_en: A manager converts a portfolio's excess return to match the market's risk and then compares it with the market's excess return.  The manager is most likely calculating which of the following performance measures?
option_c: Jensen's alpha

explanation_en: With a large sample size (75) the z-statistic is used. The z-statistic is calculated by subtracting the hypothesized parameter from the parameter that has been estimated and dividing the difference by the standard error of the sample statistic. Here, the test statistic = (sample mean – hypothesized mean) / (sample standard deviation / (sample size)1/2 = (X − µ) / (σ / n1/2) = (57,000 – 54,000) / (1,300 / 751/2) = (3,000) / (1,300 / 8.66) = 19.99.
question_en: A survey is taken to determine whether the average starting salaries of CFA charterholders is equal to or greater than $58,500 per year. What is the test statistic given a sample of 175 CFA charterholders with a mean starting salary of $67,000 and a standard deviation of $5,200?

explanation_en: Operating profit margin = (EBIT / sales) = (1,500 / 3,000) = 0.5.
question_en: Given the following income statement and balance sheet for a company: Balance Sheet Assets Year 2003 Year 2004 Cash 500 450 Accounts Receivable 600 660 Inventory 500 550 Total CA 1300 1660 Plant, prop. equip 1000 1250 Total Assets 2600 2910 Liabilities Accounts Payable 500 550 Long term debt 700 700 Total liabilities 1200 1652 Equity Common Stock 400 400 Retained Earnings 1260 1260 Total Liabilities & Equity 2600 2910 Income Statement Sales 3000 Cost of Goods Sold (1000) Gross Profit 2000 SG&A 500 Interest Expense 151 EBT 1349 Taxes (30%) 405 Net Income 944 What is the operating profit margin?

explanation_en: Security market indexes may be used as benchmarks for the performance of active managers, but the index chosen should represent the universe of securities from which the manager is choosing. Here, an index of high yield bonds would be a more appropriate benchmark.
question_en: A high yield bond fund states that through active management, the fund's return has outperformed an index of Treasury securities by 4% on average over the past five years. As a performance benchmark for this fund, the index chosen is:
option_a: inappropriate, because the index return does not reflect active management.
option_c: inappropriate, because the index does not reflect the actual bonds in which the fund invests.

explanation_en: Private equity securities are illiquid and do not trade in public securities markets. Holders of private equity must negotiate with other investors to sell the securities. Private equity securities are typically issued to qualified institutional investors.
question_en: Private equity securities most likely:
option_a: are illiquid and do not have quoted prices.
option_c: are issued to individual investors.

explanation_en: The put allows a trader to sell Basil common stock for $7.50 more than the current market value ($55.00 − $47.50). The trade is normally closed out with a cash settlement, but the trader could buy 100 shares for $47.50 per share and immediately sell them to the option writer for $55.00.
question_en: Basil, Inc., common stock has a market value of $47.50. A put available on Basil stock has a strike price of $55.00 and is selling for an option premium of $10.00. The put is:
option_c: in-the-money by $10.00.

explanation_en: To ensure compliance with the Standard, members should seek to communicate investment recommendations to all clients who have indicated an interest and also those for whom the securities are suitable. There is no need to communicate recommendations to clients for whom the securities are deemed un- suitable.
question_en: Concerning Standard III(B), Fair Dealing, which of the following actions is NOT a valid procedure for compliance with the Standard?
option_a: Communicate investment recommendations to all customers including those accounts for which the securities are not eligible for purchase.
option_b: Limit the number of people that are involved and are privy to the fact that an investment recommendation is going to be disseminated.
option_c: Communicate investment recommendations simultaneously within the firm and to customers, where possible.

explanation_en: Rating agencies' assessments of credit risk reflect the expected loss that results from a borrower (ie, bond issuer) default.  The two elements of credit risk are default probability and loss severity: Default probability is the estimated likelihood of a default occurring. Loss severity is an estimate of the decrease in value of the bondholder's claim (ie, principal and any past-due coupons) in the event of a default. Expected loss is estimated as the product of two factors: default probability and loss severity, where loss severity equals 1 − Recovery rate. The terms loss severity, loss given default, and loss severity given default are used interchangeably, and whichever expression is used is equal to 1 − Recovery rate. (Choices A and B)  Spread risk (ie, change in the difference of a bond's YTM versus a benchmark yield) and downgrade risk (ie, potential of a bond's credit rating being reduced) reflect possible changes in a bond's credit quality, but neither directly measures default probability.
question_en: When analyzing the credit risk of a bond issue, the expected loss can most likely be estimated knowing only the bond's:
option_c: default probability and loss severity.

explanation_en: It is a violation of Standard III(B) because the advisor should act first on behalf of existing clients whose needs and characteristics she already knows. It is a violation of Standard III(C) because she has never met the prospect and does not know if the new ideas are appropriate for the prospect. Thus, "both of these" is the best response.
question_en: An investment advisor goes straight from a research seminar to a meeting with a prospective new client with whom she has never been in contact. The advisor is very excited about the information she just received in the seminar and begins showing the prospect the new ideas her firm is coming up with. This is most likely a violation of:
option_c: Standard III(C), Suitability.

explanation_en: A more unionized labor force increases the bargaining power of the suppliers of labor.
question_en: An industry is experiencing a significant increase of unionized labor. In the context of Porter's Five Forces, this change most likely implies:
option_c: decreasing bargaining power of customers.

explanation_en: Business cycles measure changes in economic activity. Financial cycles measure changes in financing and credit conditions (eg, pricing, availability, risk attitudes). Credit cycles are a subset of financial cycles and describe changes in availability and pricing (ie, interest rates/yields) of private sector credit, which has direct implications for the business cycle. Credit cycles tend to be procyclical, not countercyclical, to business cycles since credit availability expands during economic expansions and contracts sharply during economic downturns. (Choice A) The credit cycle tends to peak prior to the onset of a recession and is often a precursor to the peak of the economic cycle. As the business cycle slows/contracts, lending institutions often severely restrict credit availability while increasing the cost of credit. (Choice C) Credit cycles tend to amplify the duration and magnitude of the business cycle: when the economy is expanding (contracting), creditors are more (less) willing to lend, so the supply of credit increases (decreases) and its price decreases (increases), accelerating the trend of the business cycle.
question_en: Credit cycles are least likely to:
option_c: amplify the duration and magnitude of business cycles.

explanation_en:
A high residual value estimate reduces the depreciable base and thus depreciation expense.
Long average lives reduce the annual depreciation expense for any given depreciable base. The
combination of the two would result in the lowest depreciation expense, which would lead to
the highest net income and profit margins.
question_en: A company acquires some new depreciable assets. It uses straight-line deprecation for all of its assets. Which of the following combinations of estimated residual values and useful lives is most likely to produce the highest net profit margin? Estimated residual values should be:
option_c: low with long average lives.

explanation_en: The equation for the capital asset pricing model is: E(Ri) = RF + βi[E(Rm) − RF] Beta measures the sensitivity of the stock's returns to changes in the returns on the market portfolio and is a standardized measure of the stock's systematic or non- diversifiable risk. As indicated by the CAPM equation, the expected return for any stock is related to its beta. In contrast, unsystematic risk does not affect the CAPM expected return. Therefore, according to the CAPM, expected returns are identical for assets with identical betas. Stock X has identical systematic risk but greater unsystematic risk than Stock Y, resulting in greater total risk (standard deviation).
question_en: Stephanie Dell is evaluating two stocks (X and Y) using the capital asset pricing model. Dell predicts that the betas for the two stocks will be identical but that the unsystematic risk for Stock X will be much higher than for Stock Y. According to the capital asset pricing model, in equilibrium:
option_a: Stock X will have a higher expected return than Stock Y but a standard deviation equal to Stock Y.
option_b: Stock X will have a higher standard deviation than Stock Y but an expected return equal to Stock Y.
option_c: both the expected return and standard deviation for Stock X will be higher than Stock Y.

explanation_en: Tiered pricing refers to setting prices based on a customer's volume of purchases.
question_en: Debrin Company uses a tiered pricing strategy. Debrin is most likely to:
option_a: charge higher prices during peak times of day.
option_b: offer a discount for buying a large number of units.
option_c: set a temporarily low price until it builds market share and scales up production.

explanation_en:
According to the Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting 2010 within the International
Financial Reporting Standards, as well as Concept Statement 8 under US GAAP, "the objective
of general purpose financial reporting is to provide financial information about the reporting
entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders, and other creditors in making
decisions about providing resources to the entity."
question_en: The objective of general purpose financial reporting is bestdescribed as:
option_a: facilitating resource allocation decisions by current and potential investors and creditors.
option_b: reporting an entity's economic resources and claims, and changes therein, to shareholders.
option_c: providing information about financial performance to a wide range of users.

explanation_en: Market liquidity risk is the risk of receiving less than market value when selling a bond and is reflected in the size of the bid-ask spreads. Market liquidity risk is greater for the bonds of less creditworthy issuers and for the bonds of smaller issuers with relatively little publicly traded debt. Loss severity and recovery rate refer to defaults.
question_en: The risk of receiving less than market value when selling a bond is referred to as:
option_c: market liquidity risk.

explanation_en: The correct answer properly accounts for the float adjustment in market capitalization weighting, calculating the beginning float-adjusted market cap as $336,000 and ending float-adjusted market cap as $345,000, resulting in an index value of 102.68.
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a three-stock market index:

Stock A: 5,000 shares outstanding, beginning price $40, ending price $45
Stock B: 2,000 shares outstanding, beginning price $68, ending price $60

If the index is float-adjusted market-capitalization weighted and 90% of Stock A and 100% of Stock B shares are in the public float, what is the ending index value? (Beginning index value = 100)
option_a: Correct. The index is float-adjusted market-cap weighted, so the weights are based on float-adjusted market capitalizations.
option_b: Incorrect. It ignores the float and simply computes the index on the basis of market-capitalization weighting.
option_c: Incorrect. It does make adjustment for the market float but makes the mistake of including dividends in the ending price of the stock.

explanation_en: This is an example of a permanent timing difference, as the expense passes through the income statement but is not deducted for tax purposes. Permanent differences do not result in DTAs or DTLs.
question_en: Compass Company made a donation to a charity and expensed it in the period in which it was made. The country's tax authorities do not allow charitable donations to be deducted for tax purposes. The difference between the treatment of the expense in the accounts and the tax returns will result in:
option_a: no deferred tax items being created.
option_b: the creation of a deferred tax asset.
option_c: the creation of a deferred tax liability.

explanation_en: Standard VI(A), Disclosure of Conflicts, requires members to disclose to their employer all matters, including beneficial ownership of securities, that reasonably could be expected to interfere with their duty to their employer or ability to make unbiased and objective recommendations. Disclosure of an employer's own involvement with the security is not necessary in this instance. If the report had been for external use, it would have been necessary to make all of the disclosures given as choices.
question_en: Will Lambert, CFA, is a financial analyst for Offshore Investments. He is preparing a purchase recommendation on Burch Corporation for internal use. According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, which of the following statements about disclosure of conflicts is not required? Lambert would NOT need to disclose to his employer that:
option_a: Offshore is an OTC market maker for Burch Corporation's stock.
option_b: he is a beneficiary of a pension plan of his former employer that owns a large number of shares of Burch's stock.
option_c: his wife owns 2,000 shares of Burch Corporation.

explanation_en: The accounts receivable (AR) turnover ratio measures the number of times, on average, accounts receivable is generated by credit sales and collected as cash during a fiscal period. Credit sales occur when companies allow customers to defer sales invoice payments for a short period of time (commonly 30-60 days). Companies then record the amount owed from the customers as AR. A higher AR turnover ratio implies greater efficiency in converting receivables to cash and indicates better liquidity. This efficiency can result from a firm's effectiveness in receivables collection or from its credit-extension policies (eg, granting trade discount incentives for early payment). AR turnover for the three companies are as follows: Company 1 has the highest AR turnover ratio of 3.64, which means that it is the most efficient in collecting its AR among the three companies. (Choice B) Company 2 has collected on its AR 2.50 times on average during the year. This means that it was less efficient than Company 1 at converting receivables to cash. (Choice C) Company 3 has collected on its AR 3.04 times on average during the year. This means that it was less efficient that Company 1 at converting receivables to cash.
question_en:
A consultant is evaluating several companies and has collected the following information for the fiscal year:

| Company | Credit Sales ($ millions) | Cost of Goods Sold ($ millions) | Accounts Receivable Average Balance ($ millions) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9.0 | 5.0 | 2.5 |
| 2 | 10.0 | 7.3 | 4.0 |
| 3 | 7.0 | 5.0 | 2.3 |

Which company has the best accounts receivable turnover?
option_c: Company 3

explanation_en: The risk neutral probability () of an upward price move = (1 + r – Rd) / (Ru – Rd) = (1 + 0.03 – 0.90) / (1.10 – 0.90) = 0.65. Therefore the π of a downward price move = 1 – 0.65 = 0.35. [0.65 × Max (0, $33 – $31)] + [0.35 × Max (0, $27 – $31)] = $1.30
question_en: A stock's price is currently $30 and at the end of three months when its options expire, the stock price is expected to either go up or down by 10%. What is the value of a call option with a strike price of $31?

explanation_en: Ethical conduct includes those actions that are perceived as beneficial and conforming to the ethical expectations of society, not merely what is legally required or what balances consequences.
question_en: Ethical conduct is most likely behavior that:
option_a: conforms to expectations as laid out by laws and regulations.
option_b: is perceived to be beneficial as per society's ethical expectations.
option_c: simply considers both the direct benefit and indirect consequences on others.

explanation_en: Total return includes dividend yield. Because dividends are not included in the performance of the index itself, the portfolio will outperform the index by the amount of the dividend yield.
question_en: An investor purchases 1,000 shares of each of the stocks in a price-weighted index at their closing prices (ignore transactions costs). On a total return basis, if the index stocks remain the same, this portfolio will most likely:
option_a: perform exactly like the index over time.
option_c: underperform the index over time.

explanation_en: The correct answer is C because in order to avoid violating Standard III(E), Preservation of Confidentiality, Staal should determine if applicable securities regulations require disclosing the records before she provides the confidential information concerning her client's investments.
question_en: Teresa Staal, CFA, is an investment officer in a bank trust department. She manages money for celebrities and public figures, including an influential local politician. She receives a request from the politician's political party headquarters to disclose his stock holdings. The request indicates that local law requires the disclosure. What steps should Staal most likely take to ensure she does not violate any of the Standards?
option_a: Provide the information and inform her client
option_b: Send the requested documents and inform her supervisor
option_c: Check with her firm's compliance department to determine her legal responsibilities.

explanation_en: Both of these are explicitly required by Standard V(A).
question_en: In the process of recommending an investment, in order to comply with Standard V(A), Diligence and Reasonable Basis, a CFA Institute member must:
option_a: support a recommendation with appropriate research and investigation.
option_b: have a reasonable and adequate basis for the recommendation.
option_c: do both of the above.

explanation_en:
Most fixed-coupon bonds pay interest semiannually on the same dates each year, such as every January 31 and July 31. However, interest
accrues every day between payment dates, including days when the markets are closed for trading. An investor who sells a bond between
payment dates is entitled to the interest that has accrued as of the date of sale. The accrued interest is added to the price of the bond.
The amount of accrued interest depends on the bond's day-count convention (ie, the method used to count the number of days between
coupon payments). The day-count conventions used by the CFA materials are actual/actual and 30/360, which assumes 30 days in each month
(including February) and 360 days in a year (including leap years).
(Choice A) 120 is a simplistic calculation that multiplies the number of whole months (four) by the presumed number of days in each month (30).
This is incorrect since the 30/360 convention requires that the number of days be adjusted for periods that are different than a whole month.
(Choice C) 128 is the actual number of days between July 15 and November 20, not the number of days using the 30/360 convention.
question_en: A bondholder receives a coupon payment for a semiannual-paying bond on July 15, 20X3 and then sells the bond on November 20 of the same year. If the bond uses a 30/360 day-count convention and the settlement date and sale date are the same, the number of days of accrued interest is closest to:

explanation_en: Within the asset management industry, most firms are categorized as either buy-side or sell-side. Buy-side firms are asset managers that make investment decisions for their clients. Some may specialize in one asset class (eg, emerging market equities) or style (eg, value investing). More generalized firms offer full service to clients and a diverse set of asset classes. Buy-side firms buy trading and research services from sell- side firms. Sell-side firms are broker-dealers that facilitate trading for asset managers. They are considered "sell-side" since they sell their services to buy- side firms. A sell-side firm may bundle trading services with other ancillary offerings, such as independent investment research or investment recommendations. (Choice A) Sell-side firms sell trading services, not asset management services, to buy-side firms. (Choice B) Sell-side firms, not buy-side firms, provide independent investment research as part of their services beyond trading services.
question_en: Which of the following best describes the roles of buy-side and sell-side firms?
option_a: Sell-side firms sell asset management services to buy-side firms.
option_b: Buy-side firms provide independent investment research to sell-side firms.
option_c: Buy-side firms are asset managers that buy trading services from sell-side firms.

explanation_en: The converged accounting standards concerning revenue recognition, issued in May 2014 by the IASB and FASB, are principles-based.
question_en: The approach to revenue recognition in the converged accounting standards that were issued in May 2014 is best described as:
option_c: rules-based.

explanation_en: If the QM is deemed to be deficient, this means it is lower than the discount margin (DM). The coupons are based on market reference rate (MRR) + QM, and so if the coupons being offered are less than the required return, the bond will trade below par value. If QM = DM, the bond would trade at par, and if QM was greater than DM, the bond would trade at a premium.
question_en: If the quoted margin (QM) of a floating-rate note (FRN) is deemed to be deficient, the FRN will trade at what price relative to par value?
option_c: Above par.

explanation_en: Standard VI(A) requires Grabbo to disclose to her employer her hedge fund development activity as it could interfere with her responsibilities at Atlantic, regardless of whether the funds trade in different securities or whether she works on it only during personal time.
question_en: Umi Grabbo, CFA, is a highly regarded portfolio manager for Atlantic Advisors, a mid-sized mutual fund firm investing in domestic securities. She has watched the hedge fund boom and on numerous occasions suggested that her firm create such a fund. Senior management has refused to commit resources to hedge funds. Attracted by the potential higher fees associated with hedge funds, Grabbo and several other employees begin development of their own hedge fund to invest in international securities. Grabbo and her colleagues are careful to work on the fund development only on their own time. Because Atlantic management thinks hedge funds are a fad, she does not inform her supervisor about the hedge fund creation. According to the Standards of Practice Handbook, Grabbo should most likely address which of the Standards immediately?
option_c: Additional compensation arrangements

explanation_en: At expiration, the long party will buy at the forward price and can sell at the spot price.  The forward contract requires the long party to buy the asset in the future, which means the party cannot hold the asset now.  As a result, the value of the contract is increased by the present value of the asset's holding costs and is reduced by the present value of the asset's forgone benefits.  Therefore, the forward contract's value at any time prior to expiration is equal to (spot price − present value of forward price + present value of costs − present value of benefits). In this hypothetical scenario, the storage cost of holding the asset increased since contract initiation.  Suppose that at the end of May, the present value of the forward price is 102, the spot price is 100, the present value of the benefits is 1, and the present value of the storage costs is 6.  Then the value of the forward contract is 100 − 102 + 6 − 1 = 3.  If instead the storage costs were 8, the value of the forward contract would be 100 − 102 + 8 − 1 = 5.  However, the forward price remains fixed throughout the life of the contract. Therefore, for the long party in a forward contract, all else being equal, if the storage costs of the underlying asset increase, the value of the forward contract increases (Choices A and B).
question_en: All else being equal, for a one-year forward contract initiated six months ago, an increase in the storage costs of the underlying asset implies that the contract's value to the long party most likely:
option_c: increases.

explanation_en: Call options give option holders the right to buy an underlying asset at a specified strike price at a future date. However, option holders do not have to exercise their rights. Exercise of the option depends on the price of the underlying asset relative to the option strike price. If the call is: In the money, then there is value in exercising the call. The strike price is less than the underlying asset's value, and the holder can exercise the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price, then sell the asset at the current market price and realize the difference. Out of the money, then there is no value in exercising the call. The strike price is greater than the underlying asset's price, and the option holder lets the option expire worthless. The call's exercise value depends on whether it is in the money or out of the money: Call exercise value = Max (0, Underlying asset market price − Option strike price) If a call option is in the money, then it is worth exercising and its exercise value is the underlying asset market price less the option strike price, which is greater than zero. (Choices B and C) The premium is used to calculate a position's profit but not an option's exercise value. The premium is determined when the position is created and may vary for different positions involving the same option.
question_en: The exercise value of an in-the-money call option is best described as the market price of the underlying asset minus the:
option_b: premium paid by the option buyer.
option_c: strike price plus the premium paid by the option buyer.

explanation_en:
Correlation analysis indicates the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables. However, correlation analysis has
limitations that can reduce its reliability as a summary statistic. These limitations include the following:
Outliers have significant impact. Outliers can create significant changes to the correlation between two variables. Analysts must judge
whether outliers contain information about the relationship between the variables and should therefore remain in the dataset or are noise
and should be excluded from the dataset (Choices A and B). If outliers from noise remain, they will reduce the correlation metric's
reliability.
Correlation measures only linear relationships. Variables can have a strong nonlinear (eg, logarithmic) relationship while also having
low correlation values since correlation does not account for a nonlinear relationship.
High correlation coefficients can be caused by spurious (ie, false) correlation. This occurs when:
the correlation is due to chance and not to a meaningful relationship.
calculations combine the two variables with a third variable.
the correlation results from a direct relationship to a third variable.
question_en: When conducting correlation analysis, the most appropriate approach is to exclude:
option_c: only outliers that are generated from noise.

explanation_en: The market size, which is the total revenue of all companies in the market, is $88 million. A company's market share is a ratio (not a dollar amount) of the company's revenue to the market size. With 10 companies, the average market share will be 10%. Company XYZ's market share is 20% ($17.6 million / $88 million).
question_en: A market has 10 companies and total revenue of $88 million in the last fiscal year. Company XYZ had revenue last year of $17.6 million. Which of the following statements is most accurate about this market and Company XYZ?
option_a: Company XYZ’s market share is larger than the average company in this market.
option_c: Company XYZ’s market share is $17.6 million.

explanation_en: A market order instructs the broker or exchange to obtain the best price immediately available when filling the order.
question_en: All else being equal, a reverse stock split results in:
option_a: a decrease in the number of shares and an increase in the share price.
option_b: an increase in the number of shares and a decrease in the share price.
option_c: an increase in the number of shares and an increase in the share price.

explanation_en: The coefficient of variation, CV, is the ratio of the standard deviation of a set of observations to their mean value, which measures the amount of risk (standard deviation) per unit of mean return.
question_en: Which of the following measures best quantifies the amount of risk per unit of meanreturn?
option_c: Coefficient of variation

explanation_en: The standard error of the estimate (s ) is an absolute (ie, not relative) measure of the accuracy of the regression, as reflected by the average distance between each predicted (Ŷ) and observed (Y) values of the dependent variable.  Since s  is the square root of the mean square error (MSE) , it is presented in the same units as Y.  Smaller values of s  mean that the regression line is a better fit of the data. In this scenario, s  is the correct statistic to use since the investor wants an absolute measure of the accuracy of the model.  Other measures of goodness of fit, such as the coefficient of determination (R ) and the F-statistic, provide a relative measure and are not appropriate for this case. Since this scenario does not provide the MSE, it must be calculated as the ratio of: the sum of squares error (SSE), or residual sum of squares, to the degrees of freedom, derived from the sample size (n) and the number of variables. Since there are two variables and SSE is known, the investor will need to know n to calculate s . (Choices B and C)  The regression coefficients (ie, the intercept and the slope, and the correlation between the variables are not necessary to calculate s .
question_en: An investor receives a research report that analyzes two securities through a simple linear regression.  The study discloses the coefficient of determination (R ) and the sum of squares error (SSE).  To estimate the accuracy of the model using an absolute measure of the errors, the investor will most likely need to know the:
option_c: correlation between the securities.

explanation_en: Decentralized finance (DeFi) has emerged to meet the demand for decentralized financial applications (dApps), which allow financial transactions to occur without a central system. dApps manage financial tasks on the blockchain, such as serving as a medium of exchange, a store of value, a way to tokenize underlying assets, and a means to record ownership and transfer of digital assets. They also allow for the creation of decentralized financial products and services covering lending, trading, investment, settlement, payments, and transfers. (Choice A) DeFi is not intended to reform financial regulations. Instead, it has emerged due to the need for decentralized financial applications that handle financial tasks on the blockchain. (Choice C) While DeFi offers certain technological advantages over the traditional finance system, such as saving time and reducing risk in settlements and asset transfers, it has not reached its full potential yet. Up to this point, DeFi applications have primarily been used for investors seeking leverage in their investments and speculating with digital assets.
question_en: Decentralized finance (DeFi) is most likely explored in order to:
option_b: function as a medium of exchange.
option_c: deleverage investment risk in digital assets.

explanation_en: A callable bond favors the issuer. Hence, the value of the bond is discounted by the value of the option, which means the yield will be higher.

question_en: Jim Crockett is a portfolio manager for Miami Advisors and reports to Vicki Tubbs, the Chief Investment Officer. Miami has developed a proprietary model that has been thoroughly researched and is known throughout the industry as the Miami model. The model is purely quantitative and takes a given set of client characteristics and universe of potential securities and forms a portfolio for the investor. Individual portfolio managers are responsible for selecting securities to fit into the model based on recommendations from the firm's research department and the managers' own judgment. Because of the specific nature of the inputs to the model, each manager is responsible for applying the model on his or her own computer. The basic philosophy of the process is thoroughly explained to clients. Crockett does not understand the basics of the model, but feels that since it provides pure quantitative output, he does not need to understand it. However, he misapplies the model for several of his clients. In reviewing some of Crockett's portfolios, Tubbs finds the errors and points them out to Crockett. Which of the following statements regarding Tubbs and Crockett is CORRECT?
option_a: Crockett has violated the Standards by not exercising diligence and thoroughness in making investment recommendations.
option_b: Crockett has violated the Standards by not considering the appropriateness and suitability of the investment for his clients.
option_c: Tubbs has violated the Standards by failing to supervise adequately.

explanation_en: In the four Cs of traditional credit analysis, collateral refers to the value of company assets relative to its level of indebtedness.  Collateral in this context is not narrowly focused on the value of assets pledged as collateral on secured bonds.  In this case, collateral refers to the estimated value of a company's financial, tangible and intangible assets and the degree to which their sale might mitigate creditor losses in the event of default. The two elements of credit risk are the probability of default and the severity of loss if default occurs.  The primary focus of most credit analysis is an issuer's ability to generate cash flow sufficient to make timely debt service payments (ie, avoid default).  The focus shifts to asset values (ie, collateral) when the probability of default has increased enough to concern investors. (Choice B)  Projected cash flow from company operations is an important consideration when evaluating an issuer's capacity in traditional credit analysis. (Choice C)  Affirmative and restrictive indenture provisions are an important consideration when evaluating bondholder contractual protections (ie, covenants) in traditional credit analysis.
question_en: In traditional credit analysis, collateral is most likely concerned with which of the following?
option_a: Asset values relative to level of indebtedness
option_b: Projected cash flow from company operations
option_c: Affirmative and restrictive indenture provisions

explanation_en: Generally, an option with a longer time to expiration is more valuable than a shorter-dated but otherwise identical option. However, this is not always the case for a deep-in-the-money European put option since it cannot be exercised until expiration, and its strike price must be discounted by the risk-free rate to account for this delay. Due to discounting, a longer-dated put can have less intrinsic value than a shorter-dated put. In this scenario, assume that the stock trades at zero while the put option has a strike price of €40 and a 5% risk-free rate. The present value of the strike price, discounted for one year at the risk- free rate, is about €38. This is lower than the six-month put's present value of about €39. (Choice B) A European put's value increases if a dividend is paid since the payment decreases the value of the underlying. All else equal, the one-year put should be worth more than the six-month put, given a dividend payment in nine months. (Choice C) The value of a put is directly related to the stock's volatility, regardless of the time to expiration. In this case, the values of both puts would be similarly affected by an increase in volatility.
question_en: A six-month European put option on a common stock is valued at €39, while an otherwise identical one-year put option is valued at €38. All else being equal, which of the following best describes the circumstance that results in this price difference?
option_a: The options are deep in the money.
option_b: The stock pays a dividend in nine months.
option_c: The underlying stock's volatility has increased.

explanation_en: Repurchase agreements (repos) and reverse repurchase agreements (reverse repos) have identical structures. In both transactions, the counterparties agree to an initial exchange (ie, sale) of securities for cash. The initial exchange is conditioned on the original security holder's promise to buy them back (ie, repurchase agreement). Repos are economically equivalent to a loan of cash collateralized by securities. In the repo diagram, the insurance company lending cash is not concerned with the specific security received, only that it is adequate collateral. The reverse repo has a different motivation: the hedge fund is borrowing a specific security and providing cash collateral in return. Reverse repos are often the least expensive method for borrowing securities needed to complete a short sale. A short sale is a sale of securities the seller does not own. Nonetheless, the securities must be delivered, which is the motivation for the hedge fund doing a reverse repo. Short sales may be done to speculate on declining prices or to hedge long positions. (Choice A) The hedge fund would use a repurchase agreement to earn interest since repo rates are higher than interest rates on reverse repos. (Choice B) The sale and repurchase prices in repos and reverse repos are set at transaction initiation, so neither transaction entails a direct speculation on the related security price.
question_en: When a hedge fund engages in a reverse repurchase agreement, which of the following is the most likely purpose?
option_c: Obtain securities to deliver on a short sale

option_b: High returns over a one-year period are followed by low returns over the following three years.
option_c: Low returns over a three-year period are followed by high returns over the following three years.

explanation_en:
The forward price is the future value of the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate adjusted for the future value of the net carrying costs.
Whether the forward price is greater than or less than the future value of the spot price depends on the costs and the benefits of holding the
underlying commodity:
If the benefits exceed the costs (ie, ɣ > ө), then (ɣ − ө) (1 + r)T is positive, resulting in a forward price that is less than the future value of the
spot price.
If the costs exceed the benefits (ie, ɣ < ө), then (ɣ − ө) (1 + r)T is negative, resulting in a forward price that is greater than the future value of
the spot price.
There is always a cost (eg, storage, insurance) to holding commodities, and they generate no holding period income (eg, dividends, interest). The
only benefit of holding a commodity is a convenience yield. A forward price that is greater than the future value of the spot price implies that the
holding costs exceed the benefits. In that case, the convenience yield must be less than the storage costs (Choices A and C).
question_en: .A commodity's forward price is greater than the future value of its spot price compounded at the risk-free rate. This most likely results from the commodity having a convenience yield:
option_b: that is less than the storage costs.
option_c: that is greater than the storage costs.

explanation_en: High-yield credit analysis: additional considerations Especially critical for high-yield issuers Liquidity Examples: cash on balance sheet, strong operating cash flow, bank credit facilities Financial Robust scenario analysis and stress testing take on projections added importance Leverage analysis at each level of debt required Debt structure "Top-heavy" debt structures decrease financial flexibility and are more prone to default Companies may issue high-yield debt for many reasons, but such companies tend to have weak balance sheets and/or impaired business models. Due to the greater operational risk and higher probability of default, credit analysis of high-yield bonds, compared to the analysis of investment-grade bonds, requires additional scrutiny. The priority of claims is of particular importance, and leverage calculations should be performed for every debt class. Secured creditors (eg, first and second lien) have the most senior claims on a company's cash flows and assets and rank ahead of all unsecured creditors. High-yield issuers with a large proportion of secured debt are considered "top-heavy." For top-heavy issuers, secured debt is often in the form of bank debt with stringent loan covenants, short maturities, and little room to access additional bank lines of credit. In the event of financial distress, such companies have limited ability to refinance or raise additional debt capital, leading to a higher risk of default and lower rate of recovery for creditors with a lower priority of claims (eg, senior unsecured debt) (Choices A and C).

explanation_en:
Sum of squares total
Sum of squares total (SST) = Sum of squares regression (SSR) + Sum of squares error (SSE)
A simple linear regression (SLR) can be used to assess the degree to which variations in a dependent variable are explained by variations in an
independent variable. Outputs of a regression analysis include the:
sum of squares total (SST), the variation in the observed values of the dependent variable versus its average value,
sum of squares regression (SSR), the proportion of variation of the dependent variable explained by changes in the independent variable,
and
sum of squares error (SSE), the proportion of variation of the dependent variable unexplained by changes in the independent variable.
F-statistics are used to evaluate the goodness of fit (ie, how well the regression model fits the data). F-statistics reflect the explained versus
the unexplained variation in the dependent variable, adjusted for sample size and degrees of freedom (ie, mean square regression [MSR] /
mean square error [MSE]). For a given data set, both the SSR and SSE increase as sample size increases:

| | Regression 1 | Regression 2 |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | 167.00 − 47.75 = 119.25 | 334.00 − 95.50 = 238.50 |
| MSR | 119.25 / 1 = 119.25 | 238.50 / 1 = 238.50 |
| MSE | 47.75 / (10 − 1 − 1) ≈ 5.9688 | 95.50 / (20 − 1 − 1) ≈ 5.3056 |
| F-statistic | 119.25 / 5.9688 ≈ 19.9791 | 238.50 / 5.3056 ≈ 44.9529 |

In this scenario, both the SST and SSE double when the sample size doubles. This indicates the same relative variance is exhibited by both
samples. Since the divisor in calculating the F-statistic is inversely related to sample size, other things equal, a larger sample size exhibiting the
same relative variation results in a greater value for the F-statistic (Choices A and B).
A larger sample size that exhibits the same relative variation of the dependent variable should give an analyst greater confidence regarding the
explanatory power of the independent variable.

| Regression 1 | 10 | 167.00 | 47.75 |
| Regression 2 | 20 | 334.00 | 95.50 |

Based on this information, the analyst should most likely conclude that:
option_b: both regressions have the same F-statistic.
option_c: Regression 2 has a larger F-statistic.

explanation_en: Conditional probability is the probability that one event will occur given that another event occurs. For example, an analyst may believe there is a 0.30 probability that a company will report earnings per share (EPS) of at least USD 0.20 (Event B). If Event B occurs, the analyst estimates a 0.60 probability that the company will increase its dividend (Event A). This describes a conditional probability since an of EPS of more than USD 0.20 impacts the probability of the dividend increase. Conditional probability can be higher, lower, or the same as unconditional probability. For example, the analyst may believe there is a 0.15 unconditional probability that the company will raise its dividend regardless of EPS. The conditional probability of a dividend increase given a threshold level of EPS (0.60) is higher than the unconditional probability of a dividend increase (0.15). (Choice A) Mutually exclusive events are events that cannot occur at the same time: P(A and B) = 0. Since this is the numerator of the equation for conditional probability, conditional probability for mutually exclusive events is always 0. (Choice C) The numerator for the conditional probability of B given A is P(B and A). However, P(B and A) is the same as P(A and B). This means that the conditional probability of A given B can equal the conditional probability of B given A if the probability of Events A and B (the denominator) is the same, that is if P(A) = P(B).

explanation_en:
Aggressive accounting vs. conservative accounting:
- Aggressive: Capitalizing costs; Classifying investments as trading securities; Presenting better pro forma results than IFRS or GAAP results
- Conservative: Expensing costs; Classifying investments as available-for-sale securities; Presenting pro forma results close to IFRS or GAAP results
Accounting choices affect the quality of a company's financial results. Aggressive accounting choices tend to inflate financial performance (eg, earnings, cash flow) in the current period but may understate performance in future periods. Conservative choices typically understate performance in the current period but may enhance future performance.
Capitalizing (instead of expensing) in-process research and development (R&D) costs in a reporting period assigns those costs to an asset on the balance sheet. They are then amortized periodically as an expense on the income statement. The capitalization of a cost will produce:
- higher net income in the current period since the entire cost is not expensed immediately, but
- lower net income in future periods since the remaining cost is expensed over time.
Therefore, capitalization is an aggressive accounting choice. R&D costs should be capitalized only when the product is reasonably certain to generate future revenue and is no longer considered to be in process.
(Choice A) Pro forma earnings typically include numerous management adjustments (ie, add-backs) that cause them to differ from reported earnings (ie, those under GAAP or IFRS). In general, management presents pro forma earnings that are higher than reported earnings and therefore considered aggressive.
(Choice C) When bond investments are treated as available-for-sale securities, any gains in fair value are included in other comprehensive income on the balance sheet instead of going directly to net income (earnings). Therefore, this treatment is a conservative choice.
Things to remember:
Aggressive accounting choices tend to inflate financial performance (eg, earnings, cash flow) in the current period but may understate performance in future periods. Conservative accounting choices typically understate performance in the current period but may enhance future performance. Capitalizing in-process research and development costs is considered an aggressive accounting choice.
question_en: Which of the following reporting practices is most likely considered aggressive accounting?
option_a: Presenting pro forma earnings per share (EPS) that are lower than reported EPS.
option_b: Capitalizing, instead of expensing, in-process research and development (R&D) costs.
option_c: Using the criteria of available-for-sale securities, rather than trading securities, to treat bond investment gains.

explanation_en: Monetary policy attempts to influence economic growth and inflation by increasing or decreasing the money supply and the availability of credit in the economy. question_en: Monetary policy is most accurately described as actions that influence economic activity by increasing or decreasing:

option_c: tax rates on income and consumption.

explanation_en:
Duration measures bond price sensitivity to changes in interest rates. Graphically, duration is the slope of the price/yield function. The effective
duration of a callable bond decreases as market interest rates decline below its coupon rate. Callable and noncallable bond prices behave
similarly when interest rates rise (purple curve segment), but their prices and durations diverge significantly as yields fall below bond coupon rates.
A callable bond has an embedded option giving the issuer the right to purchase (ie, call) the bond prior to maturity. The further market rates drop
below a bond's coupon, the greater the likelihood it will be called. As a result, no matter how low rates fall, the potential appreciation of a callable
bond is limited. That is reflected by the flattening slope (ie, decreasing duration) of the red segment of the callable bond price/yield curve.
question_en: A callable bond's coupon rate is 100 basis points (bps) below yields-to-maturity on noncallable bonds having the same time to maturity and credit risk. If market yields decline by 200 bps, the callable bond's effective duration most likely:
option_c: increases.

explanation_en: Oligopoly pricing theories Theory Description Kinked demand curve Compete on price Differentiate with advertising and branding Cournot assumption Firms act independently and simultaneously Equilibrium (ie, stable price and output quantity) Nash equilibrium No cooperation (ie, collusion) Firms act in their own best interest Stackelberg (ie, first mover) Firms act dependently and sequentially Leader (ie, top dog) sets quantity, others respond Collusion Firms cooperate to set quantity and price Firms act in the industry's best interest Oligopoly is a market structure in which a small number of firms sell similar products, with nonprice competition varying by market.  For example, many consumer goods companies compete by differentiating products through advertising and branding.  High barriers to entry typically protect existing firms from new entrants. Oligopolistic firms may adopt various pricing strategies.  Since the Cournot assumption supposes a competitive market, demand and marginal revenue curves are downward sloping (ie, firms are not price takers).  Supply and prices adjust naturally until, at long-run equilibrium, output quantity and price stabilize for each firm. (Choice A)  The Stackelberg (ie, first-mover) pricing theory, not the Cournot assumption, supposes that firms act sequentially, with the market leader moving first. (Choice B)  The Cournot assumption, applied to a duopoly (ie, two-firm market) in equilibrium, supposes that both firms act simultaneously and independently, without collusion (ie, cooperation), to determine production quantities to maximize profits.
question_en: For a duopoly (ie, two-firm market that is a special form of oligopoly) in equilibrium, which of the following choices best describes a characteristic of the Cournot assumption?
option_b: Firms cooperate to set output and price.
option_c: A firm's output is constant in the long run.

explanation_en:
Defined contribution plans (DC) Defined benefit plans (DB)
No future benefit guaranteed Employer promises future benefits
Employee bears responsibility for performance Employer bears responsibility for performance
Financial impact limited to expensing contributions made to Performance of plan assets can significantly impact
participants' accounts financial reporting
Accounting is straightforward and simple Accounting is complicated

A defined contribution (DC) plan is a type of employee retirement plan. Unlike a defined benefit (DB) plan, a DC plan does not guarantee the
employee any benefit at retirement. Instead, the employer establishes the plan and selects diverse investments that participants (ie, employees)
can invest in, allocating their account balance based on their individual risk and return preferences.
The funding in a DC plan can be contributions from the employer, the participant's own contributions (ie, salary deferrals), or a combination of
these. In all cases, the participant, not the employer, is responsible for the account's performance. All investment gains or losses, as well as
dividend or interest income generated by those investments, benefit the participant, not the employer (Choices A and C).
An employer receives a tax deduction for any contributions that it makes to participants' accounts. Deductibility applies whether the contributions
are contractually required (eg, collective bargaining agreements) or voluntary (eg, profit-sharing plans).

Accrual accounting Cash accounting

Example: Payment is due 30 days after invoice

A key concept of accrual accounting is that revenue is recognized when it is earned. The seller earns revenue from a sale when it has
substantially fulfilled all its obligations under the terms of the sale. The seller then reports the earned revenue. Under accrual accounting, revenue
recognition does not depend on whether the seller receives payment.
The company in this question provides its subscribers with access for one year following the subscriber's payment, so it has received payment
before it has completed its obligation. However, accounting standards require that it recognize a prorated amount of the subscription price as
revenue each month during the subscription period. Accordingly, the company will recognize 1/12th of the total subscription price each month, or
$3,000 / 12 = $250.
Note that the answer is the same whether the seller reports under IFRS or US GAAP accounting standards.
(Choice A) The company's obligation can be viewed as 12 separate monthly contracts. At the end of every month, it will have earned the
prorated share of the subscription price and will recognize the revenue associated with that month. Accounting standards do not permit the
company to delay any revenue recognition until the end of the entire subscription period. Such a delay would distort its financial picture.
(Choice C) $1,000 is the cumulative amount of income earned by the end of Month 4, not the amount earned solely for Month 4.
question_en: A company sells cloud-based accounting software. A 12-month subscription costs $3,000 payable in advance. If this company reports under IFRS standards, how much revenue will it recognize for the 4th month of each subscription?

Wellington may indicate that he passed Level II of the CFA Program and the year in which he passed, but he is not a candidate unless he is registered for the next exam or awaiting exam results. Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs addresses issues that concern the validity and security of the exams and the integrity and reputation of the CFA designation and CFA Institute.

explanation_en:
Order-driven system: priority rules for filling limit orders
The most aggressively priced orders (eg, highest-priced
Highest priority:
buys, lowest-priced sells) filled first
Price
Price takes priority over time and visibility
Orders of fully visible size have priority over those of partially
Next priority:
or fully hidden size
Visibility
Visibility takes priority over time
Next priority: Same-price orders filled based on time of receipt
Time received Earliest received = Higher priority
An order-driven system is used by nearly every stock exchange, with rules that match the buyers' and sellers' orders. Three basic rules
determine how limit orders are executed ("filled").
The first rule is based on price. Orders with the most aggressive prices (eg, highest buy price, lowest sell price) receive the highest priority. If
more than one order has the same price, priority is given to orders that are fully visible, meaning that the entire number of shares covered by the
order is known. Orders in which the size is hidden, either fully or partially (ie, iceberg orders, have lower priority than fully visible orders.
For orders with the same price and visibility, priority is based on when each order was received. The earliest-received order has the highest
priority, followed by the second earliest, etc.
In this case, Order 3 has the highest price, so it will be filled first even though it arrived last at the exchange. Orders 1 and 2 have the same price.
Order 1 arrived first, but since it is an iceberg order, it drops behind Order 2 in priority. Order 1 receives only 100 shares; Orders 2 and 3 are filled
entirely (Choices A and C).
question_en:
In an order-driven market system, the following buy limit orders for a stock are listed in the system's limit book:

| Order | Time Arrived | Number of Shares | Limit Price ($) | Special Instructions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10:05 | 100 | 15.10 | Iceberg order (total order is for 200 shares) |
| 2 | 10:07 | 200 | 15.10 |  |
| 3 | 10:08 | 200 | 15.11 |  |

Each order is listed for 200 shares. Based on the commonly used order precedence hierarchy, if the current market price is $15.10 and the exchange receives a market sell order for 500 shares, then the orders most likely to be fully executed are:
option_c: Orders 1, 2, and 3.

explanation_en: Auto loan asset-backed securities: prepayment dynamics Securitized by Amortizing auto loans and leases Nonrecourse loans Subject to prepayment risk due to Changes in interest rates Early loan payoff Vehicle ownership change Sales and trade-ins Repossessions and resale Insurance proceeds for destroyed autos Auto loan asset-backed securities (ABS) are securitized by amortizing, nonrecourse loans, which are prone to prepayments.  Prepayment risk is normally associated with changing interest rates, but auto loan ABS are also impacted by other factors.  There are two forms of prepayment risk: contraction risk and extension risk. Contraction risk is most acute when interest rates fall and lead to refinancing (eg, mortgage, auto loan), which pay loans off early.  More prepayments than expected shorten the life of the ABS, resulting in a reduction in the final maturity. Extension risk occurs when interest rates increase; higher rates result in slower prepayments than expected and lengthen the security's life (Choice B). Auto loan ABSs have other elements that affect the speed of prepayments not directly tied to interest rates, which exposes investors to more contraction risk. Examples include: borrowers who choose to pay the loan early sales and trade-ins repossessions and resales insurance proceeds for destroyed vehicles (Choice A)  Balloon risk refers to a risk of partially amortizing and interest-only loans that have balloon payments due at the end of the loan. Balloon payments are unusual for auto loans and therefore are not a risk for holders of auto loan ABS.
question_en: In a falling interest rate environment, an auto loan asset-backed security (ABS) most likely exposes an investor to:
option_c: contraction risk.

Consider the inventory equation: ending inventory = beginning inventory + purchases – cost of goods sold A write-down to NRV decreases ending inventory, with no effect on beginning inventory or purchases. For the inventory equation to hold, cost of goods sold must increase.
question_en: A U.S. GAAP firm writes down inventory to net realizable value. In the period of the writedown, what is the most likely effect on cost of goods sold?

explanation_en:
Average total cost is the cost, including fixed costs and variable costs, to produce the units. To be viable in the long run, firms must sell their
products at a price at least equal to average total cost. In the short run, it is optimal to sell at prices below average total cost if price exceeds
average variable cost. Price above variable cost means that the revenue per unit is greater than the added costs of producing it. Therefore, the
losses are smaller if the firm continues to operate rather than shut down. Any excess of price above variable cost is applied to fixed costs.
The graph above illustrates the consequences of the two short-run choices: Scenario A (continuing to operate), and Scenario B (shutting down).
The loss is greater if the firm shuts down instead of continuing operations.
(Choice A) Exiting a market is only likely if the price is expected to remain below average total cost for a long time.
(Choice C) Shutting down temporarily reduces revenue and variables costs to zero. Fixed costs are still incurred, resulting in a loss equal to fixed
costs. Sales at prices above variable costs means that there is some recovery of fixed costs, which results in a smaller loss than exiting the
market.
question_en: A firm is facing market prices that are below average total cost but above average variable cost. The optimal action for the firm in the short run is most likely to:
option_c: shut down temporarily.

explanation_en: Differences between permissioned and permissionless networks Permissioned Permissionless Speed of transaction validation Faster Slower Cost-effectiveness of transaction validation More Less Governance Centralized Decentralized Degree of decentralization Partial Total Access Limited membership Unlimited membership Digital ledger technology, which employs cryptography and algorithms, can be maintained on a permissioned or permissionless network. A permissionless network is open to any user to engage in transactions and to maintain the network. With many participants storing a copy of the same single distributed ledger, the network is decentralized, so no one user can cause the network to fail. Bitcoin creation is a well-known example of a permissionless network. In contrast, a permissioned network requires approval to join and to participate in various activities and thus is typically accessed by a limited number of authorized individuals. Such networks are generally used for enterprise purposes, enabling private entities to manage their data and operations. (Choice B) A permissionless network operates without any centralized authority for transaction validation and thus requires a larger number of members to reach consensus to validate transactions. As a result, processing speed is slower, which decreases network speed and scalability. (Choice C) Validating transactions on a permissionless network requires the work of many members, which consumes large amounts of processing power, making this type of network less cost-effective than permissioned blockchains.
question_en: Permissionless networks most likely support cryptocurrency investors by creating:
option_c: cost-effectiveness of transaction validation.

explanation_en: Typical bond contingency provisions Callability Issuer has right to redeem bond before maturity Putability Bondholder can require issuer to redeem bond before maturity Bondholder can convert bond into a predetermined number of issuer's Convertibility common shares Contingency provisions in the context of bonds are very specific and refer to the rights of the issuer and/or bondholders with respect to how a bond can be redeemed or disposed of. The most common types of contingency provisions concern whether a bond can be called, put, or converted. A putable bond gives its holder the right to require that the issuer redeem the bond before maturity. The redemption price is established in the indenture, in addition to any other relevant provisions such as when the bondholder must act. This right (ie, the put) can be valuable to the bondholder, and that value allows the issuer to pay a lower coupon rate. (Choice A) The issuer's right to defer coupon payments does not relate to redeeming or converting the bond, so it is not properly categorized as a contingency. (Choice C) Provisions concerning an issuer's ability to incur additional debt are a covenant, or promise, of actions that the issuer agrees to take (ie, affirmative covenants) or not take (ie, negative covenants).
question_en: A contingency provision contained in the indenture of a bond issued by a corporation most likely refers to:
option_a: the issuer's ability to defer coupon payments if certain conditions are met.
option_b: the bondholder's ability to force the corporation to redeem the bond before maturity.
option_c: the issuer's right to incur additional debt while some or all of the original amount is still outstanding.

explanation_en:
Companies use several methods to issue securities when raising equity capital. A rights offering is a relatively easy way for companies to raise
new capital by tapping into their existing shareholder base.
In a rights offering, existing shareholders are entitled to purchase, at a predetermined price, additional shares proportional to their existing
holdings. In this scenario, the investor has the right to buy 1 share for every 10 shares owned.
For shareholders, a disadvantage of a rights offering is that it is dilutive, forcing shareholders to commit additional capital to maintain their
proportional ownership. However, there also are advantages for shareholders, including the following:
Rights come at no cost.
Rights are a form of short-term warrant that can often be sold to other investors.
The subscription price is almost always below the market price, resulting in an immediate gain.
(Choice B) In a private placement, restricted shares (ie, shares that can be sold only to qualified investors) are sold directly to a limited number of
qualified investors. Participation in a private placement is not dependent on existing ownership.
(Choice C) A preferred stock offering is typically issued through traditional public offering methods and offers preferred stock, not additional
shares of common stock.

option_c: preferred stock offering.
