explanation_en: Certificates of deposit (CD) Nonnegotiable CD Negotiable CD Denomination ≤ USD 100,000 Usually ≥ USD 1,000,000 Early withdrawal Yes, with penalty No Tradable No Yes, in secondary market Banks receive much of their funding through retail customer deposits, but they also often turn to the wholesale funding market to obtain capital. The wholesale funding market consists of central bank funds, the interbank market, and certificates of deposit (CDs). In exchange for a deposit, a bank will issue a CD in a specific amount for a specified time and interest rate. CDs are one of the primary sources of funding for banks and similar financial institutions. CDs can be categorized as either negotiable or nonnegotiable. A nonnegotiable CD is commonly sold to the bank's retail customers. Nonnegotiable CDs pay interest at maturity, are issued in small denominations of usually less than USD 100,000, and can only be withdrawn before maturity by paying a penalty (Choice A). A negotiable CD is issued in large denominations, often USD 1 million or more, and can be traded to other investors in the secondary market. Negotiable CDs pay interest at maturity and cannot be withdrawn early. (Choice B) Both types of CDs can have maturities greater than one year. A CD with a maturity of more than one year is known as a term CD. All CDs pay interest at maturity.
question_en: A negotiable certificate of deposit (CD) is best described as having:
option_a: small denominations and a penalty for early withdrawal.
option_b: a maximum maturity of one year, and interest is paid monthly.
option_c: large denominations, and it can be traded in the secondary market.

question_en:

explanation_en: Standard III(A), Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, requires that members act for the benefit of their clients. Mader's duty is to her clients, who are shareholders of Danube. She has no duty to Danube's management, nor to the company itself, and must vote the shares accordingly.
question_en: Bertha Mader, CFA, received proxy material related to a hostile takeover attempt of Danube Industries by Balnet Company. She holds shares of Danube in most of her client accounts. Mader has a high opinion of Danube's management because they have run the company successfully and have always responded directly and honestly to her inquiries. She is not acquainted with Balnet's management team but knows they have a reputation for improving the bottom line at the companies they acquire, partly because they tend to replace upper management at their targets and assume their functions. Balnet's offer is 60% higher than the price of Danube shares before the announcement. Danube's management has contacted Mader and requested that she vote the shares she controls against the takeover because the management is concerned for their jobs and for the welfare of the company. To comply with the Code and Standards, Mader should:
option_a: delegate her proxy vote to another member of her firm due to the conflict of interest created when she was contacted by management.
option_b: vote for the takeover if it is in the best interest of Danube's shareholders, regardless of the consequences to current management.
option_c: vote for the takeover if she can get assurance that Danube's management team will remain in place.

explanation_en: Target independence means the central bank defines how inflation is computed, sets the target inflation level, and determines the horizon over which the target is to be achieved. Central banks that have operational independence are allowed to determine the policy rate. Transparency refers to the degree to which central banks report to the public on the state of the economic environment and is one of the three essential qualities of an effective central bank.
question_en: Central banks that are able to define how inflation is computed and determine its desired level are best described as having:

explanation_en: Companies typically have many options for short-term financing, including internal sources and financial intermediaries (eg, lines of credit). Mismanaging capital can result in higher costs paid or a shortage of funds. When managing funds, a company should ensure that: sufficient sources of capital are maintained to meet the company's cash needs, especially peak needs, and market rates for these sources are not excessive compared with market averages. In this scenario, selling the marketable securities is the company's cheapest option, with a 0.5% fee on sales. The company can free up funds by delaying its accounts payable payment up to 60 days, forgoing a 2% discount. ("2/10, net 60" means that the company has 60 days to pay but it can earn a 2% discount if payment is made within 10 days.) This lower cost option is preferable to liquidating bonds at a cost of 2.5% (Choice B). (Choice A) Issuing new equity in a secondary offering would be inappropriate for a company trying to meet short-term liquidity needs. Equity issuances typically take time to execute and can have high costs, which makes this option more appropriate to fund long-term needs.
question_en: A company has CAD 50 million of short-term liquidity needs. The company has the following assets and liabilities: ● CAD 20 million in marketable securities, which can be sold with a 0.5% brokerage cost ● CAD 35 million in bonds, able to be liquidated at 2.5% cost ● CAD 50 million in accounts payable with terms of 2/10, net 60 To cover its liquidity needs at lowest cost, which of the following strategies would be most appropriate for the company to use?
option_a: Issue new equity in secondary offering
option_b: Sell all the marketable securities and sell bonds
option_c: Sell all the marketable securities and delay accounts payable

explanation_en: Temporary timing differences, such as differences in depreciation methods used for accounting and tax purposes, do not typically cause statutory and effective tax rates to differ. Factors which may cause these rates to differ include: Different tax rates in different tax jurisdictions Permanent tax differences: tax credits, tax-exempt income, nondeductible expenses, and tax differences between capital gains and operating income Changes in tax rates and legislation Tax holidays in some countries

explanation_en: Creation of deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL) Balance sheet item Scenario Carrying amount > Tax base → DTL Asset Carrying amount < Tax base → DTA Carrying amount > Tax base → DTA Liability Carrying amount < Tax base → DTL The carrying amount of an asset or liability reflects the book value on the balance sheet, reported according to the applicable accounting standards. In contrast, the tax base of an asset or liability reflects the carrying value for tax purposes, according to the applicable tax code. Differences between accounting standards and tax codes may cause the carrying amount to differ from the tax base, resulting in deferred tax assets (DTA) and deferred tax liabilities (DTL). In this scenario, the firm cannot recognize the £50,000 rent payment as revenue for accounting purposes until it is fully earned in January 20X5. Instead, it records £50,000 as unearned revenue, a liability, on 30 December 20X4. For tax purposes, the firm recognizes the £50,000 as taxable cash revenue in 20X4. Since the liability's carrying value (£50,000) is greater than its tax base (£0), this creates a DTA. (Choice A) The £12,000 for the prepaid software subscription is recorded as an asset (prepaid expenses), but for tax purposes it is recognized as a cash expense in 20X4. Since the asset's carrying amount (£12,000) is greater than its tax base (£0), a DTL is created. (Choice C) For the £200,000 equipment, which is an asset, 20% of the historical cost is depreciated for accounting purposes in 20X4, so the remaining carrying amount is £160,000 or [(1 − 0.2) × 200,000]. In contrast, 40% is depreciated for tax purposes, so the remaining tax base is £120,000 or [1 − 0.4) × 200,000]. Since the asset's carrying amount (£160,000) is greater than its tax base (£120,000), a DTL is created.
question_en: A company has available-for-sale securities on its balance sheet.  If the market value of those securities increases by $100,000, the company will most appropriately record:
option_c: neither a deferred tax liability nor a deferred tax asset.

explanation_en: Dynamic pricing is a pricing model where a company charges different prices based on what time of day or time of week a purchase is made. Offering the same services at different prices on busier and slower days is an example of dynamic pricing. Tiered pricing is a pricing model based on the volume of purchases; typically, the greater the volume purchased, the greater the overall price discount. Razors-and-blades is a pricing model for multiple products; typically, one product is sold at a low price and low margin, while a second complementary product is sold at a high margin.
question_en: To generate more sales on slow days, a hair salon will be offering its services at a 50% discount on Sundays and Mondays, but it will increase its prices by 20% on Fridays and Saturdays. Which pricing model best describes the company's strategy?
option_c: Tiered pricing.

explanation_en:
Capital budgeting cash flow considerations
Characterization Definition Include
Incremental cash flows Cash flows resulting from decision to invest Yes
Sunk costs Funds spent previously No
Opportunity costs Returns from alternate use of investment funds or fixed assets Yes
Externalities Cash flow impacts on other company investments Yes
Financing costs Cost of capital to invest No
Potential investment projects should be evaluated based on their incremental cash flows. Incremental refers to changes in cash flows that
result from the decision to invest or not invest in a project. In this scenario, incremental cash flows should include:
Project cash flows: the costs of retooling the factory and operating cash flows from producing the luxury sedans;
Opportunity costs: cash flows forgone since the proceeds from selling the factory and operating cash flows from producing compact cars are
not realized (Choices A and C); and
Externalities: the reduction in net revenues from other product lines if customers buy the new luxury sedans instead of other automobiles
produced by the company.
Cash flows the company should not consider include:
Sunk costs: the funds previously spent to build and maintain the factory; and
Financing costs: the costs factored in when cash flows are discounted using an opportunity cost of capital.
Subtracting the interest expense from project cash flows amounts to double counting the financing costs.

explanation_en:
The market model uses market returns to predict the expected return of a single security. The relationship between the market return and
security's expected return is estimated through linear regression. The regression line represents an estimate for a security's return based on a
given market return.
Alpha (y-intercept) is where the market model's regression line intersects the y-axis. It represents an estimate of the security's return if the
market return is zero.
The security's beta measures the sensitivity of a security's return relative to the market's return. Note: The market always has a beta of 1. A
security with a beta higher than 1 tends to move in the same direction as the market, but the magnitude of the movement is greater.
The slope of the regression line is the individual security's beta. For a given market return, a higher beta translates to a higher expected return
for a security. A higher expected return is associated with higher risk, so a security's beta indicates its relative riskiness.
(Choice B) In the market model, a security's systematic risk (market risk) is expressed as beta, not alpha. Beta is a measure of sensitivity of a
security's return to the market's return.
(Choice C) The best estimate of a security's market return is the result of applying the complete market model formula, not just alpha. Alpha
represents the portion of a security's return not explained by the market.
question_en: When estimating expected return, which of the following statements most accurately describes the alpha coefficient in the market model?
option_a: Alpha is the intercept term of the market model.
option_b: A security's systematic risk is expressed as alpha.
option_c: Alpha is the best estimate of a security's market return.

explanation_en: Porter's five forces of strategic industry analysis provide an understanding of the underlying drivers and context that an industry operates in. The purpose of the analysis is not only to understand the competitive dynamics but also to recognize the fundamental investment merits of the industry. Structural industry attributes can vary dramatically, generating vastly different economic return profiles. Some industries generate consistent profits through an economic cycle whereas other industries struggle to generate economic profits, even during a sustained economic expansion. Industries that are forecasted to generate above-average economic profits over an economic cycle are good candidates for additional investment research. Economic profit in this context is broadly defined as generating returns above the cost of capital. (Choice B) Porter's five forces of strategic industry analysis provide an understanding of the underlying drivers and context in which an industry operates and are not directly used in portfolio construction (ie, for their diversification benefits). (Choice C) Sector and industry classification schemes are generally a useful starting place for assessing industries, but strategic industry analysis would include a much deeper and more thorough examination of the industry.

Taylor convinces a government cotton inspector to issue a warning that the Texas cotton crop is in danger from insect infestation. The price of cotton soars. Taylor immediately shorts cotton futures. explanation_en: Commodity indexes Exposure to underlying commodities gained through derivatives Derivative price performance can vary significantly from physical commodity price Underlying commodity exposure can vary substantially between indexes Widely viewed as an inflation hedge Historically low correlations to other asset classes Commodity indexes use futures or other derivative contracts to gain exposure to the underlying commodities in each index. This makes the indexes more investable and easier to replicate with greater price transparency than direct commodity investments. An index may have exposure to more than one commodity, and each commodity in the index may have a different weight. Futures prices, while certainly affected by changes in the underlying commodity, are also affected by carrying costs and returns on the collateral required for futures investments. These factors mean that the price of the index is almost certain to differ from the commodity's futures price. Likewise, an underlying commodity's return as measured by a change in its spot price is almost certain to differ from the commodity index's return as measured by a change in its futures price. (Choice A) Unlike other alternative investment indexes (eg, hedge funds, private equities), commodity indexes are based on observable market prices of commodity derivatives and therefore not subject to the selective reporting that leads to backfill and survivorship bias. (Choice B) Underlying commodity exposure and weighting methods can vary substantially between indexes and therefore are not standardized.
question_en: Commodity indexes are most likely:
option_a: subject to backfill and survivorship bias.
option_b: directly comparable since weighting methods are standardized.
option_c: to have performance differences versus the underlying commodities.

explanation_en:
The ex-dividend date (ie, ex-date) is the first day that a company's shares trade without rights to the dividend. Since shares purchased on or
after the ex-date do not convey the right to receive the dividend, the share price typically falls by the amount of the dividend on the ex-date.
The ex-dividend date is directly tied to the settlement process (eg, T + 2) since shares purchased on or after the ex-dividend date settle after the
holder-of-record date (ie, record date).
(Choice A) The dividend payment date is announced when the company declares the dividend and is the day the company will actually transfer
funds to those entitled to the dividend.
(Choice B) The declaration date is the date the company announces the specifics of the dividend (eg, size, payment date). Since the declaration
date is often weeks or months before the record date, the shares can still be bought with rights to the dividend.
question_en: The ex-dividend date is best described as the date when:
option_b: the company declares the amount and timing of the dividend.
option_c: the stock trades for the first time without the right to the dividend.

explanation_en:
The coupon rate of a floating-rate note (ie, FRN or floater) is based on a reference rate (eg, LIBOR). The quoted margin is the yield that is
added to the reference rate to determine each period's coupon rate. The quoted margin typically does not change during the life of the bond. The
coupon rate of the FRN in this scenario is the LIBOR rate plus 35 basis points (bps), or 3.25% + 0.35% = 3.60%.
The discount margin of an FRN (also called the required margin) is an adjustment to the rate used to discount the bond's cash flows. The
discount margin represents the additional yield required given the risks of an FRN. When the bond is issued, the discount margin is the same as
the quoted margin, but changes in the bond's risks cause the discount margin to change. Any change in the discount margin affects the bond's
present value, not its coupon rate.
(Choice A) 3.10% results from adding the discount margin (−15 bps), rather than the quoted margin, to the reference rate.
(Choice C) 3.45% results from inappropriately adding the sum of the quoted margin and discount margin (20 bps) to the reference rate.
question_en: A floating-rate note has a quoted margin of 35 basis points (bps) and a discount margin of −15 bps. If the relevant reference rate is 3.25% on the bond's reset date, the new coupon rate is most likely:

explanation_en: Increases in government spending cause an increase in GDP. More infrastructure spending causes the aggregate demand to increase. Consequently, an increase in government spending is an expansionary fiscal policy. The immediate impact of increased spending on highways and bridges is the additional sales revenue for the firms that supply the materials and machinery used in the construction projects. The firms involved in the construction—and their equipment and materials suppliers—will hire additional workers. As a result, aggregate demand is further stimulated by the increased income that workers spend on consumption. (Choice A) A tax on vehicle fuel raises consumers' costs. This puts downward pressure on GDP and is therefore a contractionary policy. (Choice C) Raising corporate income taxes reduces investments and hiring. This is a contractionary policy, not an expansionary policy.
question_en: An increase in which of the following would most appropriately be considered expansionary fiscal policy?
option_a: New excise taxes on vehicle motor fuel
option_b: Infrastructure spending on highways and bridges
option_c: Reducing budget deficits by raising corporate income taxes

explanation_en: The price return of an index is the weighted average return of the asset prices of the index's constituents: PR_Index = w1 x PR1 + w2 x PR2 + ... + wN x PRN, where each asset's price return PRi = (Ending price - Beginning price) / Beginning price. An asset's price return is the percent change in its price over a given period. Unlike an index or asset's total return, the price return excludes any dividend or interest income from the assets since investors anticipate such income and adjust asset prices accordingly. To find the price return of an index, multiply each asset's price return by its weighting in the index. For a value-weighted (market cap-weighted) index, each asset's weight in the index is its beginning market capitalization as a percentage of the total beginning market cap in the index: Asset A: 13.50 x 700,000 = 9,450,000, so 9,450,000 / 61,675,000 is approximately 15.3%; Asset B: 56.50 x 450,000 = 25,425,000, approximately 41.2%; Asset C: 67.00 x 400,000 = 26,800,000, approximately 43.5%; total beginning market cap = 61,675,000. With the assets' weightings calculated, the index's price return is calculated from the individual assets' price returns: Asset A: (11.50 - 13.50) / 13.50 is approximately -14.8%, and -14.8% x 15.3% is approximately -2.27%; Asset B: (55.00 - 56.50) / 56.50 is approximately -2.7%, and -2.7% x 41.2% is approximately -1.09%; Asset C: (69.00 - 67.00) / 67.00 is approximately 3.0%, and 3.0% x 43.5% is approximately 1.30%. Total index price return = -2.1%. Therefore, the price return of the index is -2.1%. (Choice B) -1.5% results from weighting the assets by their prices, not their market caps. (Choice C) -1.1% results from including the assets' dividend income in the return calculation. Price returns exclude income from dividends. Things to remember: The price return of an index is the weighted average return of the prices of the index's constituent assets. An asset's price return is the percent change in its price over a certain period.

explanation_en: Hypothesis tests are classified as either parametric or nonparametric. Parametric tests are based on distributional assumptions (eg, normally distributed) whereas nonparametric tests are used when few assumptions about the underlying population can be made. The correlation between two populations (ρ) can be calculated using a parametric measure (ie, the pairwise or Pearson correlation) or a nonparametric measure (eg, the Spearman rank correlation coefficient). Both measures are similar, but while the Pearson correlation assumes that data is normally distributed, the Spearman rank correlation makes no assumptions about the dataset's distribution. Instead, it ranks the observations and calculates the differences between the rank of each pair. In this instance, the Spearman rank correlation is given (0.7311) and it should be used since the investor believes that the distribution is not normally distributed. The hypothesis test based on this nonparametric measure is calculated as: Since the calculated t-statistic is greater than the critical t-value, there is evidence that the population correlation is different from zero and the null hypothesis should be rejected (Choice A). (Choice C) 9.00 is obtained by incorrectly calculating the t-statistic with the Pearson correlation, which is a parametric measure and should not be used since the distribution is believed to deviate from a normal distribution.

explanation_en:
The efficient frontier contains the best portfolios an investor can find using risky assets. The efficient frontier represents all portfolios of risky
assets in the investment opportunity set with the highest expected return for a given level of risk. The efficient frontier is a continuum of optimal
portfolios.
Portfolio B is an optimal portfolio that has an expected return of 12% with a risk of 30%. All portfolios to the right of Portfolio B (where expected
return is 12%) have risk greater than 30%; therefore, these portfolios are suboptimal to (ie, less efficient than) Portfolio B. Any point above or to
the left of Portfolio B is unattainable by any combination of risky assets since it is not part of the investment opportunity set.
The global minimum-variance portfolio, Portfolio A, is the portfolio with the lowest possible risk (15%) on the efficient frontier. While
portfolios along the red curved line are minimum variance portfolios, they are not part of the efficient frontier. Portfolio C is suboptimal to Portfolio
B since both have the same portfolio risk (30%), although Portfolio B has a higher expected return (12%). The efficient frontier is the blue curved
line.
(Choice A) The efficient frontier represents portfolios of only risky assets and does not include risk-free assets at any return level.
(Choice B) Risk-averse investors would prefer any portfolio along the efficiency frontier above the global minimum-variance portfolio. Portfolios
below this level have higher risk and lower return. Selecting these portfolios is not a behavior pattern of risk-averse investors.
question_en: Under modern portfolio theory, the efficient frontier most accurately represents portfolios:
option_a: of risk-free and risky assets with the lowest risk for a given expected return.
option_b: preferred by risk-averse investors below the global minimum-variance portfolio.
option_c: in the investment opportunity set with the highest expected return for a given level of risk.

explanation_en: A firm's supply function reflects the quantities it will produce at various prices.  All firms maximize profits at the level of output at which marginal cost (MC) = marginal revenue (MR); therefore, a firm's MC curve can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output.  In a market with perfect competition, where a firm has perfectly elastic demand (ie, it is a price taker) and price (P) = MR, MC can also be used to determine the price that maximizes profit (ie, price at which MC = MR = P).  Thus, the MC curve reflects the firm's willingness to supply and defines its supply curve. In other market structures, such as oligopoly, monopoly, and monopolistic competition, P ≠ MR due to inelasticity of demand.  The optimal price is determined by the demand curve, which reflects the inelastic demand.  Although MC can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output, the MC curve does not reflect the firm's willingness to supply at various prices and does not define the supply curve (Choices A and C). For a firm in perfect competition, long-run equilibrium means producing a quantity of output that minimizes the firm's average total cost, which equals the market price for its product.  At this level of output economic profit is zero, so Total cost = Total revenue, or Price per unit × Quantity of units sold = Average total cost per unit × Units sold. Under the monopoly and monopolistic competition structures, firms have some pricing power, but any new price must be offered to all customers; therefore, MR ≠ Change in price multiplied × Change in quantity sold.  Although the relationship between the average revenue and MR is similar under both structures, in general, the demand curve for monopolistic competitors is flatter (ie, more elastic).
question_en: If firms' supply curves can be used to determine the optimal, profit-maximizing price, those firms are most likely operating in:
option_c: monopolistic competition.

explanation_en: Monte Carlo simulation is a technique that generates random samples from specific probability distributions. One of the advantages of Monte Carlo simulation is that the user can conduct what-if analyses by changing the assumptions underlying the inputs used to analyze the data. Monte Carlo analysis generates a result that is an average of thousands of trials (ie, simulation). Its accuracy depends on its standard deviation. A large standard deviation indicates a wide variability of possible outcomes. For example, the simulation might result in a price of $5, but it could be as low as $4 or as high as $6. Therefore, when an investment decision requires a precise result, Monte Carlo simulation may be inappropriate (Choice A). Monte Carlo simulation can incorporate multiple inputs. For example, the derivative in this scenario may be impacted by interest rate volatility, changes in the issuer's credit rating, and the correlation of bond prices and economic conditions. Each variable has its own probability distribution, and unless the user knows or can reasonably estimate the distributions, the simulation would produce meaningless results (Choice C).
question_en: An analyst is determining the appropriate price for a complex call option on a bond. Monte Carlo simulation is most appropriate to use if the analyst:
option_b: can only use estimates for the inputs.
option_c: is unsure of the probability distributions for the inputs.

explanation_en: Deferred tax assets (DTA) arise when a company's taxable income temporarily exceeds its pretax income. The imbalance causes the company to pay more in taxes than it reports as tax expense on its income statement. This occurs when the company pays tax on cash it receives in the current period but for which it will not earn and recognize as revenue until a future period. The carrying value and tax base of an item are similar concepts. Carrying value refers to an item's value that the company reports in its financial reporting. The tax base is the value that the company uses for the same item when it calculates its tax obligations. The company pays tax on the advance payment in 20X8, even though it does not recognize the cash as revenue in 20X8 since it has not performed the agreed-upon services. It creates a liability (eg, deferred revenue) of £20,000 to account for the cash, and the liability's 20X8 carrying value is £20,000. The cash's 20X8 tax base equals zero since it was taxed when received in 20X8. This difference results in a DTA. A DTA is the difference between the item's carrying value and its tax base, multiplied by the tax rate: (20,000 − 0) × 25% = £5,000. When the tax rate increases to 30% in 20X9, the DTA also increases: (20,000 − 0) × 30% = £6,000, an increase of £1,000. (Choice A) The increase in DTA from £5,000 to £6,000 causes tax expense to decline, not increase, by £1,000. (Choice B) The company paid the tax on the customer advance in 20X8, so that has no impact on its tax obligations for 20X9.
question_en: In 20X8, a security company received payment of £20,000 for services that it will not perform until 20X9. If the statutory tax rate increases from 25% to 30% in 20X9, the effect of this advance payment in 20X9 most likely causes an increase in:

explanation_en: A company can be analyzed as a combination of systems and processes that add value in the production of goods or services for the customer. Commonly used models for this analysis assess a company's: Supply chain: internal and external steps in production and delivery Value chain: internal systems and processes that support the firm's operating and administrative activities Value proposition is the measure of value added for customers by the firm's competitive advantages. This includes value created within the supply chain (eg, convenient delivery) and other areas, such as: Product differentiation Sales processes Customer service and support Pricing In this case, the option for customer delivery through a local retailer is part of the e-commerce company's supply chain (Choice B). The convenience created for customers by using the retailer is part of company's value proposition (Choice C).
question_en: An e-commerce company offers customers the option to pick up orders from an independent local retailer. Using the retailer is least likely to be part of the e-commerce company's:
option_c: value proposition.

explanation_en: Text analytics are used to analyze unstructured data in text (or voice) forms, for example identifying how often a word appears in a report. Corporate exhaust is the potentially useful data that businesses generate from retail transactions and bank data. In natural language processing, computers and artificial intelligence are used to interpret human language.
question_en: An analyst would like to use fintech to assess how often the word "assumption" is used in a company's annual financial report. This application is best described as:
option_c: natural language processing.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in behavior that undermines the integrity of CFA Institute, its programs, and the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter.  To uphold the integrity of the charter, the CFA Institute takes care to ensure that confidential information about exams is not shared by anyone.  For Members and Candidates, sharing such information is a violation of the Standard. Members may not disclose: questions that are set to appear on the exam or are under consideration, any parts of the deliberation process related to the exam, or information related to the grading of questions. Graders may not share information with anyone outside of the development or grading process.  Since Han is not part of the grading process, Yoo may not discuss any information relating to the grading of questions, whether it is specific details or general information.  By doing so, she violates the Standard.  If this information were shared with other participants in the grading process, it would not violate the Standard. (Choices A and C)  Han does not violate the Standard since he is not part of the exam's development, administering, or grading process and therefore does not know any information to disclose.  His only source of information is a social media post.
question_en: Soomin Yoo, CFA, is helping grade the most recent Level 3 exam.  At dinner one evening, she discusses the grading process with a friend, Minsoo Han, CFA, who is not participating in the grading process. Yoo states "I'm surprised how many people are missing the question on fixed income investing strategies.  It didn't come across to me as that difficult." Han responds "If that's the case, candidates might be in trouble.  I read on a social media post that the multiple-choice section also had more fixed income questions than in other recent exams." According to the Standards, is it most likely that:
option_a: both Yoo and Han have violated the Standards.
option_b: Yoo has violated the Standards but Han has not.
option_c: Han has violated the Standards but Yoo has not.

explanation_en: Acting as the counterparty for all buyers and sellers is the primary role of the clearinghouse. By providing liquidity, the clearinghouse may also help lower transaction costs indirectly.
question_en: In futures markets, the primary role of the clearinghouse is to:
option_a: reduce transaction costs by making contract prices public.
option_b: act as guarantor to both sides of a futures trade.
option_c: prevent arbitrage and enforce federal regulations.

explanation_en: In an efficient market, assets' market values should reflect their intrinsic values. Book values seldom equal market or intrinsic values because book values do not reflect investors' expectations.
question_en: A market can be characterized as efficient if assets':
option_a: book values equal their market values.
option_b: intrinsic values equal their book values.
option_c: market values equal their intrinsic values.

explanation_en: The policy statement outlines broad objectives and constraints but does not get into the details of specific stocks for investment.
question_en: Which of the following is NOT a rationale for the importance of the policy statement in investing? It:
option_a: forces investors to understand their needs and constraints.
option_b: helps investors understand the risks and costs of investing.
option_c: identies specic stocks the investor may wish to purchase.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation requires Members and Candidates to avoid any practices that deceive market participants through the distortion of securities prices or trading volume.  Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing misleading information) and transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard is not meant to prevent the use of legitimate strategies that limit a trade's impact on the market when trading large positions or low- liquidity stocks.  The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is whether the trading strategy is intended to deceive market participants.  If the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, Annika Goncharov uses a legitimate strategy of breaking up a large position of a low-liquidity stock to limit the impact of the sale on the price.  Annika's strategy has not violated the Standard (Choice B).  Boris Goncharov intends to distort market prices by making market participants believe there are more buyers of Bright Sky Capital's stock than there are.  Since market participants cannot see that Boris is driving both the buying and the selling activity, the trading is deceptive and has violated the Standard (Choice C).
question_en: Annika and Boris Goncharov are siblings, CFA charterholders, and investors of Bright Sky Capital (BSC).  Annika and Boris hold more than RUB 100 million each in BSC stock, and each plans to sell 10% to diversify their separate portfolios.  However, BSC is a lightly traded stock, and the siblings agree that large sales would likely cause the company's stock price to decline. Annika decides to break up her sales into small batches of limit orders and sell them over multiple days to minimize the impact on the stock's price.  Still, Annika's sales cause BSC's stock price to decline.  Boris similarly decides to sell his holdings in batches, but he simultaneously purchases half the amount he sells to ensure the stock price is unaffected by his trades.  Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is most likely violated by:
option_c: neither Boris nor Annika.

explanation_en: The quality of a firm's earnings is considered to be low if they are not sustainable or if they are not of a sufficient level to provide an adequate return to investors. When financial reports do not conform with GAAP, the user cannot evaluate the quality of earnings in terms of adequacy or sustainability.
question_en: The quality of a company's reported earnings is low when they:
option_c: are lower than for the prior-year period.

explanation_en: The GIPS-compliant firm definition must be the corporation, subsidiary, or division that holds itself out to the client as a specific business entity. If the firm has different geographic locations, this firm definition should include all the locations.
question_en: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the GIPS requirement for definition of the firm?
option_a: The firm must be the distinct business entity held out to clients.
option_b: If a firm has offices in different geographical locations, the firm definition may include just the primary location where all the investment decisions are made.
option_c: The firm definition may include the corporation or a subsidiary of the corporation, but the firm cannot be defined as simply a “division” of the corporation.

explanation_en: Securitization refers to the process of bundling (ie, pooling) cash-generating loans and receivables, such as auto loans or credit card receivables, to create asset-backed securities (ABS). The cash flows from these assets (ie, payments from the borrowers) are used to pay the bonds' interest and principal. Securitization has many benefits, including the redistribution of the risk of the underlying collateral. Credit enhancements allow investors to tailor their interest rate and credit risk exposure. However, the level of inherent credit risk on this collateral does not change. Therefore, securitization is not guaranteed to reduce the overall credit risk to investors. If losses on the collateral are particularly high, the credit enhancements can fail to provide the intended protection. (Choices A and B) One benefit of securitization is that it allows financial institutions to sell loans and use the proceeds to provide more lending. Securitization also provides a funding source for companies in addition to equity and bond issuance because companies that originate loans and receivables can sell these assets directly to financial intermediaries.
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a benefit of securitization? Securitization provides:
option_a: lenders with the ability to finance more loans.
option_b: companies with an alternate source of funding.
option_c: investors with less inherent credit risk from the underlying collateral.

explanation_en: National governments may seek to limit foreign investment in certain domestic industries, for example, those that are seen as essential for national defense. A government seeking to keep domestic interest rates low or support domestic asset prices would be more likely to restrict capital outflows.
question_en: Which of the following objectives would a national government most likely pursue by placing restrictions on inflows of foreign capital?
option_c: Keeping domestic interest rates low.

explanation_en: Typical hedge fund fee structure Fee Basis for calculation Specific details Management Assets under management (AUM) Typically 1%−3% of AUM annually Does not depend on fund's profitability Always calculated before incentive fee Performance or incentive Annual returns Can be net or gross of management fee Can be subject to hurdle rate and/or high-water mark Hedge funds often levy both a management fee and an incentive fee.  If fees are calculated independently, calculations are on a gross basis. An incentive fee is often contingent on: profits being greater than a hurdle rate, which is the minimum performance that a fund must achieve before earning a performance fee, and/or Assets under management (AUM) being above a high-water mark (HWM), which is the base asset value used to calculate the incentive fee.  The HWM represents the fund's previous peak value of AUM at which incentive fees have been paid. In this case, the fee structure's management and incentive fees are on a gross basis (ie, independently), subject to a high-water mark, since the fund does not collect an incentive fee on assets that have already been subject to that fee (Choices A and B).
question_en: A hedge fund's fees are calculated independently, and the fund does not collect an incentive fee on assets that have already been subject to that fee.  Which of the following best describes this fee structure?
option_a: Management and incentive fees are on a net basis, subject to a hurdle rate
option_b: Management fees are on a gross basis and incentive fees are on a net basis
option_c: Management and incentive fees are on a gross basis, subject to a high-water mark

explanation_en: The vintage year is typically defined as the year a private equity or venture capital fund makes its first investment. The year of the first capital commitment is not necessarily the same as the year of the first investment by the fund into a portfolio company, because there might be a lag between when the capital is committed and when it is deployed.
question_en: The vintage year is the year in which a private equity fund:
option_c: sells its rst investment.

The early retirement option embedded in callable bonds creates uncertainty about future cash flows. Two types of duration are used to evaluate
the effect of early retirement options on cash flows payable over an uncertain time horizon:
Effective duration assumes parallel shifts in the benchmark yield curve, and
key rate duration is based on a change in the shape (ie, shaping risk) of the benchmark yield curve.
A bond's key rate duration is calculated by assuming changes in one or more yields on the benchmark yield curve. A steepening of the yield curve
could result from a decrease in short-term rates, an increase in long-term rates, or a combination of both. The assumed change in the benchmark
curve is used to evaluate the effect on the embedded call option and cash flows over the life of the bond.
(Choice A) Yield volatility affects bond values but is not a factor measured by key rate duration.
(Choice B) Corporate bond yields reflect a benchmark government bond yield and a yield spread over that benchmark. The spread reflects the
issuer's credit risk and the bond issue's liquidity risk. Key rate duration is based on changes in the benchmark yield curve, so it does not directly
incorporate changes in yield spreads.
question_en: All else being equal, key rate duration is most appropriate for assessing the interest rate risk of callable bonds if:
option_c: the yield curve is steepening.

explanation_en: The correct answer is B because investors in mezzanine bond classes seek to earn a potentially higher yield than comparably rated corporate bonds by gaining exposure to debt products they may not otherwise be able to purchase.
question_en: The motivation for investing in the mezzanine tranche of a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) is most likely to:
option_a: benefit from the credit protection provided by the senior tranche.
option_b: earn a higher yield than that on a comparably rated corporate bond.
option_c: receive a return in excess of what is paid out to all other bond classes.

explanation_en: The maximum gain for option sellers (ie, shorts) is limited to the option premium from the option sale and occurs when the option is out of the money.  In such cases, put holders will not exercise their right to sell since the underlying could be sold at the higher market price. If the option is in the money, put holders will exercise their right to sell the asset at the higher strike price, and the short put is obligated to buy the asset at the higher price.  The short put's loss at exercise is the difference between the strike price and the market price, and if that difference is greater than the premium received when the option was sold, the seller has a net loss.  As the underlying asset price decreases, the put seller faces increasing losses.  However, since underlying asset prices cannot fall below zero, the maximum loss is limited. (Choice B)  Short calls have limited gains and unlimited losses.  Call sellers' gains are limited to the premium received.  Potential losses are unlimited since losses increase as underlying asset prices increase, with no theoretical limit. (Choice C)  No asset or derivative has unlimited potential gains and losses.  Short option maximum gains are always limited.
question_en: Which of the following best describes the maximum potential gains and losses on a short put at expiration?
option_c: Unlimited gains and unlimited losses

explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires Members and Candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when conducting investment transactions and to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest. A Member or Candidate's participation in private placements and initial public offerings (IPOs) requires an especially high standard of care. The potential for conflicts of interest is more significant for investment personnel at large investment firms. Investment personnel (eg, Liang) may be offered special enticements, such as access to private placements or IPOs, as payback for doing business (eg, largest client) with the broker (eg, Trusted Brokers) offering the securities. Another concern is that once the private placement goes public, there is an incentive for the Member or Candidate who bought into the private placement and holds the now-public company's stock to offer and/or buy the securities for clients (or, in this case, for the fund) whether suitable or not. Participation in private placements should be strictly limited to special situations in which there is no potential for even the appearance of conflicts of interest. Therefore, Liang violated the Standard by involving himself in a situation that potentially had the appearance of impropriety. (Choices B and C) Liang appropriately considered the investment for the fund first and found it unsuitable. However, this is not where the violation occurred.
question_en: Shreya Batra, CFA, is an equity analyst for S&K Financial (SKF).  SKF creates an online forum solely for its paying clients and encourages its analysts to post their research reports following public dissemination so clients can discuss the reports among themselves.  Batra recommends that her clients join the forum so they can take part in the discussions.  However, she warns each client that posts on the forum can be seen by any SFK client and that they should avoid posting confidential or sensitive information.  Following the release of a new report about Fox Property Group, Batra posts the report to SFK's forum.  One client posts, "This has really got me thinking.  I should invest in Fox when I sell my company next year.  We can discuss it during our meeting next month."  Batra knows the sale of the client's company is confidential and deletes the post as soon as she sees it, an hour after it was posted.  Has Batra most likely violated Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality?
option_b: No, since the client – not Batra – posted the information on the forum
option_c: No, since Batra provided adequate warning to clients about posting confidential information

explanation_en: Both ownership of Braden stock and the possible consulting work present potential conflicts of interest for Smith and must be disclosed within the report to comply with Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts.
question_en: Donald Smith, CFA, has been assigned by his employer to write a report for clients on Braden Corporation. Smith has 1,000 shares of Braden that he bought three years ago and has been discussing a consulting contract with Braden to write guidelines for their investor relations department. If Smith writes the report on Braden Corporation, he must disclose within the report:
option_a: both his ownership of Braden shares and his prospective consulting work.
option_b: and to his employer his prospective consulting work but not his ownership of Braden shares.
option_c: his ownership of Braden shares but need only disclose his prospective consulting work to his employer.

explanation_en:
A forward contract allows its owner to buy an underlying asset for a predetermined price in the future. Therefore the contract owner does not incur
any costs and forgoes the benefits of the asset prior to purchase. In contrast, the holder of an asset pays the holding costs and receives the
benefits of holding the asset. The cost of carry is the net value of these costs and benefits. If the costs outweigh the benefits, the cost of carry is
negative.
To calculate the spot price from the forward price, add the cost of carry to the present value of the forward price. The present value is
calculated by discounting the forward price at the risk-free rate. In this scenario, the asset's forward price is £98, the cost of carry is £2.25, and the
risk-free rate is 2%. Substitute to calculate the spot price:
(Choice A) £98.28 is the result of discounting the cost of carry before adding it to the present value of the forward price. This is incorrect since
cost of carry is already expressed as a present value; therefore, it doesn't need to be discounted.
(Choice C) £100.25 is the result of failing to discount the forward price before adding it to the cost of carry.
question_en: An asset has a one-year forward price of £98, and its one-year cost of carry has a present value of £2.25. If the risk-free rate is 2%, the current arbitrage-free spot price of the asset is closest to:

explanation_en: Correct because, unlike financial assets, most digital assets do not have an inherent value based on underlying assets or on the potential cash flow.
question_en: Compared to traditional financial assets, digital assets:
option_a: can be invested in through indirect investment vehicles such as ETFs.
option_b: are generally recorded in private ledgers maintained by central intermediaries.
option_c: do not have an inherent value based on underlying assets or on potential cash flows.

explanation_en: Compared to the other two groups, shareholders have the greatest potential gains from riskier strategies and can diversify their holdings across firms in order to reduce the influence of company specific risk. While senior managers can gain from company outperformance, they typically prefer less risk than shareholders because managers' risk of poor company performance on the value of their options and on their careers cannot be easily diversified away.
question_en: The stakeholder group that typically prefers the greatest amount of business risk is:
option_c: senior managers.

explanation_en:
A peer group is a collection of companies with similar business activities and economics, making their equity valuation comparable.
Ideally, a company's peer group should consist only of companies with similar business models, who share similar customer demand drivers, cost
structures, and access to capital. Companies that share these attributes provide a good basis for comparing equity valuations of peer group
members.
Analysts can find management's comments in the annual report. The commentary may provide valuable insight into the competitive environment
or industry dynamics. It is an essential step in the process of constructing a peer group.
(Choice A) A common starting place for peer group creation is the various standard industry classification systems (eg, GICS, RGS, ICB), but
constructing a well-defined peer group for equity valuation requires further analysis.
(Choice C) Although total revenue, operating margins, and debt levels are important considerations, information regarding business models and
the drivers of economic performance is necessary for making an informed judgment on peer group inclusion.
question_en: With regard to forming an appropriate equity peer group, which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: Standard industry classification systems are adequate.
option_b: Named competitors in an annual report are an important consideration.
option_c: Total revenue, operating margins, and debt levels are the most important considerations.

explanation_en: Portfolio risk will decrease when adding an asset with a correlation of 0.5 (less than +1) to the portfolio, as imperfect correlation provides diversification benefits that reduce overall portfolio risk despite the asset and portfolio having equal standard deviations.
question_en:
An analyst gathers the following information about a two-asset portfolio and a third asset that is not part of the current portfolio:

- **Portfolio standard deviation of returns:** 20%,
- **Asset's standard deviation of returns:** 20%,
- **Correlation of returns between the asset and the portfolio:** 0.5.

If the asset is added to the portfolio, the portfolio standard deviation will most likely:
option_c: increase.

explanation_en:
The number of financial analysts who follow or analyze a security or asset should be positively
related to market efficiency. Therefore, if more analysts cover a company, the market for this
company's shares will most likely become more efficient.
question_en: If the number of financial analysts who follow or analyze a company increases substantially, then the market for this company's shares will mostlikely become:
option_c: more attractive for active investors.

question_en: An investment consists of a payment of $10,000 today (t = 0) and an ordinary annuity of $10,000 per year for 9 years, where the first payment occurs one year from today. What is the present value of this investment at a 6% discount rate?

explanation_en: Caledonia's basic EPS = (net income − preferred stock dividends) / (weighted average common shares outstanding) = [$460,000 − ($1,000 × 1,000 × 0.08)] / 2,300,000 = $0.17. Using the treasury stock method, if the warrants were exercised, cash inflow would be 10,000 × 100 × $1.50 = $1,500,000. The number of Caledonia shares that could be purchased with the inflow, using the average share price, is $1,500,000 / $2 = 750,000. The net increase in common shares outstanding would have been 1,000,000 − 750,000 = 250,000. Diluted EPS = $380,000 / (2,300,000 + 250,000) = $0.15.

explanation_en: Floating rate debt instruments (ie, floaters or FRNs) do not pay a fixed coupon.  Instead, coupon payments are based on a reference rate such as LIBOR, which can fluctuate from one coupon period to the next. The present value of a floater is calculated as the sum of its discounted cash flows.  The formula shows the required inputs.  Two variables—the quoted margin and discount margin—affect the present value of each payment: To determine the quoted margin, calculate the coupon payment using a financial calculator.  Each quarterly payment for this bond is approximately 0.6151 per 100 par value, with a coupon rate of 0.6151% per quarter, since the bond's quarterly yield is 0.8750% (based on an annual yield of 3.5%, the sum of the 3-month LIBOR of 3% and the discount margin of 0.5%).  Once the payment is known, the quoted margin in terms of basis points (bps) is calculated using the formula shown above: This means that the bond's interest payment is the 3-month LIBOR minus 54 bps.  The quoted margin can be positive or negative. (Choice A)  - 153 bps is the quoted margin if the coupon payments are discounted by specifying the denominator in the present value formula as (1 – discount margin)  instead of (1 + discount margin) . (Choice C)  50 bps is the quoted margin that makes the bond's price equal to par value.
question_en: A 2-year floating rate note is priced at 98 per 100 par value and pays interest quarterly based on the 3-month LIBOR.  It has a discount margin of 50 basis points (bps) and uses a 30/360 day-count convention.  If the three-month LIBOR is 3% throughout the life of the bond, the quoted margin is closest to:
option_c: 50 bps.

explanation_en:
Analysts use valuation models to estimate the intrinsic value of a stock to determine whether it is valued fairly. Common forms of valuation models
include multiplier, present value, and asset based.
With an asset-based valuation model, a firm's estimated equity value (ie, value to shareholders) is assumed to be equal to the current fair value
of assets minus the fair value of liabilities. Analysts often start with the book values of line items on the balance sheet and make fair value
adjustments to derive their market values. Since all inputs are based on current data, no long-term growth rate (g) is needed; g is used as an
input for forecasting future cash flows (eg, dividends, free cash flows).
(Choice A) When a multiplier model is justified (ie, justified P/E), it typically is derived from a present value model (eg, discounted free cash flow,
dividend discount model), that includes g as an input.
(Choice B) Present value models (eg, dividend discount model) typically require g for forecasting a company's future financial results (eg,
dividends, free cash flows). Once forecasts are made, they are discounted to the present at an appropriate discount rate (eg, WACC) to derive an
intrinsic value.
question_en: Which of the following least likely requires a future long-term growth rate for valuation purposes?
option_c: Asset-based valuation model

explanation_en: In accordance with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity, Callahan must only issue recommendations that reflect his own independent judgment. If Dening will not permit him to do so, Callahan must refuse to cover the firm under the conditions specified.
question_en: William Callahan, CFA, is an energy analyst. His supervisor, Nancy Dening, CFA, has recently decided to let Callahan cover a few of the firms that Dening had been covering previously. Dening gives Callahan specific instructions not to change her prior recommendation on one of these firms, Mayfield Energy. Callahan's least appropriate action is to:
option_a: tell Dening that he cannot cover Mayfield Energy under those restrictions.
option_b: perform his own independent analysis of Mayfield and reach an independent conclusion.
option_c: use ambiguous language in the report, in order to not mislead the investor while complying with his employer’s instructions.

explanation_en: In periods of high demand for bonds, spreads will move tighter, and narrower spreads help bond performance, whereas wider spreads hurt bond performance.
question_en: Over a given holding period, performance of credit-risky bonds will most likely benefit from:
option_c: weakening economic conditions.

explanation_en:
Blake violated Standard II(B) regarding the Integrity of Capital Markets by engaging in a
practice that is likely to artificially inflate trading volume.
question_en: Justin Blake, CFA, a retired portfolio manager, owns 20,000 shares of a small public company that he would like to sell because he is worried about the company's prospects. He posts messages on several internet bulletin boards. The messages read, "This stock is going up once the pending patents are released, so now is the time to buy. The stock is a buy at anything below $3. I have done some close research on these guys." According to the Standards of Practice Handbook, Blake most likely violated the Code and Standards associated with:
option_a: Integrity of Capital Markets, but not Conflicts of Interest.
option_b: neither Integrity of Capital Markets nor Conflicts of Interest.
option_c: Integrity of Capital Markets, and Conflicts of Interest. 5

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: The information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, Disclosure is required by law, or The client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information." Standard III (E) Preservation of Confidentiality requires that Members and Candidates not disclose a client's information unless is it required by law or if the client gives explicit permission. Conservative application of this Standard suggests that analysts should not disclose anything that the client may give or share with them unless the client gives authorization. However, a client may accidentally share communications intended for only the advisor with others. To comply with the Standard, advisors must try to prevent accidental disclosures by instructing clients on the proper use of social media. Since Bender reiterated instructions regarding the use of her social media page, she does not violate the Standard; immediately removing Faber's post also would align with meeting the Standard (Choice B). (Choice C) The use of social media is common, and its use is not an immediate violation. If an advisor chooses to contact clients using social media, the Member or Candidate must give clients clear instructions on its use to comply with the Standard.
question_en: Meng Bo, CFA, is a research analyst for Grant Capital.  She currently has a hold rating on Spire Data Center Investments (SDCI).  SDCI is considering a secondary public offering.  Meng is approached by Hao Liang, an investment banker for Grant who is trying to win SDCI's business for its offering.  Hao tells Meng, "We'll have a better chance of winning SDCI's offering if we have a buy rating on them.  Can you take another look and see if you can upgrade them?" Meng reviews SDCI's business again and does not see any change to her base case, which she views as the most likely outcome.  However, Meng believes that, in a best-case scenario, SDCI could outperform its peers and be worthy of a buy rating.  She still views the best-case scenario as unlikely, but its probability increases with the funds from the secondary offering.  Meng writes a new report with a buy rating, stating that she expects SDCI to achieve its best-case scenario and outperform peers, and sends it to clients.  Has Meng most likely violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
option_b: No, since the new rating is backed by her best-case scenario
option_c: No, since she thoroughly reviewed SDCI's business before changing the rating

explanation_en: Sources of industry size estimates Government agencies Third-party consultants Company presentations As part of their research, analysts frequently estimate the size of an industry (eg, by revenue, units). This helps determine sales potential and market shares for companies within the industry. Size is often difficult to estimate accurately for industries since many companies are private and do not disclose sales. Given this limitation, analysts have optional data sources, including: Government agencies, which often collect data and make their own estimates Third-party consultants, which use surveys to collect data from private companies (Choice A) In addition, many publicly traded companies disclose their own estimates in their investor presentations. Such estimates are often based on data from proprietary sources, which may be combined with third-party estimates (Choice B). When estimating industry size, analysts can sum the reported revenue from publicly traded companies to estimate part of the market. However, total revenue from the financial statements of public companies' filings (eg, annual reports, earnings presentations) should not be used for companies with multiple business lines; in those cases, only revenue from the segment(s) within that industry should be used in the estimate. Using total revenue from all companies within an industry would likely overstate the size of that industry.
question_en: Which of the following would be the least appropriate data source for measuring the size of an industry by its total revenue?
option_b: Investor presentations by publicly traded companies
option_c: Reported total firm revenue from companies in the industry

explanation_en: A mismatch between an investor's holding period (or investment horizon) and a bond's Macaulay duration results in exposure to two types of interest rate risk: price risk and reinvestment risk.  An investment horizon that is longer than the Macaulay duration results in exposure to reinvestment risk.  An investment horizon shorter than the Macaulay duration creates price risk. A 10-year coupon bond will have a Macaulay duration of less than 10 years, but significantly longer than 2 years.  At the end of the investment horizon, the bond will still have 8 years until its maturity.  If the bond's YTM has increased or decreased by even a relatively modest amount (eg, 0.50%), the price change will be much greater than the reinvestment income on 2 years of coupon income. The duration mismatch can work to the investor's advantage.  If yields decline, the investor's 2-year horizon return will be greater than the bond's YTM at purchase.  However, the mismatch becomes a disadvantage for the investor if yields rise since the price decrease will exceed the additional reinvestment income. (Choice B)  Liquidity risk refers to the ability to convert an investment into cash at a price close to the bond's fair value.  The investment would not create significant exposure to liquidity risk since government bonds are typically more liquid than other fixed income securities. (Choice C)  Investors have exposure to reinvestment risk when their investment horizons are longer than the Macaulay durations of their bond holdings.
question_en: An investor with a 2-year investment horizon buys a 10-year government bond that pays a 3% annual coupon.  The resulting mismatch between the 10-year bond's duration and the investment horizon results in the investor having the greatest exposure to:
option_c: reinvestment risk.

explanation_en: The two countries are a part of an economic union. In an economic union, there is (1) free trade among members, (2) common restrictions (tariffs) on imports from non-members, (3) free movement of production factors (labor), and (4) common economic institutions and coordination of economic policies. While a customs union has common tariffs on imports from non-union countries and free trade, it does not allow workers to cross the borders freely and does not have common economic institutions. A monetary union requires all of the listed items and a common currency.
question_en: Two countries trade freely with each other and have agreed to specific tariffs on imports from other countries. explanation_en: Behavioral biases that impact financial decisions are categorized as either cognitive errors or emotional biases. Cognitive errors result from flawed logic; emotional biases are decisions made from subconscious influences or emotions. Cognitive errors are classified as either belief perseverance bias: firmly adhering to previously held beliefs and ignoring facts, or processing errors: illogical or irrational financial decision-making that can be corrected with better education, information, or advice. Representativeness bias is a form of belief perseverance bias in which new information is classified based on past views or experiences. Base- rate neglect is a form of representativeness bias in which new information is processed through the lens of a specific view or belief, while the general evidence counter to that view is often ignored. In this scenario, the analyst ignored the evidence of general economic weakness, preferring to believe a specific data point (ie, company guidance) that validated the analyst's view. (Choice A) Cognitive cost is the effort involved in processing new information. Very technical data (eg, pharmaceutical trial data, technical specifics of a new semiconductor) requires strenuous effort to process and carries a high cognitive cost. In this instance, the cognitive cost of processing the new information was low. (Choice C) Sample-size neglect is the assumption that information affecting small sample reflects the broader trend. That was not the case here since the analyst did not extrapolate the company's situation to a wider group.
question_en: A classically trained fundamental buy-side analyst has done extensive company-specific due diligence on a cyclical industrial company. Such credit enhancements would be explained in the bond indenture.

explanation_en: Ricardian equivalence Fiscal deficits have no net effect on the economy. Government's choice is essentially to tax now or to tax in the future. Private sector increases savings by an amount equal to the deficit to pay future taxes. Fiscal deficits have little effect on private consumption and investment decisions. Policymakers should favor monetary policy tools over fiscal deficits. Ricardian equivalence is an economic theory suggesting that fiscal deficits and tax cuts have no net effect on the economy. According to this theory, the private sector reacts to these fiscal policy actions by increasing savings to pay for inevitable future tax increases; this reaction leaves national savings (ie, the sum of all public and private savings) unchanged. For example, a government enacts a tax cut to stimulate the economy but needs to borrow an equivalent amount to cover current spending. According to the Ricardian equivalence theory, these actions would have no net effect on the economy since the private sector would increase its savings by an amount equal to the tax cut to ensure there would be enough to repay the debt in the future. Thus, there would be no change in income available for consumption and no change to aggregate demand. (Choice A) The Fisher effect theorizes that real (ie, inflation-adjusted) interest rates are stable. It is not a theory about reaction to fiscal policies. (Choice B) Money neutrality refers to the idea that in the long run, an increase in the money supply only affects nominal price factors (eg, wages, exchange rates) and has no impact on real variables such as production and employment.
question_en: An economist states: "Fiscal deficits and tax cuts have no net effect on the economy since the private sector offsets these policy actions by increasing savings to pay for future tax increases." The economist's statement best reflects which of the following?
option_c: Ricardian equivalence

explanation_en:
Modified duration quantifies the sensitivity of a bond's price to a change in its yield. Therefore, modified duration can be used to estimate a
bond's percentage price change using the formula in the exhibit. The calculated percentage price change is only an approximation. Errors in
estimates of price change arise as a result of the curvilinear relationship between price and yield (green function); duration assumes a linear
relationship.
Duration, the slope of the blue tangent line, measures the sensitivity of price to yield changes at current market values, allowing the use of
duration as a measure of risk. Duration's primary application is quantifying the sensitivity of bond prices and the value of bond portfolios to interest
rate changes.
Consider the consequence for two bonds with different durations. For equal declines in their YTM, the bond with the longer duration would have a
larger percentage price increase. If their yields rose by the same number of basis points, the longer-duration bond would have a larger
percentage price decrease.
(Choice B) Macaulay duration is usually interpreted as a measure of a bond's life. It is the present value–weighted average time until the receipt
of a bond's remaining contractual cash flows.
(Choice C) Duration is sometimes mistakenly believed to quantify bond price volatility. Volatility quantifies dispersion of outcomes (eg, returns).
Duration quantifies sensitivity, not volatility.

option_b: weighted average time to receipt of the bond's cash flows.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in any conduct that would undermine the integrity of the CFA Institute or any CFA Institute program, including the CFA Program exams.  A specific requirement in connection with this Standard is a pledge that candidates must sign before taking any Level exam.  The pledge reads, in part, "After this exam, I will not disclose ANY portion of this exam…" Wyll, by referencing areas that the Ethics questions did not address, violated Standard VII(A) and the pledge.  It is immaterial that he did not discuss specific questions.  His statement that certain areas of the candidate body of knowledge were not tested, especially since it was posted soon after he took the exam, is considered assistance to future candidates.  This assistance undermines the integrity of the exam and is prohibited under the Standard. However, general opinions about the difficulty of an exam that do not address specific questions or topics or CFA Institute's policies and procedures do not violate the Standard.  Wyll's opinions that the exam was "easy" and that CFA Institute's recommendation is unwarranted regarding time needed to study for Level II do not violate the Standard (Choice C).

explanation_en:
The forward price is the future value of the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate and adjusted for the future value of the net carrying costs.
If there is a net cost to holding the commodity, the forward price is greater than the spot price.
If there is a net benefit to holding the commodity, the forward price is less than the spot price.
In this case, since the forward price is less than the spot price, there must be a net benefit. Since there are positive costs, there must also be a
benefit(s) greater than the carrying costs. The convenience yield is the nonmonetary benefit of holding the asset. Monetary benefits include
dividends or interest paid by the asset while it is held.
In this illustration using crude oil, since the 3-month forward price is $48 and the future value of the spot price and holding costs is $55, the
convenience yield is $7 per barrel.
Convenience yields usually arise during shortages and situations when short selling the underlying commodity is difficult. Commercial users
continue to hold the commodity despite the incentive to sell at relatively higher spot price. For example, oil refiners need inventories of crude oil to
run their operations. Maintaining the value of the business (ie, convenience yield) is more important than making a trading profit by selling at
current spot prices.
(Choice A) Storage costs are a carrying cost of holding the asset and are avoided by instead holding the forward. Storage costs explain the
forward price being greater than, not less than, the spot price.
(Choice C) Counterparty credit risk does not affect the forward price.
question_en: A commodity has some positive carrying costs. If the commodity's forward price is less than its spot price, which of the following best explains this scenario?
option_c: Counterparty credit risk

explanation_en: Derivatives are an extremely efficient means of hedging risk for natural buyers and sellers. The modern derivatives market is based on the idea of trading a product today for delivery at some point in the future. For example, a wheat farmer who is planting today can sell a portion of the harvest for future delivery to a bread maker. This allows both parties to prudently plan for the future because the price and delivery date have been determined with certainty. Short-term speculators take the opposite side of the trade from natural buyers or sellers, which allows natural market participants to lay off risk. As derivatives enable the efficient transfer of risk from one party to another, speculators play a critical role by accepting risk, improving market liquidity, and reducing transaction costs. This is much different from pure gambling, which has little to no redeeming value for society as a whole. (Choice B) Although the underlying premise of the derivatives market is based on hedging, speculators can and do make leveraged one-way bets that add risks for lenders and counterparties. (Choice C) One of the major attractions of the derivatives market for short-term speculators is the low capital and collateral requirements, which in extreme situations may put other investors at risk.
