explanation_en: Specific identification is the inventory method that results in the matching of the physical flow of the particular items sold and would be most suitable for high-end custom-built motorcycles that are not ordinarily considered interchangeable.
question_en: The method a high-end custom-built motorcycle manufacturer uses to value its inventory results in the matching of the physical flow of the particular items sold, and the items remaining in inventory, to their actual cost. Which of the following inventory valuation methods is the manufacturer most likely using?
option_c: Weighted average cost

explanation_en: Shares of open-end mutual funds trade at NAV. The others may deviate from NAV.
question_en: Which of the following pooled investment shares is least likely to trade at a price different from its NAV?
option_c: Open-end mutual fund shares.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs mandates that Members and Candidates maintain the reputation, integrity, validity, and security of CFA Institute exams and programs.  The Standard prohibits behavior that would compromise the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. Candidates taking the exam must sign the Candidate Pledge, which identifies behaviors that are prohibited before, during, and after the test. These behaviors include: giving or receiving information about the exam before or during the exam, and providing information about the exam to others after the exam, including broad topic areas tested, until it is publicly released by CFA Institute. In this scenario, Himari Sato violates the Standard by disclosing information about the exam.  Even though she did not disclose information about specific questions, she did disclose that the number of questions about derivatives was at the bottom of the given range.  Learning this could give those who have not yet taken the exam an unfair advantage. (Choice A)  The Standard allows Members and Candidates to share opinions that disagree with CFA Institute policies (eg, allowing only two types of calculators) and stances on key issues (eg, advocacy articles). (Choice B)  Members and Candidates are allowed to share opinions about the exams or CFA Institute as long as the opinions do not reveal specific information about the exams.
question_en: Himari Sato just got home from taking Level I of the CFA exam.  She goes onto a popular online forum and writes, "Just got back from Level I. Definitely a hard exam, much harder than I expected based on my studying, but I think I passed!  However, I still disagree with CFA Institute's policy of providing ranges for the weights of each subject on the exam.  Just tell us what to expect!  I studied way too hard for derivatives, but the number of questions was at the bottom of the range.  I wasted so much time on this."  Sato violated the Standards by:
option_a: disagreeing with CFA Institute's exam policies.
option_b: expressing an opinion on the difficulty of the exam.
option_c: providing information about topics tested on the exam.

explanation_en: Standard III(D) requires compliance with GIPS standards as the best method to present performance for members managing assets, and Standard I(A) requires adherence to applicable laws and regulations, which when stricter than the Code and Standards, must be followed.
question_en: Not visible in the provided image - this appears to be the solution section only
option_a: Incorrect because complying with the GIPS standards is voluntary. Compliance with the GIPS standards is not typically required by legal or regulatory authorities. Therefore, the member is not required to communicate investment performance information to her clients in accordance with the GIPS standards.
option_b: Correct because Standard III(D), Performance Presentation, for members and candidates who are showing the performance history of the assets they manage, compliance with the GIPS standards is the best method to meet their obligations under Standard III(D). Members and candidates should encourage their firms to comply with the GIPS standards. Clearly then, Standard III(D) does not require a member to comply with the GIPS standards; complying with the GIPS Standards is only encouraged.
option_c: Incorrect because complying with the GIPS standards is voluntary. Compliance with the GIPS standards is not typically required by legal or regulatory authorities. Also, according to Standard I(A), Knowledge of the Law, if applicable law is stricter than the requirements of the Code and Standards, members and candidates must adhere to applicable law; otherwise, they must adhere to the Code and Standards. Because compliance with the GIPS standards is not required under applicable law, the member is not required to communicate investment performance information to her clients in accordance with the stricter of the GIPS standards and the Code and Standards.

explanation_en: The installment sales method of revenue recognition does not result in permanent differences between pretax and taxable income. Premium payments on life insurance of key employees is an expense on the financial statements, but is not deducted on tax returns. Tax exempt interest is recognized as revenue on the financial statements. These items result in permanent differences between pretax income and taxable income.
question_en: A permanent difference between pretax and taxable income is least likely to arise when a firm:
option_b: uses the installment sales method for nancial reporting.
option_c: pays premiums on life insurance of key employees.

explanation_en: In a limited partnership, general partners typically receive a greater share of profits than limited partners because general partners manage the business and make business decisions. Limited partners have limited financial liability. They are typically not involved in key business decisions, and they do not appoint/remove general partners.
question_en: In a limited partnership, limited partners:
option_a: typically receive a smaller share of profits than general partners.
option_b: are responsible for managing the business, but they have limited financial liability.
option_c: are not involved in business decisions, but they appoint/remove general partners.

explanation_en: A hedge fund typically is more likely to use leverage, is less liquid, and charges higher fees than a traditional mutual fund.
question_en: Compared to a traditional mutual fund, a hedge fund is more likely to feature:
option_c: higher liquidity.

explanation_en: As the name suggests, a tax holiday is usually a temporary exemption from having to pay taxes in some tax jurisdiction. Because of the temporary nature, the key issue for the analyst is to determine when the holiday will terminate, and how the termination will affect taxes payable in the future.
question_en: While evaluating the financial statements of Omega, Inc., the analyst observes that the effective tax rate is 7% less than the statutory rate. The source of this difference is determined to be a tax holiday on a manufacturing plant located in South Africa. This item is most likely to be:
option_a: continuous in nature, so the termination date is not relevant.
option_b: sporadic in nature, and the analyst should try to identify the termination date and determine if taxes will be payable at that time.
option_c: sporadic in nature, but the effect is typically neutralized by higher home country taxes on the repatriated profits.

explanation_en: A value-weighted index is biased toward large-cap stocks because the impact of a given percentage price change of a large-cap stock is larger than the impact of the same percentage price change of a small-cap stock, which is a source of bias for value-weighted indexes.
question_en: A value-weighted equity index is most likely biased by a stock that:
option_c: has a large market capitalization.

explanation_en:
Security market indices serve as market proxies when measuring risk-adjusted performance.
Alpha, the difference between thereturn of the actively managed portfolio and the return of the
passive portfolio, is a measure of risk-adjusted return.
question_en: Security market indices can be used to calculate alphas, which are best described as:
option_a: the systematic risk of a security, using the index as a proxy for the entire market.
option_b: the difference between the return of the actively managed portfolio and the return of the passive portfolio.
option_c: a measure of marketsentiment.

explanation_en: Analysts use both external and internal information when researching companies; it is critical for insightful financial statement analysis. External information refers to information not published by the company. Internal information refers to information produced by the company. explanation_en:
Covariance describes the linear relationship between returns of two assets relative to each other. If two assets' returns tend to move in the
same direction at the same time, the assets have positive covariance. If the returns tend to move in opposite directions, the assets have negative
covariance. Zero covariance means there is no linear relationship between the assets.
Covariance is important in portfolio management since assets with negative covariance can be combined to create a lower-risk portfolio. In this
question, each asset's weight and the portfolio's variance are given. Each asset's variance is the square of its standard deviation. Calculating
covariance is accomplished by rearranging the terms in the equation above:

| Steps | Calculations |
|---|---|
| Insert variables into the two-asset variance equation | sigma_p^2 = wa^2 sigma_a^2 + wb^2 sigma_b^2 + 2 wa wb Cov_ab; 0.07 = (0.25)^2(0.25)^2 + (0.75)^2(0.35)^2 + (2 x 0.25 x 0.75 x Cov_ab) |
| Rearrange to isolate and solve for covariance | (0.07 - 0.0039 - 0.0689) / 0.3750 = Cov_ab; Cov_ab = -0.0028 / 0.3750 = -0.0075 |

In this scenario, the covariance is negative since the sum of the product of each asset's squared weight and its variance is greater than the
portfolio's variance (Choices B and C). However, covariance indicates only the direction of each asset relative to the other; it does not provide
any information about the strength of the linear relationship. The correlation coefficient provides information about both the direction and strength
of the linear relationship.

(Choice B)  The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) is not a dividend discount model and is used to find the expected return of a security, not its current intrinsic value.  The CAPM can be used to find the required rate of return, a variable of the two-stage DDM. explanation_en: Forward commitment derivatives Futures Forwards Swaps Trading venue Exchange-traded Over-the-counter Over-the-counter Legal counterparty Exchange clearinghouse Contract counterparty Contract counterparty Contract terms Standardized Negotiated Negotiated Gain/loss realization Daily settlement At expiration Periodically (eg, semiannual) Futures, forwards, and most swaps are forward commitment derivatives that involve an exchange of contractual obligations between the counterparties.  Gains and losses on each derivative are settled at different frequencies. Futures gains and losses are paid as they are marked to market, and they are settled daily.  Positions are valued based on the day's closing price.  Any change in value from the previous day results in a cash deposit (ie, gains) or withdrawal (ie, losses). Forward contracts are settled at expiration (Choice B).  The short party must sell the underlying asset to the long party at the agreed price set at contract initiation.  The gain (loss) for the counterparties is the difference between the agreed price and the market price of the underlying. Forward commitment swaps are settled at a negotiated frequency (eg, semiannually) (Choice C).  On designated payment dates, the counterparties transfer cash equal to the difference between the value of the payment series (eg, fixed versus floating) that each is obligated to pay. Daily settlement of futures is designed to minimize counterparty credit risk by avoiding the build-up of unrealized gains and losses.  When settlement occurs only periodically or at expiration, underlying price movements can result in large unrealized gains and losses.  The larger one party's unrealized gain is, the greater its credit risk exposure to the counterparty that must make good on its loss.
question_en: Payments of gains and losses on futures contracts are most likely made:
option_c: as negotiated by the counterparties.

A profession becomes respected by having its members create and maintain trust with stakeholders. Professions create trust when members' conduct reflects the profession's ethical principles. explanation_en: Investors must be compensated for bearing risk when providing capital to companies. Equity investors base their required rate of return on expected future cash flows. Since these are uncertain and unknown, different investors will have different estimates of the company's future cash flows. This leads to different investors having different required rates of return. Since companies seek to issue capital at the lowest potential cost, a company will issue equity capital at the lowest rate that will allow it to raise sufficient capital, which becomes the company's cost of equity. Investors with required rates of return less than or equal to this rate will purchase the company's securities; those that have higher required rates of return will not. For a given amount of equity issued, the company's cost of equity will be a single rate. Investors will have varied required rates of return, which often differ from a company's cost of equity. (Choice B) A company taking on riskier projects would most likely increase both its cost of equity and investors' required rate of return, assuming the investors would be aware of the projects. This is not a reason for differences between the cost of equity and investors' required rates of return. (Choice C) The company's cost of debt, not its cost of equity, is calculated after tax. Interest expense is a tax-deductible expense for the company, but dividends are not.

the selling price and the bond's carrying value. If the purchase price is at any value other than 100% of par value, the carrying value will
change over time.
For bonds purchased at a price above or below 100% of par, the premium or discount must be amortized over the time to maturity. This process
results in carrying value at maturity equal to 100% of par. Thus, for bonds held to maturity, there will never be a capital gain or loss.
For bonds sold prior to maturity, the carrying value is based on the YTM at the bond's purchase. The carrying value is determined by using the
YTM at the bond's purchase to discount the coupons and principal over the remaining time to maturity.

explanation_en: The elements (ie, phases) of the risk management framework incorporate the enterprise-wide spectrum of risk management activities and help management stay within the company's risk tolerance while pursuing strategic goals. These elements can be summarized as follows: Leadership determines the overall strategic operating goals, risk budget, and risk tolerance. Management allocates capital to risky projects and manages daily operations. The risk infrastructure (eg, people, systems) gathers, measures, monitors, and reports risk positions. How frequently a company monitors its risk position may vary among entities and depends upon the size of the organization, available resources, and to what degree risk affects decision-making. For example, a large multinational entity may opt for daily monitoring, whereas a smaller regional firm may choose monthly monitoring. (Choice B) Leadership determines the company's risk budget during the risk governance phase. In the context of risk management, risk infrastructure refers to the people and systems that support the implementation of risk management with data collection, measurement, monitoring, and reporting. During the identification phase, the company analyzes risk drivers (eg, economic factors, industry's intensity of competition, specific company factors). Things to remember The risk management framework includes risk governance, risk infrastructure, policies and procedures, identification, measurement, monitoring, reporting, and strategizing. explanation_en:
Total risk, or standard deviation of returns (σ), combines systematic risk (market risk) and nonsystematic risk (nonmarket risk). Using either the Sharpe ratio or M-squared (M2) equation is proper when evaluating managers based on the highest return adjusted for total risk.

Both M-squared and the Sharpe ratio calculate total risk-adjusted performance for each manager because each reflects total risk (as captured by standard deviation, σ). Both also evaluate a portfolio's excess return (ie, return greater than the risk-free rate) compared to that portfolio's standard deviation.

Both the unscaled Sharpe ratio and the M2, in percentage terms, give identical rankings when comparing manager's performance. As shown below, Manager 1 has the highest Sharpe ratio and M-squared results:

Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf)/σp; M-squared = (Rp − Rf)(σm/σp) + Rf

Manager 1: Sharpe = (13% − 2%)/18% = 0.61; M-squared = (13% − 2%)(14%/18%) + 2% = 10.56%
Manager 2: Sharpe = (7% − 2%)/12% = 0.42; M-squared = (7% − 2%)(14%/12%) + 2% = 7.83%
Manager 3: Sharpe = (14% − 2%)/22% = 0.55; M-squared = (14% − 2%)(14%/22%) + 2% = 9.64%

Things to remember:
Standard deviation measures total risk whereas beta measures systematic risk.

explanation_en: A bond's yield describes and quantifies its return.  There are several types of yields used for bonds.  One measure is its current yield, which is the bond's annual coupon payments divided by its flat price (ie, the price usually quoted by dealers, which does not account for accrued interest). Current yield has two main drawbacks that limit its usefulness in analyzing or comparing bonds: It accounts only for interest payments, so it ignores a bond's capital appreciation (or loss) and is also ineffective for bonds that do not pay interest (ie, zero-coupon bonds). It fails to include accrued interest in the denominator, which has the effect of making current yield too high.  A bond's full price is its flat price plus accrued interest (Choice B). (Choice C)  Coupon interest divided by par value is a bond's coupon rate.
question_en: A bond's current price is 95 per 100 par value.  Its current yield is best described as its annual coupon payments divided by its:
option_c: par value.

option_c: a long call and a short risk-free zero-coupon bond.

explanation_en: Overconfidence bias occurs when an analyst has too much faith in their own work. Sharing forecasts with others, widening confidence intervals, and using scenario analysis are all appropriate ways to mitigate the impact of overconfidence bias.

option_c: employ scenario analysis in forecasting.

explanation_en: The capital market line (CML) is the practical form of the capital allocation line (CAL).  The CAL represents theoretical portfolios combining the optimal risky portfolio and a risk-free asset.  The CML replaces the optimal risky portfolio with the real market portfolio (eg, the S&P 500 Index) and replaces the risk-free asset with short-term domestic government bonds. Analysts using the CML assume that markets are informationally efficient.  This means that markets provide all the information investors need, and all investors find the same valuation.  With uniformity of securities' valuations, it is very difficult for investors to outperform the market consistently. This assumption compels investors to follow a passive investing strategy.  Under these conditions, using a stock index—such as the S&P 500 Index—as a proxy for the market portfolio is logical. Under the CAL, the definition of the optimal risky portfolio not only includes stocks and bonds but also includes thousands of different types of asset classes.  Some of these are unavailable due to legal restrictions (eg, Class A China Stock to non-Chinese investors) and some are nontradable (eg, private property).  Therefore, the optimal risky portfolio does not exist in the real world. (Choice A)  The efficient frontier represents all theoretical portfolios of risky assets in the investment opportunity set to that offer the highest expected return at each level of risk.  Portfolios on the efficient frontier do not hold the risk-free asset. (Choice C)  The security market line shows rates of return for individual assets, not for a portfolio of assets.  It depicts one security's expected return as a function of systematic risk.
question_en: A portfolio consisting of the S&P 500 Index ETF and US Treasury bills is most likely on the:
option_c: security market line.

explanation_en:
Oligopoly pricing theories
Theory Description
Compete on price

Cournot assumption
Equilibrium: stable price and output quantity
No cooperation (ie, no collusion)

Oligopolistic firms may adopt various pricing strategies. Nash equilibrium is perhaps best known as "game theory" in reference to a set of optimal
strategies used by two or more market participants to maximize their profits. Although this theory assumes that each firm acts in its own best
interest, it also assumes that firms will consider their competitors' responses to an action. For example, a firm could try to increase profits by
raising prices but may also consider the loss of market share to competitors that do not raise their prices.
(Choice A) Under the collusion pricing theory, firms seek to maximize industry profits, not firm profits. Also, as the name suggests, market firms
cooperate to manipulate the market equilibrium; under Nash equilibrium, firms do not collude, even though they might benefit from doing so.
(Choice C) The Cournot assumption, applied to a duopoly (ie, two-firm market) in equilibrium, assumes that both competitive firms act
independently and simultaneously. Firms act to determine production quantities and maximize profits, without collusion and without anticipating
each other's actions.
question_en: An oligopolist's pricing strategy includes anticipating competitor reactions and acting in the firm's self-interest. This firm is most likely pursuing which of the following pricing strategies?
option_c: Cournot assumption

explanation_en: Investors are risk averse. Given a choice between assets with equal rates of expected return, the investor will always select the asset with the lowest level of risk. Risk aversion does not imply that an investor will choose the less risky of two assets in all cases, or that an investor is unwilling to accept greater risk to achieve a greater expected return.
question_en: Risk aversion means that an individual will choose the less risky of two assets:
option_a: even if it has a lower expected return.
option_c: if they have the same expected return.

option_b: expected return over the level of ination.

explanation_en: Categories of alternative investing in the oil and gas sector Category Characteristics Upstream Exploration and extraction Drilling and oil field services companies Midstream Refining and processing Gasoline, heating oil, and jet fuel refineries Downstream Makers of end-user goods from refined petroleum products Plastics and chemicals manufacturers Commodity investing focuses on physical resources, which include energy-related products like coal and crude oil.  In addition to gaining direct exposure to commodities through futures contracts, alternative investment vehicles also invest in the companies that mine and refine those products. In the oil and gas sector, companies are divided into three broad categories.  Upstream companies explore for and extract the basic product, such as crude oil.  Midstream companies refine the crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and heating oil.  Downstream companies create other products or services (eg, tires, retail gas stations) from the refined commodity. An oil and gas sector hedge fund that focuses on midstream companies most likely invests in a gasoline refinery.  A drilling company is an upstream company (Choice B), and a plastics manufacturer is an example of a downstream company (Choice C).
question_en: A hedge fund that concentrates on midstream oil and gas investments is most likely to invest in:
option_c: plastics manufacturers.

Her statement that total return "could" exceed 20% is appropriately phrased as an opinion.
question_en: Janet Coleman, CFA, is preparing a research report on Union Utilities. If investors buy the stock now at around $50 a share, their total return could exceed 20%." With regard to the Standard on communication with clients and prospective clients, Coleman:
option_b: violated the Standard because she promised a specic return on an investment.
option_c: violated the Standard because she failed to distinguish opinion from fact.

explanation_en: A Type I error is the rejection of the null when the null is actually true. The significance level of the test (alpha) (which is one minus the confidence level) is the probability of making a Type I error. A Type II error is the failure to reject the null when it is actually false.
question_en: John Jenkins, CFA, is performing a study on the behavior of the mean P/E ratio for a sample of small-cap companies. Which of the following statements is most accurate?
option_a: A Type I error represents the failure to reject the null hypothesis when it is, in fact, false.
option_b: One minus the confidence level of the test represents the probability of making a Type II error.
option_c: The significance level of the test represents the probability of making a Type I error.

Because owners have potentially unlimited upside from a company's growth, they are more likely to favor actions that increase a company's potential growth rate.
question_en: Increasing a company's risk exposure in an effort to increase its growth rate is most likely to be favored by:
option_c: both lenders and owners.

explanation_en: Differences may exist between forward and futures prices for otherwise identical contracts if futures prices are correlated with interest rates. If futures prices are negatively correlated with interest rates, daily settlement of long futures contracts will require cash when interest rates are increasing and produce cash when interest rates are decreasing. As a result the futures price will be lower than the forward price. The difference in price does not provide an arbitrage opportunity or suggest that investors should prefer forward or futures contracts.
question_en: Bea Moran wants to establish a long derivatives position in a commodity she will need to acquire in six months. Moran observes that the six-month forward price is 45.20 and the six- month futures price is 45.10. This difference most likely suggests that for this commodity:

option_b: futures prices are negatively correlated with interest rates.
option_c: there is an arbitrage opportunity among forward, futures, and spot prices.

explanation_en: ROE measures the profit a company creates from using its equity. DuPont analysis entails decomposing ROE into different components: profitability, efficiency, and leverage. By understanding the components of ROE, a company can determine more particularly how it can improve its ROE. ROE is the product of the company's return on assets (ROA) and the amount of leverage it uses. ROA (ie, the ratio of net income to asset value) can also be expressed as the product of profit margin and asset turnover. The more profit the company produces and the more efficiently it uses its assets, the higher its ROE. A company can also increase ROE by borrowing, which increases its leverage. Using DuPont analysis, ROE is the product of the net profit margin, total asset turnover, and leverage. Company C has the highest ROE, 27.0% since its low efficiency is offset by a high profit margin (Choices A and B).

explanation_en:
The portfolio standard deviation, sigma_p, is a measure of risk. For a standard deviation of a two-asset portfolio, the portfolio standard deviation is a
function of the weight and risk of the portfolio's assets and the correlation between two assets. It expresses the degree of dispersion of how
portfolio returns occur around its mean. The greater the dispersion, the higher the risk.
The data given in this question are all expected values; this does not change how the portfolio standard deviation is calculated. Both expected
standard deviation and standard deviation from historical data are calculated from the same equation.
To find portfolio standard deviation, input the weights, standard deviations, variances of the portfolio's assets, and the correlation coefficients
between all pairs of assets. For this question, find the weights of treasury bond (T) and the stock (S) from the return requirement.
In a two-asset portfolio, restate the weight of one of the funds as the difference of the total portfolio minus the other fund's weight.

wT rT + wS rS = Rp
(1 - wS) rT + wS rS = Rp
(1 - wS) 0.04 + wS 0.12 = 0.09
0.04 - 0.04wS + 0.12wS = 0.09
0.08wS = 0.05
wS = 0.625

Once the weight of stock (wS) is found, solve for the weight of the treasury bond (wT):
wT = 1 - wS
wT = 1 - 0.625
wT = 0.375

For the expected standard deviations of T (treasury bond) and S (stock), calculate the values by taking the square root of the variance.
sigma_T^2 = 0.01, sigma_S^2 = 0.04
sigma_T = sqrt(0.01), sigma_S = sqrt(0.04)
sigma_T = 0.10, sigma_S = 0.20

Now that all the components have been calculated, input all values into the standard deviation of the two-asset portfolio equation and solve:
sigma_p = sqrt(wa^2 sigma_a^2 + wb^2 sigma_b^2 + 2 wa wb rho_ab sigma_a sigma_b)
sigma_p = sqrt((0.375)^2(0.01) + (0.625)^2(0.04) + 2(0.375)(0.625)(0.25)(0.10)(0.20))
sigma_p = sqrt(0.0014 + 0.0156 + 0.0023)
sigma_p = sqrt(0.0193)
sigma_p = 0.1389

(Choice A) This choice misapplies the variance of the assets and then squares them as if the variance were the standard deviation. This understates portfolio risk.
(Choice C) This option does not square the weights of the assets and therefore overstates portfolio risk.

explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the adviser's responsibility for assessing the suitability of investments for each client.  This responsibility entails researching a client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance.  These form the building blocks of the client's investment policy statement (IPS) and determine the suitability of proposed investments. Clients sometimes wish to make investments that do not align with their IPSs.  In such a case, the Member or Candidate should discuss the proposed investment with the client before making the trade, explaining why the investment diverges from the IPS.  If the investment has minimal impact on the portfolio, the Member or Candidate can purchase the investment without modifying the IPS after receiving the proper client approval, subject to the firm's guidelines. In this scenario, Munira Alam may purchase Force Gaming Inc. (FGI) stock for Rahmi Hadi's portfolio since she educated him on the deviation between the stock's risk profile and the IPS and received Hadi's acknowledgment that the position is inconsistent with his current IPS. (Choice B)  Alam would have to consider ceasing her advisory relationship with Hadi only if the unsolicited trade were material to Hadi's portfolio and he refused to update his IPS. (Choice C)  Alam does not have to refuse to purchase FGI stock even though it does not align with Hadi's IPS.  Since the trade will be immaterial to Hadi's portfolio, Alam only needs to educate Hadi and have him acknowledge that the trade is inconsistent with his IPS.
question_en: Munira Alam, CFA, is a financial adviser for Rahmi Hadi.  Hadi reads a report about Force Gaming Inc. (FGI) and calls Alam to purchase the stock.  After thorough research, Alam concludes that FGI is too risky for the parameters of Hadi's investment policy statement (IPS), although the amount of the proposed purchase would have only a minimal effect on his overall portfolio.  She calls Hadi to inform him about the risk.  Hadi acknowledges Alam's warning but insists that FGI stock be added to his portfolio, even if the IPS must be modified.  To comply with the Standards, Alam should:
option_a: purchase FGI based on Hadi's request.
option_b: cease her advisory relationship with Hadi.
option_c: refuse to purchase FGI for Hadi's portfolio.

explanation_en:
The price of a bond is the bond's present value: the sum of the present values of its coupon and principal (ie, par value) payments over the
remaining time to maturity. Each cash flow is discounted by the market yield to maturity (YTM), expressed as a periodic rate, over the number of
periods between the pricing date and the date each cash flow is due.
The quickest solution to the problem is obtained with a financial calculator, using the following inputs:
Number of periods (N) n × m = 4 × 2 = 8
Periodic discount rate (i) r ÷ m = 4.50% ÷ 2 = 2.25(%)
Periodic payments (PMT) (c × FV) ÷ m = (0.05 × 100) ÷ 2 = 2.5
Par value (FV) 100
c = coupon rate; FV = par value
For bonds with a compounding frequency (m) of more than once per year, the number of periods (N), coupon payments (PMT), and market
discount rate (i) must be adjusted from the given annual values to the periodic values. The market discount rate is also called the required yield or
the required rate of return.
(Choice A) 98.2075 results from using the market discount rate to determine the coupon payments and using the coupon rate to discount the
cash flows. Note that since the bond's coupon rate is greater than its yield, it is currently priced at a premium: the price must be greater than the
par value. Thus, any answer choice less than par value is incorrect.
(Choice B) 101.7938 would be the price if the bond paid coupons once per year.

option_c: administrative expenses.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action." Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members and candidates to exercise diligence and thoroughness when making investment decisions.  While there is no exact policy or procedure that the Standard demands, appropriate and diligent research must be completed. Here, Rosa believes that the funds of Broadwick Investment Partners (BIP) are an ideal investment based on her memory and experience while working at BIP.  However, BIP may have changed its investment process or the funds' underlying securities over the last six months; based on current research, she might have a different investment recommendation. To comply with the Standard, regardless of limited time or personal relationships, Rosa must exercise diligence by conducting her own thorough review of the funds.  Memory or past experiences are inadequate justifications and are not reasonable bases to make investment decisions (Choice A). (Choice B)  Rosa does not violate the Standard by having a personal relationship with another investment manager.  While Danek does assist Rosa, Rosa must do her own work in making an investment recommendation.

explanation_en: The theory of semi-strong form market efficiency holds that market prices contain all publicly available information. One consequence of this theory is that investors cannot achieve abnormal returns without using material, nonpublic information. Market anomalies are persistent market events that are inconsistent with semi-strong form efficiency, that is, price changes that cannot be explained by available or newly released public information. The earnings surprise anomaly is due to the lack of a complete and immediate price adjustment to unexpected news from an earnings report. Since there is a lag between the release of the earnings report (which becomes public information) and the subsequent price adjustment, it is possible to generate abnormal returns for a short time. This is inconsistent with semi-strong form market efficiency. (Choice A) The initial public offering (IPO) anomaly indicates that, on average, investors purchasing shares through an IPO may be able to earn short-term abnormal profits. IPOs are frequently underpriced, allowing investors to earn abnormal returns; however, market prices adjust quickly, supporting semi-strong market efficiency. (Choice C) A closed-end fund discount is the persistent 4–10% discount to net asset value (NAV) observed in these funds' prices. The discount does not result in abnormal returns due to transaction costs, liquidity, and the potential for NAV miscalculations.
question_en: Which of the following market anomalies is inconsistent with semi-strong form market efficiency?
option_c: Closed-end fund discount

explanation_en: Geopolitical risk types Risk Characteristics Examples Specific date Event Country elections Known risk Climate change Ongoing Thematic Cyber threats Known and evolving risk Terrorism Surprise Natural disaster Exogenous Unknown risk Pandemic Geopolitical risk represents the risk from political changes, natural disasters, and other factors that affect international relations. Risks differ in their timing and predictability. Thematic risks are known and can remain present for an extended period as they evolve and change in scope or frequency. Awareness of a thematic risk allows companies and investors to manage the risk through preparation. Populism is a type of political movement and a known risk that continues evolving over time. Therefore, a growth in populism is a thematic geopolitical risk and, as such, its potential effects can be incorporated by investors into their risk analysis. (Choice A) Event risks (eg, government elections) occur on specific dates that are known in advance. In contrast, political movements such as populism develop over time and thus are not considered specific events. (Choice C) Exogenous risks involve surprising events that are often uncontrollable, whereas a political movement is a more predictable and ongoing risk.
question_en: The growth in populism is most likely consistent with which type of geopolitical risk?
option_c: Exogenous

explanation_en: The zero volatility spread (Z-spread) is the interest rate that is added to each zero-coupon bond spot rate that will cause the present value of the risky bond's cash flows to equal its market value. The nominal spread is the spread that is added to the YTM of a similar maturity government bond that will then equal the YTM of the risky bond. The zero volatility spread (Z-spread) is the spread that results when the cost of the call option in percent is added to the option adjusted spread.
question_en: The zero volatility spread (Z-spread) is the spread that:
option_a: is added to each spot rate on the government yield curve that will cause the present value of the bond's cash flows to equal its market price.
option_b: is added to the yield to maturity of a similar maturity government bond to equal the yield to maturity of the risky bond.
option_c: results when the cost of the call option in percent is subtracted from the option adjusted spread.

correct answer.

(Choice B) 7.00% is the result of incorrectly assuming the EAR is equal to the annual continuously compounded rate of return.

explanation_en: Short-term funding available to banks Demand deposits (checking accounts) Retail deposits Savings accounts Money market accounts Central bank funds Wholesale funds Interbank deposits Certificates of deposit Short-term loan-like agreements Repurchase agreements ("repos") Repo and reverse repo Not particular to banks Debt maturities < 360 days Commercial paper Not particular to banks Financial institutions like banks have greater funding needs than nonfinancial companies since, in addition to projects like expansions and acquisitions, they engage in financial operations such as making loans and investing. Banks obtain much of their funding through the retail deposits of their customers. However, when the amount of loans made to customers exceeds the funds available from retail accounts, they most commonly turn to wholesale funds: central bank funds, interbank deposits, and certificates of deposit. Banks will use wholesale funds first, after retail deposits, since interest costs can be less than with retail deposits, repurchase agreements, and commercial paper. Wholesale funds are also important in managing any potential fixed/floating balance sheet mismatch between assets and liabilities. Repurchase agreements are another commonly used source of funds available to banks and other companies. (Choice B) Demand deposits (checking accounts) are a type of retail deposit. (Choice C) Bank financial assets tend to be relatively short-term, and therefore result in a variable rate of interest. Banks normally first turn to lower-cost wholesale funds before issuing debt in the form of bonds. If banks issue bonds, the bonds are likely to have a floating (not fixed) coupon rate.
question_en: A bank expects to originate more loans than can be funded by retail deposits. Banks in this situation most commonly utilize funding from:

explanation_en: The rebalancing policy specifies when the actual asset allocation should be realigned to the strategic allocation. The Appendices section of the investment policy statement (IPS) contains the client's strategic asset allocation and rebalancing policy. The strategic asset allocation specifies the target weight of different asset classes based on the client's investment risk and return objectives and constraints. Over time, market values of investments change, which cause the actual allocation to stray from the strategic allocation. Rebalancing (ie, buying and selling securities) the portfolio from actual weights back to strategic weights ensures that the portfolio's asset classes remain proportional to meet the client's risk and return objectives. The frequency of rebalancing is determined by evaluating the risk of being misallocated versus the costs of rebalancing. (Choice A) Best execution refers to a trading process that seeks to maximize the value of a portfolio within its prescribed objectives and constraints. It is part of the firm's investment management process and not part of an individual client's IPS. (Choice C) Per CFA Institute, the Appendices of the IPS describe the strategic asset allocation and the rebalancing policy. Although minimizing transaction costs improves the client's performance, the rebalancing policy describes when the manager realigns the portfolio, not how to minimize transaction costs.
question_en: Within a client's investment policy statement, the rebalancing policy most likely addresses changes in which of the following?
option_c: The process of minimizing transaction costs

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation concerns actions that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the profession and financial markets.  The Standard applies whether the information is prepared for clients, colleagues, or the public.  Misrepresentation can include: Plagiarism:  quoting information without acknowledgement or citation Omission:  presenting incomplete information or data in order to mislead Exaggeration:  inflating professional credentials or performance results Here, Hossi violates the Standard by claiming she authored the report (ie, plagiarism).  The slight changes in wording she made are not enough to make it her work.  Although the chief financial officer granted verbal permission to use the report, this does not absolve Hossi of the need to disclose the original source (Choice A). (Choice B)  There is nothing in the Standards that prevents Hossi from collecting her full fee for this assignment.  By collecting only a flat fee that was neither based on her recommendation nor tied to the client's future stock performance, and by disclosing who paid for the report, Hossi has followed the recommendations under Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity.

explanation_en: If a random variable is lognormally distributed, this means its natural log is normally distributed. If a variable is lognormally distributed, it can be defined and analyzed with reference to the mean and variance of its associated normal distribution (ie, the distribution of the natural log of X). The related normal distribution is simpler to work with than the lognormal distribution. Analyzing a lognormal distribution is more complex than analyzing a normal distribution. It is bounded by zero to the left and is asymmetrical. In addition, calculating its mean and variance is cumbersome. However, it can be analyzed via its associated normal distribution, making the lognormal distribution useful for conducting statistical tests on lognormally distributed data like asset prices. (Choice B) The natural log of a lognormally distributed random variable is distributed according to a normal distribution, not another lognormal distribution. (Choice C) A chi-squared distribution is the distribution of a random variable that is the sum of squares of one or more independent standard normal random variables. The natural log of a lognormally distributed random variable is not chi-square distributed.
question_en: If a random variable X is lognormally distributed, its natural log most likely follows a:
option_c: chi-squared distribution.

explanation_en: Investment constraints Time horizon Length of investment objective Taxes Status, treatment of application Need for cash during the time Liquidity horizon All laws in the jurisdiction Legal Special legal status (eg, pension) Special A special aspect of the client circumstances When constructing an investment policy statement (IPS), an advisor will have to consider multiple investment constraints that influence how the client's assets should be invested. Unique circumstances refer to any aspect of the client's situation that is not covered by one of the other investment constraints. Unique circumstances include: A client's beliefs and values (eg, religious, ethical) Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices Portions of a client's wealth not included in the manager's portfolio and thus not under its control The advisor must consider all a client's assets, even those outside the advisor's control, when constructing an IPS. Specifically, the assets should be included in planning to meet risk and return objectives using diversification. For example, if a client's retirement plan is heavily invested in the stock of that client's employer, the client is exposed to the risk of that employer twice: both through the stock value and through a source of income. The advisor must include this unique circumstance in the client's IPS in order to meet the client's risk objective. (Choice A) An insurance company having more uneven and uncertain cash flow than its peers is a factor affecting the company's cash needs and therefore would be a liquidity constraint. (Choice C) A pension fund being legally restricted from holding more than 50% of its assets in equities is a legal restriction on the pension's investments and therefore would be a legal and regulatory constraint.

option_b: An individual's retirement plan is heavily invested in employer common stock.
option_c: A pension fund is legally restricted from holding more than 50% of its assets in equities.

Common-sized cash flow statements may be reported as a percentage of net revenue. Increases in assets indicate a use of cash and are
shown as negative numbers on a common-sized cash flow statement; decreases are shown as positive figures. In this question, inventory is
increasing, so it decreases cash flow and is shown as a negative percentage of net revenue. Increases in liabilities suggest a source of cash.
Increases in liabilities are shown as positive figures and decreases as negative figures on common-sized statements of cash flow.
(Choice B) Accounts payable increases when a company purchases assets on credit and decreases as the company pays off those assets. It is
the increase, not the decrease, in accounts payable that increases cash flow.
(Choice C) Accounts receivable increases when a company extends credit to customers and decreases when the company collects cash from
them. It is the increase, not the decrease, in accounts receivable that decreases cash flow.

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV focuses on the duty to employers. Under Standard IV(B), members and candidates must not accept gifts that may create a conflict of interest with their employer unless all parties involved give written consent. Here, all the answer choices are valid constraints of the Standards, but only one is associated with Standard IV. This is a way of testing knowledge of the Standards themselves. Although most exam questions will address applications of the Standards, it is possible that there will be a question like this on the exam. (Choice A) Judging the suitability of an investment using the total portfolio approach is an application of Standard III(C) Suitability, not Standard IV Duty to Employers. Standard III is about a member's or candidate's duty to clients. (Choice C) Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs , not Standard IV Duty to Employers, requires members and candidates to act in a manner that does not compromise the reputation of the CFA Institute.

explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must:… a. Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this information regularly. b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action." Standard III(C) Suitability requires Members and Candidates that are advisors to properly assess the suitability of each potential investment for each client before making investment decisions.  To do this, an advisor must first gather information on each client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance.  This information is used to develop an investment policy statement (IPS), which is then used to develop an appropriate investment program for the client. Without gathering and understanding the appropriate information, an advisor has no way of knowing if specific investments meet criteria for suitability for the client.  Therefore, investing a client's assets before gathering appropriate information violates the Standard.  In this scenario, Chen invests Zhao's assets before getting information on Zhao's financial circumstances and objectives.  Even though Zhao said to invest her assets however Chen saw fit, Chen had no way to know if the investments were suitable for Zhao.  Therefore, Chen violated the Standards (Choice A). (Choice B)  Members and Candidates do not need client approval for every specific investment to adhere to the Standard.  Once the IPS is created, the advisors can invest within the confines of the IPS without approval for each investment.
question_en: Chen Hong, CFA, is an independent investment advisor.  Through a referral from an existing client, Chen contacts Zhao Qiuping.  Chen briefly meets with Zhao, who is leaving for vacation the next day.  Zhao agrees to be Chen's client and sends him money that is currently in her savings account.  They are not able to discuss the details of Zhao's financial circumstances and objectives at the meeting, but Zhao tells Chen that he can invest the money however he sees fit and agrees that they will meet again to create a detailed investment policy statement when Zhao returns. Chen invests a portion of Zhao's funds in several stocks of companies that Chen has invested in other clients' funds, since Chen believes the stock prices will increase and Chen does not want Zhao to miss out.  By the time Zhao returns, her investment portfolio is up 4%.  With regards to Zhao's investments, Chen:
option_a: was in full compliance with the Standards.
option_b: violated the Standards by not getting approval from Zhao for each investment.
option_c: violated the Standards by investing Zhao's funds before gathering appropriate information.

explanation_en:
Return on common equity (ROCE) gauges the amount of residual net income (after accounting for preferred dividends) generated relative to
common equity. Preferred dividends are subtracted from net income since common shareholders receive distributions only after preferred
shareholders receive their dividends. Greater ROCE ratios suggest that a company is more effective in using common equity to generate a return
for common shareholders.
ROCE should not be confused with ROE (return on equity). ROE measures the return for all equity investors (preferred and common) and is
calculated as net income / average total equity.
(Choice B) 5.18% results from failing to subtract preferred dividends from net income. ROCE measures return for common shareholders only, so
distributions to preferred shareholders (ie, preferred dividends) should be taken out.
(Choice C) 6.18% results from incorrectly using EBIT, instead of net income, in the calculation. EBIT measures profits before interest and taxes,
which reduce income available to common shareholders.
question_en:

explanation_en: The financial statement analysis framework consists of six steps: 1. State the objective and context. Determine what questions the analysis is meant to answer, the form in which it needs to be presented, and what resources and how much time are available to perform the analysis. 2. Gather data. Acquire the company's financial statements and other relevant data on its industry and the economy. Ask questions of the company's management, suppliers, and customers, and visit company sites. 3. Process the data. Make any appropriate adjustments to the financial statements. Calculate ratios. Prepare exhibits such as graphs and common-size balance sheets. 4. Analyze and interpret the data. Use the data to answer the questions stated in the first step. Decide what conclusions or recommendations the information supports. 5. Report the conclusions or recommendations. Prepare a report and communicate it to its intended audience. Be sure the report and its dissemination comply with the Code and Standards that relate to investment analysis and recommendations. 6. Update the analysis. Repeat these steps periodically and change the conclusions or recommendations when necessary.
question_en: In the financial statement analysis framework, using the data to address the objectives of the analysis and deciding what conclusions or recommendations the information supports is best described as:
option_c: reporting the conclusions.

LIFO is allowed under U.S. GAAP but is not allowed under IFRS. Thus, Lincoln should choose LIFO and Continental should choose average cost in order to minimize pre-tax financial income.

Assuming an inflationary environment and stable inventory quantities, which permissible cost flow assumption will minimize each firm's pre-tax financial income? Lincoln Continental Corporation Incorporated

explanation_en: Beta is a measure of market (systematic) risk. Beta estimates an asset's sensitivity to market movements. An asset with a beta of 1 has the same relative risk and the same expected return as the market's return. An asset with a beta of 1.20 has 20% more risk than the market. With respect to capital market theory, beta is the main component of the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). The CAPM is used to estimate a security's expected return based on the security's beta, the market's expected return, and the risk-free rate. (Choices A and C) Beta is a measure of a security's systematic risk. Total risk comprises both systematic risk and nonsystematic risk.
question_en: According to the capital asset pricing model, beta best measures the sensitivity of an asset's return to:

Forward rates and spot rates are related and each can be derived from the other (as shown in the image above).  However, solving for spot rates is not required to calculate a bond's value.  Instead, the forward rates can be applied directly to solve the discount rates at each cash flow and, subsequently, the present value. In this scenario, since each coupon is 2.50 (100 × 0.025): (Choice B)  104.01 is the bond's price if 1y1y (not 0y1y) is used as the starting point of the discounting calculations. (Choice C)  104.57 is the bond's price if each forward rate is applied individually to each cash flow, as if they were spot rates.

explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Expansionary monetary policies encourage more rapid growth of GDP by stimulating economic activity, including business and consumer investment and consumption. Since businesses borrow to invest in additional plant and equipment and consumers borrow to increase purchases of goods and services, policies that stimulate lending and borrowing are expansionary. A policy rate (ie, official interest rate or official policy rate) is the interest rate a central bank charges when it lends money to commercial banks. Setting the policy rate below a neutral rate of interest means the central bank is attempting to increase the real GDP growth rate by: reducing the cost of borrowing from the central bank, which encourages commercial banks to use additional reserves to make loans, increasing the supply of available credit; and lowering borrowing rates generally since commercial bank base lending rates are often tied to the policy rate, stimulating demand for credit. Since this policy leads to increased lending and borrowing and should stimulate economic growth, it is expansionary. (Choice A) When central banks sell government securities, they reduce bank reserves since commercial banks pay for the securities using reserves. This discourages lending and borrowing and slows GDP growth; therefore, it is a contractionary monetary policy. (Choice C) Raising the reserve requirement to reduce excess reserves inhibits commercial banks' ability to make loans; therefore, it is not an expansionary policy.
question_en: Which of the following monetary policy actions is most likely expansionary?
option_a: Selling government securities through open market operations
option_b: Lowering the policy rate to a level below the neutral interest rate
option_c: Raising reserve requirements to reduce the amount of excess reserves

option_a: A positive (negative) adjustment to net income when accounts payable increases (decreases).
option_b: A negative adjustment to net income regardless of whether accounts payable increases or decreases.

explanation_en: One common approach to the categorization of industry growth is a matrix that identifies companies by their pace of growth and sensitivity to the business cycle (ie, cyclicality). For pace of growth, industries are broken into: Growth industries, which have not fully penetrated their addressable market and therefore have growth factors specific to both the industry and the overall market Mature industries, which have saturated their market and are growing at the same pace as the economy or even declining (eg, when companies that have developed substitutes take market share) For cyclicality, industries are broken into: Cyclical industries, which are highly sensitive to the business cycle Defensive industries, which are less sensitive to the business cycle One drawback of this categorization system is that a company operating within an industry may not be categorized the same as that industry or other companies within it.  For instance, a new entrant into a mature, defensive industry may have faster growth and more cyclicality than its established competitors. (Choice A)  Although defensive companies are less sensitive to business cycles, they are usually still affected by slowdowns in spending. Therefore, even defensive companies' revenues often decline during recessions. (Choice C)  Investors who agree on a company's degree of cyclicality can still value the company differently if they have different expectations regarding the severity and length of the business cycle.
question_en: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion regarding industry growth categorization?
option_a: Defensive companies typically experience modest revenue growth even during recessions.
option_b: Companies within the same industry may have differing growth and cyclicality characteristics.
option_c: Investors that agree on a company's degree of cyclicality will typically have similar valuations.

explanation_en: Industries evolve over time and experience different levels of growth and profitability in each stage of their life cycle. Each stage exhibits different characteristics that affect the competitive dynamics of an industry, such as level of product demand, intensity of competition, and profitability. The shakeout stage is characterized by slowing growth, fierce competition, and diminishing profitability. In the shakeout stage, growth in demand is slow since the overall industry can attract few new customers (Choice A). Companies are forced to take existing market share away from competitors to grow, leading to fierce competition. The slowdown in demand also pressures many companies to reduce costs through restructuring (Choice C).
question_en: Which of the following is least likely a characteristic of the shakeout stage in an industry's life cycle?
option_c: Frequent company restructuring

explanation_en: An indicator variable, also called a dummy variable, takes on the value of 0 or 1 to represent mutually exclusive categories (eg, yes/no, growth/value, before/after).  It can be used as the independent variable (X) in a regression model.  In this scenario, X is an indicator variable that assigns the value of 1 to the months with sales campaigns and 0 to the months without a sales campaign. The scatterplot on the left shows two distinct trends since revenues peak in months with sales campaigns (in green).  Consequently, the time- series regression model does not fit the data appropriately.  In the second graph, using the indicator variable as X concentrates all sales data in two columns: when X = 0 and when X = 1. The intercept and the slope have singular interpretations when X is an indicator variable: Intercept is the average revenue in the months without sales campaigns (ie, when X = 0) Slope is the average difference in revenues of months without sales campaigns (ie, when X = 0) and with sales campaigns (ie, when X = 1) (Choice C) As a result, the average revenue in months with sales campaigns is the sum of the intercept and the slope (Choice A)

explanation_en: The Treynor ratio and Jensen's alpha are used to evaluate risk-adjusted portfolio performance. The Treynor ratio compares the portfolio's returns in excess of the risk-free rate with the portfolio's systematic risk as measured by beta. Jensen's alpha calculates the difference between a portfolio's actual (eg, average return) and expected returns consistent with the portfolio's systematic risk according to CAPM. In this scenario, the manager uses both measures to compare three funds. Treynor ratios are solved using the equation above. Jensen's alpha is more easily solved by comparing the actual and expected returns. Substituting all terms into the equation would give the same answer, but the more direct approach is to recognize that Jensen's alpha is the difference between the actual (ie, average) and expected returns. The only choice that meets both criteria is Fund Y. (Choice A) Fund X has a Jensen's alpha that exceeds −0.5%, but its ex post Treynor ratio, based on actual returns, is below 3%; therefore, this fund would not be selected. (Choice C) Fund Z has a Treynor ratio greater than 3%, but its Jensen's alpha is below −0.5%; therefore, this fund would not be selected.

A portfolio manager is considering three funds to add to a portfolio and gathers the following data:

| | Fund X | Fund Y | Fund Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| Actual average return (%) | 5.13 | 4.98 | 7.29 |
| Expected return (%) | 5.59 | 4.83 | 7.81 |
| Beta | 1.18 | 0.95 | 1.85 |

The manager will add only funds with Jensen's alpha above −0.5% and a, ex post Treynor ratio greater than 3%. If the risk-free rate is 1.7% and the market has averaged a 5% return, the manager's most appropriate choice is:

explanation_en: Industries usually evolve over time in a predictable pattern, allowing analysts to predict present and future expected performance based on the industry life cycle. Each stage exhibits different characteristics that reflect the competitive dynamics (eg, product demand, intensity of competition) that lead to varying levels of growth and profitability. Determining where an industry is in its life cycle can provide helpful context for analysis of a company in that industry as it almost certainly will affect investment returns. Industry life-cycle analysis has limitations since it assumes all industries follow a predictable path. External factors (eg, technological, regulatory, social) can divert an industry's path along the cycle. For example, stages may become longer/shorter than expected and can be skipped or repeated. This makes industry life-cycle analysis most useful when an industry is relatively stable and less useful during periods of rapid change (Choice A). (Choice B) Not all companies in an industry will experience similar performance (eg, growth, profitability). Also, different companies, even within the same industry, may be in various stages of the company life cycle.
question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of industry life-cycle analysis?
option_a: The model is most useful when industries are in periods of rapid change.
option_b: Companies in the same industry can be expected to exhibit similar performance.
option_c: External factors can cause an industry to deviate from the expected progress of the cycle.

explanation_en: The efficient market hypothesis (EMH) specifies three forms of market efficiency: weak, semi-strong, and strong. Weak-form EMH holds that historical market data is reflected in market prices. Technical analysis involves using historical trading and volume data as the basis to buy and sell. If historical market data has already influenced prices, then it is not possible to produce consistent, abnormal returns (ie, returns better than expected returns) using technical analysis. (Choices B and C) If markets are weak-form efficient, historical price and volume information are immediately reflected in market prices. Other publicly available information (eg, company financial reports) and material nonpublic (insider) information may not be reflected in prices under weak-form EMH. Therefore, it is possible for an investor to achieve consistent, abnormal returns by trading on publicly available information or insider information.
question_en: A country's financial markets are weak-form efficient. This implies that it is impossible to obtain consistent, abnormal returns in the country's markets using:
option_c: fundamental analysis.

explanation_en:
There are three general sources of funds companies use to finance operations:
issuing common or preferred stock,
borrowing (eg, loans, bonds), and
generating cash from operations.
Ultimately, these amounts are reflected on balance sheets as debt or equity. The proportional split between the amounts of debt and equities is a
company's capital structure.
Although many companies have a target capital structure, various factors influence a company's reliance on different funding sources and may
result in the actual capital structure not matching the target. However, refinancing maturing debt at a lower interest rate does not change the
capital structure since the amount of debt is unchanged. All else equal, reducing the interest rate on debt lowers the company's WACC, but it
would not alter the company's capital structure.
(Choice A) Greater than anticipated net operating cash flow results in cash in excess of amounts budgeted for other purposes (eg, debt
retirement, investments). All else equal, this increases equity capital, raising it above the targeted proportion of the capital structure.
(Choice C) A company may opportunistically issue equity securities if management perceives its common stock is overpriced. For a company
operating at its target capital structure, issuing additional shares increases equity above the targeted proportion of the capital structure.
question_en: All else being equal, which of the following factors is least likely to cause a company's actual capital structure to diverge from its target capital structure? The company:
option_a: generated greater than anticipated operating cash flow.
option_b: refinanced maturing debt at a lower rate to reduce the cost of debt.
option_c: issued equity when management perceived company stock was overvalued.

explanation_en: Utility has two terms: the expected return and a negative term based on the portfolio risk weighted by risk aversion. For an identical portfolio, the investor with a higher risk aversion (A) would calculate a lower utility (U). 1 U Er A 2
question_en: When considering a portfolio that is optimal for one investor, a second investor with a higher risk aversion would most likely:

explanation_en: Systematic vs. nonsystematic risk Total risk = Systematic risk + Nonsystematic risk Systematic risk Nonsystematic risk Also known as market risk or Also known as nonmarket risk or firm- nondiversifiable risk specific risk Inherent in the market Specific to firm or industry Cannot be eliminated by diversification Can be eliminated by diversification Examples: interest rate shifts, stock Examples: business litigation, market crashes cyberattacks Risky assets have both systematic and nonsystematic risk. The total risk of an asset comprises both systemic and nonsystemic risk. Systematic risk (market risk) is the intrinsic risk of the financial system and cannot be reduced or eliminated. It is associated with macroeconomic risks which impact all assets (eg, wars, recessions, interest rates). Nonsystematic risk usually refers to the risk of an individual company or an industry (eg, a pharmaceutical company facing a class action lawsuit). To eliminate the nonsystematic risk of a portfolio, choose assets whose returns are not correlated with one another. Rational investors add such assets until the nonsystematic risk is eliminated to create a fully diversified portfolio (Choices A and C).
question_en: If a portfolio is fully diversified, it most likely eliminates which type of risk(s)?
option_b: Nonsystematic risk but not systematic risk
option_c: Systematic risk but not nonsystematic risk

explanation_en:
Factors influencing revenue forecasts with inflation
Inelastic: raising prices increases revenues
Price elasticity of demand
Elastic: raising prices may decrease revenues
Geographic mix of revenues must be considered
Inflation rates in different countries
Differences in inflation rates usually affect exchange rates
Inflation does not affect all input costs equally
Changes in relevant costs
Proper identification of affected relevant costs is essential
Passing full costs to customers preserves margins
Pricing strategy
Partial increase in prices may increase market share
To forecast revenues and costs, analysts need to understand the following:
product price sensitivity, or the price elasticity of demand,
differences in inflation rates across countries,
variation in the company's relevant costs, and
pricing strategies.
Understanding how a company's significant input costs (eg, raw material, products for reselling) are affected by inflation can give the analyst
insights into how different strategies of price adjustment may affect margins.
In this situation, the company increases its prices in line with the change in Country A's CPI (ie, general inflation), most likely to preserve margins.
The final effect of this increase depends on the characteristics of the industry and the company. For example, if the increase in the company's
costs exceeds the CPI rate, and therefore exceeds the rate of increase in the company's global prices, then gross margin percentage will most
likely decrease.
(Choice A) If demand for the company's products is highly price inelastic, an increase in price will have little effect on quantity demanded and will
likely increase revenues. Therefore, the analyst should predict an increase in revenues in the financial model.
(Choice B) If competitors in other countries are increasing their prices by more than the inflation in Country A, the company's global prices will be
relatively lower than competitors', despite the increase based on the CPI rate. This will likely result in an increase in market share, not a reduction.
question_en: Country A is currently in an inflationary environment. A multinational corporation that sources most of its inputs from Country A increases its global prices based on the change in Country A's general consumer price index (CPI). All else equal, this strategy will most likely reduce:
option_a: revenues if demand is highly price inelastic.
option_b: market share if competitors in other countries raise prices by a higher rate.
option_c: gross margin percentage if input costs increase more than Country A's CPI.

explanation_en:
Like modified duration and effective duration, money duration is a measure of a bond's price sensitivity to a change in its yield-to-maturity.
Whereas modified and effective durations estimate percentage price change, money duration estimates price change in currency units of the
bond's denomination.
For noncallable bonds, money duration is a bond's modified duration multiplied by its full price. Consequently, the bond with the greatest
sensitivity on a percentage basis (ie, highest modified duration) does not necessarily have the greatest money duration. In this question, the bond
with the greatest modified duration (the 20-year, zero-coupon bond) has the smallest money duration since it has a much lower price per 100 par
value compared to the coupon bonds.
question_en: An analyst has gathered information on Bonds X, Y, and Z: Assuming the coupon bonds pay interest annually and there is no accrued interest, which of the bonds most likely has the greatest money duration per 100 of par value?
option_c: Bond Z

explanation_en: Economies experience business cycle phases of trough, expansion, peak, and contraction. Each phase is associated with certain characteristics regarding GDP growth and inflation. Expansion is divided into early (ie, recovery) and late phases (ie, boom). During an early expansion phase, consumers begin to spend more, and GDP growth becomes moderately positive. Businesses begin to purchase inventory but are hesitant to hire new employees until there is evidence of further economic growth (Choice C). During the late expansion phase, consumer spending increases even further, and GDP growth becomes accelerated. Businesses rehire full time employees and invest in heavy capital equipment. (Choice A) The peak phase follows late expansion and is characterized by decelerating GDP growth and a slowdown in hiring.
question_en: An economy is experiencing accelerated GDP growth and businesses have started hiring full-time workers and ordering heavy equipment. This economy is most likely in the:

explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a derivative in which the underlying is a future interest rate. A 30-day FRA on 60-day LIBOR is the same economically as a 60-day loan that starts in 30 days. The long party to an FRA is the borrower, and the short party is the lender. A lender takes a short position in a 30-day FRA to hedge against a decline in interest rates. The image above shows the relevant timeframes for an FRA. Assume that today, both sides expect 60-day LIBOR to be 5% in 30 days. If 60-day LIBOR is less than 5% on Day 30, the lender receives from the borrower an amount based on the difference between 5% and the 60-day LIBOR rate in effect on Day 30. The lender can replicate a short position in an FRA through a portfolio of long and short positions on zero-coupon bonds with maturities that correspond to the FRA's time horizons. The diagram below demonstrates how this is done: If interest rates decrease in the first 30 days, the price of both bonds increases. The lender will have a positive return for the long position in the 90-day bond and a negative return for the short position in the 30-day bond. The 90-day bond's price will increase more than the 30-day bond's price will decrease, so the lender's net return is positive. Economically, this is identical to a short position in an FRA. (Choice A) This is the equivalent of being short a 30-day FRA, where the underlying is 30-day LIBOR. (Choice C) This is the equivalent of being long a 30-day FRA, where the underlying is 60-day LIBOR.
question_en: An investor can most closely create a synthetic short position in a 30-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 60-day LIBOR by simultaneously:
option_a: buying a 60-day zero-coupon bond and selling a 30-day zero-coupon bond.
option_b: buying a 90-day zero-coupon bond and selling a 30-day zero-coupon bond.
option_c: buying a 30-day zero-coupon bond and selling a 90-day zero-coupon bond.

question_en: The Federal Reserve has decided to increase the federal funds rate (the interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans). To implement this policy, the Federal Reserve will most likely:
